Practice Set · Completion-Scored

Assignment

Lesson 6-1
Answer Key: Two Languages for One Rotation
Full worked solutions for all 6 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1
Degrees to radians: Convert each to radians, reduced to lowest terms: ① \(150^\circ\)   ② \(-240^\circ\)   ③ \(315^\circ\).
SOLUTION
Master equation: multiply degrees by \(\dfrac{\pi}{180}\).

① \(150^\circ \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{150\pi}{180}\). \(\gcd(150,180)=30\), so this reduces to \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\).

② \(-240^\circ \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{180} = -\dfrac{240\pi}{180}\). \(\gcd(240,180)=60\), so this reduces to \(-\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\).

③ \(315^\circ \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{315\pi}{180}\). \(\gcd(315,180)=45\), so this reduces to \(\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\).
Final Answer: ① \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\)  ·  ② \(-\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\)  ·  ③ \(\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\)
PROBLEM 2
Radians to degrees: Convert each to degrees: ① \(\dfrac{7\pi}{12}\)   ② \(-\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\)   ③ \(\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\).
SOLUTION
Master equation: multiply radians by \(\dfrac{180}{\pi}\) (the \(\pi\)'s cancel).

① \(\dfrac{7\pi}{12} \cdot \dfrac{180}{\pi} = 7 \cdot \dfrac{180}{12} = 7 \cdot 15 = 105^\circ\).

② \(-\dfrac{5\pi}{6} \cdot \dfrac{180}{\pi} = -5 \cdot \dfrac{180}{6} = -5 \cdot 30 = -150^\circ\).

③ \(\dfrac{11\pi}{6} \cdot \dfrac{180}{\pi} = 11 \cdot \dfrac{180}{6} = 11 \cdot 30 = 330^\circ\).
Final Answer: ① \(105^\circ\)  ·  ② \(-150^\circ\)  ·  ③ \(330^\circ\)
PROBLEM 3
An "ugly" angle: Convert \(250^\circ\) to radians. It will not reduce to a familiar friend like \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) or \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) — show that the conversion factor works regardless.
SOLUTION
The same master equation applies no matter how the angle looks: \(250^\circ \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{250\pi}{180}\). \(\gcd(250,180) = 10\), so this reduces to \(\dfrac{25\pi}{18}\). Check: \(\gcd(25,18)=1\), so \(\dfrac{25\pi}{18}\) is fully reduced — it simply is not one of the "nice" denominators (2, 3, 4, or 6) that come from the special angles, and that is perfectly fine. As a decimal, \(\dfrac{25\pi}{18} \approx 4.36\) radians.
Final Answer: \(\dfrac{25\pi}{18}\) rad \(\approx 4.36\) rad
PROBLEM 4
Estimate without a calculator: Decide whether 4 radians is more or less than \(240^\circ\), using only the fact that 1 radian is a little less than \(60^\circ\). Show your reasoning in words, then check your estimate against the exact conversion.
SOLUTION
If 1 radian is a little less than \(60^\circ\), then 4 radians is 4 copies of "a little less than \(60^\circ\)," which must land a little less than \(4 \times 60^\circ = 240^\circ\). So the estimate says 4 radians is less than \(240^\circ\).

Check against the exact conversion: \(4 \cdot \dfrac{180}{\pi} \approx 229.18^\circ\), which is indeed less than \(240^\circ\) — the estimate holds. (For the curious: 1 radian is short of \(60^\circ\) by about \(2.70^\circ\); four radians accumulate that shortfall to about \(10.82^\circ\), and \(240^\circ - 229.18^\circ \approx 10.82^\circ\) exactly — the "little less" was not vague at all, it was precisely trackable.)
Final Answer: 4 radians \(\approx 229.18^\circ\), which is less than \(240^\circ\) — confirming the estimate.
PROBLEM 5 — Explain why
Two students both type sin(60) into their calculators and get two different answers: one gets \(0.866\), the other gets \(\approx -0.305\). In three or four sentences, explain exactly what happened to produce two different results from the same keystrokes, and how each student should check which one is correct for the situation they meant to solve.
MODEL SOLUTION
The keystrokes were identical, but the calculators were in different angle modes. The first student's calculator was in degree mode: \(\sin(60^\circ) = 0.866\), the familiar value from a 30-60-90 triangle. The second student's calculator was in radian mode, so it computed \(\sin(60 \text{ rad})\) — interpreting "60" as 60 whole radians, almost \(9.5\) full revolutions around the circle. Reducing \(60\) radians by multiples of \(2\pi\) leaves a coterminal angle of \(60 - 9(2\pi) \approx 3.45\) radians, which lands in the third quadrant (between \(\pi\) and \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\)), where sine is negative: \(\sin(3.45) \approx -0.305\), matching the second result exactly.

Each student should check by asking what units the original problem intended. If the problem meant "\(60^\circ\)," a first-quadrant acute angle, the answer must be positive and less than 1 — \(0.866\) fits, \(-0.305\) does not. If the problem genuinely meant "60 radians," the huge input (almost 9.5 full turns) is itself a signal to pause and confirm that is really what was intended before trusting the output. The fix in either case is the same: check the calculator's mode indicator against the units the problem is actually using, every time, before reading off a trig value.
Final Answer: \(0.866 = \sin(60^\circ)\) in degree mode; \(-0.305 \approx \sin(60 \text{ rad})\) in radian mode (60 rad reduces to \(\approx 3.45\) rad, in Quadrant III). Always match the calculator's mode to the problem's intended units before trusting the result.
PROBLEM 6 — Honors stretch
Prove that no whole number of degrees, other than \(0^\circ\), converts to a radian measure that is itself a whole number. (Hint: suppose \(n^\circ\) converts to a whole number \(M\) radians, for some nonzero integer \(n\). Write the conversion equation, solve it for \(\pi\), and use the fact that \(\pi\) is irrational — it cannot equal a ratio of two integers — to reach a contradiction.)
SOLUTION
Proof by contradiction. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that some nonzero integer \(n\) of degrees converts to exactly \(M\) radians, where \(M\) is also an integer. The conversion equation is \[ M = n \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{180} \] Solve this equation for \(\pi\): \[ \pi = \dfrac{180M}{n} \] First check \(M\): if \(M = 0\), the equation \(M = n\pi/180\) forces \(n\pi = 0\), and since \(\pi \ne 0\), that forces \(n = 0\) — contradicting the assumption that \(n\) is nonzero. So \(M\) must also be nonzero.

With both \(M\) and \(n\) nonzero integers, \(\dfrac{180M}{n}\) is a ratio of two integers — a rational number. But the equation above claims this ratio equals \(\pi\), and \(\pi\) is irrational: it cannot be written as a ratio of any two integers. This is a contradiction.

Since assuming a nonzero integer \(n^\circ\) converts to an integer \(M\) radians leads to a contradiction, no such \(n\) exists. The only integer degree measure that converts to an integer radian measure is the trivial case \(n=0\) (which converts to \(M=0\) radians).
Final Answer: If \(n^\circ \to M\) rad with \(n, M\) nonzero integers, then \(\pi = \dfrac{180M}{n}\), a ratio of integers — contradicting \(\pi\)'s irrationality. So no nonzero integer number of degrees ever converts to a nonzero integer number of radians.
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the calculator should show)
Problems 1–3: in degree mode, \(\sin(150) = \sin\!\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)\) once switched to radian mode with the converted answer typed in — both modes must return the identical output if the conversion is correct. Problem 5 is the whole lesson in miniature: typing sin(60) in degree mode and again in radian mode should reproduce \(0.866\) and \(-0.305\) exactly, confirming the mode-mismatch explanation above.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) requires a genuine, visible attempt at all 6 problems, including the honors stretch. Radian answers must be left as reduced fractions of \(\pi\) (not decimals) except where a problem specifically calls for one — check that Problem 1's three answers are in lowest terms. Problems 4 and 5 need full-sentence reasoning, not a bare number. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips elsewhere if the method is sound — release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).

Lesson 6-2
Answer Key: One Angle, One Distance, One Planet
Full worked solutions for all 6 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1
Coterminal in degrees: Find the angle coterminal with each, in \([0^\circ, 360^\circ)\):   ① \(520^\circ\)   ② \(-250^\circ\).
SOLUTION
Add or subtract full \(360^\circ\) rotations until the result lands in \([0^\circ,360^\circ)\).

① \(520^\circ\) is past one full turn: \(520^\circ - 360^\circ = 160^\circ\), and \(160^\circ\) is already in range.

② \(-250^\circ\) is negative, so add a full turn: \(-250^\circ + 360^\circ = 110^\circ\), in range.
Final Answer: ① \(160^\circ\)  ·  ② \(110^\circ\)
PROBLEM 2
Coterminal in radians: Find the angle coterminal with each, in \([0, 2\pi)\):   ① \(\dfrac{17\pi}{6}\)   ② \(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).
SOLUTION
Add or subtract full \(2\pi\) rotations (write \(2\pi\) with the same denominator to combine).

① \(\dfrac{17\pi}{6} - 2\pi = \dfrac{17\pi}{6} - \dfrac{12\pi}{6} = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\), which is in \([0,2\pi)\).

② \(-\dfrac{\pi}{4} + 2\pi = -\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{8\pi}{4} = \dfrac{7\pi}{4}\), which is in \([0,2\pi)\).
Final Answer: ① \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\)  ·  ② \(\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\)
PROBLEM 3
Arc length and sector area: A circle has radius 8 cm. Find the arc length and sector area for a central angle of \(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\) radians. Give exact values (in terms of \(\pi\)) and rounded decimals.
SOLUTION
\(\theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\) is already in radians, so both formulas apply directly.

Arc length: \(s = r\theta = 8 \cdot \dfrac{3\pi}{4} = \dfrac{24\pi}{4} = 6\pi \approx 18.85\) cm.

Sector area: \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}(8)^2 \cdot \dfrac{3\pi}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}(64)\cdot\dfrac{3\pi}{4} = 32 \cdot \dfrac{3\pi}{4} = 24\pi \approx 75.40\) cm\(^2\).
Final Answer: \(s = 6\pi \approx 18.85\) cm; \(A = 24\pi \approx 75.40\) cm\(^2\)
PROBLEM 4
Solving for the angle: An arc 21 inches long is cut off by a central angle on a circle of radius 9 inches. Find the angle in radians (exact fraction) and in degrees (rounded to the nearest hundredth).
SOLUTION
Solve \(s = r\theta\) for \(\theta\): \(\theta = \dfrac{s}{r} = \dfrac{21}{9} = \dfrac{7}{3}\) rad (already in lowest terms).

Convert to degrees: \(\dfrac{7}{3} \cdot \dfrac{180}{\pi} = \dfrac{1260}{3\pi} = \dfrac{420}{\pi} \approx 133.69^\circ\).
Final Answer: \(\theta = \dfrac{7}{3}\) rad \(\approx 133.69^\circ\)
PROBLEM 5 — Explain why
A classmate computes an arc length by writing \(s = r\theta = 10 \cdot 45 = 450\), using \(\theta = 45^\circ\) directly. In three or four sentences, explain what has gone wrong, why the arithmetic itself is not the problem, and what the classmate must do before the formula can be trusted.
MODEL SOLUTION
The multiplication \(10 \times 45 = 450\) is arithmetically correct — the arithmetic is not the problem. The problem is that the formula \(s = r\theta\) is only true when \(\theta\) is measured in radians; it was derived directly from the radian's own definition (the ratio of arc length to radius), so plugging in a degree measure breaks that derivation entirely. The result, 450, is not just wrong but obviously absurd once checked against reality: the full circumference of this circle is only \(2\pi(10) \approx 62.8\), so no arc on this circle can possibly be 450 units long — the answer exceeds the entire circle more than seven times over.

Before trusting the formula, the classmate must convert \(45^\circ\) to radians first: \(45^\circ \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) rad, then compute \(s = 10 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{4} = 2.5\pi \approx 7.85\), a value that easily fits within the circle's circumference.
Final Answer: The classmate must convert \(45^\circ\) to \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) rad first. Correct arc length: \(s = 10 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{4} = 2.5\pi \approx 7.85\), not 450.
PROBLEM 6 — Honors stretch (measure a planet)
Two observers stand on the same north–south line. At a certain moment, the sun's angle from directly overhead differs between the two cities by \(5^\circ\), and the north–south distance between the cities is measured as 555 km. ① Convert \(5^\circ\) to radians. ② Using \(s = r\theta\) with \(s = 555\) km, estimate the planet's radius. ③ Find the estimated circumference two ways: once from your radius using \(C = 2\pi r\), and once directly from the ratio "\(5^\circ\) is what fraction of \(360^\circ\)?" without any radius at all. Confirm both methods agree. ④ In one sentence, name the one assumption about sunlight that makes this whole method work.
SOLUTION
① \(5^\circ \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{5\pi}{180} = \dfrac{\pi}{36} \approx 0.0873\) rad.

② The \(5^\circ\) angle at the planet's center subtends the 555 km arc between the two cities, so \(s = r\theta \Rightarrow r = \dfrac{s}{\theta} = \dfrac{555}{\pi/36} = \dfrac{555 \cdot 36}{\pi} = \dfrac{19{,}980}{\pi} \approx 6{,}359.83\) km.

③ Method A (via radius): \(C = 2\pi r = 2\pi \cdot \dfrac{19{,}980}{\pi} = 2(19{,}980) = 39{,}960\) km — the \(\pi\)'s cancel exactly, leaving a clean whole number.
Method B (direct ratio, no radius): if \(5^\circ\) corresponds to an arc of 555 km, and \(5^\circ\) is \(\dfrac{5}{360} = \dfrac{1}{72}\) of a full \(360^\circ\) circle, then the full circumference is \(72\) times the arc: \(C = 555 \times 72 = 39{,}960\) km.
Both methods agree exactly: \(39{,}960\) km.

④ The method depends on the sun's rays arriving at the two cities essentially parallel — the sun is so far away that its light rays are, for practical purposes, parallel lines by the time they reach the planet, which is exactly what lets the measured difference in shadow angle at the two cities equal the true central angle at the planet's own center between them (as in the Eratosthenes example from the lesson).
Final Answer: \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{36}\) rad; \(r \approx 6{,}359.83\) km; \(C = 39{,}960\) km by both methods. Key assumption: the sun's rays reach the planet essentially parallel.
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the calculator should show)
Problem 3: 8*(3pi/4) should return \(\approx 18.85\); 0.5*8^2*(3pi/4) should return \(\approx 75.40\). Problem 6: 555*36/pi should return \(\approx 6359.83\), and 555*(360/5) should return exactly \(39960\), matching \(2\pi r\) computed from that radius.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) requires a genuine, visible attempt at all 6 problems, including the honors stretch. Every arc-length or sector-area computation (Problems 3, 4, 6) must show the radian conversion step explicitly, not skip straight to a decimal — that conversion step is the whole point of the lesson. Problem 5 needs full-sentence reasoning, not a bare correction. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips elsewhere if the method is sound — release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).

Assignment 6-3 · Practice Set: SOH-CAH-TOA, Proven and Practiced
Practice Set · Completion-Scored
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 6-3
Answer Key: SOH-CAH-TOA, Proven and Practiced
Full worked solutions for all 5 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1
Side from angle: A right triangle has an acute angle of \(27^\circ\) and a hypotenuse of 15 units. Find both legs, rounded to the nearest hundredth. Check your answer against the Pythagorean theorem.
SOLUTION
Relative to the \(27^\circ\) angle, the hypotenuse is known and both legs (opposite and adjacent) are unknown — use sine for the opposite leg, cosine for the adjacent leg.

Opposite leg: \(\sin(27^\circ) = \dfrac{\text{opp}}{15} \Rightarrow \text{opp} = 15\sin(27^\circ) \approx 15(0.45399) \approx 6.81\).

Adjacent leg: \(\cos(27^\circ) = \dfrac{\text{adj}}{15} \Rightarrow \text{adj} = 15\cos(27^\circ) \approx 15(0.89101) \approx 13.37\).

Pythagorean check: \(6.81^2 + 13.37^2 \approx 46.38 + 178.76 = 225.14 \approx 225 = 15^2\) (the small discrepancy is only from rounding the legs to hundredths before squaring; the unrounded values satisfy the theorem exactly).
Final Answer: opposite \(\approx 6.81\); adjacent \(\approx 13.37\); Pythagorean check confirms (up to rounding).
PROBLEM 2
Angle from two sides: A right triangle has legs 9 and 40, with hypotenuse 41 (check this is a valid right triangle first). Find both acute angles, rounded to the nearest hundredth of a degree, using two different ratios and confirming they agree.
SOLUTION
Validity check: \(9^2 + 40^2 = 81 + 1{,}600 = 1{,}681 = 41^2\). ✓ Valid right triangle.

Angle opposite the leg of 9 (call it \(\alpha\)): using tangent, \(\tan\alpha = \dfrac{9}{40} \Rightarrow \alpha = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{9}{40}\right) \approx 12.68^\circ\). Cross-check with sine: \(\sin\alpha = \dfrac{9}{41} \Rightarrow \alpha = \sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{9}{41}\right) \approx 12.68^\circ\) — the two ratios agree.

Angle opposite the leg of 40 (call it \(\beta\)): using tangent, \(\tan\beta = \dfrac{40}{9} \Rightarrow \beta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{40}{9}\right) \approx 77.32^\circ\). Cross-check with sine: \(\sin\beta = \dfrac{40}{41} \Rightarrow \beta \approx 77.32^\circ\) — agrees again.

Sum check: \(12.68^\circ + 77.32^\circ = 90.00^\circ\), confirming the two acute angles of a right triangle are complementary.
Final Answer: \(\alpha \approx 12.68^\circ\), \(\beta \approx 77.32^\circ\) (sum \(=90^\circ\), confirmed by both tangent and sine ratios).
PROBLEM 3
Two unknowns from one angle and one side: A right triangle has an acute angle of \(63^\circ\) and an adjacent leg of length 22. Find the opposite leg and the hypotenuse, each rounded to the nearest hundredth.
SOLUTION
The adjacent leg is known; tangent connects adjacent to opposite, and cosine connects adjacent to hypotenuse.

Opposite leg: \(\tan(63^\circ) = \dfrac{\text{opp}}{22} \Rightarrow \text{opp} = 22\tan(63^\circ) \approx 22(1.96261) \approx 43.18\).

Hypotenuse: \(\cos(63^\circ) = \dfrac{22}{\text{hyp}} \Rightarrow \text{hyp} = \dfrac{22}{\cos(63^\circ)} \approx \dfrac{22}{0.45399} \approx 48.46\).

Pythagorean check: \(43.18^2 + 22^2 \approx 1{,}864.5 + 484 = 2{,}348.5\), and \(48.46^2 \approx 2{,}348.4\) — matches (up to rounding).
Final Answer: opposite \(\approx 43.18\); hypotenuse \(\approx 48.46\)
PROBLEM 4 — Explain why
Triangle A has an acute angle \(\theta\) with opposite leg 3 and hypotenuse 5. Triangle B has the same angle \(\theta\) but is three times larger in every dimension. In three or four sentences, explain why \(\tan\theta\) must come out identical in both triangles, using the AA similarity argument from the lesson — not just by computing both values and noting they match.
MODEL SOLUTION
Triangle A and Triangle B are both right triangles that share the acute angle \(\theta\); since two angles are forced to match (the right angle and \(\theta\)), the third angle must match too, so AA similarity guarantees the two triangles are similar. Similarity means every pair of corresponding sides is scaled by the exact same factor — here, \(k=3\), since Triangle B is three times larger in every dimension: \(\text{opp}_B = 3\cdot\text{opp}_A\) and \(\text{adj}_B = 3\cdot\text{adj}_A\).

Since \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}\), computing it for Triangle B gives \(\tan\theta_B = \dfrac{3\cdot\text{opp}_A}{3\cdot\text{adj}_A} = \dfrac{\text{opp}_A}{\text{adj}_A} = \tan\theta_A\) — the scale factor \(3\) appears in both the numerator and the denominator and cancels algebraically. This is exactly why tangent (and sine and cosine) can be defined as a function of the angle alone: similarity guarantees the ratio is scale-invariant by construction, for every possible scale factor, not merely for this one pair of numbers.
Final Answer: The shared angle \(\theta\) plus the shared right angle force AA similarity, so every side scales by the same factor \(k\); in \(\tan\theta = \text{opp}/\text{adj}\), that \(k\) cancels between numerator and denominator, so \(\tan\theta_A = \tan\theta_B\) necessarily.
PROBLEM 5 — Honors stretch
In a right triangle, \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{5}{13}\). Without finding \(\theta\) in degrees at any point, find \(\cos\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) exactly, as fractions. (Think about which whole-number right triangle has a side ratio of 5 to 13, and use the Pythagorean theorem to find the missing side.)
SOLUTION
\(\sin\theta = \dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}} = \dfrac{5}{13}\), so take opposite \(=5\) and hypotenuse \(=13\). Find the adjacent leg with the Pythagorean theorem: \[ \text{adj} = \sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = \sqrt{169-25} = \sqrt{144} = 12 \] This is the classic 5-12-13 Pythagorean triple. Now read off the remaining ratios directly: \[ \cos\theta = \dfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}} = \dfrac{12}{13}, \qquad \tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}} = \dfrac{5}{12} \]
Final Answer: \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{12}{13}\), \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{5}{12}\)
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the calculator should show)
Degree mode: 15sin(27) → \(\approx 6.81\); 15cos(27) → \(\approx 13.37\); tan-1(9/40) and sin-1(9/41) should both return \(\approx 12.68^\circ\). For Problem 5, sin-1(5/13) gives \(\theta \approx 22.62^\circ\); confirm \(\cos(\theta) \approx 0.923\) and \(\tan(\theta) \approx 0.417\) match \(\frac{12}{13}\) and \(\frac{5}{12}\) once rounded.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) requires a genuine, visible attempt at all 5 problems, including the honors stretch. Every problem must explicitly name which side is opposite, adjacent, and hypotenuse relative to the angle in use, and every side-finding answer (Problems 1 and 3) must show a Pythagorean or second-ratio check, per the assignment's own success criteria. Problem 4 needs full-sentence AA-similarity reasoning, not just numerical agreement. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips elsewhere if the method is sound — release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).

Quarter / Unit
Q3 · Unit 6
Right Triangle Trigonometry
Lesson
Lesson 6-4
Keys To
Assignment 6-4 · Focus Set: The Surveyor's Record
⭐ Focus Assignment · Method-Graded (2 problems)
Points
Assignment
16 pts
Lesson 6-4
Answer Key: The Surveyor's Record
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems. Problems 3 and 6 carry gold-badged scoring guidance for the rubric — those are the only two problems graded for method; the rest are checked for honest completion.
PROBLEM 1
Angle of elevation: From a point 120 ft from the base of an office building, the angle of elevation to the roofline is \(48^\circ\). Find the building's height, rounded to the nearest tenth of a foot.
SOLUTION
Diagram: a right triangle with the horizontal line of sight along the ground (120 ft, the adjacent leg to the \(48^\circ\) angle) and the building's height \(h\) as the opposite leg. \[ \tan(48^\circ) = \dfrac{h}{120} \Rightarrow h = 120\tan(48^\circ) \approx 120(1.11061) \approx 133.3 \]
Final Answer: \(h \approx 133.3\) ft
PROBLEM 2
Angle of depression: From the top of an 85 m cliff, the angle of depression to a boat is \(9^\circ\). Find the horizontal distance from the base of the cliff to the boat, rounded to the nearest tenth of a meter.
SOLUTION
The angle of depression from the cliff top down to the boat equals the angle of elevation from the boat up to the cliff top (alternate interior angles with the horizontal). In the right triangle formed, the cliff height (85 m) is opposite that \(9^\circ\) angle, and the unknown horizontal distance \(d\) is adjacent. \[ \tan(9^\circ) = \dfrac{85}{d} \Rightarrow d = \dfrac{85}{\tan(9^\circ)} \approx \dfrac{85}{0.15838} \approx 536.7 \]
Final Answer: \(d \approx 536.7\) m
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 3
A survey crew cannot reach the base of a radio tower (a highway is in the way). From point \(A\), the angle of elevation to the top of the tower is \(22^\circ\). The crew then walks 175 ft directly toward the tower to point \(B\) and measures the angle of elevation as \(38^\circ\). Complete the full discipline, every step labeled: ① diagram; ② set up; ③ solve; ④ check; ⑤ verdict.
SOLUTION
① Diagram: the tower stands vertically with unknown height \(h\) at its base. Point \(B\) lies an unknown distance \(x\) from the base; point \(A\) lies \(175\) ft farther back, so \(A\) is \(x+175\) from the base. Both triangles share the same vertical side \(h\), and the \(22^\circ\) angle at \(A\) sits inside the larger triangle that contains the smaller \(38^\circ\) triangle at \(B\).

② Set up — one tangent equation from each station: \[ \text{From } B: \quad \tan(38^\circ) = \dfrac{h}{x} \qquad \text{From } A: \quad \tan(22^\circ) = \dfrac{h}{x+175} \]
③ Solve — both equations describe the same \(h\), so set them equal after solving each for \(h\): \[ h = x\tan(38^\circ) \qquad \text{and} \qquad h = (x+175)\tan(22^\circ) \] \[ x\tan(38^\circ) = (x+175)\tan(22^\circ) \] \[ x\tan(38^\circ) - x\tan(22^\circ) = 175\tan(22^\circ) \] \[ x\big(\tan(38^\circ)-\tan(22^\circ)\big) = 175\tan(22^\circ) \] \[ x = \dfrac{175\tan(22^\circ)}{\tan(38^\circ)-\tan(22^\circ)} \approx \dfrac{175(0.40403)}{0.78129-0.40403} \approx \dfrac{70.71}{0.37726} \approx 187.4 \text{ ft} \] Then: \(h = x\tan(38^\circ) \approx 187.4(0.78129) \approx 146.4\) ft.

④ Check — substitute \(x \approx 187.4\) into the other station's equation: \(h = (x+175)\tan(22^\circ) \approx (362.4)(0.40403) \approx 146.4\) ft. Both stations agree on the same height ✓.

⑤ Verdict: "The radio tower stands approximately 146.4 feet tall, and survey point \(B\) lies approximately 187.4 feet from the tower's base."
Final Answer: \(x \approx 187.4\) ft (B to base); \(h \approx 146.4\) ft (tower height); both station equations confirm the same height.
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): both tangent equations are set up correctly, matching each station's angle to the correct pair of legs (\(h\) over \(x\) at \(B\); \(h\) over \(x+175\) at \(A\)); the two equations are correctly combined by solving each for \(h\) and setting them equal. (2): method sound but one conceptual slip — e.g., the \(175\) ft added to the wrong station's distance, or the two tangent equations set up with the angles swapped. (0): the method does not use two stations at all (e.g., only one triangle solved, ignoring the second sighting).

Reasoning (4): all five labeled steps (diagram / setup / solve / check / verdict) are present and each follows from the last; the check step actually recomputes \(h\) from the other station's equation and confirms agreement, rather than simply asserting the answer is correct. (2): most steps shown, but the check is skipped or the verdict merely restates the numbers without a sentence a client could read. (0): an answer appears with little supporting algebra.

Presentation & precision (4): a clearly labeled diagram shows both triangles sharing the height \(h\), with \(x\) and \(175\) marked distinctly; all five steps are labeled in order; the algebra combining the two equations is shown line by line. (2): organized with a labeling lapse (e.g., the diagram omits one of the two distances, or a step is folded invisibly into another). (0): scattered or illegible; the five steps cannot be followed.

Intellectual honesty (4): the algebra combining the two tangent equations is shown in full (not skipped to the answer); the check step is a genuine independent recomputation, not a restatement; the verdict sentence reports exactly what was found, with rounding stated. (2): the check is asserted ("both agree") without showing the recomputed number. (0): the answer appears reverse-engineered or copied, with no combining algebra shown.
PROBLEM 4
Two depressions, one comparison: From the top of a 45 m cliff, an observer sights a boat at an angle of depression of \(15^\circ\) and, farther out, a lighthouse at an angle of depression of \(6^\circ\). Find the horizontal distance from the boat to the lighthouse.
SOLUTION
Each sighting forms its own right triangle with the cliff (45 m) as the leg opposite the depression angle, and the horizontal distance from the cliff's base as the adjacent leg. Since the lighthouse is farther out, it has the smaller depression angle.

Distance to boat: \(\tan(15^\circ) = \dfrac{45}{d_{\text{boat}}} \Rightarrow d_{\text{boat}} = \dfrac{45}{\tan(15^\circ)} \approx \dfrac{45}{0.26795} \approx 167.9\) m.

Distance to lighthouse: \(\tan(6^\circ) = \dfrac{45}{d_{\text{light}}} \Rightarrow d_{\text{light}} = \dfrac{45}{\tan(6^\circ)} \approx \dfrac{45}{0.10510} \approx 428.1\) m.

Distance between boat and lighthouse: \(d_{\text{light}} - d_{\text{boat}} \approx 428.1 - 167.9 = 260.2\) m.
Final Answer: \(\approx 260.2\) m between the boat and the lighthouse.
PROBLEM 5 — Explain why
In Problem 3, the angle at \(B\) (\(38^\circ\)) is larger than the angle at \(A\) (\(22^\circ\)). In three or four sentences, explain why the closer observation point must always produce the larger angle of elevation to the same object, and what it would mean if a real field crew's data showed the opposite.
MODEL SOLUTION
For a fixed tower height \(h\), the angle of elevation \(\theta\) at horizontal distance \(x\) satisfies \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{h}{x}\). As \(x\) gets smaller (the observer moves closer), the fraction \(\dfrac{h}{x}\) gets larger, and since tangent is an increasing function on \(0^\circ\) to \(90^\circ\), a larger tangent means a larger angle \(\theta\). This is not a coincidence of the specific numbers \(22^\circ\) and \(38^\circ\) — it is a geometric certainty for any fixed height: the closer station must always report the larger angle.

If a real field crew's data ever showed the opposite — a smaller angle from the closer point — that would signal a measurement or setup error, not a valid new geometry: a misread instrument, an angle assigned to the wrong station, the two stations not actually lying on a straight line through the base, or the object's apparent height changing between readings. The crew should treat such a result as a red flag requiring re-measurement, not as data to be trusted and reported.
Final Answer: Since \(\tan\theta = h/x\) increases as \(x\) decreases, the closer station must always report the larger angle; data showing the opposite signals a measurement or setup error, not a valid alternative geometry.
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 6
A crew measures the angle of elevation to the top of a cell tower as \(30^\circ\) from a point 250 ft from its base, and reports the height. ① Compute the reported height using \(30^\circ\). ② Suppose the true angle was \(31^\circ\) (one degree of instrument misreading). Recompute the height using \(31^\circ\). ③ Find the exact difference between the two computed heights. ④ Paragraph: what would this difference mean for a real project, and what specific practice should a responsible surveyor follow?
SOLUTION
① Reported height at \(30^\circ\): \[ \tan(30^\circ) = \dfrac{h_{30}}{250} \Rightarrow h_{30} = 250\tan(30^\circ) \approx 250(0.57735) \approx 144.34 \text{ ft} \]
② Recomputed height at \(31^\circ\): \[ h_{31} = 250\tan(31^\circ) \approx 250(0.60086) \approx 150.22 \text{ ft} \]
③ Exact difference: \[ h_{31} - h_{30} \approx 150.22 - 144.34 = 5.88 \text{ ft} \]
④ Paragraph: A single degree of instrument misreading — something a surveyor could easily make while sighting by eye — produced nearly 5.9 feet of error in the reported height, on a modest 250 ft baseline. That is roughly a 4% swing, and for many purposes it might not matter. But if this tower's height is being used to determine a required clearance from an aircraft flight path, or a required setback from a property line, a discrepancy of almost 6 feet could be the exact margin between a project that legally clears its obstruction limit and one that violates it. A responsible surveyor should never report a single angle reading as though it were exact. Instead, the crew should take several independent readings of the same angle and average them to reduce random error, use a longer baseline distance where the site allows (a longer baseline makes the computed height less sensitive to a fixed angular error, since the same one-degree slip changes \(\tan\theta\) by a smaller relative amount when \(\theta\) itself corresponds to a longer sight line), and report the result together with a stated margin of error — for example, "\(\approx 147\) ft \(\pm 6\) ft" — so that anyone relying on the number, whether a builder, a pilot, or a zoning officer, knows how much cushion the figure actually carries.
Final Answer: \(h_{30} \approx 144.34\) ft; \(h_{31} \approx 150.22\) ft; difference \(\approx 5.88\) ft. Recommended practice: repeated readings, a longer baseline, and reporting the height with a stated margin of error — the surveyor's responsibility is to the honesty of the number, not just the number.
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): both heights are computed correctly with \(\tan\theta = h/250\), and the difference is computed from the two correct values. (2): method sound but one conceptual slip — e.g., using sine or cosine instead of tangent, or comparing the wrong pair of values. (0): the method does not compute two separate heights at all (e.g., only one angle used, or the "difference" invented without a second computation).

Reasoning (4): all four labeled parts are present; the paragraph in part ④ draws an explicit, reasoned line from the numeric difference to a real consequence (a specific type of project where the discrepancy would matter), not a vague claim that "errors are bad." (2): the numeric parts are correct but the paragraph asserts a consequence without connecting it back to the specific size of the computed difference. (0): the paragraph is generic and could have been written without doing the computation at all.

Presentation & precision (4): both tangent computations are shown in full with labeled steps; the difference is computed and clearly labeled; the paragraph is a genuine four-to-six-sentence paragraph, not a list of fragments. (2): organized with a labeling or rounding lapse (e.g., the difference computed from rounded intermediate values without noting the rounding). (0): scattered or illegible; the four parts cannot be followed.

Intellectual honesty (4): the paragraph names one specific practice (repeated readings, longer baseline, or a stated margin of error) and explicitly ties it to the unit's virtue of responsibility, rather than a platitude like "be more careful." (2): a specific practice is named but the connection to responsibility is only implied, not stated. (0): the paragraph offers no specific, actionable practice at all.
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
From the top of a 100 m cliff, a surveyor sights the base of a distant tower at an angle of depression of \(25^\circ\), and the top of that same tower at an angle of elevation of \(10^\circ\) (the tower is tall enough that its top rises above the cliff's own height). ① Find the horizontal distance from the base of the cliff to the base of the tower. ② Find how far the tower's top rises above the cliff-top's own elevation. ③ Combine your results to find the tower's total height. ④ In one sentence, explain why this problem needed two right triangles sharing the same horizontal distance.
SOLUTION
① The line from the cliff top to the tower's base looks down at \(25^\circ\); the cliff's height (100 m) is opposite that angle, and the unknown horizontal distance \(d\) is adjacent: \[ \tan(25^\circ) = \dfrac{100}{d} \Rightarrow d = \dfrac{100}{\tan(25^\circ)} \approx \dfrac{100}{0.46631} \approx 214.5 \text{ m} \]
② The line from the cliff top to the tower's top looks up at \(10^\circ\), over the same horizontal distance \(d\). The rise above the cliff-top's own elevation, call it \(r\), is opposite that angle: \[ \tan(10^\circ) = \dfrac{r}{d} \Rightarrow r = d\tan(10^\circ) \approx 214.5(0.17633) \approx 37.8 \text{ m} \]
③ The tower's total height (base to top) is the cliff's own height (which carries the tower's base up to the cliff-top's elevation level) plus the additional rise above that level: \[ \text{total height} = 100 + r \approx 100 + 37.8 = 137.8 \text{ m} \]
④ Two triangles were needed because the tower's base sits below the observer's eye level (an angle of depression) while its top sits above the observer's eye level (an angle of elevation) — these are two different vertical relationships to the same horizontal sightline, so no single right triangle can capture both extents at once; both triangles do, however, share the identical horizontal leg \(d\), which is what lets the two be combined.
Final Answer: \(d \approx 214.5\) m; rise above cliff-top \(\approx 37.8\) m; total tower height \(\approx 137.8\) m. Two triangles are needed because the base (depression) and top (elevation) sit on opposite sides of the observer's horizontal sightline.
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
Problem 3: x=175tan(22)/(tan(38)-tan(22)) (degree mode) should return \(\approx 187.42\), matching the hand-computed \(x\); then x*tan(38) should return \(\approx 146.43\), matching \(h\). Problem 6: 250tan(30) and 250tan(31) should return \(\approx 144.34\) and \(\approx 150.22\); their difference should match \(\approx 5.88\) computed by hand.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC

Apply this rubric to the two ⭐ method problems (3 and 6). The rest of the set is checked for honest completion only. This same four-criterion standard governs every hand-graded item in this course, all year.

Criteria Excellent (4) Proficient (3) Developing (2) Beginning (1) Pts
Understanding of the material

Lesson 6-5
Answer Key: Coordinates That Never Sleep
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems, for grading and self-correction release. The leading VR artifact has no single correct answer — see the completion checklist below in place of a fabricated student submission.
🥽 VR ARTIFACT — completion checklist, not a scored answer
This piece of the submission (the Walking the Unit Circle session artifact) has no single correct student narration, so this key gives you what to look for rather than an invented example. Do not deduct for phrasing — check for the presence and correctness of these items:
  • Labeled-circle snapshot present and shows all sixteen positions from the Unit Circle Plaza reference card, each with a coordinate sticky-note attached (spawn point at \(\theta = 0\) reads \((1, 0)\); the quadrantal points at \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), \(\pi\), \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\) read \((0,1)\), \((-1,0)\), \((0,-1)\) respectively — spot-check two or three non-quadrantal labels against Lesson 6-6/6-8's special-angle values once those are covered, since 6-5 supplied them on a reference card rather than deriving them).
  • Whiteboard-narration snapshot present and contains genuine written sentences (not a single word or blank) connecting the walker's height above the floor at a stop to the wall graph's \(y\)-value at the matching \(x\) — the core idea is that height above the floor is \(\sin\theta\) at that angle, traced live by the marker on \(y = \sin x\).
  • Both snapshots are placed first in the PDF, ahead of the seven written problems.
Full credit for this component is presence + genuine content, exactly as with any other completion-scored piece of this assignment.
PROBLEM 1
Quadrantal points: Find the exact coordinates \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\) for \(\theta = -\pi\), \(\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{2}\), \(\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), and \(\theta = 4\pi\). For each, briefly explain the reasoning (which direction you rotated, or how many full laps you subtracted).
SOLUTION
\(\theta = -\pi\): rotating clockwise by \(\pi\) lands at the same point as rotating counterclockwise by \(\pi\) — the western point. Coordinates \((-1, 0)\).

\(\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{2}\): subtract one full lap (\(2\pi = \dfrac{4\pi}{2}\)): \(\dfrac{5\pi}{2} - \dfrac{4\pi}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), the northern point. Coordinates \((0, 1)\).

\(\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\): add one full lap to land on a positive coterminal angle: \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2\pi = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\), the southern point. Coordinates \((0, -1)\).

\(\theta = 4\pi\): subtract two full laps (\(4\pi - 2(2\pi) = 0\)), landing back at the eastern spawn point. Coordinates \((1, 0)\).
Final Answer: \(\theta=-\pi \to (-1,0)\); \(\theta=\frac{5\pi}{2}\to(0,1)\); \(\theta=-\frac{\pi}{2}\to(0,-1)\); \(\theta=4\pi\to(1,0)\).
PROBLEM 2
Missing coordinate (Quadrant III): An angle \(\theta\) terminates in Quadrant III with \(\cos\theta = -\dfrac{5}{13}\). Find \(\sin\theta\), showing the identity step and the sign reasoning separately.
SOLUTION
Identity step: \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1 \Rightarrow \sin^2\theta = 1 - \left(-\dfrac{5}{13}\right)^2 = 1 - \dfrac{25}{169} = \dfrac{144}{169} \Rightarrow \sin\theta = \pm\dfrac{12}{13}\).

Sign reasoning: in Quadrant III both coordinates are negative, so \(\sin\theta < 0\).
Final Answer: \(\sin\theta = -\dfrac{12}{13}\)
PROBLEM 3
Missing coordinate (Quadrant II): An angle \(\theta\) terminates in Quadrant II with \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{8}{17}\). Find \(\cos\theta\), showing the identity step and the sign reasoning separately.
SOLUTION
Identity step: \(\cos^2\theta = 1 - \sin^2\theta = 1 - \dfrac{64}{289} = \dfrac{225}{289} \Rightarrow \cos\theta = \pm\dfrac{15}{17}\).

Sign reasoning: in Quadrant II, \(x\) is negative and \(y\) is positive, so \(\cos\theta < 0\).
Final Answer: \(\cos\theta = -\dfrac{15}{17}\)
PROBLEM 4
Judge the claim: A classmate claims \(\left(\dfrac{7}{25}, \dfrac{24}{25}\right)\) could be a terminal point \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\). Judge the claim by checking it against the unit circle's own equation, and state your verdict in a sentence.
SOLUTION
Check \(x^2 + y^2 = 1\): \[ \left(\frac{7}{25}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{24}{25}\right)^2 = \frac{49}{625} + \frac{576}{625} = \frac{625}{625} = 1 \]
Final Answer: The sum is exactly \(1\), so the point does lie on the unit circle — the claim is true, and this point could indeed be a terminal point.
PROBLEM 5
Circle or function? Solve \(x^2 + y^2 = 1\) for \(y\), and explain in a sentence what the \(\pm\) reveals about the vertical line test. Then explain, in two or three sentences, how defining sine and cosine by angle \(\theta\) — rather than solving the circle's equation directly for \(y\) in terms of \(x\) — sidesteps that problem and still produces one well-defined output for every input.
SOLUTION
\[ x^2+y^2=1 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; y^2 = 1-x^2 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; y = \pm\sqrt{1-x^2} \] The \(\pm\) means that (for any \(x\) strictly between \(-1\) and \(1\)) a vertical line through that \(x\) hits the circle at two points, one above and one below the axis — so the circle fails the vertical line test and \(y\) is not a function of \(x\).

Defining sine and cosine by angle \(\theta\) sidesteps this entirely: each value of \(\theta\) names one specific amount of rotation, which lands at exactly one point on the circle — never two. The input is no longer an \(x\)-coordinate that two points might share; it is a rotation, and a given rotation has only one terminal point. So \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\) is a genuine function of \(\theta\), producing exactly one ordered pair for every real number \(\theta\), even though the circle itself is not a function of \(x\).
Final Answer: \(y=\pm\sqrt{1-x^2}\); the \(\pm\) shows the circle fails the vertical line test. Defining sine/cosine by rotation angle \(\theta\) instead of by \(x\)-coordinate gives each input exactly one terminal point, so it is a genuine function even though the circle's own equation is not.
PROBLEM 6 — Explain why
In three or four sentences, explain why \(-1 \le \sin\theta \le 1\) and \(-1 \le \cos\theta \le 1\) for every real number \(\theta\), with no exceptions. Argue from the definition of the terminal point, not from a memorized fact.
MODEL SOLUTION
By definition, \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\) is the terminal point of angle \(\theta\) on the unit circle, meaning it satisfies \(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\) for every real \(\theta\), with no exceptions. Since \(\sin^2\theta \ge 0\) always, \(\cos^2\theta = 1 - \sin^2\theta \le 1\), which forces \(-1 \le \cos\theta \le 1\); the identical argument with the roles swapped forces \(-1 \le \sin\theta \le 1\). Geometrically, this is just the statement that every point on a circle of radius \(1\) is exactly distance \(1\) from the origin, so neither coordinate alone can ever exceed that distance.
Final Answer: Because \(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1\) with both squares nonnegative, neither \(\cos\theta\) nor \(\sin\theta\) can exceed \(1\) in absolute value — each coordinate of a point on the unit circle is bounded by the circle's own radius.
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
Tracking a satellite: A geostationary communications satellite orbits at radius \(R = 42{,}164\) km, and its position at a given moment corresponds to angle \(\theta\) with \(\cos\theta = -0.6\), with the satellite in the upper half of its orbit. ① Find \(\sin\theta\) exactly. ② The satellite's actual position in kilometers is \((R\cos\theta,\, R\sin\theta)\). Compute both coordinates. ③ In one sentence, explain why ground controllers cannot afford a sign error on \(\sin\theta\) here.
SOLUTION
① \(\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta = 1 - 0.36 = 0.64 \Rightarrow \sin\theta = \pm0.8\). Upper half means \(\sin\theta > 0\), so \(\sin\theta = 0.8\).

② \(x = R\cos\theta = 42{,}164 \times (-0.6) = -25{,}298.4\) km. \(y = R\sin\theta = 42{,}164 \times 0.8 = 33{,}731.2\) km.

③ A sign error on \(\sin\theta\) would flip the satellite's \(y\)-coordinate to \(-33{,}731.2\) km — placing it over \(67{,}000\) km away from its actual location, on the opposite side of the orbital plane's reference line, which would misdirect any antenna pointing or collision-avoidance calculation built from that position.
Final Answer: \(\sin\theta = 0.8\); position \((-25{,}298.4,\ 33{,}731.2)\) km; a sign error would place the satellite about \(67{,}462\) km from its true position, on the wrong side of the reference plane.
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
For problems 2–4, plotting the candidate point alongside \(x^2+y^2=1\) in Desmos should show the point sitting exactly on the circle for problem 4 (both radii check out), and problems 2–3's completed points \(\left(-\frac{5}{13},-\frac{12}{13}\right)\) and \(\left(-\frac{15}{17},\frac{8}{17}\right)\) should likewise land exactly on the circle in Quadrant III and Quadrant II respectively.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for the VR artifact (per the completion checklist above) plus a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the setup is sound — watch specifically for students confusing which coordinate is which (writing \(\cos\theta\) where \(\sin\theta\) is meant, or vice versa) in problems 2–3 and 7. Release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).

Lesson 6-6
Answer Key: Cutting Two Shapes for Six Values
Full worked solutions for all 8 problems. Problems 3 and 6 carry gold-badged scoring guidance for the rubric — those are the only two problems graded for method; the rest are checked for honest completion.
PROBLEM 1
Rescale the square: Bisect a square of side length 4 along its diagonal. Find the exact side lengths of the resulting right triangle, then state \(\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\), \(\cos\frac{\pi}{4}\), and \(\tan\frac{\pi}{4}\) in lowest terms. Compare your three values to Lesson 6-6's — what changed, and what didn't?
SOLUTION
A square of side \(4\) has diagonal \(d = \sqrt{4^2+4^2} = \sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt2\). Bisecting along the diagonal gives a right isosceles triangle with legs \(4\), \(4\) and hypotenuse \(4\sqrt2\). \[ \sin\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{4}{4\sqrt2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2} = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}, \qquad \cos\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}, \qquad \tan\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{4}{4} = 1 \] Comparison: the side lengths themselves changed (\(4, 4, 4\sqrt2\) here instead of the lesson's numbers), but all three ratios came out identical to Lesson 6-6's — confirming that sine, cosine, and tangent depend only on the triangle's angles, not its size.
Final Answer: Legs \(4, 4\), hypotenuse \(4\sqrt2\); \(\sin\frac{\pi}{4}=\cos\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\), \(\tan\frac{\pi}{4}=1\) — the same ratios as the lesson, only the raw lengths changed.
PROBLEM 2
Rescale the equilateral triangle: Bisect an equilateral triangle of side length 6 along its altitude. Find the exact lengths of all three sides of the resulting right triangle, then state \(\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\), \(\cos\frac{\pi}{6}\), \(\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\), and \(\cos\frac{\pi}{3}\) in lowest terms.
SOLUTION
Bisecting an equilateral triangle of side \(6\) along its altitude splits the base into two segments of \(3\) each and keeps the full side \(6\) as the hypotenuse. The altitude \(h\) satisfies \[ h^2 + 3^2 = 6^2 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; h^2 = 36-9 = 27 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; h = \sqrt{27} = 3\sqrt3 \] So the right triangle has legs \(3\) and \(3\sqrt3\), hypotenuse \(6\). \[ \sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{3}{6} = \frac12, \qquad \cos\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{3\sqrt3}{6} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}, \qquad \sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{3\sqrt3}{6} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}, \qquad \cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{3}{6} = \frac12 \]
Final Answer: Sides \(3\), \(3\sqrt3\), \(6\); \(\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac12\), \(\cos\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\sin\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\cos\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac12\).
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 3
Starting from an equilateral triangle with side length \(s\): ① construct — draw the altitude, find its length in terms of \(s\) using the Pythagorean theorem; ② extract six values — \(\sin\), \(\cos\), \(\tan\) at both \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) and \(\frac{\pi}{3}\); ③ verify — confirm both Pythagorean-identity checks; ④ explain why building with a general side \(s\) proves the ratios never depend on size, connecting to similar triangles.
SOLUTION
① Construct. The altitude from one vertex of an equilateral triangle with side \(s\) bisects the opposite side into two segments of length \(\frac{s}{2}\), and bisects the \(60°\) apex angle. By the Pythagorean theorem, with hypotenuse \(s\) and one leg \(\frac{s}{2}\): \[ h^2 + \left(\frac{s}{2}\right)^2 = s^2 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; h^2 = s^2 - \frac{s^2}{4} = \frac{3s^2}{4} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; h = \frac{s\sqrt3}{2} \] The resulting right triangle has legs \(\frac{s}{2}\) (opposite the \(30°=\frac{\pi}{6}\) angle) and \(\frac{s\sqrt3}{2}\) (opposite the \(60°=\frac{\pi}{3}\) angle), hypotenuse \(s\).

② Extract six values. \[ \sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{s/2}{s} = \frac12, \qquad \cos\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{s\sqrt3/2}{s} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}, \qquad \tan\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{s/2}{s\sqrt3/2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3} = \frac{\sqrt3}{3} \] \[ \sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{s\sqrt3/2}{s} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}, \qquad \cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{s/2}{s} = \frac12, \qquad \tan\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{s\sqrt3/2}{s/2} = \sqrt3 \] ③ Verify. \[ \sin^2\frac{\pi}{6}+\cos^2\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac14+\frac34 = 1 \;\;\checkmark \qquad \sin^2\frac{\pi}{3}+\cos^2\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac34+\frac14 = 1 \;\;\checkmark \] ④ Explain why. Because \(s\) is left as a general side rather than a fixed number, it cancels completely out of every ratio above — each value came out as a pure number ($\frac12$, $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, etc.) with no \(s\) remaining. That cancellation is exactly what similar triangles guarantee: every equilateral triangle has the same three \(60°\) angles, so any two equilateral triangles are similar regardless of size, and similar triangles have proportional corresponding sides — which is precisely why the ratio of two sides (sine, cosine, or tangent) is the same constant no matter which equilateral triangle you started from.
Final Answer: \(h = \frac{s\sqrt3}{2}\); \(\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac12\), \(\cos\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\tan\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\); \(\sin\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\cos\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac12\), \(\tan\frac{\pi}{3}=\sqrt3\); both identity checks confirmed; \(s\) cancels because all equilateral triangles are similar.
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): the altitude is correctly derived via the Pythagorean theorem with \(\frac{s}{2}\) as the bisected leg, and all six ratios are read off the correct pair of sides. (2): method sound but one conceptual slip — e.g., bisecting the wrong side, or swapping which leg is opposite which angle. (0): the six values are quoted from memory with no triangle constructed.

Reasoning (4): all four labeled stages are present and follow from each other; the similar-triangles explanation in ④ genuinely argues from proportional sides, not restated as a rule. (2): the six values are correct but the similar-triangles explanation is thin or generic. (0): answers appear with little or no supporting reasoning.

Presentation & precision (4): triangle drawn and labeled, all four stages clearly marked, exact values fully simplified and rationalized (\(\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\), not \(\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\)). (2): organized with a labeling or rationalizing lapse. (0): scattered or illegible.

Intellectual honesty (4): the verification in ③ is carried out as actual arithmetic with \(s\)-free fractions, not asserted; the cancellation of \(s\) is shown, not assumed. (2): the verification is stated as true without being computed. (0): values appear reverse-engineered from a memorized table.
PROBLEM 4
A kite in the wind: A kite string makes an angle of \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) with the level ground, and the string itself is 100 m long. Find the kite's exact height above the ground and its exact horizontal distance from the flyer, then give both as decimals rounded to the nearest tenth of a meter.
SOLUTION
The string is the hypotenuse. Height is opposite the angle, horizontal distance is adjacent: \[ \text{height} = 100\sin\frac{\pi}{3} = 100\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} = 50\sqrt3 \text{ m} \] \[ \text{horizontal} = 100\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = 100\cdot\frac12 = 50 \text{ m} \] Decimal: \(\sqrt3 \approx 1.7320508\), so \(50\sqrt3 \approx 86.6\) m.
Final Answer: Height \(=50\sqrt3\approx86.6\) m; horizontal distance \(=50\) m exactly.
PROBLEM 5
Order without a calculator: Without computing a single decimal, order \(\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\), \(\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\), and \(\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\) from least to greatest. Justify your order using the triangles — which side gets longer as the angle grows — not a memorized ranking.
SOLUTION
\(\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac12\), \(\sin\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\), \(\sin\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\) — all three share the denominator \(2\), and \(1 < \sqrt2 < \sqrt3\), so the numerators alone settle the order without any decimal ever being computed.

Triangle justification: in a right triangle with a fixed hypotenuse, sine is the ratio of the side opposite the angle to that hypotenuse. As the angle grows from \(30°\) to \(45°\) to \(60°\), the side opposite it swings farther from the hypotenuse's line and grows longer relative to the fixed hypotenuse — so a larger angle always produces a larger opposite leg, and hence a larger sine ratio.
Final Answer: \(\sin\frac{\pi}{6} < \sin\frac{\pi}{4} < \sin\frac{\pi}{3}\), since \(\frac12<\frac{\sqrt2}{2}<\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\) and a larger angle always has a longer opposite leg relative to a fixed hypotenuse.
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 6
Starting from a square with side length \(s\): ① construct — the diagonal via the Pythagorean theorem; ② extract three values — \(\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\), \(\cos\frac{\pi}{4}\), \(\tan\frac{\pi}{4}\); ③ combine families — compute \(\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\cos\frac{\pi}{6}+\cos\frac{\pi}{4}\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\) as a single simplified fraction; ④ bonus thread — this equals \(\sin\frac{5\pi}{12}\); speculate why in one sentence.
SOLUTION
① Construct. A square of side \(s\) has diagonal \(d\) with \(d^2 = s^2+s^2 = 2s^2 \Rightarrow d = s\sqrt2\).

② Extract three values. \[ \sin\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{s}{s\sqrt2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2} = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}, \qquad \cos\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}, \qquad \tan\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{s}{s} = 1 \] ③ Combine families (using problem 3's \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) values \(\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac12\), \(\cos\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\)): \[ \sin\frac{\pi}{4}\cos\frac{\pi}{6}+\cos\frac{\pi}{4}\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac12 = \frac{\sqrt6}{4} + \frac{\sqrt2}{4} = \frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4} \] ④ Bonus thread. Since \(\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{3\pi}{12}+\frac{2\pi}{12} = \frac{5\pi}{12}\), and this computation produced exactly \(\sin\frac{5\pi}{12}\) by combining the \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) and \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) values in the pattern \(\sin A\cos B + \cos A\sin B\), it's reasonable to guess that this specific combination pattern computes the sine of the sum of two angles, \(A+B\) — as if sine somehow "distributes" across addition in this particular cross-multiplied form, rather than simply adding \(\sin A+\sin B\).
Final Answer: \(d=s\sqrt2\); \(\sin\frac{\pi}{4}=\cos\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\), \(\tan\frac{\pi}{4}=1\); combined value \(\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\) (matching \(\sin\frac{5\pi}{12}\)); the pattern plausibly computes \(\sin(A+B)\) — to be confirmed in Unit 7.
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): the diagonal is correctly derived via the Pythagorean theorem, the three \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) values are correctly extracted, and the combination in ③ is computed with the correct cross-multiplied pattern. (2): method sound but one conceptual slip — e.g., adding \(\sin\frac{\pi}{4}+\cos\frac{\pi}{6}\) instead of the requested cross-product pattern. (0): the combination step is skipped or the values are quoted without construction.

Reasoning (4): all four labeled stages follow from each other, and the bonus-thread speculation in ④ genuinely connects the \(\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{5\pi}{12}\) angle sum to the pattern used, not a vague guess. (2): the arithmetic is correct but the speculation in ④ does not connect the angle sum to the computation pattern. (0): little or no supporting reasoning.

Presentation & precision (4): square drawn and labeled, all four stages clearly marked, the combined fraction fully simplified as \(\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\) with common denominator shown. (2): organized with a simplification or labeling lapse. (0): scattered or illegible.

Intellectual honesty (4): the combination arithmetic in ③ is shown step by step (each product computed separately before combining), not jumped to; the speculation in ④ is presented as a guess, not asserted as a proven fact. (2): the combination is shown but the final simplification is unexplained. (0): the final fraction appears copied or reverse-engineered.
PROBLEM 7 — Explain why
In three or four sentences, explain why cutting a square along its diagonal always produces an isosceles right triangle whose hypotenuse is exactly \(\sqrt2\) times a leg, no matter how large or small the square is. Argue from similar triangles.
MODEL SOLUTION
Every square has four right angles and four equal sides, so any two squares are similar to each other — one is simply a uniform scaling of the other by some factor \(k\). If a unit square (side \(1\)) has diagonal \(\sqrt2\) by the Pythagorean theorem, then scaling every length by \(k\) turns the side into \(k\) and the diagonal into \(k\sqrt2\), so the ratio diagonal-to-side stays exactly \(\sqrt2\) regardless of \(k\). Because similar figures preserve the ratios between corresponding lengths even as the absolute lengths change, the hypotenuse-to-leg ratio of \(\sqrt2\) is a genuine constant of "square-ness," not a coincidence of any one square's size.
Final Answer: All squares are similar (same angles, proportional sides), so scaling a unit square (diagonal \(\sqrt2\)) by any factor \(k\) preserves the diagonal-to-side ratio at exactly \(\sqrt2\) — a property of the shape, not the size.
PROBLEM 8 — Honors stretch
The hexagon confirms itself: A regular hexagon is inscribed in a circle of radius 10. ① State the hexagon's exact side length and explain why it equals the radius. ② Bisect one of its six equilateral triangles and find the exact legs of the resulting 30-60-90 triangle. ③ Using this triangle's own hypotenuse, compute \(\cos\frac{\pi}{6}\) and \(\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\) and confirm they match the unit-circle values. ④ Explain why this had to work out.
SOLUTION
① A regular hexagon inscribed in a circle divides into six triangles from the center, each with two sides equal to the radius (\(10\)) and a central angle of \(\frac{360°}{6}=60°\). A triangle with two equal sides and the included angle \(60°\) is forced to be equilateral (its two base angles must also each be \(60°\), since the angles sum to \(180°\) and the triangle is isosceles), so the third side — the hexagon's own side — also equals \(10\). Side length \(=10=\)radius.

② Bisecting this equilateral triangle (side \(10\)) along its altitude gives hypotenuse \(10\), short leg \(5\), and long leg \(h\) with \(h^2+5^2=10^2 \Rightarrow h^2=75 \Rightarrow h=5\sqrt3\).

③ Using this triangle's own hypotenuse (\(10\), not \(2\), not the unit circle): \[ \cos\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{5\sqrt3}{10} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}, \qquad \sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{5}{10} = \frac12 \] These match the unit-circle values from Lesson 6-6 exactly.

④ Why it had to work out: this radius-\(10\) 30-60-90 triangle is similar to the radius-\(1\) 30-60-90 triangle built directly on the unit circle — both come from bisecting an equilateral triangle, and all equilateral triangles are similar to each other regardless of size. Similar triangles have identical corresponding-side ratios by definition, so no matter what radius the hexagon is drawn on, the sine and cosine ratios extracted from it must equal the unit circle's values exactly.
Final Answer: Side \(=10\) (equals the radius because each of the six central triangles is forced equilateral); 30-60-90 legs \(5\) and \(5\sqrt3\), hypotenuse \(10\); \(\cos\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac12\), matching the unit circle exactly — guaranteed because all 30-60-90 triangles are similar, regardless of the circle's radius.
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
Typing sin(pi/6), cos(pi/6), sin(pi/3), cos(pi/3), sin(pi/4), and cos(pi/4) into Desmos should return \(0.5\), \(0.8660...\), \(0.8660...\), \(0.5\), \(0.7071...\), \(0.7071...\) — matching \(\frac12\), \(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\frac12\), \(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\), \(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\) to four decimal places. Problem 6's combined value \(\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\) should match sin(5pi/12) to the same precision.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Focus Assignment — 16 pts, method-graded on Problems 3 and 6 only)
Problems 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, and 8 are checked for honest, visible completion only — do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound, and release this key after the due date for self-correction. Problems 3 and 6, the two ⭐ method problems, carry the entire 16-point rubric (Understanding / Reasoning / Presentation & Precision / Intellectual Honesty, 4 pts each), applied holistically across both problems together — use the per-problem scoring guidance above as the concrete anchor. Budget roughly 1–2 minutes per student for the two method problems, per the course's designated-problems-only grading model.

Practice Set · Completion-Scored
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 6-7
Answer Key: Four Functions, No New Geometry
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1
All six from a point: The terminal point of angle \(\theta\) is \(\left(-\dfrac{8}{17}, \dfrac{15}{17}\right)\). Find \(\sin\theta\), \(\cos\theta\), \(\tan\theta\), \(\cot\theta\), \(\sec\theta\), and \(\csc\theta\).
SOLUTION
The terminal point is \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\), so \(\cos\theta = -\dfrac{8}{17}\) and \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{15}{17}\) directly. \[ \tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \frac{15/17}{-8/17} = -\frac{15}{8}, \qquad \cot\theta = \frac{1}{\tan\theta} = -\frac{8}{15} \] \[ \sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta} = -\frac{17}{8}, \qquad \csc\theta = \frac{1}{\sin\theta} = \frac{17}{15} \]
Final Answer: \(\sin\theta=\frac{15}{17}\), \(\cos\theta=-\frac{8}{17}\), \(\tan\theta=-\frac{15}{8}\), \(\cot\theta=-\frac{8}{15}\), \(\sec\theta=-\frac{17}{8}\), \(\csc\theta=\frac{17}{15}\).
PROBLEM 2
All six from a special angle: Using Lesson 6-6's exact values, find all six trigonometric function values at \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\).
SOLUTION
From Lesson 6-6: \(\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac12\), \(\cos\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\). \[ \tan\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1/2}{\sqrt3/2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3} = \frac{\sqrt3}{3}, \qquad \cot\frac{\pi}{6} = \sqrt3 \] \[ \sec\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3/2} = \frac{2}{\sqrt3} = \frac{2\sqrt3}{3}, \qquad \csc\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{1/2} = 2 \]
Final Answer: \(\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac12\), \(\cos\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\tan\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\), \(\cot\frac{\pi}{6}=\sqrt3\), \(\sec\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}\), \(\csc\frac{\pi}{6}=2\).
PROBLEM 3
Combined exact value: Using Lesson 6-6's exact values, compute \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}\cdot\sec\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \cot\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) as a single simplified exact number.
SOLUTION
\(\tan\frac{\pi}{4} = 1\). \(\sec\frac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{\cos(\pi/3)} = \dfrac{1}{1/2} = 2\). \(\cot\frac{\pi}{6} = \sqrt3\) (from problem 2). \[ \tan\frac{\pi}{4}\cdot\sec\frac{\pi}{3} - \cot\frac{\pi}{6} = (1)(2) - \sqrt3 = 2-\sqrt3 \]
Final Answer: \(2-\sqrt3\)
PROBLEM 4
Full domain, two functions: State the complete domain of \(\tan\theta\) and of \(\csc\theta\), using \(k\) for an arbitrary integer. For each, explain which coordinate must equal zero to create the gap, and where on the circle that happens.
SOLUTION
\(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\) is undefined exactly where \(\cos\theta = 0\), i.e., where the terminal point's \(x\)-coordinate is zero — the top and bottom of the circle, \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}+k\pi\).

\(\csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}\) is undefined exactly where \(\sin\theta = 0\), i.e., where the terminal point's \(y\)-coordinate is zero — the left and right of the circle, \(\theta = k\pi\).
Final Answer: \(\tan\theta\): domain is all reals except \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}+k\pi\) (where \(x=\cos\theta=0\)). \(\csc\theta\): domain is all reals except \(\theta = k\pi\) (where \(y=\sin\theta=0\)).
PROBLEM 5
Judge the claim: A classmate claims, "\(\csc\theta\) is undefined only when \(\cos\theta = 0\)." Judge the claim, correct it if it is wrong, and give one specific angle that shows the correct rule in action.
SOLUTION
The claim is false. \(\csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}\), so it is undefined exactly where \(\sin\theta = 0\), not where \(\cos\theta = 0\).

Counterexample: at \(\theta = 0\), \(\sin\theta = 0\) so \(\csc\theta\) is undefined, yet \(\cos\theta = 1 \ne 0\) — showing \(\csc\theta\) can be undefined even when \(\cos\theta\) is nowhere near zero.
Final Answer: The claim is false; \(\csc\theta\) is undefined when \(\sin\theta = 0\) (e.g., \(\theta = 0\), where \(\cos\theta = 1\)).
PROBLEM 6 — Explain why
In three or four sentences, explain why sine and cosine are defined for every real number while the other four functions are not. Argue from what a coordinate is versus what a quotient requires.
MODEL SOLUTION
Sine and cosine are, by definition, the \(y\)- and \(x\)-coordinates of the terminal point on the unit circle — every real angle \(\theta\) has exactly one terminal point, so these coordinates always exist and are always finite numbers, with nothing that could go wrong. The other four functions, though, are all built as quotients of sine and cosine (\(\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\), \(\cot\theta=\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\), \(\sec\theta=\frac{1}{\cos\theta}\), \(\csc\theta=\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\)), and a quotient is only defined when its denominator is nonzero. Since \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) each equal zero at specific angles, any function with one of them in the denominator inherits a gap at exactly those angles — a limitation coordinates themselves never carry, but division always can.
Final Answer: Sine/cosine are coordinates, which always exist; the other four are quotients built from sine and cosine, which are undefined wherever their denominator (\(\sin\theta\) or \(\cos\theta\)) equals zero.
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
A new identity: Start from \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\). ① Divide every term by \(\cos^2\theta\) (assume \(\cos\theta \ne 0\)), simplify using \(\tan\theta\) and \(\sec\theta\). ② State the new identity. ③ Verify numerically at \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}\). ④ Explain why it cannot hold at \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\).
SOLUTION
① Divide by \(\cos^2\theta\): \[ \frac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} + \frac{\cos^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} = \frac{1}{\cos^2\theta} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \left(\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)^2 + 1 = \left(\frac{1}{\cos\theta}\right)^2 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \tan^2\theta + 1 = \sec^2\theta \] ② New identity: \(\tan^2\theta + 1 = \sec^2\theta\).

③ Verify at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}\): \(\tan\frac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\sin(\pi/3)}{\cos(\pi/3)} = \dfrac{\sqrt3/2}{1/2} = \sqrt3\), so left side \(= (\sqrt3)^2+1 = 3+1 = 4\). \(\sec\frac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{\cos(\pi/3)} = \dfrac{1}{1/2}=2\), so right side \(= 2^2 = 4\). Both sides equal \(4\). ✓

④ Why it fails at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\): at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\), \(\cos\theta = 0\), so both \(\tan\theta\) and \(\sec\theta\) are undefined (division by zero) — and the identity was derived by dividing the original equation by \(\cos^2\theta\) in the first place, a step that explicitly required \(\cos\theta \ne 0\). At \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\), both sides of the new identity are simply undefined, not unequal.
Final Answer: \(\tan^2\theta+1=\sec^2\theta\); verified at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}\) (both sides \(=4\)); fails at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\) because \(\cos\theta=0\) makes both \(\tan\theta\) and \(\sec\theta\) undefined, and the derivation itself required \(\cos\theta\ne0\).
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
Typing tan(pi/6), cot(pi/6), sec(pi/6), and csc(pi/6) should confirm problem 2's values decimally. For problem 7, graphing y = tan(x)^2 + 1 and y = sec(x)^2 together should show the two curves sitting exactly on top of each other everywhere \(\cos x \ne 0\), with matching vertical asymptotes at \(x=\frac{\pi}{2}+k\pi\).
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound — watch specifically for the signature error of inverting the wrong ratio (writing \(\cot\theta = \sin\theta/\cos\theta\) instead of \(\cos\theta/\sin\theta\), or confusing \(\sec\) with \(\csc\)). Release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).

pages.html:

Lesson 6-8
Answer Key: Three Reflections, Twelve Angles
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1
\(\pi-x\): Find \(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\) and \(\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\), stating which special angle and which symmetry you used.
SOLUTION
\(\dfrac{3\pi}{4} = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), so this uses the \(\pi-x\) symmetry with reference angle \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\): \(\cos(\pi-x) = -\cos x\), \(\sin(\pi-x) = \sin x\). \[ \cos\frac{3\pi}{4} = -\cos\frac{\pi}{4} = -\frac{\sqrt2}{2}, \qquad \sin\frac{3\pi}{4} = \sin\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\sqrt2}{2} \]
Final Answer: \(\cos\frac{3\pi}{4} = -\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\), \(\sin\frac{3\pi}{4} = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\).
PROBLEM 2
\(\pi+x\): Find \(\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\) and \(\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\), stating which special angle and which symmetry you used.
SOLUTION
\(\dfrac{4\pi}{3} = \pi + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), so this uses the \(\pi+x\) symmetry with reference angle \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\): \(\cos(\pi+x) = -\cos x\), \(\sin(\pi+x) = -\sin x\). \[ \cos\frac{4\pi}{3} = -\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = -\frac12, \qquad \sin\frac{4\pi}{3} = -\sin\frac{\pi}{3} = -\frac{\sqrt3}{2} \]
Final Answer: \(\cos\frac{4\pi}{3} = -\frac12\), \(\sin\frac{4\pi}{3} = -\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\).
PROBLEM 3
\(2\pi-x\): Find \(\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\) and \(\sin\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\), stating which special angle and which symmetry you used.
SOLUTION
\(\dfrac{7\pi}{4} = 2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), so this uses the \(2\pi-x\) symmetry with reference angle \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\): \(\cos(2\pi-x) = \cos x\), \(\sin(2\pi-x) = -\sin x\). \[ \cos\frac{7\pi}{4} = \cos\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}, \qquad \sin\frac{7\pi}{4} = -\sin\frac{\pi}{4} = -\frac{\sqrt2}{2} \]
Final Answer: \(\cos\frac{7\pi}{4} = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\), \(\sin\frac{7\pi}{4} = -\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\).
PROBLEM 4
All six, one angle: Find all six trigonometric function values at \(\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\), starting from the correct symmetry and Lesson 6-6's values, then building the remaining four functions as in Lesson 6-7.
SOLUTION
\(\dfrac{5\pi}{6} = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\): \(\pi-x\) symmetry with reference angle \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\). \[ \cos\frac{5\pi}{6} = -\cos\frac{\pi}{6} = -\frac{\sqrt3}{2}, \qquad \sin\frac{5\pi}{6} = \sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac12 \] Building the remaining four from these two: \[ \tan\frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{1/2}{-\sqrt3/2} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt3} = -\frac{\sqrt3}{3}, \qquad \cot\frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{\tan(5\pi/6)} = -\sqrt3 \] \[ \sec\frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{-\sqrt3/2} = -\frac{2}{\sqrt3} = -\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}, \qquad \csc\frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{1/2} = 2 \]
Final Answer: \(\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}=\frac12\), \(\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\tan\frac{5\pi}{6}=-\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\), \(\cot\frac{5\pi}{6}=-\sqrt3\), \(\sec\frac{5\pi}{6}=-\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}\), \(\csc\frac{5\pi}{6}=2\).
PROBLEM 5
Derive a tangent identity: Using \(\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x\) and \(\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x\), derive a simplified expression for \(\tan(\pi - x)\) in terms of \(\tan x\). Verify numerically at \(x = \frac{\pi}{6}\).
SOLUTION
\[ \tan(\pi-x) = \frac{\sin(\pi-x)}{\cos(\pi-x)} = \frac{\sin x}{-\cos x} = -\frac{\sin x}{\cos x} = -\tan x \] Verify at \(x=\frac{\pi}{6}\): \(\tan\left(\pi-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \tan\frac{5\pi}{6} = -\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\) (from problem 4). And \(-\tan\frac{\pi}{6} = -\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\) (from Lesson 6-7's value \(\tan\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\)). Both sides equal \(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\). ✓
Final Answer: \(\tan(\pi-x) = -\tan x\); verified numerically at \(x=\frac{\pi}{6}\), both sides \(=-\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\).
PROBLEM 6 — Explain why
In three or four sentences, explain why \(\cos(-x) = \cos x\) but \(\sin(-x) = -\sin x\), using the \(2\pi-x\) reflection. Then state, with a one-sentence justification, whether you expect \(\tan(-x)\) to equal \(\tan x\) or \(-\tan x\).
MODEL SOLUTION
The angle \(-x\) is coterminal with \(2\pi-x\) (they differ by exactly one full lap: \(-x + 2\pi = 2\pi - x\)), so \(-x\) and \(2\pi-x\) land at the identical terminal point and share the identical function values. The \(2\pi-x\) reflection is a flip across the \(x\)-axis: the \(x\)-coordinate (cosine) is preserved, while the \(y\)-coordinate (sine) flips sign. Substituting \(-x\) for \(x\) in that same reflection rule gives \(\cos(2\pi-(-x))=\cos(-x)=\cos x\) directly, alongside \(\sin(-x) = -\sin x\) — exactly the pattern of a reflection across the \(x\)-axis, applied to angle \(x\) itself.

Prediction for \(\tan(-x)\): I expect \(\tan(-x) = -\tan x\), because \(\tan(-x) = \dfrac{\sin(-x)}{\cos(-x)} = \dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x} = -\tan x\) — the sign flip in the numerator carries straight through the quotient since the denominator is unchanged.
Final Answer: \(-x\) is coterminal with \(2\pi-x\), whose reflection across the \(x\)-axis preserves \(x\) (cosine) and flips the sign of \(y\) (sine) — giving \(\cos(-x)=\cos x\), \(\sin(-x)=-\sin x\). Predicted: \(\tan(-x) = -\tan x\).
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
The reciprocal functions' parity: Using \(\cos(-x) = \cos x\) and \(\sin(-x) = -\sin x\): ① Prove whether \(\sec(-x)\) equals \(\sec x\) or \(-\sec x\). ② Prove whether \(\csc(-x)\) equals \(\csc x\) or \(-\csc x\). ③ Prove whether \(\cot(-x)\) equals \(\cot x\) or \(-\cot x\). ④ State the general pattern for even vs. odd.
SOLUTION
① \(\sec(-x) = \dfrac{1}{\cos(-x)} = \dfrac{1}{\cos x} = \sec x\). — even, matches \(\sec x\).

② \(\csc(-x) = \dfrac{1}{\sin(-x)} = \dfrac{1}{-\sin x} = -\dfrac{1}{\sin x} = -\csc x\). — odd, matches \(-\csc x\).

③ \(\cot(-x) = \dfrac{\cos(-x)}{\sin(-x)} = \dfrac{\cos x}{-\sin x} = -\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x} = -\cot x\). — odd, matches \(-\cot x\).

④ General pattern: every function built purely from cosine (cosine itself and its reciprocal, secant) is even — unchanged when \(x\) is replaced by \(-x\). Every function that carries a sine in its definition, whether as the function itself, its reciprocal, or in a ratio with cosine (sine, cosecant, tangent, cotangent), is odd — it flips sign when \(x\) is replaced by \(-x\), because sine itself flips sign while cosine does not.
Final Answer: \(\sec(-x)=\sec x\) (even); \(\csc(-x)=-\csc x\) (odd); \(\cot(-x)=-\cot x\) (odd). Pattern: cosine and secant are even; sine, cosecant, tangent, and cotangent are all odd, since every one of the latter four carries a sine that flips sign while any accompanying cosine does not.
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
Plotting the completed points from problems 1–3 — \(\left(-\frac{\sqrt2}{2},\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)\), \(\left(-\frac12,-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\), \(\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2},-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)\) — against \(x^2+y^2=1\) should show each landing exactly on the circle, in Quadrants II, III, and IV respectively. For problem 7, y = sec(x) should overlap y = sec(-x) exactly, and y = csc(x) should overlap y = -csc(-x) exactly.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound — watch specifically for the signature error of applying the wrong symmetry (using \(\pi+x\) sign rules on a \(\pi-x\) angle, or vice versa) in problems 1–4. Release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).
