Lesson 6-9
Answer Key: Reference Angles and Reasonable Answers
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1
Reference angle fluency: find the reference angle for each — ① \(250^\circ\) ② \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\) ③ \(-200^\circ\) ④ \(400^\circ\). Show the quadrant for each before you state the reference angle.
SOLUTION
① \(250^\circ\) lies between \(180^\circ\) and \(270^\circ\) — Quadrant III. Reference angle \(=250^\circ-180^\circ=30^\circ\).
② \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\) lies between \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\pi\) — Quadrant II. Reference angle \(=\pi-\dfrac{5\pi}{6}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\).
③ \(-200^\circ\) is coterminal with \(-200^\circ+360^\circ=160^\circ\), which lies between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\) — Quadrant II. Reference angle \(=180^\circ-160^\circ=20^\circ\).
④ \(400^\circ\) is coterminal with \(400^\circ-360^\circ=40^\circ\), which lies between \(0^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\) — Quadrant I. Reference angle \(=40^\circ\) (a Quadrant I angle is its own reference angle).
Final Answer: ① \(30^\circ\) (QIII)  ·  ② \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) (QII)  ·  ③ \(20^\circ\) (QII)  ·  ④ \(40^\circ\) (QI).
PROBLEM 2
All six, exactly: evaluate all six trigonometric functions of \(\theta = 225^\circ\), stating the quadrant and sign pattern before you write a single value.
SOLUTION
\(225^\circ\) lies between \(180^\circ\) and \(270^\circ\) — Quadrant III. Reference angle \(=225^\circ-180^\circ=45^\circ\). In Quadrant III: sine negative, cosine negative, tangent positive (and their reciprocals match). \[ \sin225^\circ=-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2} \quad \cos225^\circ=-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2} \quad \tan225^\circ=1 \] \[ \csc225^\circ=-\sqrt2 \quad \sec225^\circ=-\sqrt2 \quad \cot225^\circ=1 \]
Final Answer: \(\sin=-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\), \(\cos=-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\), \(\tan=1\), \(\csc=-\sqrt2\), \(\sec=-\sqrt2\), \(\cot=1\).
PROBLEM 3
All six, radians: evaluate all six trigonometric functions of \(\theta = \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\).
SOLUTION
\(\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\) lies between \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\) and \(2\pi\) — Quadrant IV. Reference angle \(=2\pi-\dfrac{11\pi}{6}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\). In Quadrant IV: sine negative, cosine positive, tangent negative. \[ \sin\dfrac{11\pi}{6}=-\dfrac12 \quad \cos\dfrac{11\pi}{6}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \quad \tan\dfrac{11\pi}{6}=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3} \] \[ \csc\dfrac{11\pi}{6}=-2 \quad \sec\dfrac{11\pi}{6}=\dfrac{2\sqrt3}{3} \quad \cot\dfrac{11\pi}{6}=-\sqrt3 \]
Final Answer: \(\sin=-\frac12\), \(\cos=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\tan=-\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\), \(\csc=-2\), \(\sec=\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}\), \(\cot=-\sqrt3\).
PROBLEM 4
Two roads, one answer: evaluate \(\sin(-150^\circ)\) and \(\cos(-150^\circ)\) two ways — coterminal + reference angle, and even/odd symmetry — and show both agree.
SOLUTION
Road 1 — coterminal angle: \(-150^\circ+360^\circ=210^\circ\), which lies in Quadrant III. Reference angle \(=210^\circ-180^\circ=30^\circ\). QIII: sine and cosine both negative. \[ \sin210^\circ=-\dfrac12 \qquad \cos210^\circ=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \] Road 2 — even/odd symmetry: sine is odd (\(\sin(-\theta)=-\sin\theta\)); cosine is even (\(\cos(-\theta)=\cos\theta\)). \[ \sin(-150^\circ)=-\sin(150^\circ)=-\left(\dfrac12\right)=-\dfrac12 \qquad \cos(-150^\circ)=\cos(150^\circ)=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \] Both roads land on the same two values.
Final Answer: \(\sin(-150^\circ)=-\dfrac12\), \(\cos(-150^\circ)=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\) — confirmed by both methods.
PROBLEM 5
Technology, checked: for \(\tan(100^\circ)\) and \(\cot(1.8)\) (radians), state quadrant/reference angle/expected sign first, then compute and confirm.
SOLUTION
\(\tan(100^\circ)\): \(100^\circ\) lies between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\) — Quadrant II. Reference angle \(=180^\circ-100^\circ=80^\circ\). In QII, sine positive and cosine negative, so tangent (sine over cosine) is negative. Since \(\tan(80^\circ)\) is large (close to a vertical asymptote at \(90^\circ\)), expect a large negative decimal. \[ \tan(100^\circ) = -\tan(80^\circ) \approx -5.6713 \] This matches the sign prediction (negative) and the size prediction (large in magnitude).

\(\cot(1.8)\) (radians): \(1.8\) rad lies between \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\approx1.571\) and \(\pi\approx3.142\) — Quadrant II. Reference angle \(=\pi-1.8\approx1.342\) rad. In QII, cosine negative and sine positive, so cotangent (cosine over sine) is negative. \[ \sin(1.8)\approx0.9738 \qquad \cos(1.8)\approx-0.2272 \qquad \cot(1.8)=\dfrac{\cos(1.8)}{\sin(1.8)}\approx-0.2333 \] Negative, as predicted, and modest in size since the reference angle is not close to either \(0\) or \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
Final Answer: \(\tan(100^\circ)\approx-5.6713\); \(\cot(1.8)\approx-0.2333\). Both confirm the hand-predicted sign before the calculator was trusted.
PROBLEM 6 — Explain why
Explain why the reference-angle method never needs more than the first-quadrant special values. Use magnitude and sign, and say what job each does.
MODEL SOLUTION
Every reference angle, by definition, is the acute angle between the terminal side and the \(x\)-axis — so it is always a Quadrant I angle, no matter which quadrant the original angle actually terminates in. The reference angle supplies the magnitude: the size of the ratio, read straight from the first-quadrant special values already memorized. The quadrant of the original angle then supplies the sign, via ASTC, since the coordinates that build each ratio simply flip sign as the terminal side crosses into each quadrant while the underlying triangle's proportions stay identical. Splitting the work this way — one first-quadrant fact for size, one quadrant-lookup for sign — means the six ratios for every one of infinitely many angles can be built from the same small first-quadrant table.
Final Answer: Magnitude comes from the (always Quadrant I) reference angle; sign comes from ASTC applied to the original angle's quadrant. Together they rebuild any angle's values from the first-quadrant table alone.
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
\(\sin\theta=-0.28\), \(\theta\) in Quadrant III. Find \(\cos\theta\) exactly, \(\tan\theta\) exactly, then use inverse sine to find one valid \(\theta\) in degrees; verify it lands in QIII.
SOLUTION
① \(\sin\theta=-0.28=-\dfrac{7}{25}\). Using the Pythagorean identity: \[ \cos^2\theta = 1-\sin^2\theta = 1-\left(\dfrac{7}{25}\right)^2 = 1-\dfrac{49}{625}=\dfrac{576}{625} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \cos\theta=\pm\dfrac{24}{25}=\pm0.96 \] Quadrant III requires cosine negative, so \(\cos\theta=-\dfrac{24}{25}=-0.96\).

② \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{-7/25}{-24/25} = \dfrac{7}{24}\) (both negatives cancel, and \(7\)-\(24\)-\(25\) is a Pythagorean triple, so the fraction is already in lowest terms).

③ A calculator's inverse sine returns the reference angle for magnitude \(0.28\): \(\sin^{-1}(0.28)\approx16.26^\circ\). Since \(\theta\) must terminate in Quadrant III, add this reference angle to \(180^\circ\): \[ \theta \approx 180^\circ+16.26^\circ = 196.26^\circ \approx 196.3^\circ \] Verify: \(196.3^\circ\) lies between \(180^\circ\) and \(270^\circ\) — Quadrant III, as required. Checking the sine: \(\sin(196.3^\circ)=-\sin(16.3^\circ)\approx-0.281\approx-0.28\) ✓.
Final Answer: \(\cos\theta=-\dfrac{24}{25}=-0.96\); \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{7}{24}\); \(\theta\approx196.3^\circ\), confirmed in Quadrant III.
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the calculator should show)
Problem 2's sin(225°) and cos(225°) should both return \(\approx-0.7071\), matching \(-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\). Problem 5's tan(100°) should return \(\approx-5.6713\) and (in radian mode) 1/tan(1.8) should return \(\approx-0.2333\) — if a student's Desmos is in the wrong angle mode for either, the decimal returned will not match the hand estimate, which is exactly the mode-check discipline the lesson trains.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound — release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it. Common spots to watch: Problem 1④'s \(400^\circ\) mistakenly treated as already needing a full reference-angle case analysis rather than simply subtracting one rotation first; Problem 4 stating the even/odd identities backwards (cosine is the even one); Problem 5 skipping the written sign/size prediction and only reporting the calculator's decimal; Problem 7② failing to recognize the \(7\)-\(24\)-\(25\) triple and instead carrying an unsimplified or decimal-only \(\tan\theta\).

Quarter / Unit
Q3 · Unit 6
Right Triangle Trigonometry
Lesson
Lesson 6-10
Keys To
Assignment 6-10 · Practice Set: Three Seeds, One Circle
Practice Set · Completion-Scored
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 6-10
Answer Key: Three Seeds, One Circle
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1
Generate and verify: using the \(\pi/3\) seed and the sign rule, find \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\) for \(\theta=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\); verify \(x^2+y^2=1\).
SOLUTION
\(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\) lies between \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\) and \(2\pi\) — Quadrant IV. Reference angle \(=2\pi-\dfrac{5\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\), confirming the \(\pi/3\) seed: \(\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3},\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=\left(\dfrac12,\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\). In QIV, cosine is positive and sine is negative: \[ (\cos\theta,\sin\theta) = \left(\dfrac12, -\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) \] Verify: \(\left(\dfrac12\right)^2+\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac14+\dfrac34 = 1\) ✓.
Final Answer: \(\left(\dfrac12, -\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\).
PROBLEM 2
Generate and verify: using the \(\pi/4\) seed and the sign rule, find the pair for \(\theta=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\); verify \(x^2+y^2=1\).
SOLUTION
\(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\) lies between \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\pi\) — Quadrant II. Reference angle \(=\pi-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\), the \(\pi/4\) seed: \(\left(\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2},\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)\). In QII, cosine negative, sine positive: \[ (\cos\theta,\sin\theta) = \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right) \] Verify: \(\dfrac24+\dfrac24 = 1\) ✓.
Final Answer: \(\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)\).
PROBLEM 3
Generate and verify: using the \(\pi/6\) seed and the sign rule, find the pair for \(\theta=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\); verify \(x^2+y^2=1\).
SOLUTION
\(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\) lies between \(\pi\) and \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\) — Quadrant III. Reference angle \(=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}-\pi=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\), the \(\pi/6\) seed: \(\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2},\dfrac12\right)\). In QIII, both cosine and sine are negative: \[ (\cos\theta,\sin\theta) = \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, -\dfrac12\right) \] Verify: \(\dfrac34+\dfrac14 = 1\) ✓.
Final Answer: \(\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, -\dfrac12\right)\).
PROBLEM 4
Read a function from the point: using the coordinates from Problems 1 and 2, evaluate \(\cot\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right)\) and \(\sec\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)\).
SOLUTION
From Problem 1, \(\left(\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{3},\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right)=\left(\dfrac12,-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\): \[ \cot\dfrac{5\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\cos(5\pi/3)}{\sin(5\pi/3)} = \dfrac{1/2}{-\sqrt3/2} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3} \] From Problem 2, \(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{4}=-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\): \[ \sec\dfrac{3\pi}{4} = \dfrac{1}{\cos(3\pi/4)} = \dfrac{1}{-\sqrt2/2} = -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt2}=-\sqrt2 \]
Final Answer: \(\cot\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right)=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\); \(\sec\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)=-\sqrt2\).
PROBLEM 5
Find the planted error: audit all six claimed coordinate pairs (magnitude check, then sign check); name the failing row and give the corrected value.
SOLUTION
Run both checks on every row — magnitude (\(x^2+y^2=1\)) first, then sign (does the pair's sign pattern match ASTC for that angle's quadrant):
  • \(\pi/4\), claimed \(\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2},\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)\): magnitude \(\frac12+\frac12=1\) ✓. QI — both positive expected, both positive claimed ✓. Passes both.
  • \(2\pi/3\), claimed \(\left(-\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\): magnitude \(\frac14+\frac34=1\) ✓. \(2\pi/3\) is QII (reference \(\pi/3\)) — cosine negative, sine positive expected; claimed matches ✓. Passes both.
  • \(5\pi/4\), claimed \(\left(-\frac{\sqrt2}{2},-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)\): magnitude \(\frac12+\frac12=1\) ✓. \(5\pi/4\) is QIII — both negative expected, both negative claimed ✓. Passes both.
  • \(4\pi/3\), claimed \(\left(\frac12,-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\): magnitude \(\frac14+\frac34=1\) ✓ — passes the magnitude check. But \(4\pi/3\) lies between \(\pi\) and \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\) — Quadrant III, where both cosine and sine must be negative. The claimed cosine, \(+\frac12\), has the wrong sign. This row fails the sign check.
  • \(5\pi/3\), claimed \(\left(\frac12,-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\): magnitude \(\frac14+\frac34=1\) ✓. \(5\pi/3\) is QIV — cosine positive, sine negative expected; claimed matches ✓. Passes both.
  • \(7\pi/4\), claimed \(\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2},-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)\): magnitude \(\frac12+\frac12=1\) ✓. \(7\pi/4\) is QIV — cosine positive, sine negative expected; claimed matches ✓. Passes both.
The lone failure is the \(4\pi/3\) row: it survives the magnitude check (both candidate signs give the same squares) but fails the sign check, since Quadrant III demands a negative cosine.
Final Answer: The \(4\pi/3\) row fails its sign check (Quadrant III needs cosine negative). Corrected value: \(\left(-\dfrac12, -\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\).
PROBLEM 6 — Explain why
Why aren't the \(\pi/6\) and \(\pi/3\) seeds interchangeable, even though both use \(\frac12\) and \(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\)? Give one quick check to tell them apart at a glance.
MODEL SOLUTION
The two seeds share the same pair of numbers but assign them to opposite coordinates: the \(\pi/6\) seed is \(\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2},\dfrac12\right)\) (larger value on cosine, since \(\pi/6\) is close to the \(x\)-axis), while the \(\pi/3\) seed is \(\left(\dfrac12,\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\) (larger value on sine, since \(\pi/3\) is close to the \(y\)-axis). Swapping them silently swaps which axis carries the larger value, producing a genuinely different point on the circle. A quick check: compare the angle to \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) (\(45^\circ\), halfway between the axes) — an angle closer to \(0\) (like \(\pi/6\)) should have the larger value on cosine, while an angle closer to \(\pi/2\) (like \(\pi/3\)) should have the larger value on sine. The size of the reference angle itself tells you which axis it leans toward.
Final Answer: The seeds assign the same two numbers to opposite coordinates. Quick check: an angle closer to \(0\) leans its larger value onto cosine; an angle closer to \(\pi/2\) leans it onto sine.
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
Using only the three seeds and the sign rule, evaluate all six trig functions of \(\theta=\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\); verify with \(\tan\theta\cdot\cot\theta=1\).
SOLUTION
\(\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\) lies between \(\pi\) and \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\) — Quadrant III. Reference angle \(=\dfrac{5\pi}{4}-\pi=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\), the \(\pi/4\) seed: \(\left(\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2},\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)\). In QIII, both cosine and sine are negative: \[ \cos\dfrac{5\pi}{4}=-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2} \qquad \sin\dfrac{5\pi}{4}=-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2} \] \[ \tan\dfrac{5\pi}{4}=\dfrac{-\sqrt2/2}{-\sqrt2/2}=1 \qquad \csc\dfrac{5\pi}{4}=-\sqrt2 \qquad \sec\dfrac{5\pi}{4}=-\sqrt2 \qquad \cot\dfrac{5\pi}{4}=1 \] Verify: \(\tan\theta\cdot\cot\theta = (1)(1) = 1\) ✓, confirming tangent and cotangent are genuine reciprocals here.
Final Answer: \(\sin=-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\), \(\cos=-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\), \(\tan=1\), \(\csc=-\sqrt2\), \(\sec=-\sqrt2\), \(\cot=1\); consistency check \(\tan\theta\cdot\cot\theta=1\) confirmed.
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the plotted points should show)
Plotting \(\left(\frac12,-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\), \(\left(-\frac{\sqrt2}{2},\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)\), and \(\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2},-\frac12\right)\) against x^2+y^2=1 should show all three landing exactly on the circle. If a student instead plots the uncorrected \(4\pi/3\) claim, \(\left(\frac12,-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\), it will sit exactly on the circle too (the magnitude was never the problem) — but visibly in Quadrant IV instead of the Quadrant III position \(4\pi/3\) actually terminates in, which is the giveaway a graph makes obvious that arithmetic alone can hide.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound — release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it. Common spots to watch: Problem 5 students who catch the wrong sign but misidentify which row it's in, or who run only one of the two checks; Problem 5 students reporting the error as a magnitude failure rather than a sign failure (the magnitude of the \(4\pi/3\) row is actually fine — the giveaway is exclusively the sign); Problem 6 students who describe the seeds as "different because they're different values" without naming the axis-lean explanation; Problem 7 losing a sign on \(\csc\) or \(\sec\) since Quadrant III makes every one of the six functions negative except tangent and cotangent.

pages.html:
🔒 TEACHER ANSWER KEY — INTERNAL USE ONLY. Do not post, link, or share this page with students.

PRECALCULUS HONORS — ANSWER KEY
Quarter / Unit
Q3 · Unit 6
Right Triangle Trigonometry
Lesson
Lesson 6-11
Keys To
Assignment 6-11 · Focus Set: The Field Report
⭐ Focus Assignment · Method-Graded (2 problems)
Points
Assignment
16 pts
Lesson 6-11
Answer Key: The Field Report
Full worked solutions for all 6 problems. Problems 3 and 4 carry gold-badged scoring guidance for the rubric — those are the only two problems graded for method; the rest are checked for honest completion.
PROBLEM 1 — Warmup
A drone hovers at \(150\) m. The angle of depression to a landmark is \(24^\circ\). Find the horizontal distance to the landmark.
SOLUTION
The angle of depression from the drone equals the angle of elevation from the landmark (alternate interior angles with the horizontal). In the right triangle formed, the drone's altitude (\(150\) m) is the side opposite the \(24^\circ\) angle, and the horizontal distance \(d\) is the adjacent side: \[ \tan(24^\circ) = \dfrac{150}{d} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; d = \dfrac{150}{\tan(24^\circ)} = \dfrac{150}{0.4452} \approx 336.9 \text{ m} \]
Final Answer: \(d \approx 336.9\) m.
PROBLEM 2 — Warmup
Convert a compass heading of \(205^\circ\) to standard position; state the quadrant, reference angle, and the sign of each displacement component.
SOLUTION
Compass headings are measured clockwise from north; standard-position angles are measured counterclockwise from east. The conversion is \(\text{standard} = 90^\circ - \text{heading}\) (adjusted into \([0^\circ,360^\circ)\)): \[ \text{standard} = 90^\circ - 205^\circ = -115^\circ \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; -115^\circ+360^\circ = 245^\circ \] \(245^\circ\) lies between \(180^\circ\) and \(270^\circ\) — Quadrant III. Reference angle \(=245^\circ-180^\circ=65^\circ\). A heading of \(205^\circ\) points between due south (\(180^\circ\)) and due west (\(270^\circ\)), so the boat moves south and west — both the east and north displacement components must be negative, exactly what Quadrant III's sign pattern (cosine negative, sine negative) predicts.
Final Answer: Standard angle \(245^\circ\), Quadrant III, reference angle \(65^\circ\); both east and north displacement components negative.
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 3
The two-station survey: elevation \(41^\circ\) at station 1; walk \(55\) m directly away, elevation \(26^\circ\) at station 2. Declare variables, set up both equations, solve the system, verify with the unused equation, and check physical reasonableness.
SOLUTION
① Declare and set up. Let \(h\) = tower height, \(x\) = horizontal distance from station 1 to the tower's base. From station 1: \[ \tan(41^\circ) = \dfrac{h}{x} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; h = x\tan(41^\circ) \] From station 2, now a distance \(x+55\) from the base: \[ \tan(26^\circ) = \dfrac{h}{x+55} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; h = (x+55)\tan(26^\circ) \] ② Solve the system. Set the two expressions for \(h\) equal: \[ x\tan(41^\circ) = (x+55)\tan(26^\circ) \] \[ 0.8693x = 0.4877x + 0.4877(55) = 0.4877x + 26.82 \] \[ 0.3816x = 26.82 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; x \approx 70.3 \text{ m} \] \[ h = x\tan(41^\circ) \approx 70.3(0.8693) \approx 61.1 \text{ m} \] ③ Verify with the other station's equation: \[ h = (x+55)\tan(26^\circ) = (70.3+55)(0.4877) = (125.3)(0.4877) \approx 61.1 \text{ m} \;\;\checkmark \] Both stations agree on the same height, confirming the solution.

④ Height and reasonableness: the tower is approximately \(61.1\) m tall — a very reasonable height for a radio tower (roughly 200 ft). The second station's distance, \(125.3\) m, exceeds the first station's distance, \(70.3\) m, by exactly \(125.3-70.3=55\) m, precisely the distance walked — a second check that the system was set up and solved correctly.
Final Answer: Tower height \(h\approx61.1\) m; original distance \(x\approx70.3\) m. Verified against the unused station equation and against the required \(55\) m gap between stations.
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): both station equations are set up correctly with \(h\) opposite and the horizontal leg adjacent to each elevation angle, and the second station's distance is correctly written as \(x+55\) (not \(x-55\) or \(55-x\)). (2): one equation correct, the other has a sign or setup error (commonly \(x-55\)). (0): tangent ratio inverted (adjacent over opposite) or elevation angle misapplied.

Reasoning (4): the system is solved algebraically with every step shown (not guessed or solved by calculator black-box), and the verification step actually substitutes back into the equation not used to solve, genuinely recovering the same height. (2): system solved correctly but verification skipped or merely restates the same equation used to solve. (0): no real system-solving shown, height simply asserted.

Presentation & precision (4): variables declared in a labeled sentence before use, both equations displayed before combining, algebra shown in clean vertical steps, final height and distance boxed with units. (2): organized with a labeling or unit lapse. (0): scattered or illegible; the two-equation structure cannot be followed.

Intellectual honesty (4): the physical-reasonableness sentence is a genuine check (naming that \(61\) m is sensible for a radio tower, and confirming the \(55\) m gap holds), not a rote closing line. (2): reasonableness sentence present but generic ("this seems right"). (0): no reasonableness check, or the \(55\) m gap check is fabricated to match rather than genuinely computed.
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 4
The heading report: a boat sails heading \(128^\circ\) for \(18\) nm, then heading \(205^\circ\) for \(12\) nm. Convert both headings, find displacement components, sum them, find distance and reciprocal bearing, close with a field report.
SOLUTION
① Convert both headings using \(\text{standard} = 90^\circ - \text{heading}\) (mod \(360^\circ\)): \[ \text{Leg 1: } 90^\circ-128^\circ=-38^\circ+360^\circ=322^\circ \quad\text{(QIV, reference } 38^\circ\text{)} \] \[ \text{Leg 2: } 90^\circ-205^\circ=-115^\circ+360^\circ=245^\circ \quad\text{(QIII, reference } 65^\circ\text{)} \] ② East/north components (east \(=r\cos(\text{standard})\), north \(=r\sin(\text{standard})\)): \[ \text{Leg 1: East}=18\cos(322^\circ)=18(0.7880)\approx14.18 \text{ nm} \quad(+\text{, QIV cosine positive}) \] \[ \text{North}=18\sin(322^\circ)=18(-0.6157)\approx-11.08 \text{ nm} \quad(-\text{, QIV sine negative}) \] \[ \text{Leg 2: East}=12\cos(245^\circ)=12(-0.4226)\approx-5.07 \text{ nm} \quad(-\text{, QIII cosine negative}) \] \[ \text{North}=12\sin(245^\circ)=12(-0.9063)\approx-10.88 \text{ nm} \quad(-\text{, QIII sine negative}) \] ③ Sum the components: \[ \text{Total East} = 14.18+(-5.07) = 9.11 \text{ nm} \qquad \text{Total North} = -11.08+(-10.88) = -21.96 \text{ nm} \] ④ Distance and reciprocal bearing: \[ \text{Distance} = \sqrt{(9.11)^2+(-21.96)^2} = \sqrt{83.0+482.2} = \sqrt{565.2} \approx 23.8 \text{ nm} \] To return to the marina, the boat must travel along the vector opposite its position, \((-9.11,\,+21.96)\) — negative east (west), positive north. The reference angle for the return course is \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{9.11}{21.96}\right)\approx22.5^\circ\), and since the return vector points west-of-north, the compass bearing is \(360^\circ-22.5^\circ\approx337^\circ\).

⑤ Field report: “The vessel's current position is approximately \(23.8\) nautical miles from the marina. To return directly, steer a course of approximately \(337^\circ\).”
Final Answer: Total displacement \(\approx(9.1\text{ nm E}, -22.0\text{ nm N})\); distance from marina \(\approx23.8\) nm; reciprocal bearing \(\approx337^\circ\).
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): both headings converted correctly with the formula shown, correct quadrant and reference angle named for each, and all four displacement components computed with the correct trig ratio and sign matching ASTC. (2): one heading conversion or one component's sign is wrong but the overall method is sound. (0): headings used directly as standard-position angles with no conversion.

Reasoning (4): the four components are summed correctly, the distance is found via the Pythagorean theorem on the summed components (not the individual legs), and the reciprocal bearing is derived from the return vector's own quadrant, not guessed. (2): distance/bearing computed but the return-vector's quadrant reasoning for the bearing is skipped, arriving at the right number without showing why the \(360^\circ-\text{reference}\) form was chosen. (0): no real derivation of distance or bearing shown.

Presentation & precision (4): each leg's conversion, components, and running sums organized in clearly labeled rows or steps; the closing field report is a clean two-sentence document a dispatcher could act on without re-deriving anything. (2): organized with a labeling lapse (e.g., legs not clearly distinguished). (0): scattered; the four components cannot be traced to their legs.

Intellectual honesty (4): every conversion and sign is shown as an explicit step, not silently assumed from the final answer; the field report states the numbers plainly rather than hedging or overstating precision. (2): the final numbers are correct but one intermediate sign or conversion is unstated. (0): components or bearing appear reverse-engineered from an assumed answer.
PROBLEM 5
The AI cross-examination: give your Problem 4 work to an AI tutor, ask it to check the heading conversions and displacement directions, copy its response, and render your own verdict.
GRADING GUIDANCE (no single correct answer — the response is student-generated)
There is no fixed "correct" AI response to check against — what is graded is the judging. Look for:
  • An actual AI response copied onto the page (two or three sentences), not fabricated or trivial.
  • A verdict that engages the mathematics specifically — if the AI flags a real conversion or sign error, the student should show the fix; if the AI's check is itself wrong (e.g., it misapplies the \(90^\circ-\text{heading}\) formula, or asserts a direction that contradicts ASTC for the stated quadrant), the student should refute it by re-deriving the conversion or citing a compass-direction sanity check (e.g., "heading \(205^\circ\) is between south and west, so both components must be negative — the AI's claim of a positive north component is wrong").
  • Either outcome earns full credit: a sound refutation of a bad AI claim, or a genuine correction if the AI catches something real. What must not appear is a verdict that merely restates "the AI is right" or "the AI is wrong" without checking the specific claim against the conversion formula or ASTC.
Final Answer: Grade for the quality of the judgment (was every claim actually verified against the conversion formula or ASTC before ruling?), not for which side of the argument the student lands on.
PROBLEM 6 — Honors stretch
A hazard is detected on a true bearing of \(313^\circ\) at \(8.5\) nm. Convert to standard position, find the (east, north) position, and explain the error from plotting the bearing directly as a standard-position angle.
SOLUTION
① \(\text{standard} = 90^\circ-313^\circ=-223^\circ+360^\circ=137^\circ\). \(137^\circ\) lies between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\) — Quadrant II. Reference angle \(=180^\circ-137^\circ=43^\circ\).

② \(\text{East}=8.5\cos(137^\circ)=8.5(-0.7314)\approx-6.2\) nm; \(\text{North}=8.5\sin(137^\circ)=8.5(0.6820)\approx5.8\) nm. Position \(\approx(-6.2, 5.8)\) — \(6.2\) nm west and \(5.8\) nm north of the ship, matching the physical sense of a bearing between northwest (\(315^\circ\)) and north (\(360^\circ\)).

③ The error: a bearing of \(313^\circ\) points toward the northwest — north and west of the ship. If a navigator instead plotted \(313^\circ\) as though it were already a standard-position angle (measured counterclockwise from east), it would fall in Quadrant IV, giving a positive east component and a negative north component — placing the hazard to the east and south of the ship instead of to its actual west and north. That is not a small rounding error; it points the hazard into the opposite quadrant entirely, which could mean steering directly toward danger the navigator believes is safely behind.
Final Answer: Standard angle \(137^\circ\); hazard position \(\approx(-6.2, 5.8)\) nm. Plotting \(313^\circ\) directly as a standard-position angle would place the hazard in the opposite quadrant (east-southeast instead of west-northwest).
💡 DESMOS / EXCEL CHECK
For Problem 4, a two-row Excel traverse table (distance, heading, standard angle, east component, north component) should sum to East \(\approx9.11\), North \(\approx-21.96\) — matching the hand computation. Plotting both legs tip-to-tail as vectors from the origin in Desmos should show the final position landing at approximately \((9.1, -22.0)\), about \(23.8\) units from the origin.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Focus Assignment — 16 pts, method-graded on Problems 3 and 4 only)
Problems 1, 2, 5, and 6 are checked for honest, visible completion only — do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound, and release this key after the due date for self-correction. Problems 3 and 4, the two ⭐ method problems, carry the entire 16-point rubric (Understanding / Reasoning / Presentation & Precision / Intellectual Honesty, 4 pts each), applied holistically across both problems together. Budget roughly 1–2 minutes per student for the two method problems, per the course's designated-problems-only grading model. The most common fatal error in Problem 3 is writing the second station's distance as \(x-55\) instead of \(x+55\) (the surveyor walks away); the most common fatal error in Problem 4 is skipping the heading-to-standard-position conversion and using the compass heading directly in the sine/cosine formulas, which silently swaps the roles of the east and north components.

Answer Key: Unit 6 Test
Full worked solutions for all 11 problems (Part A: 1–8, Part B: 9–10, Part C: 11), for grading against the standing 4-criterion rubric.
📊 POINT ALLOCATION SUMMARY (which problems supply evidence for which criterion)
The rubric is holistic across the whole test (each of the four criteria scored out of 10, 40 pts total) rather than problem-by-problem, but each part carries most of the weight for particular criteria:
  • Understanding of the material (10 pts): primarily Part A (1–8) — degree–radian conversion, arc length and sector area, right-triangle solving, unit-circle special values, and reference-angle/ASTC evaluation, including a calculator used only after a hand prediction.
  • Quality of reasoning (10 pts): primarily Part B (9–10) and Part C (11) — the 30-60-90 seed values derived as a genuine geometric argument, the two-station system solved and its necessity explained, and the ADA-ramp problem's connection to Unit 4's one-to-one/horizontal-line-test criterion made explicitly, not merely gestured at.
  • Presentation & precision (10 pts): distributed across all parts — neat vertical work, aligned equals signs, exact values kept in radical form where the angle is special, units carried on every field-problem answer.
  • Intellectual honesty (10 pts): the signed honor line plus honest handling throughout — any problem left incomplete should carry a note of where and why the student stopped, which earns credit here rather than losing it.
📝 PART A — FLUENCY (Lessons 6-1 through 6-10)
PROBLEM 1
Degree–radian fluency: convert \(315^\circ\) to radians; convert \(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\) radians to degrees.
SOLUTION
\[ 315^\circ \times \dfrac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \dfrac{315\pi}{180} = \dfrac{7\pi}{4} \] \[ \dfrac{5\pi}{3} \times \dfrac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \dfrac{5(180^\circ)}{3} = 300^\circ \]
Final Answer: \(315^\circ=\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\); \(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}=300^\circ\).
PROBLEM 2
Coterminal angle for \(-750^\circ\) in \([0^\circ,360^\circ)\); convert to radians; sector with central angle \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\) and radius \(9\) cm — arc length and area.
SOLUTION
① Add full rotations of \(360^\circ\) until the result lies in \([0^\circ,360^\circ)\): \[ -750^\circ + 360^\circ = -390^\circ \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; -390^\circ+360^\circ = -30^\circ \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; -30^\circ+360^\circ = 330^\circ \] (three full rotations added: \(-750^\circ+3(360^\circ)=-750^\circ+1080^\circ=330^\circ\)).
② \(330^\circ \times \dfrac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \dfrac{330\pi}{180}=\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\).
③ Arc length \(s=r\theta = 9\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)=6\pi\) cm. Area \(A=\dfrac12 r^2\theta = \dfrac12(81)\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)=\dfrac{81\pi}{3}=27\pi\) cm\(^2\).
Final Answer: Coterminal angle \(330^\circ=\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\); arc length \(6\pi\) cm; sector area \(27\pi\) cm\(^2\).
PROBLEM 3
Right triangle: one leg \(=14\), the angle opposite it is \(38^\circ\). Find the hypotenuse, other leg, third angle; verify with the Pythagorean theorem.
SOLUTION
The known leg (\(14\)) is opposite \(38^\circ\); sine relates opposite to hypotenuse: \[ \sin(38^\circ) = \dfrac{14}{\text{hyp}} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \text{hyp} = \dfrac{14}{\sin(38^\circ)} = \dfrac{14}{0.6157} \approx 22.74 \] The other leg is adjacent to \(38^\circ\); tangent relates opposite to adjacent: \[ \tan(38^\circ) = \dfrac{14}{\text{adj}} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \text{adj} = \dfrac{14}{\tan(38^\circ)} = \dfrac{14}{0.7813} \approx 17.92 \] Third angle \(=90^\circ-38^\circ=52^\circ\).

Verify: \(14^2+17.92^2 = 196+321.1 = 517.1\); \(22.74^2=517.1\) ✓ (matching within rounding).
Final Answer: Hypotenuse \(\approx22.74\); other leg \(\approx17.92\); third angle \(52^\circ\).
PROBLEM 4
Evaluate \(\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\), \(\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\), \(\tan\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\) exactly, stating quadrant and reference angle.
SOLUTION
\(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\) lies between \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\) and \(2\pi\) — Quadrant IV. Reference angle \(=2\pi-\dfrac{5\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\). In QIV: sine negative, cosine positive, tangent negative. \[ \sin\dfrac{5\pi}{3}=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \qquad \cos\dfrac{5\pi}{3}=\dfrac12 \qquad \tan\dfrac{5\pi}{3}=-\sqrt3 \]
Final Answer: \(\sin=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\cos=\dfrac12\), \(\tan=-\sqrt3\).
PROBLEM 5
Evaluate all six trigonometric functions of \(\theta=120^\circ\) exactly, stating the sign pattern first.
SOLUTION
\(120^\circ\) lies between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\) — Quadrant II. Reference angle \(=180^\circ-120^\circ=60^\circ\). In QII: sine positive, cosine negative, tangent negative. \[ \sin120^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \quad \cos120^\circ=-\dfrac12 \quad \tan120^\circ=-\sqrt3 \] \[ \csc120^\circ=\dfrac{2\sqrt3}{3} \quad \sec120^\circ=-2 \quad \cot120^\circ=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3} \]
Final Answer: \(\sin=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\cos=-\frac12\), \(\tan=-\sqrt3\), \(\csc=\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}\), \(\sec=-2\), \(\cot=-\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\).
PROBLEM 6
Evaluate \(\sec250^\circ\) to four decimal places; predict quadrant, reference angle, and sign before computing.
SOLUTION
\(250^\circ\) lies between \(180^\circ\) and \(270^\circ\) — Quadrant III. Reference angle \(=250^\circ-180^\circ=70^\circ\). In QIII, cosine is negative, so secant (its reciprocal) must also be negative. \[ \cos250^\circ = -\cos70^\circ \approx -0.34202 \] \[ \sec250^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\cos250^\circ} \approx \dfrac{1}{-0.34202} \approx -2.9238 \] Negative, exactly as predicted.
Final Answer: \(\sec250^\circ\approx-2.9238\).
PROBLEM 7
\(\sin\theta=0.6\), \(\theta\) in Quadrant II. Using \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\), find \(\cos\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) exactly.
SOLUTION
\(\sin\theta=0.6=\dfrac35\). \[ \cos^2\theta = 1-\sin^2\theta = 1-\dfrac9{25}=\dfrac{16}{25} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \cos\theta=\pm\dfrac45 \] Quadrant II requires cosine negative: \(\cos\theta=-\dfrac45=-0.8\). \[ \tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{3/5}{-4/5} = -\dfrac34 \]
Final Answer: \(\cos\theta=-\dfrac45\); \(\tan\theta=-\dfrac34\).
PROBLEM 8
From \(40\) m away, the angle of elevation to the top of a building is \(55^\circ\). Find the building's height.
SOLUTION
The height is opposite the elevation angle; the \(40\) m distance is adjacent: \[ \tan(55^\circ) = \dfrac{h}{40} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; h = 40\tan(55^\circ) = 40(1.4281) \approx 57.1 \text{ m} \]
Final Answer: \(h\approx57.1\) m.
📝 PART B — REASONING (write these as arguments)
PROBLEM 9
Derive the seeds themselves: equilateral triangle side \(2\), altitude to a \(30\)-\(60\)-\(90\) split. Find the altitude, read off \(\sin30^\circ,\cos30^\circ,\sin60^\circ,\cos60^\circ\), and explain why deriving beats memorizing.
MODEL SOLUTION
① Dropping the altitude from one vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side bisects that side, so the resulting right triangle has hypotenuse \(2\) (the original side) and one leg \(1\) (half the base). By the Pythagorean theorem: \[ (\text{altitude})^2 + 1^2 = 2^2 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; (\text{altitude})^2 = 4-1=3 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \text{altitude}=\sqrt3 \] ② The altitude also bisects the equilateral triangle's \(60^\circ\) apex angle into two \(30^\circ\) angles. In the resulting right triangle: the side of length \(1\) (half the base) sits opposite the \(30^\circ\) angle, the altitude \(\sqrt3\) sits opposite the \(60^\circ\) angle, and the hypotenuse is \(2\): \[ \sin30^\circ=\dfrac{1}{2} \qquad \cos30^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \qquad \sin60^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \qquad \cos60^\circ=\dfrac{1}{2} \] ③ These four numbers are exactly the seed for the reference angle \(30^\circ\) (and, by cofunction symmetry, \(60^\circ\)) — the same \(\pi/6\)/\(\pi/3\) seed family used throughout the unit. Deriving them geometrically, from an equilateral triangle and the Pythagorean theorem, is more trustworthy than memorizing four unrelated facts because the derivation can be reconstructed from first principles at any time, closing off the risk of misremembering which value belongs to which function — a risk that pure memorization always carries.
Final Answer: Altitude \(=\sqrt3\); \(\sin30^\circ=\frac12\), \(\cos30^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\sin60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\cos60^\circ=\frac12\) — the \(30^\circ\)/\(60^\circ\) seed, reconstructible from first principles.
PROBLEM 10
Two-station field problem: elevation \(42^\circ\), walk \(35\) m away, elevation \(24^\circ\). Set up, solve, verify, and explain why one station alone cannot determine the height.
MODEL SOLUTION
① Let \(h\)=height, \(x\)=distance from station 1 to the base. \[ \tan(42^\circ)=\dfrac{h}{x} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; h=x\tan(42^\circ) \qquad\qquad \tan(24^\circ)=\dfrac{h}{x+35} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; h=(x+35)\tan(24^\circ) \] ② Solve: \[ x\tan(42^\circ) = (x+35)\tan(24^\circ) \] \[ 0.9004x = 0.4452x + 0.4452(35) = 0.4452x+15.58 \] \[ 0.4552x = 15.58 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; x\approx34.2 \text{ m} \] \[ h = x\tan(42^\circ) \approx 34.2(0.9004) \approx 30.8 \text{ m} \] ③ Verify using the equation not used to solve for \(x\): \[ h=(x+35)\tan(24^\circ) = (34.2+35)(0.4452) = (69.2)(0.4452) \approx 30.8 \text{ m} \;\;\checkmark \] ④ Why one station is not enough: a single station's equation, \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{h}{x}\), has two unknowns — the height \(h\) and the distance \(x\) — and one equation cannot determine two unknowns; infinitely many \((h,x)\) pairs satisfy it. Walking a known distance to a second station introduces a second, independent equation relating the same two unknowns (now to \(x+35\) rather than \(x\)), and two independent equations in two unknowns is exactly what a system needs to pin down a single solution.
Final Answer: Tower height \(h\approx30.8\) m, distance \(x\approx34.2\) m, confirmed by the unused station equation. One station's equation alone leaves two unknowns (\(h\) and \(x\)) undetermined; the second station supplies the second independent equation the system needs.
📝 PART C — SYNTHESIS (this unit meets Unit 4)
PROBLEM 11
ADA ramp: \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{12}\). Find \(\theta\) in \((0^\circ,90^\circ)\); find a second solution in \((0^\circ,360^\circ)\); connect the need for a restricted domain to Unit 4's one-to-one/horizontal-line-test criterion; explain why \((0^\circ,90^\circ)\) is the physically forced restriction.
MODEL SOLUTION
① Using the calculator's inverse tangent key on \(\dfrac{1}{12}\approx0.08333\): \[ \theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{12}\right) \approx 4.7636^\circ \approx 4.8^\circ \]
② Tangent repeats every \(180^\circ\), so a second solution is \(\theta+180^\circ\): \[ 4.8^\circ + 180^\circ = 184.8^\circ \] \(184.8^\circ\) lies between \(180^\circ\) and \(270^\circ\) — Quadrant III, with reference angle \(4.8^\circ\). By ASTC, Quadrant III makes both sine and cosine negative, so their ratio (tangent) is positive — confirming \(\tan(184.8^\circ)\) is also positive and equal to \(\tan(4.8^\circ)=\dfrac{1}{12}\).

③ Connect to Unit 4: Part ② just exhibited two different inputs, \(4.8^\circ\) and \(184.8^\circ\), that produce the identical output \(\dfrac{1}{12}\) under tangent — and in fact every angle of the form \(4.8^\circ+180^\circ k\) does the same. A function that sends more than one input to the same output fails the horizontal line test, which in Unit 4 was the certifying criterion for whether a function is one-to-one; tangent over its full domain is not one-to-one, so "the angle whose tangent is \(\frac{1}{12}\)" has no single well-defined answer — the question itself is ambiguous until the domain is restricted. Restricting to \(0^\circ<\theta<90^\circ\) removes every repeat: within that interval tangent passes the horizontal line test and becomes genuinely one-to-one, which is exactly the property Unit 4 required before a function could be assigned a well-defined inverse. That restricted tangent is what the inverse tangent key on a calculator actually computes.

④ Close the loop: \(0^\circ<\theta<90^\circ\) is not an arbitrary mathematical convenience here — it is the only range of angles a right triangle's interior angle can physically occupy, since an angle of \(0^\circ\) or \(90^\circ\) would collapse the triangle entirely, so the domain restriction Unit 4's invertibility criterion demands turns out to be identical to the domain the physical geometry already forces.
Final Answer: \(\theta\approx4.8^\circ\); second solution \(184.8^\circ\) (QIII, reference \(4.8^\circ\), tangent positive there too). Tangent over its full domain fails the horizontal line test (not one-to-one), so it has no well-defined inverse until restricted to \(0^\circ<\theta<90^\circ\) — exactly the interval a real right-triangle angle is forced to occupy.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC

The whole test is graded against the standing four-criterion rubric, each criterion scored out of 10. Part A supplies most of the evidence for understanding and precision; Parts B and C supply most of the evidence for reasoning.

Criteria What excellent looks like Pts
Understanding of the material Degree–radian conversions, arc length and sector area, right-triangle solving, and reference-angle/ASTC evaluation all executed correctly and fluently, with notation exact throughout. 10 pts
Quality of reasoning The 30-60-90 derivation reads as a real geometric argument; the two-station system is solved and its necessity explained; the Part C connection to Unit 4's one-to-one/horizontal-line-test criterion is made explicitly and correctly, not merely gestured at. 10 pts
Presentation & precision Clean vertical work throughout, aligned equals signs, exact values kept in radical form where the angle is special, units carried on every field-problem answer, pages in order — forty points of work a stranger could follow. 10 pts
Intellectual honesty Honor line signed and honored; work shown as actually done; any problem you could not finish carries an honest note of where and why you stopped — which earns respect here, never punishment. 10 pts
Total: 40 pts
📊 GRADING NOTE (Test — 40 pts, rubric-graded)
Score holistically against the four-criterion rubric printed on the test page (10 pts each). Common partial-credit spots: Problem 2① dropping a full rotation in the coterminal-angle addition (landing on \(-30^\circ\) instead of continuing to \(330^\circ\)) — deduct from Understanding since \([0^\circ,360^\circ)\) was the stated requirement; Problem 3's leg/hypotenuse ratios swapped (using cosine where sine was needed, since the given leg is opposite, not adjacent) — deduct from Understanding; Problem 6 skipping the written sign/quadrant prediction and reporting only the calculator's decimal — deduct from Reasoning even if the number is correct, since the problem explicitly requires the prediction first; Problem 9's altitude-length step done correctly but the final "why derive, not memorize" sentence merely restated as "it's easier to remember" without naming the reconstructibility argument — deduct from Reasoning; Problem 10's system solved correctly but the "why one station is insufficient" explanation naming only "you need more information" without identifying the two specific unknowns \(h\) and \(x\) — deduct from Reasoning; Problem 11③ stating that tangent "isn't one-to-one" without explicitly citing the two equal outputs from ② as the evidence, or omitting the explicit link to Unit 4's horizontal-line-test language — deduct from Reasoning, since the problem asks the connection to be made explicitly, not simply asserted. An honestly noted incomplete answer should never cost Intellectual Honesty points — that criterion rewards the honesty, not the completeness.

Practice Set · Completion-Scored
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 7-1
Answer Key: Unrolling the Circle
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1
Build the sine table: Using the unit circle's exact values, complete a table of \(\sin\theta\) for \(\theta = 0,\ \frac{\pi}{6},\ \frac{\pi}{4},\ \frac{\pi}{3},\ \frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{2\pi}{3},\ \frac{3\pi}{4},\ \frac{5\pi}{6},\ \pi\). Then describe, in one sentence, the shape the plotted points would trace.
SOLUTION
Reading the \(y\)-coordinate of the terminal point at each angle straight off the unit circle:
\(\theta\)\(0\)\(\frac{\pi}{6}\)\(\frac{\pi}{4}\)\(\frac{\pi}{3}\)\(\frac{\pi}{2}\)\(\frac{2\pi}{3}\)\(\frac{3\pi}{4}\)\(\frac{5\pi}{6}\)\(\pi\)
\(\sin\theta\)\(0\)\(\frac12\)\(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\)\(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\)\(1\)\(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\)\(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\)\(\frac12\)\(0\)
The values rise from \(0\) up to \(1\) and back down to \(0\), symmetric about \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\).
Final Answer: Table as above. The points trace a single symmetric hump (arch) rising from \(0\) to a peak of \(1\) at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\), then falling back to \(0\) at \(\theta=\pi\).
PROBLEM 2
Build the cosine table: Using the unit circle's exact values, complete a table of \(\cos\theta\) for the same nine angles as Problem 1. Then explain, in one sentence, how this table's shape compares to Problem 1's.
SOLUTION
Reading the \(x\)-coordinate of the terminal point at each angle:
\(\theta\)\(0\)\(\frac{\pi}{6}\)\(\frac{\pi}{4}\)\(\frac{\pi}{3}\)\(\frac{\pi}{2}\)\(\frac{2\pi}{3}\)\(\frac{3\pi}{4}\)\(\frac{5\pi}{6}\)\(\pi\)
\(\cos\theta\)\(1\)\(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\)\(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\)\(\frac12\)\(0\)\(-\frac12\)\(-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\)\(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\)\(-1\)
Final Answer: Table as above. Unlike sine's table, which rises then falls back to \(0\), cosine's table decreases steadily the whole way from \(1\) to \(-1\) — over this domain cosine is tracing the descending half of its own wave, since its own hump is centered at \(\theta=0\) rather than at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\).
PROBLEM 3
Evaluate by periodicity: Find \(\sin\dfrac{17\pi}{6}\) by first reducing the angle to an equivalent one inside \([0,2\pi)\), showing that reduction step.
SOLUTION
\[ \frac{17\pi}{6} - 2\pi = \frac{17\pi}{6} - \frac{12\pi}{6} = \frac{5\pi}{6} \] \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\) lies in \([0,2\pi)\), so \(\sin\frac{17\pi}{6} = \sin\frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac12\).
Final Answer: \(\sin\frac{17\pi}{6} = \frac12\)
PROBLEM 4
Evaluate by periodicity: Find \(\cos\dfrac{11\pi}{4}\) by the same reduction method.
SOLUTION
\[ \frac{11\pi}{4} - 2\pi = \frac{11\pi}{4} - \frac{8\pi}{4} = \frac{3\pi}{4} \] \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\) lies in \([0,2\pi)\), so \(\cos\frac{11\pi}{4} = \cos\frac{3\pi}{4} = -\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\).
Final Answer: \(\cos\frac{11\pi}{4} = -\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\)
PROBLEM 5
Name the features: State the period, amplitude, and midline of both \(y=\sin x\) and \(y=\cos x\), and explain in one sentence how each number can be read directly off the unit circle rather than memorized as an isolated fact.
SOLUTION
Both \(y=\sin x\) and \(y=\cos x\) have period \(2\pi\), amplitude \(1\), and midline \(y=0\). The period is the angle of one full revolution around the circle, after which the terminal point (and hence the coordinate) repeats exactly; the amplitude is the circle's own radius, the farthest a coordinate can ever get from zero; and the midline is the circle's center height, since the coordinate swings symmetrically between \(-1\) and \(1\) around the origin.
Final Answer: Period \(=2\pi\), amplitude \(=1\), midline \(y=0\) for both functions — each number is a direct feature of the unit circle itself (one revolution, the radius, and the circle's center), not an arbitrary memorized value.
PROBLEM 6 — Explain why
Using the unit circle's own definition of sine as a coordinate, explain in three or four sentences why \(\sin(\theta+2\pi)=\sin\theta\) must hold for every real number \(\theta\), not merely for the values already listed in a table.
MODEL SOLUTION
Sine is defined as the \(y\)-coordinate of the terminal point reached by sweeping through angle \(\theta\) around the unit circle. Adding \(2\pi\) to \(\theta\) means sweeping through one additional complete revolution — since \(2\pi\) is exactly the angle of a full trip around the circle, the terminal point after \(\theta+2\pi\) lands in precisely the same place as the terminal point after \(\theta\) alone. Because the two angles produce the identical terminal point, and sine is nothing more than that point's \(y\)-coordinate, the two sine values must also be identical. This reasoning never referred to a specific angle or a table entry — it depends only on \(2\pi\) being one full revolution — so it applies to every real \(\theta\), including angles far outside any table ever written.
Final Answer: \(\sin(\theta+2\pi)=\sin\theta\) because adding \(2\pi\) is one full revolution, returning to the identical terminal point — and identical terminal points must share the identical \(y\)-coordinate, for any \(\theta\) whatsoever.
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
Evaluate \(\sin\dfrac{100\pi}{3}\). You will need to subtract multiples of \(2\pi\) more than once to land inside \([0,2\pi)\) — show every subtraction. Then, in one sentence, explain why this repeated-subtraction process works no matter how large the original angle is.
SOLUTION
Writing \(2\pi=\frac{6\pi}{3}\) so every step shares a denominator of \(3\): \[ \frac{100\pi}{3}-\frac{6\pi}{3}=\frac{94\pi}{3} \quad\rightarrow\quad \frac{94\pi}{3}-\frac{6\pi}{3}=\frac{88\pi}{3} \quad\rightarrow\quad \frac{88\pi}{3}-\frac{6\pi}{3}=\frac{82\pi}{3} \quad\rightarrow\ \cdots \] Each subtraction removes exactly one full revolution (\(\frac{6\pi}{3}\)). Continuing this same subtraction a total of \(16\) times (since \(\frac{100\pi}{3}\div 2\pi = \frac{50}{3}\approx16.7\), so \(16\) full revolutions fit): \[ \frac{100\pi}{3} - 16\left(\frac{6\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{100\pi}{3}-\frac{96\pi}{3} = \frac{4\pi}{3} \] \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\) lies in \([0,2\pi)\). This angle is in Quadrant III with reference angle \(\frac{4\pi}{3}-\pi=\frac{\pi}{3}\), where sine is negative: \[ \sin\frac{4\pi}{3} = -\sin\frac{\pi}{3} = -\frac{\sqrt3}{2} \]
Final Answer: \(\sin\frac{100\pi}{3} = -\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\). The process works for any size angle because each subtraction of \(2\pi\) is one full revolution and therefore never changes the terminal point (Problem 6) — so no matter how many revolutions must be removed, the sine value of what's left is guaranteed to equal the sine value of the original angle.
💡 DESMOS CHECK
Typing sin(17pi/6), cos(11pi/4), and sin(100pi/3) directly into Desmos should return \(0.5\), \(\approx-0.7071\), and \(\approx-0.866\) respectively — matching \(\frac12\), \(-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\), and \(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\) decimally.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound — watch specifically for the signature error of reducing to an angle correctly but then reading the wrong exact value off the circle, or reducing by the wrong number of revolutions in Problem 7. Release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).

pages.html:
🔒 TEACHER ANSWER KEY — INTERNAL USE ONLY. Do not post, link, or share this page with students.

Trigonometric Functions
Lesson
Lesson 7-2
Keys To
Assignment 7-2 · Practice Set: Three Parameters, Three Jobs
Practice Set · Completion-Scored
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 7-2
Answer Key: Three Parameters, Three Jobs
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1
Fluency: State the amplitude, period, and midline of \(y=5\sin(4x)\).
SOLUTION
\(A=5\), \(B=4\), \(D=0\). \[ \text{Amplitude}=|A|=5, \qquad \text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{|B|}=\frac{2\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}, \qquad \text{Midline: } y=0 \]
Final Answer: Amplitude \(=5\); period \(=\frac{\pi}{2}\); midline \(y=0\).
PROBLEM 2
Fluency: State the amplitude, period, and midline of \(y=-2\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)+4\).
SOLUTION
\(A=-2\), \(B=\frac13\), \(D=4\). \[ \text{Amplitude}=|{-2}|=2, \qquad \text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{1/3}=6\pi, \qquad \text{Midline: } y=4 \]
Final Answer: Amplitude \(=2\); period \(=6\pi\); midline \(y=4\).
PROBLEM 3
Fluency with reflection: State the amplitude, period, and midline of \(y=-4\sin(x)+2\), and explain in one sentence what the negative sign in front of the \(4\) does to the graph's direction.
SOLUTION
\(A=-4\), \(B=1\), \(D=2\). \[ \text{Amplitude}=|{-4}|=4, \qquad \text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{1}=2\pi, \qquad \text{Midline: } y=2 \] The negative sign reflects the graph over its midline: where an unreflected sine curve rises from the midline as \(x\) increases from \(0\), this curve immediately falls instead.
Final Answer: Amplitude \(=4\); period \(=2\pi\); midline \(y=2\). The negative sign flips (reflects) the graph vertically over its midline, reversing its direction of travel.
PROBLEM 4
Build the equation: A sinusoidal graph has a maximum of \(9\), a minimum of \(3\), and a period of \(\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\). Assuming it is a sine function with no phase shift, find its equation.
SOLUTION
Midline is the average of max and min; amplitude is the distance from the midline to either extreme: \[ D=\frac{9+3}{2}=6, \qquad A=9-6=3 \] From the period: \(\dfrac{2\pi}{B}=\dfrac{2\pi}{5} \;\Rightarrow\; B=5\).
Final Answer: \(y=3\sin(5x)+6\)
PROBLEM 5
Table and range: Build a table of values for \(y=2\sin(2x)-1\) at \(x=0,\ \frac{\pi}{4},\ \frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{3\pi}{4},\ \pi\) (one full period), then state the graph's range.
SOLUTION
\(x\)\(0\)\(\frac{\pi}{4}\)\(\frac{\pi}{2}\)\(\frac{3\pi}{4}\)\(\pi\)
\(2x\)\(0\)\(\frac{\pi}{2}\)\(\pi\)\(\frac{3\pi}{2}\)\(2\pi\)
\(y=2\sin(2x)-1\)\(-1\)\(1\)\(-1\)\(-3\)\(-1\)
The amplitude is \(2\) and the midline is \(y=-1\), so the range runs from \(-1-2=-3\) up to \(-1+2=1\) — matching the extreme values in the table.
Final Answer: Table as above; range \(=[-3,1]\).
PROBLEM 6 — Explain why
In three or four sentences, explain why multiplying the input \(x\) by a number \(B>1\) before applying sine compresses the graph horizontally rather than stretching it. Use the period formula and a specific example (such as \(B=4\)) to justify your answer.
MODEL SOLUTION
The period of \(y=\sin(Bx)\) is \(\frac{2\pi}{B}\), and since \(B\) sits in the denominator, making \(B\) larger makes the period smaller — the graph must complete its entire cycle over a shorter stretch of the \(x\)-axis, which is exactly what a horizontal compression means. For example, with \(B=4\), the period becomes \(\frac{2\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}\), one-quarter of the parent sine's period of \(2\pi\): four full copies of the wave now fit in the space the parent used for just one. Multiplying \(x\) by \(4\) before evaluating sine makes every input "arrive" at a given output value four times sooner, which squeezes the whole graph inward rather than stretching it outward.
Final Answer: Because period \(=\frac{2\pi}{B}\), a larger \(B\) shortens the period, compressing the graph horizontally — e.g., \(B=4\) gives period \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), one-quarter of \(2\pi\).
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
A Ferris wheel has a diameter of \(40\) m, a hub \(22\) m above the ground, and completes one full revolution every \(8\) minutes. Modeling a rider's height above the ground \(y\) (in meters) as a function of time \(t\) (in minutes) with \(y=A\sin(Bt)+D\), find \(A\), \(B\), and \(D\), and write the complete equation.
SOLUTION
The wheel's radius (half its \(40\) m diameter) is the amplitude, since the rider swings this far above and below the center of the wheel: \(A=20\). The hub is the center of the wheel's circular path, so it is the midline height: \(D=22\). From the period (one revolution every \(8\) minutes): \[ \frac{2\pi}{B}=8 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; B=\frac{2\pi}{8}=\frac{\pi}{4} \]
Final Answer: \(A=20\), \(B=\frac{\pi}{4}\), \(D=22\); \(y=20\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}t\right)+22\).
💡 DESMOS CHECK
For Problem 4, graph y = 3 sin(5x) + 6 and trace to confirm a maximum of \(9\) and minimum of \(3\). For Problem 7, graph y = 20 sin(pi/4 x) + 22 and trace to confirm the height oscillates between \(2\) m and \(42\) m, with one full cycle completing every \(8\) units of \(t\).
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, a correctly labeled amplitude on every problem (reported as a positive number even where \(A\) itself is negative — Problem 3 is the check), and the Wave Machine whiteboard snapshot with its spatial-recording link included as a page in the PDF. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound. The most common miss in Problem 7 is swapping the hub height and the radius — confirm students used the diameter's half (\(20\)) as \(A\) and the hub height itself (\(22\)) as \(D\). Release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it.

Assignment 7-3 · Focus Set: Factor Before You Trust It
⭐ Focus Assignment · Method-Graded (2 problems)
Points
Assignment
16 pts
Lesson 7-3
Answer Key: Factor Before You Trust It
Full worked solutions for all 6 problems. Problems 3 and 4 carry gold-badged scoring guidance for the rubric — those are the only two problems graded for method; the rest are checked for honest completion.
PROBLEM 1 — Warmup
State the amplitude, period, and midline of \(y=4\cos(2x)-3\).
SOLUTION
\(A=4\), \(B=2\), \(D=-3\). \[ \text{Amplitude}=|4|=4, \qquad \text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{2}=\pi, \qquad \text{Midline: } y=-3 \]
Final Answer: Amplitude \(=4\); period \(=\pi\); midline \(y=-3\).
PROBLEM 2 — Warmup, factor first
State the amplitude, period, midline, and phase shift of \(y=\sin(4x-\pi)\). Show the factoring step.
SOLUTION
Factor \(B=4\) out of the argument: \[ 4x-\pi = 4\left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \] Check: \(4\left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=4x-\pi\). ✓ So \(A=1\), \(B=4\), \(D=0\), \(C=\frac{\pi}{4}\). \[ \text{Amplitude}=1, \qquad \text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}, \qquad \text{Midline: } y=0, \qquad \text{Phase shift}=\frac{\pi}{4}\ \text{(right, since \(C>0\))} \]
Final Answer: Amplitude \(=1\); period \(=\frac{\pi}{2}\); midline \(y=0\); phase shift \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) right.
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 3
The unprepared equation. Consider \(y=-5\cos(2\pi x+\pi)+7\). ① Factor the coefficient of \(x\) out of the argument, showing the step, and check your factoring by distributing it back out. ② State the amplitude, period, midline, and phase shift (with direction). ③ Verify by evaluating the function at \(x=C\) (the phase-shift point) and confirming the result is consistent with the sign of \(A\). ④ Explain why your verification produced a minimum rather than a maximum at that point, given the sign of \(A\).
SOLUTION
① Factor. The coefficient of \(x\) is \(2\pi\): \[ 2\pi x+\pi = 2\pi\left(x+\frac12\right) = 2\pi\left(x-\left(-\frac12\right)\right) \] Check by distributing back: \(2\pi\left(x-\left(-\frac12\right)\right)=2\pi x + 2\pi\left(\frac12\right)=2\pi x+\pi\). ✓ So \(A=-5\), \(B=2\pi\), \(D=7\), \(C=-\frac12\).

② State the features. \[ \text{Amplitude}=|{-5}|=5, \qquad \text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{2\pi}=1, \qquad \text{Midline: } y=7, \qquad \text{Phase shift}=-\frac12\ \text{(left, since \(C<0\))} \] ③ Verify at \(x=C=-\frac12\). The argument becomes \(2\pi\left(-\frac12-\left(-\frac12\right)\right)=2\pi(0)=0\): \[ y=-5\cos(0)+7 = -5(1)+7 = 2 \] Since the graph's range is \([D-|A|,\,D+|A|]=[7-5,\,7+5]=[2,12]\), the value \(y=2\) at this point is the graph's minimum — consistent with \(A\) being negative.

④ Why a minimum, not a maximum: the parent cosine reaches its maximum value of \(1\) wherever its argument equals \(0\). Here the argument is \(0\) at \(x=C\), so the parent cosine's output there is \(1\) — but the coefficient \(A=-5\) is negative, which reflects the entire graph over its midline, turning every parent maximum into a minimum (and vice versa). That is why evaluating at the phase-shift point produces \(D+A=7+(-5)=2\), the minimum, rather than \(D+|A|=12\), the maximum.
Final Answer: Amplitude \(=5\); period \(=1\); midline \(y=7\); phase shift \(\frac12\) left. Verification at \(x=-\frac12\) gives \(y=2\), the minimum, because \(A=-5\) reflects the parent cosine's maximum at the phase-shift point into a minimum.
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): the argument is factored correctly into \(2\pi\left(x+\frac12\right)\) (or equivalently \(x-\left(-\frac12\right)\)), the factoring is checked by distributing back out, and all four features (amplitude, period, midline, phase shift with direction) are correctly stated. (2): factoring attempted but the sign of \(C\) or the direction (left/right) is wrong. (0): the constant term \(\pi\) is read directly as the phase shift, with no factoring of \(B=2\pi\) attempted.

Reasoning (4): the verification substitution at \(x=C\) is actually performed (not merely asserted), and the explanation in part ④ correctly connects the negative \(A\) to a reflection of the parent cosine's maximum into a minimum. (2): the substitution is performed correctly but the explanation of why it's a minimum is vague or missing the reflection argument. (0): no real substitution shown, or the explanation misidentifies the cause.

Presentation & precision (4): the factoring step, the four stated features, and the verification are each clearly labeled and easy to follow in order; a reader could check the factoring without hunting for it. (2): organized with a minor labeling lapse. (0): scattered or illegible; the factoring step cannot be located.

Intellectual honesty (4): the check-by-distributing-back step is genuinely shown, not skipped or asserted; the explanation in part ④ is a real argument from the sign of \(A\), not a restated conclusion. (2): the distributing-back check is stated but not actually carried out. (0): the phase shift or verification appears reverse-engineered from an assumed correct answer.
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 4
The reverse direction. A sinusoidal graph, assumed cosine-shaped, has a maximum value of \(10\) at \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\), a minimum value of \(-2\), and completes one full cycle every \(\pi\) units. ① Find the midline and amplitude from the maximum and minimum. ② Find \(B\) from the period. ③ Find the phase shift \(C\), explaining why a cosine-shaped graph's maximum tells you \(C\) directly. ④ Write the complete equation and verify it by evaluating at \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\), confirming it reproduces the given maximum of \(10\).
SOLUTION
① Midline and amplitude. \[ D=\frac{10+(-2)}{2}=4, \qquad A=10-4=6 \] ② Find \(B\). Period \(=\pi\): \[ \frac{2\pi}{B}=\pi \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; B=2 \] ③ Find \(C\). A parent cosine graph reaches its maximum exactly where its argument \(B(x-C)\) equals \(0\), which happens precisely at \(x=C\). Since this graph's maximum is given directly at \(x=\frac{\pi}{3}\), that \(x\)-value is \(C\) — no secondary computation (such as locating a zero-crossing) is needed, because the maximum location and the phase-shift point coincide for a cosine-shaped graph: \[ C=\frac{\pi}{3} \] ④ Write and verify. \[ y=6\cos\left(2\left(x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right)+4 \] At \(x=\frac{\pi}{3}\): argument \(=2\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=2(0)=0\), so \[ y=6\cos(0)+4=6(1)+4=10 \] matching the given maximum of \(10\). ✓
Final Answer: \(y=6\cos\left(2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\right)+4\). Midline \(y=4\); amplitude \(6\); \(B=2\); phase shift \(C=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\). Verified: at \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\), \(y=10\).
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): midline and amplitude correctly computed from the average and half-difference of max/min; \(B\) correctly found from the period formula; \(C\) correctly identified as \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) directly from the given maximum's location. (2): midline/amplitude and \(B\) correct, but \(C\) is derived incorrectly (e.g., treated as needing a zero-crossing calculation) even though the final numeric value happens to be right, or a sign/direction error appears. (0): maximum and minimum swapped, or period formula inverted (\(B=\pi/2\pi\) or similar).

Reasoning (4): part ③'s explanation correctly reasons that a cosine-shaped graph's maximum occurs exactly where its argument is \(0\), which is why the maximum's \(x\)-location directly gives \(C\); the verification in part ④ is an actual substitution that reproduces \(10\). (2): the correct value of \(C\) is stated but the explanation of why the maximum reveals \(C\) directly is thin or missing. (0): \(C\) is asserted with no justification connecting it to the maximum's location.

Presentation & precision (4): all four steps (midline/amplitude, \(B\), \(C\), equation-and-verification) appear as distinct, clearly labeled steps; the final equation is boxed and the verification substitution is easy to follow. (2): organized with a labeling lapse. (0): scattered; the four steps cannot be distinguished.

Intellectual honesty (4): the verification substitution genuinely reproduces \(10\) as shown, not asserted; no step is skipped and reverse-fit to the known answer. (2): verification stated as true without showing the substitution. (0): the equation appears back-solved from the answer rather than built from the four steps.
PROBLEM 5
The AI cross-examination: Give your AI tutor the function \(y=3\sin(2x-\pi)+1\) with the instruction: “State the phase shift of this function, showing your work.” Copy the AI's response onto your page, then write your own verdict, verifying with your own factoring before you rule.
GRADING GUIDANCE (no single correct answer — the response is student-generated)
The correct, independently-derived answer to check the student's verdict against: factor \(B=2\) out of the argument first, \[ 2x-\pi = 2\left(x-\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \] so the true phase shift is \(C=\frac{\pi}{2}\) (a shift right). Note this is the exact identity used in this week's lesson's own AI Checkpoint example (\(y=\sin(2x-\pi)\)), where the documented AI error is reading the unfactored constant term (\(\pi\)) directly as the phase shift instead of dividing out \(B=2\) first — an answer of \(\pi\) instead of the correct \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), overstated by exactly a factor of \(B\).
There is no fixed "correct" AI response to check against — what is graded is the judging. Look for:
  • An actual AI response copied onto the page (not fabricated or trivial).
  • A verdict that engages the mathematics specifically: if the AI reports a phase shift of \(\pi\) (or otherwise skips factoring \(B\) out of the argument), the student should catch this and show the correct factored form and the true value \(\frac{\pi}{2}\); if the AI's response already factored correctly and reported \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), the student should confirm it independently by performing the same factoring step themselves and saying so.
  • Either outcome earns full credit: a sound correction of a bad AI claim, or a genuine independent confirmation of a correct one. What must not appear is a verdict that merely restates "the AI is right" or "the AI is wrong" without the student's own factoring step to back it up.
Final Answer: Grade for the quality of the judgment (was the argument actually factored by the student before ruling on the AI's claim?), not for which side of the argument the student lands on. Independently verified correct value: phase shift \(C=\frac{\pi}{2}\), right.
PROBLEM 6 — Honors stretch
Consider \(y=-2\sin\left(3\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)-1\). ① State its amplitude, period, midline, and phase shift (with direction), noting that this argument is already factored. ② Evaluate the function at \(x=-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) (the phase-shift point) and at \(x=0\) (one quarter-period later), showing full substitution work at each. ③ Explain why the value at \(x=-\frac{\pi}{6}\) is the midline rather than a maximum or minimum, given that the parent sine function is rising through its midline at that same point in its own cycle.
SOLUTION
① State the features. Writing \(3\left(x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=3\left(x-\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)\), so \(A=-2\), \(B=3\), \(D=-1\), \(C=-\frac{\pi}{6}\): \[ \text{Amplitude}=|{-2}|=2, \qquad \text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{3}, \qquad \text{Midline: } y=-1, \qquad \text{Phase shift}=-\frac{\pi}{6}\ \text{(left)} \] ② Evaluate. Quarter period \(=\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\), and \(-\frac{\pi}{6}+\frac{\pi}{6}=0\), confirming \(x=0\) is indeed one quarter-period after the phase-shift point.
At \(x=-\frac{\pi}{6}\): argument \(=3\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=3(0)=0\), so \(y=-2\sin(0)-1=-2(0)-1=-1\).
At \(x=0\): argument \(=3\left(0+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=3\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{\pi}{2}\), so \(y=-2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)-1=-2(1)-1=-3\).

③ Why the midline, not an extreme: for the parent sine function, an argument of \(0\) is always where the curve crosses its own midline while rising (\(\sin(0)=0\), and sine is increasing there) — extremes occur only where the argument is \(\pm\frac{\pi}{2}\), not \(0\). Since the argument is exactly \(0\) at \(x=-\frac{\pi}{6}\), that point is a midline-crossing regardless of \(A\)'s sign: \(A\) only controls whether the curve is rising or falling through the midline at that instant (here, negative \(A\) means the transformed graph is actually falling through \(y=-1\) as \(x\) increases, the reverse of the parent), never whether a midline-crossing occurs there in the first place.
Final Answer: Amplitude \(=2\); period \(=\frac{2\pi}{3}\); midline \(y=-1\); phase shift \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) left. \(y(-\frac{\pi}{6})=-1\) (midline); \(y(0)=-3\) (minimum, since negative \(A\) reflects the parent's rising quarter-point into a falling one). The value at the phase-shift point is the midline because an argument of \(0\) is always a midline-crossing for sine, never an extreme.
💡 DESMOS / EXCEL CHECK
For Problem 3, graphing y = -5cos(2πx+π)+7 and y = -5cos(2π(x+0.5))+7 on separate lines in Desmos should show the two curves sitting exactly on top of each other, with a minimum of \(2\) at \(x=-0.5\). For Problems 4 and 6, an Excel table with columns for \(x\), the argument \(B(x-C)\), and the resulting \(y\)-value at four or five chosen \(x\)-values should reproduce the hand-computed values at the verification points exactly.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Focus Assignment — 16 pts, method-graded on Problems 3 and 4 only)
Problems 1, 2, 5, and 6 are checked for honest, visible completion only — do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound, and release this key after the due date for self-correction. Problems 3 and 4, the two ⭐ method problems, carry the entire 16-point rubric (Understanding / Reasoning / Presentation & Precision / Intellectual Honesty, 4 pts each). Budget roughly 1–2 minutes per student for the two method problems, per the course's designated-problems-only grading model. The most common fatal error in Problem 3 is reading the constant term \(\pi\) directly off the unfactored argument as the phase shift instead of dividing \(B=2\pi\) out first; the most common fatal error in Problem 4 is swapping which given value (max vs. min) becomes the midline versus mistakenly averaging incorrectly, or computing \(C\) via a needless zero-crossing search instead of recognizing that a cosine-shaped maximum's \(x\)-location is \(C\).
