Practice Set · Completion-Scored
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 7-12
Answer Key: One Circle, Three Identities
Full worked solutions for all 6 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1 — From sine to all five
Given \(\sin\theta = -\dfrac{5}{13}\) with \(\theta\) in Quadrant IV, find \(\cos\theta\), \(\tan\theta\), \(\sec\theta\), \(\csc\theta\), and \(\cot\theta\).
SOLUTION
By the Pythagorean identity: \(\cos^2\theta = 1-\sin^2\theta = 1-\dfrac{25}{169} = \dfrac{144}{169}\), so \(\cos\theta = \pm\dfrac{12}{13}\). Quadrant IV has cosine positive, so \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{12}{13}\). \[ \tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{-5/13}{12/13} = -\dfrac{5}{12}, \qquad \sec\theta = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{13}{12}, \qquad \csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta} = -\dfrac{13}{5}, \qquad \cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta} = -\dfrac{12}{5} \] Check: \(\tan^2\theta+1 = \dfrac{25}{144}+1=\dfrac{169}{144}\), and \(\sec^2\theta = \left(\dfrac{13}{12}\right)^2=\dfrac{169}{144}\) — the companion identity holds.
Final Answer: \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{12}{13}\), \(\tan\theta=-\dfrac{5}{12}\), \(\sec\theta=\dfrac{13}{12}\), \(\csc\theta=-\dfrac{13}{5}\), \(\cot\theta=-\dfrac{12}{5}\).
PROBLEM 2 — From cosine to all five
Given \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{7}{25}\) with \(\theta\) in Quadrant I, find \(\sin\theta\), \(\tan\theta\), \(\sec\theta\), \(\csc\theta\), and \(\cot\theta\).
SOLUTION
By the Pythagorean identity: \(\sin^2\theta = 1-\cos^2\theta = 1-\dfrac{49}{625} = \dfrac{576}{625}\), so \(\sin\theta = \pm\dfrac{24}{25}\). Quadrant I has sine positive, so \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{24}{25}\). \[ \tan\theta = \dfrac{24/25}{7/25} = \dfrac{24}{7}, \qquad \sec\theta = \dfrac{1}{7/25} = \dfrac{25}{7}, \qquad \csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{24/25} = \dfrac{25}{24}, \qquad \cot\theta = \dfrac{7}{24} \] Check: \(\tan^2\theta+1 = \dfrac{576}{49}+1 = \dfrac{625}{49}\), and \(\sec^2\theta=\left(\dfrac{25}{7}\right)^2=\dfrac{625}{49}\) — matches.
Final Answer: \(\sin\theta=\dfrac{24}{25}\), \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{24}{7}\), \(\sec\theta=\dfrac{25}{7}\), \(\csc\theta=\dfrac{25}{24}\), \(\cot\theta=\dfrac{7}{24}\).
PROBLEM 3 — Simplify
Simplify \(\dfrac{\sec^2\theta-1}{\tan^2\theta}\) to a single number, showing which companion identity makes it possible.
SOLUTION
The companion identity \(\tan^2\theta+1=\sec^2\theta\), rearranged, states \(\sec^2\theta-1=\tan^2\theta\). Substitute directly into the numerator: \[ \dfrac{\sec^2\theta-1}{\tan^2\theta} = \dfrac{\tan^2\theta}{\tan^2\theta} = 1 \] This holds wherever both sides are defined (\(\cos\theta\ne0\) for \(\sec\theta,\tan\theta\) to exist, and \(\tan\theta\ne0\) so the denominator is not zero). Numeric check at \(\theta=50^\circ\): \(\sec^250^\circ-1\approx2.4203-1=1.4203\), and \(\tan^250^\circ\approx1.4203\) — the ratio is \(1\).
Final Answer: \(1\), using the companion identity \(\sec^2\theta-1=\tan^2\theta\).
PROBLEM 4 — Judge the claim
“\(\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta\) is only true when \(\theta\) is in Quadrant I — in the other quadrants you need a different identity.” Judge the claim and correct it if it is wrong.
SOLUTION
The claim is false. The identity \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\) comes directly from substituting the unit-circle point \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\) into \(x^2+y^2=1\); every angle's terminal side meets the unit circle at exactly one such point, in every quadrant, with no exception. Squaring a coordinate destroys its sign (a negative \(x\)- or \(y\)-coordinate squares to the same positive value a positive one would), so the identity never depended on which quadrant — and therefore which signs — \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) carried in the first place.

Counterexample outside Quadrant I: at \(\theta=210^\circ\) (Quadrant III), \(\cos210^\circ=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\) and \(\sin210^\circ=-\dfrac12\). Then \(\sin^2210^\circ=\dfrac14\) and \(1-\cos^2210^\circ = 1-\dfrac34=\dfrac14\) — they match, confirming the identity holds outside Quadrant I exactly as well as inside it.
Final Answer: The claim is false; \(\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta\) holds in every quadrant because squaring erases the sign of \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) (verified at \(\theta=210^\circ\): both sides \(=\tfrac14\)).
PROBLEM 5 — Explain why
The identity \(1+\cot^2\theta=\csc^2\theta\) fails at \(\theta=0\), \(\theta=\pi\), and every integer multiple of \(\pi\). Explain why, tracing the failure back to the specific division step used to derive it.
MODEL SOLUTION
The identity \(1+\cot^2\theta=\csc^2\theta\) was derived by dividing every term of \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\) through by \(\sin^2\theta\), a step that is only algebraically valid where \(\sin\theta\ne0\) (dividing by zero is undefined). At \(\theta=0,\pi,2\pi,\dots\) (every integer multiple of \(\pi\)), the terminal point on the unit circle sits exactly on the \(x\)-axis, where the \(y\)-coordinate — which is \(\sin\theta\) by definition — equals zero. At those exact angles, both \(\cot\theta=\cos\theta/\sin\theta\) and \(\csc\theta=1/\sin\theta\) are themselves undefined, since each has \(\sin\theta\) in its denominator. So the identity does not merely become false at these points; both of its sides simply fail to exist, which is exactly what the derivation's own division-by-\(\sin^2\theta\) step predicted would happen wherever \(\sin\theta=0\).
Final Answer: The identity was produced by dividing through by \(\sin^2\theta\), valid only where \(\sin\theta\ne0\); at \(\theta=k\pi\), \(\sin\theta=0\), so \(\cot\theta\) and \(\csc\theta\) are themselves undefined there — the domain gap traces directly to the derivation's own division step.
PROBLEM 6 — Honors stretch: from tangent alone
Given \(\tan\theta=2\) with \(\theta\) in Quadrant III, find all six trigonometric function values without a calculator, starting from \(\sec^2\theta=1+\tan^2\theta\).
SOLUTION
\[ \sec^2\theta = 1+\tan^2\theta = 1+2^2 = 5 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \sec\theta = \pm\sqrt5 \] Quadrant III has cosine negative, so \(\sec\theta=1/\cos\theta\) is also negative: \(\sec\theta = -\sqrt5\). \[ \cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sec\theta} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5} = -\dfrac{\sqrt5}{5} \] Since \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = 2\), \(\sin\theta = 2\cos\theta = 2\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt5}{5}\right) = -\dfrac{2\sqrt5}{5}\). Both \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) are negative, consistent with Quadrant III. \[ \csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta} = \dfrac{1}{-2\sqrt5/5} = -\dfrac{5}{2\sqrt5} = -\dfrac{\sqrt5}{2}, \qquad \cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta} = \dfrac{1}{2} \] Check (Pythagorean identity): \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta = \dfrac{20}{25}+\dfrac{5}{25} = \dfrac{25}{25}=1\) ✓. Check (companion): \(1+\cot^2\theta = 1+\dfrac14=\dfrac54\), and \(\csc^2\theta=\left(\dfrac{\sqrt5}{2}\right)^2=\dfrac54\) — matches.
Final Answer: \(\sin\theta=-\dfrac{2\sqrt5}{5}\), \(\cos\theta=-\dfrac{\sqrt5}{5}\), \(\tan\theta=2\), \(\cot\theta=\dfrac12\), \(\sec\theta=-\sqrt5\), \(\csc\theta=-\dfrac{\sqrt5}{2}\).
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the calculator should show)
For problems 1, 2, and 6, find \(\theta\) itself in Desmos with arcsin(, arccos(, or arctan(, adjusted into the correct quadrant, then evaluate the remaining functions directly at that angle. For problem 6, \(\theta\approx180^\circ+63.43^\circ\approx243.43^\circ\) (Quadrant III, reference angle \(\arctan2\approx63.43^\circ\)); typing sin(243.43°) should return \(\approx-0.894\), matching \(-2\sqrt5/5\approx-0.8944\).
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 6 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound — watch specifically for the signature error of choosing the wrong sign after taking a square root (forgetting to consult the quadrant before fixing the sign of \(\cos\theta\), \(\sin\theta\), or \(\sec\theta\)). Release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).

Practice Set · Completion-Scored
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 7-13
Answer Key: One Side at a Time
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1
Simplify: \(\cos\theta\tan\theta\).
SOLUTION
Convert to sine and cosine first. Since \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\): \[ \cos\theta\tan\theta = \cos\theta\cdot\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \sin\theta \] The \(\cos\theta\) factors cancel — legal here because this is a single expression being simplified, not an equation or identity with two sides.
Final Answer: \(\sin\theta\)
PROBLEM 2
Verify: \(\sec x\sin x = \tan x\).
SOLUTION
Transform the left side only. Convert \(\sec x\) to cosine: \[ \sec x\sin x = \frac{1}{\cos x}\cdot\sin x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} = \tan x \] The left side now reads exactly as the right side — verified. The right side was never touched.
Final Answer: Verified: \(\sec x\sin x = \tan x\).
PROBLEM 3
Verify: \(\dfrac{1-\sin^2x}{\cos x}=\cos x\) (assume \(\cos x\ne0\)).
SOLUTION
Transform the left side only. By the Pythagorean identity, \(1-\sin^2x=\cos^2x\): \[ \frac{1-\sin^2x}{\cos x} = \frac{\cos^2x}{\cos x} = \cos x \] The left side now matches the right side exactly — verified, right side untouched.
Final Answer: Verified: \(\dfrac{1-\sin^2x}{\cos x}=\cos x\).
PROBLEM 4
Simplify to a single term: \(\csc x - \sin x\).
SOLUTION
Convert to sine first, then combine over a common denominator: \[ \csc x-\sin x = \frac{1}{\sin x}-\sin x = \frac{1-\sin^2x}{\sin x} \] By the Pythagorean identity, \(1-\sin^2x=\cos^2x\): \[ = \frac{\cos^2x}{\sin x} = \cos x\cdot\frac{\cos x}{\sin x} = \cos x\cot x \] Check at \(x=30^\circ\): \(\csc30^\circ-\sin30^\circ = 2-0.5=1.5\). \(\cos30^\circ\cot30^\circ = (0.8660)(1.7321)\approx1.5\). Matches.
Final Answer: \(\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\sin x}\), equivalently \(\cos x\cot x\).
PROBLEM 5 — Judge the claim
A classmate says, “You can prove any identity by squaring both sides and showing the results are equal.” Judge this claim. Is it a valid proof method? Connect your answer to the lesson's AI checkpoint.
SOLUTION
The claim is false. Squaring both sides operates on both sides of an equation whose equality has not yet been established — exactly the "operate on both sides of an unproven claim" fallacy the lesson's AI checkpoint exposed (begging the question). Reaching a true statement after squaring does not show the original, unsquared identity was true.

Counterexample that exposes the method: consider the false claim \(\sin x = -\sin x\) (true only at \(x=0,\pi,\dots\), false in general — e.g., at \(x=30^\circ\), \(0.5\ne-0.5\)). Squaring both sides gives \(\sin^2x=\sin^2x\), which is true for every \(x\). The squaring method would "verify" this false identity, because squaring erases the sign difference between an expression and its negative — two expressions can have equal squares while being genuinely unequal. That is precisely why the method is invalid: it cannot distinguish a true identity from one that is only true up to a sign.
Final Answer: The claim is false. Squaring both sides is another form of operating on both sides of an unproven equation, and it can "verify" false identities whenever the two sides are negatives of each other (e.g., \(\sin x=-\sin x\)).
PROBLEM 6 — Explain why
In three or four sentences, explain why a valid identity proof may only transform one side of the page, and connect that rule to this unit's virtue of self-government.
MODEL SOLUTION
A valid identity proof may transform only one side because touching both sides of an unproven equation quietly assumes the two sides are already equal — the very thing the proof was supposed to establish, and exactly the fallacy the AI checkpoint's cross-multiplication committed. Restricting the work to one side, and rewriting it with only already-established identities and legal algebra until it becomes the untouched other side, is the only method that actually demonstrates equality rather than merely producing some true statement from an assumed premise. That restraint is self-government made visible inside an algebra step: the discipline to refuse the shortcut that would make the proof easier but would secretly beg the question, even when no one is watching to catch it.
Final Answer: Touching both sides assumes the equality being proved; transforming one side alone actually demonstrates it — the self-governed refusal of an easier but circular shortcut.
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
Verify \((\sin x+\cos x)^2 = 1+2\sin x\cos x\) by expanding the left side and applying the Pythagorean identity. Then, without proof, state what you notice \(2\sin x\cos x\) looks like it might be related to — you will meet the exact identity in the next lesson.
SOLUTION
Transform the left side only. Expand the square: \[ (\sin x+\cos x)^2 = \sin^2x+2\sin x\cos x+\cos^2x = (\sin^2x+\cos^2x)+2\sin x\cos x \] By the Pythagorean identity, \(\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1\): \[ = 1+2\sin x\cos x \] The left side now matches the right side exactly — verified, right side untouched. Check at \(x=30^\circ\): left side \(=(\sin30^\circ+\cos30^\circ)^2=(0.5+0.8660)^2=(1.3660)^2\approx1.8660\); right side \(=1+2(0.5)(0.8660)=1+0.8660=1.8660\). Matches.

What \(2\sin x\cos x\) resembles: the expression \(2\sin x\cos x\) — two, times sine, times cosine, of the same angle — has exactly the shape of a doubled product, which looks like it could be an entire trigonometric function of \(2x\) in disguise, the same way this lesson turned \(\sin\theta\cot\theta\) into a single named function. (Lesson 7-16 proves \(\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta\) directly.)
Final Answer: Verified: \((\sin x+\cos x)^2=1+2\sin x\cos x\). \(2\sin x\cos x\) appears to be a single trigonometric function of \(2x\) in disguise — the double-angle sine, formalized in Lesson 7-16.
💡 DESMOS CHECK
For Problem 2, graphing y = sec(x)sin(x) and y = tan(x) together should show the two curves sitting exactly on top of each other everywhere both are defined, with matching gaps at \(x=\frac{\pi}{2}+k\pi\). For Problem 7, graphing y = (sin(x)+cos(x))^2 and y = 1+2sin(x)cos(x) together should coincide everywhere, and also coincide with y = 1+sin(2x) — a preview of next lesson's double-angle identity.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound — watch specifically for the signature error this lesson targets: performing the same operation on both sides of an unproven identity (cross-multiplying, squaring both sides) rather than transforming one side alone. Release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).

pages.html:
🔒 TEACHER ANSWER KEY — INTERNAL USE ONLY. Do not post, link, or share this page with students.

Quarter / Unit

Trigonometric Functions
Lesson
Lesson 7-14
Keys To
Assignment 7-14 · Focus Set: Proof and Exact Value
⭐ Focus Assignment · Method-Graded (2 problems)
Points
Assignment
16 pts
Lesson 7-14
Answer Key: Proof and Exact Value
Full worked solutions for all 6 problems. Problems 3 and 4 carry gold-badged scoring guidance for the rubric — those are the only two problems graded for method; the rest are checked for honest completion.
PROBLEM 1 — Warmup
Find the exact value of \(\cos75^\circ\), writing \(75^\circ=45^\circ+30^\circ\), and verify your answer against a decimal approximation.
SOLUTION
\[ \cos75^\circ = \cos(45^\circ+30^\circ) = \cos45^\circ\cos30^\circ-\sin45^\circ\sin30^\circ \] \[ = \left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)\!\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)-\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)\!\left(\frac12\right) = \frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4} \] Verify: \(\dfrac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}\approx\dfrac{2.4495-1.4142}{4}\approx\dfrac{1.0353}{4}\approx0.2588\), matching a calculator's \(\cos75^\circ\approx0.2588\).
Final Answer: \(\cos75^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}\approx0.2588\).
PROBLEM 2 — Warmup
Using the sum formula for sine, verify that \(\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x\). State the values of \(\sin\pi\) and \(\cos\pi\) you used.
SOLUTION
\[ \sin(x+\pi) = \sin x\cos\pi+\cos x\sin\pi \] Using \(\cos\pi=-1\) and \(\sin\pi=0\): \[ = \sin x(-1)+\cos x(0) = -\sin x \] The left side now matches the right side exactly — verified.
Final Answer: Verified using \(\cos\pi=-1\), \(\sin\pi=0\): \(\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x\).
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 3
Prove that \(\sin(\alpha-\beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta-\cos\alpha\sin\beta\) for all angles \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), starting from the boxed cosine-difference formula and the cofunction relationships \(\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\sin\theta\) and \(\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\cos\theta\). State your starting facts, carry out the substitution one line at a time, confirm the final line matches the claimed formula, and verify numerically at a chosen pair of angles.
SOLUTION
① State the starting facts. We may use, as already established: the cosine-difference formula \(\cos(\alpha-\beta)=\cos\alpha\cos\beta+\sin\alpha\sin\beta\); the cofunction facts \(\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\sin\theta\) and \(\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\cos\theta\) for every \(\theta\); and the even/odd facts \(\cos(-x)=\cos x\), \(\sin(-x)=-\sin x\), both direct consequences of the unit circle. Nothing about \(\sin(\alpha-\beta)\) itself is assumed anywhere below.

② Rewrite \(\sin(\alpha-\beta)\) using the cofunction fact. Since \(\sin\theta=\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)\) for every \(\theta\), set \(\theta=\alpha-\beta\): \[ \sin(\alpha-\beta) = \cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-(\alpha-\beta)\right) = \cos\!\left(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\alpha\right)+\beta\right) \] ③ Turn the sum into a difference. Let \(A=\frac{\pi}{2}-\alpha\), so the right side is \(\cos(A+\beta)=\cos(A-(-\beta))\). Apply the cosine-difference formula with angles \(A\) and \(-\beta\): \[ \cos(A-(-\beta)) = \cos A\cos(-\beta)+\sin A\sin(-\beta) \] Using \(\cos(-\beta)=\cos\beta\) and \(\sin(-\beta)=-\sin\beta\): \[ = \cos A\cos\beta - \sin A\sin\beta \] ④ Substitute the cofunction values of \(A\). Since \(A=\frac{\pi}{2}-\alpha\): \(\cos A = \cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\alpha\right)=\sin\alpha\), and \(\sin A=\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\alpha\right)=\cos\alpha\): \[ \cos A\cos\beta-\sin A\sin\beta = \sin\alpha\cos\beta-\cos\alpha\sin\beta \] ⑤ Confirm the final line. Tracing back: \(\sin(\alpha-\beta) = \cos\!\left(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\alpha\right)+\beta\right) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta-\cos\alpha\sin\beta\), exactly the claimed formula. QED — no step assumed the result being proved; every substitution traced back to the boxed cosine-difference formula and the two cofunction facts.

⑥ Verify numerically at \(\alpha=50^\circ\), \(\beta=20^\circ\) (neither \(0^\circ\) nor \(90^\circ\)). Left side: \(\sin(30^\circ)=0.5\). Right side, computed independently: \(\sin50^\circ\cos20^\circ-\cos50^\circ\sin20^\circ \approx (0.7660)(0.9397)-(0.6428)(0.3420) \approx 0.7198-0.2198 = 0.5000\). Both sides agree.
Final Answer: Proved: \(\sin(\alpha-\beta)=\sin\alpha\cos\beta-\cos\alpha\sin\beta\), derived entirely from the cosine-difference formula and the cofunction facts. Verified numerically at \(\alpha=50^\circ,\beta=20^\circ\): both sides \(=0.5\).
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): the student correctly rewrites \(\sin(\alpha-\beta)\) as \(\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-(\alpha-\beta)\right)\), correctly restructures the resulting sum as a difference to apply the given formula, and correctly substitutes the cofunction values of \(A=\frac{\pi}{2}-\alpha\). (2): the general strategy is right but one substitution (e.g., the even/odd step, or which cofunction value goes where) is mishandled. (0): the student simply restates the sine-difference formula as already known, or assumes \(\sin(\alpha-\beta)\) to derive itself.

Reasoning (4): every line follows from a fact stated in step 1 or a line already derived; no step assumes the sine-difference formula being proved; the numeric verification computes both sides independently rather than by construction. (2): the chain of substitution is mostly sound but one link is asserted without justification (e.g., the cofunction values used without stating why). (0): the "proof" is circular, or no real derivation chain is shown.

Presentation & precision (4): starting facts declared before use, each substitution on its own labeled line, the final line explicitly matched against the claimed formula. (2): organized with a labeling or alignment lapse. (0): scattered; the chain from starting facts to final formula cannot be followed.

Intellectual honesty (4): the numeric verification is a genuine independent computation of both sides (not reverse-engineered to match); any uncertainty about a step is named rather than glossed over. (2): numeric check present but one side is computed by assuming the formula already holds rather than independently. (0): numeric verification is fabricated or omitted while claimed as done.
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 4
Find the exact value of \(\sin105^\circ\): decompose \(105^\circ\) as a sum of two known angles, apply the sum formula, simplify completely, verify numerically, and state what you notice about how the answer compares to \(\cos15^\circ\).
SOLUTION
① Decompose: \(105^\circ = 60^\circ+45^\circ\), two angles the unit circle knows exactly.

② Apply the sum formula for sine: \[ \sin105^\circ=\sin(60^\circ+45^\circ)=\sin60^\circ\cos45^\circ+\cos60^\circ\sin45^\circ \] \[ = \left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\!\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)+\left(\frac12\right)\!\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right) = \frac{\sqrt6}{4}+\frac{\sqrt2}{4} \] ③ Simplify: \[ \sin105^\circ = \frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4} \] The denominator is already rational; no further simplification is possible.

④ Verify numerically: \(\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\approx\dfrac{2.4495+1.4142}{4}\approx\dfrac{3.8637}{4}\approx0.9659\), matching a calculator's \(\sin105^\circ\approx0.9659\).

⑤ Comparison to \(\cos15^\circ\): Lesson 7-14's Example 2 found \(\cos15^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\) — the identical value. This is not a coincidence: \(\sin105^\circ=\cos(90^\circ-105^\circ)=\cos(-15^\circ)=\cos15^\circ\) by the cofunction relationship together with the fact that cosine is even, so the two expressions were guaranteed to match before any arithmetic was done.
Final Answer: \(\sin105^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\approx0.9659\), equal to \(\cos15^\circ\) by the cofunction relationship (not coincidence).
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): the decomposition uses two angles with known exact values, the sum formula for sine is applied correctly with no sign errors, and the exact value is fully simplified. (2): decomposition and formula correct but the final simplification is left incomplete (e.g., unrationalized or uncombined fraction). (0): wrong formula applied (e.g., cosine sum formula used for a sine problem) or an invalid decomposition (angles without known exact values).

Reasoning (4): the numeric verification is an honest independent decimal computation compared against a calculator value, and the closing comparison to \(\cos15^\circ\) is explained by the cofunction relationship (not just noted as a curiosity). (2): numeric check performed but the \(\cos15^\circ\) comparison is stated without the cofunction explanation. (0): no real numeric verification, or the comparison sentence is absent.

Presentation & precision (4): each of the five requested steps (decompose / apply / simplify / verify / compare) is clearly labeled and shown in order; the exact value is boxed and fully reduced. (2): organized with a lapse in labeling one step. (0): steps merged or missing; the reader cannot tell decomposition from simplification.

Intellectual honesty (4): the decimal comparison in step 3 is performed before, not after, checking against Lesson 7-14's \(\cos15^\circ\) value, so the "not a coincidence" claim is actually earned rather than asserted. (2): correct final answer, but the honesty of the coincidence claim is unclear (asserted with no supporting cofunction argument). (0): the comparison step is fabricated or skipped while claimed as complete.
PROBLEM 5
The AI cross-examination: give your Problem 4 work to an AI tutor, ask it to check the exact-value computation, copy its response, and render your own verdict.
GRADING GUIDANCE (no single correct answer — the response is student-generated)
There is no fixed "correct" AI response to check against — what is graded is the judging. Look for:
  • An actual AI response copied onto the page (two or three sentences), not fabricated or trivial.
  • A verdict that engages the mathematics specifically — if the AI flags a real error (a wrong decomposition, a sign slip in applying the sum formula, an unsimplified radical), the student should show the fix using the numeric comparison already built in Problem 4; if the AI's check is itself wrong (e.g., it claims \(105^\circ=60^\circ+45^\circ\) requires a different sign pattern, or miscomputes the decimal comparison), the student should refute it by recomputing the decimal check independently.
  • Either outcome earns full credit: a sound refutation of a bad AI claim, or a genuine correction if the AI catches something real. What must not appear is a verdict that merely restates "the AI is right" or "the AI is wrong" without re-checking the specific claim against the decimal comparison from Problem 4.
Final Answer: Grade for the quality of the judgment (was every claim actually verified against the decimal comparison before ruling?), not for which side of the argument the student lands on.
PROBLEM 6 — Honors stretch
Find the exact value of \(\cos105^\circ\) two different ways: (a) as \(\cos(60^\circ+45^\circ)\); and (b) as \(\cos(180^\circ-75^\circ)\), first proving in one line that \(\cos(180^\circ-\theta)=-\cos\theta\), then applying it to \(\cos75^\circ\). Confirm both methods agree.
SOLUTION
Method (a) — direct sum formula: \[ \cos105^\circ = \cos(60^\circ+45^\circ) = \cos60^\circ\cos45^\circ-\sin60^\circ\sin45^\circ = \left(\frac12\right)\!\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)-\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\!\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right) = \frac{\sqrt2-\sqrt6}{4} \]
Method (b) — via \(\cos(180^\circ-\theta)=-\cos\theta\): prove this one-line identity the same way the lesson handled \(\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x\): \[ \cos(180^\circ-\theta) = \cos180^\circ\cos\theta+\sin180^\circ\sin\theta = (-1)\cos\theta+(0)\sin\theta = -\cos\theta \] Apply it with \(\theta=75^\circ\): \(\cos105^\circ=\cos(180^\circ-75^\circ)=-\cos75^\circ\). From Problem 1, \(\cos75^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}\), so: \[ \cos105^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4} = \frac{\sqrt2-\sqrt6}{4} \] Confirm agreement: both methods give \(\dfrac{\sqrt2-\sqrt6}{4}\), identically. Numerically, \(\dfrac{1.4142-2.4495}{4}\approx\dfrac{-1.0353}{4}\approx-0.2588\), matching a calculator's \(\cos105^\circ\approx-0.2588\).
Final Answer: \(\cos105^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt2-\sqrt6}{4}\approx-0.2588\) by both methods.
💡 DESMOS CHECK
Typing sin(105 deg) and cos(105 deg) directly into Desmos should return \(\approx0.9659\) and \(\approx-0.2588\), confirming Problems 4 and 6. The match confirms the algebra; it does not replace the hand derivation, which is what earns the credit on the two method problems.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Focus Assignment — 16 pts, method-graded on Problems 3 and 4 only)
Problems 1, 2, 5, and 6 are checked for honest, visible completion only — do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound, and release this key after the due date for self-correction. Problems 3 and 4, the two ⭐ method problems, carry the entire 16-point rubric (Understanding / Reasoning / Presentation & Precision / Intellectual Honesty, 4 pts each), applied holistically across both problems together. Budget roughly 1–2 minutes per student for the two method problems, per the course's designated-problems-only grading model. The most common fatal error in Problem 3 is treating the sine-difference formula as already known instead of deriving it strictly from the cosine-difference formula and cofunction facts; the most common fatal error in Problem 4 is a sign slip in the sum formula (writing \(\sin60^\circ\cos45^\circ-\cos60^\circ\sin45^\circ\) instead of \(+\)), which silently turns \(\sin105^\circ\) into \(\sin15^\circ\)'s value instead.

Lesson 7-15
Answer Key: Exact Values and Cofunctions
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1
Find the exact value of \(\cos105^\circ\), writing \(105^\circ = 60^\circ + 45^\circ\), and verify it numerically.
SOLUTION
\[ \cos105^\circ=\cos(60^\circ+45^\circ)=\cos60^\circ\cos45^\circ-\sin60^\circ\sin45^\circ \] \[ = \left(\frac12\right)\!\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)-\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\!\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right) = \frac{\sqrt2}{4}-\frac{\sqrt6}{4} = \frac{\sqrt2-\sqrt6}{4} \] Verify: \(\dfrac{\sqrt2-\sqrt6}{4}\approx\dfrac{1.4142-2.4495}{4}\approx\dfrac{-1.0353}{4}\approx-0.2588\), matching a calculator's \(\cos105^\circ\approx-0.2588\).
Final Answer: \(\cos105^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt2-\sqrt6}{4}\approx-0.2588\).
PROBLEM 2
Find the exact value of \(\tan15^\circ\), writing \(15^\circ = 45^\circ - 30^\circ\), and verify it numerically.
SOLUTION
\[ \tan15^\circ = \frac{\tan45^\circ-\tan30^\circ}{1+\tan45^\circ\tan30^\circ} = \frac{1-\frac{1}{\sqrt3}}{1+\frac{1}{\sqrt3}} = \frac{\sqrt3-1}{\sqrt3+1} \] Rationalize by multiplying by \(\dfrac{\sqrt3-1}{\sqrt3-1}\): \[ = \frac{(\sqrt3-1)^2}{(\sqrt3+1)(\sqrt3-1)} = \frac{3-2\sqrt3+1}{3-1} = \frac{4-2\sqrt3}{2} = 2-\sqrt3 \] Verify: \(2-\sqrt3\approx2-1.7321\approx0.2679\), matching a calculator's \(\tan15^\circ\approx0.2679\).
Final Answer: \(\tan15^\circ = 2-\sqrt3\approx0.2679\).
PROBLEM 3
Verify: \(\sin(\alpha+\beta)\sin(\alpha-\beta) = \sin^2\alpha-\sin^2\beta\).
SOLUTION
Transform the left side alone. Expand both factors, then multiply as a difference of squares: \[ \sin(\alpha+\beta)\sin(\alpha-\beta) = (\sin\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\sin\beta)(\sin\alpha\cos\beta-\cos\alpha\sin\beta) = \sin^2\alpha\cos^2\beta-\cos^2\alpha\sin^2\beta \] Replace \(\cos^2\beta=1-\sin^2\beta\) and \(\cos^2\alpha=1-\sin^2\alpha\) (Pythagorean identity), then expand and cancel: \[ = \sin^2\alpha(1-\sin^2\beta)-(1-\sin^2\alpha)\sin^2\beta = \sin^2\alpha-\sin^2\alpha\sin^2\beta-\sin^2\beta+\sin^2\alpha\sin^2\beta = \sin^2\alpha-\sin^2\beta \] The two \(\sin^2\alpha\sin^2\beta\) terms cancel exactly, leaving the right side untouched throughout. Check at \(\alpha=50^\circ,\beta=20^\circ\): left side \(=\sin70^\circ\sin30^\circ\approx(0.9397)(0.5)\approx0.4699\); right side \(=\sin^250^\circ-\sin^220^\circ\approx(0.7660)^2-(0.3420)^2\approx0.5868-0.1170\approx0.4698\). Matches.
Final Answer: Verified: \(\sin(\alpha+\beta)\sin(\alpha-\beta)=\sin^2\alpha-\sin^2\beta\).
PROBLEM 4 — Cofunction
Simplify \(\dfrac{\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)}{\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)}\) to a single named function, showing the cofunction substitutions you used.
SOLUTION
By the cofunction identities, \(\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)=\cos x\) and \(\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)=\sin x\): \[ \frac{\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)}{\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)} = \frac{\cos x}{\sin x} = \cot x \]
Final Answer: \(\cot x\)
PROBLEM 5 — Judge the claim
A classmate says, “The cofunction identities mean sine and cosine are really the same function.” Judge this claim, correct it if it is wrong, and state precisely what a cofunction identity actually relates.
SOLUTION
The claim is false. A cofunction identity does not say sine and cosine give the same value at the same angle — it relates a function's value at an angle \(\theta\) to its cofunction's value at the complementary angle \(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\): \(\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\cos\theta\), not \(\sin\theta=\cos\theta\).

Counterexample: at \(\theta=30^\circ\), \(\sin30^\circ=0.5\) but \(\cos30^\circ\approx0.8660\) — clearly different values, so sine and cosine are not "the same function." What is true is that \(\sin60^\circ=\cos30^\circ\approx0.8660\) (\(60^\circ\) and \(30^\circ\) being complementary), which is the correct cofunction relationship the classmate is misremembering.
Final Answer: The claim is false. A cofunction identity relates a function's value at \(\theta\) to its cofunction's value at the complementary angle \(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\), not to the same function at the same angle.
PROBLEM 6 — Explain why
In three or four sentences, explain why every cofunction identity pairs sine with cosine, tangent with cotangent, and secant with cosecant — and never any other combination — arguing from a right triangle's two complementary acute angles.
MODEL SOLUTION
In a right triangle, the two acute angles \(\theta\) and \(90^\circ-\theta\) are complementary, and each acute angle's "opposite" side is the other angle's "adjacent" side — the two legs simply trade roles depending on which angle you stand at. Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, and cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse; since \(\theta\)'s opposite leg is \((90^\circ-\theta)\)'s adjacent leg, \(\theta\)'s sine is exactly \((90^\circ-\theta)\)'s cosine, using the same two sides relabeled. The same swap happens for tangent (opposite over adjacent) and cotangent (adjacent over opposite), and for secant (hypotenuse over adjacent) and cosecant (hypotenuse over opposite), because each of those pairs is built from precisely the two legs that exchange roles between the complementary angles. No other pairing is possible, because no other two functions are built from that same pair of sides in reversed order — sine and tangent, for instance, use different side-ratios entirely, so swapping the angle does not turn one into the other.
Final Answer: Complementary acute angles swap "opposite" and "adjacent"; each cofunction pair uses exactly the same two sides in reversed roles, and no other pair of functions shares that same side-ratio structure.
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
Verify \(\cos(\alpha+\beta)\cos(\alpha-\beta)=\cos^2\alpha-\sin^2\beta\). Then verify it a second way, numerically, at two different pairs of angles of your own choosing, and state whether both checks agree with your algebraic proof.
SOLUTION
Transform the left side alone. Expand both factors, then multiply as a difference of squares: \[ \cos(\alpha+\beta)\cos(\alpha-\beta) = (\cos\alpha\cos\beta-\sin\alpha\sin\beta)(\cos\alpha\cos\beta+\sin\alpha\sin\beta) = \cos^2\alpha\cos^2\beta-\sin^2\alpha\sin^2\beta \] Replace \(\cos^2\beta=1-\sin^2\beta\) and \(\sin^2\alpha=1-\cos^2\alpha\) (Pythagorean identity): \[ = \cos^2\alpha(1-\sin^2\beta)-(1-\cos^2\alpha)\sin^2\beta = \cos^2\alpha-\cos^2\alpha\sin^2\beta-\sin^2\beta+\cos^2\alpha\sin^2\beta = \cos^2\alpha-\sin^2\beta \] The two \(\cos^2\alpha\sin^2\beta\) terms cancel exactly, leaving the right side untouched — verified algebraically.

Numeric check 1 at \(\alpha=50^\circ,\beta=20^\circ\): left side \(=\cos70^\circ\cos30^\circ\approx(0.3420)(0.8660)\approx0.2962\); right side \(=\cos^250^\circ-\sin^220^\circ\approx(0.6428)^2-(0.3420)^2\approx0.4132-0.1170\approx0.2962\). Matches.

Numeric check 2 at \(\alpha=40^\circ,\beta=25^\circ\): left side \(=\cos65^\circ\cos15^\circ\approx(0.4226)(0.9659)\approx0.4081\); right side \(=\cos^240^\circ-\sin^225^\circ\approx(0.7660)^2-(0.4226)^2\approx0.5868-0.1786\approx0.4082\). Matches (agreeing to rounding).
Final Answer: Verified algebraically; both independent numeric checks (\(\alpha=50^\circ,\beta=20^\circ\) and \(\alpha=40^\circ,\beta=25^\circ\)) agree with the algebraic proof.
💡 DESMOS CHECK
Problems 1 and 2 confirm decimally with cos(105 deg) and tan(15 deg) typed directly into Desmos. For Problem 3 or 7, graphing both sides as two functions of \(\alpha\) (holding \(\beta\) fixed, e.g. \(\beta=20^\circ\)) should show the curves sitting exactly on top of each other for every \(\alpha\).
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound — watch specifically for the signature cofunction error: assuming a sign flip where none exists (e.g., writing \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=-\cos\theta\)), or crossing the pairing (matching sine with tangent instead of cosine). Release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).

10 pts
Lesson 7-16
Answer Key: One Substitution Away
Full worked solutions for all 6 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1 — Full set from a ratio
Given \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{5}{13}\) with \(\theta\) in Quadrant IV, find \(\sin2\theta\), \(\cos2\theta\), and \(\tan2\theta\). Verify your \(\cos2\theta\) using at least two of its three equivalent forms.
SOLUTION
In Quadrant IV, cosine is positive and sine is negative. With \(\cos\theta=\frac{5}{13}\), the reference triangle is the \(5\text{-}12\text{-}13\) right triangle, so \(\sin\theta=-\dfrac{12}{13}\). \[ \sin2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = 2\!\left(-\frac{12}{13}\right)\!\left(\frac{5}{13}\right) = -\frac{120}{169} \] For \(\cos2\theta\), the form \(2\cos^2\theta-1\) is fastest since \(\cos\theta\) is already known: \[ \cos2\theta = 2\!\left(\frac{5}{13}\right)^{\!2}-1 = \frac{50}{169}-\frac{169}{169} = -\frac{119}{169} \] Verify with the other two forms: \(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta=\dfrac{25}{169}-\dfrac{144}{169}=-\dfrac{119}{169}\) ✓; and \(1-2\sin^2\theta=1-\dfrac{288}{169}=-\dfrac{119}{169}\) ✓. All three forms agree. \[ \tan2\theta = \frac{\sin2\theta}{\cos2\theta} = \frac{-120/169}{-119/169} = \frac{120}{119} \] Reasonableness check: \(\theta\) in QIV with \(\cos\theta=\frac{5}{13}\approx0.385\) puts \(\theta\approx292.6^\circ\), so \(2\theta\approx585.2^\circ\equiv225.2^\circ\), which lands in Quadrant III — where both sine and cosine are negative, exactly matching the signs found above.
Final Answer: \(\sin2\theta=-\dfrac{120}{169}\), \(\cos2\theta=-\dfrac{119}{169}\), \(\tan2\theta=\dfrac{120}{119}\).
PROBLEM 2 — Exact-value callback
Use the double-angle formula for cosine, together with \(\sin15^\circ\) and \(\cos15^\circ\) from Lessons 7-14/7-15, to compute \(\cos30^\circ\). Confirm your answer matches the familiar unit-circle value.
SOLUTION
\[ \cos30^\circ = \cos(2\cdot15^\circ) = \cos^215^\circ-\sin^215^\circ \] Using \(\cos15^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\) and \(\sin15^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}\), squared exactly: \[ \cos^215^\circ = \frac{(\sqrt6+\sqrt2)^2}{16} = \frac{6+2\sqrt{12}+2}{16} = \frac{8+4\sqrt3}{16} = \frac{2+\sqrt3}{4}, \qquad \sin^215^\circ = \frac{(\sqrt6-\sqrt2)^2}{16} = \frac{8-4\sqrt3}{16} = \frac{2-\sqrt3}{4} \] \[ \cos^215^\circ-\sin^215^\circ = \frac{(2+\sqrt3)-(2-\sqrt3)}{4} = \frac{2\sqrt3}{4} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2} \] Decimal check: \(\cos15^\circ\approx0.9659\), \(\sin15^\circ\approx0.2588\); \((0.9659)^2-(0.2588)^2\approx0.9330-0.0670\approx0.8660\), which equals \(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\approx0.8660\).
Final Answer: \(\cos30^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\) — exactly the familiar unit-circle value, reached by an entirely different road.
PROBLEM 3 — Solve
Solve \(\sin2\theta=\sin\theta\) on \([0,2\pi)\). List every solution and verify each one.
SOLUTION
\[ 2\sin\theta\cos\theta-\sin\theta=0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \sin\theta(2\cos\theta-1)=0 \] So either \(\sin\theta=0\), giving \(\theta=0,\ \pi\); or \(\cos\theta=\dfrac12\), giving \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\).

Verify each:
\(\theta=0\): \(\sin0=0\) and \(\sin0=0\) — equal. ✓
\(\theta=\pi\): \(\sin2\pi=0\) and \(\sin\pi=0\) — equal. ✓
\(\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}\): \(\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\approx0.8660\) and \(\sin\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\approx0.8660\) — equal. ✓
\(\theta=\frac{5\pi}{3}\): \(\sin\frac{10\pi}{3}=\sin\frac{4\pi}{3}=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\approx-0.8660\) and \(\sin\frac{5\pi}{3}=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\approx-0.8660\) — equal. ✓
Final Answer: \(\theta \in \left\{0,\ \dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pi,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right\}\).
PROBLEM 4 — Judge the claim
A classmate says, “\(\sin2\theta\) always equals \(2\sin\theta\).” Judge this claim, and prove it false or true with a specific numeric counterexample or confirmation.
SOLUTION
The claim is false. The correct identity is \(\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta\) — the claim drops the necessary \(\cos\theta\) factor, treating the "\(2\)" as though it distributes into the function linearly.

Counterexample at \(\theta=30^\circ\): true value \(\sin60^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\approx0.8660\); claimed value \(2\sin30^\circ=2(0.5)=1.0\). Since \(0.8660\ne1.0\), the claim fails.
Final Answer: False. \(\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta\), not \(2\sin\theta\); at \(\theta=30^\circ\), \(\sin60^\circ\approx0.8660\ne1.0=2\sin30^\circ\).
PROBLEM 5 — Explain why
In three or four sentences, explain why setting \(\beta=\alpha\) in an already-proven sum formula produces a new, equally valid identity — rather than a coincidence that happens to work for this one substitution.
MODEL SOLUTION
The sum formula \(\sin(\alpha+\beta)=\sin\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\sin\beta\) was proved for every pair of angles \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) independently, with no restriction on how they relate to each other. Because a universally true statement remains true for any particular substitution of its variables, it must in particular remain true for the special case where \(\beta\) happens to equal \(\alpha\) — the same way "for all \(x\), \(x+0=x\)" being true guarantees \(5+0=5\) without a fresh proof. Setting \(\beta=\alpha\) introduces no new unproven assumption; it is simply evaluating an already-established universal fact at one specific pair of inputs. A coincidence, by contrast, would be an unexplained numerical pattern with no logical guarantee behind it — and that is exactly what this substitution is not.
Final Answer: The sum formula holds for all \(\alpha,\beta\); a universally true statement must hold for the special case \(\beta=\alpha\) too, so no new proof — and no coincidence — is needed.
PROBLEM 6 — Honors stretch
Derive the triple-angle formula \(\cos3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\) by writing \(\cos3\theta=\cos(2\theta+\theta)\) and applying the sum formula and the double-angle formulas for cosine. Verify your derived formula numerically at \(\theta=30^\circ\).
SOLUTION
Write \(\cos3\theta=\cos(2\theta+\theta)\) and apply the cosine sum formula: \[ \cos3\theta = \cos2\theta\cos\theta-\sin2\theta\sin\theta \] Substitute \(\cos2\theta=2\cos^2\theta-1\) and \(\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta\): \[ = (2\cos^2\theta-1)\cos\theta - (2\sin\theta\cos\theta)\sin\theta = 2\cos^3\theta-\cos\theta-2\sin^2\theta\cos\theta \] Replace \(\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta\) (Pythagorean identity): \[ = 2\cos^3\theta-\cos\theta-2\cos\theta(1-\cos^2\theta) = 2\cos^3\theta-\cos\theta-2\cos\theta+2\cos^3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta \] Verify at \(\theta=30^\circ\): left side \(\cos90^\circ=0\). Right side: \(4\cos^330^\circ-3\cos30^\circ = 4(0.8660)^3-3(0.8660) \approx 4(0.6495)-2.5981 \approx 2.5981-2.5981 = 0\). Both sides equal \(0\).
Final Answer: \(\cos3\theta=4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\), derived from the sum formula and double-angle formulas alone; verified at \(\theta=30^\circ\), both sides \(=0\).
💡 DESMOS CHECK
For Problem 3, graphing y = sin(2x) and y = sin(x) together on \([0,2\pi]\) in Desmos should show intersections exactly at \(x=0,\frac{\pi}{3},\pi,\frac{5\pi}{3}\), matching the algebraic solution set. For Problem 6, graphing y = cos(3x) and y = 4cos(x)^3-3cos(x) together should show the two curves sitting exactly on top of each other everywhere.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 6 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound — watch specifically for the signature error this lesson targets: writing \(\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\) (dropping the \(\cos\theta\) factor), or picking a valid but slower form of \(\cos2\theta\) than the ratio given actually supports (not itself an error, but worth a note if the reference triangle step is skipped entirely). Release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty). This set is good rehearsal for the Unit 7 test next week.

Answer Key: Halving an Angle Honestly
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems, for grading and self-correction release. Every half-angle sign below is verified by locating the quadrant of the half-angle itself, never the original angle.
PROBLEM 1
Exact values from a half-angle: using \(105^\circ = \dfrac{210^\circ}{2}\), find the exact values of \(\sin105^\circ\) and \(\cos105^\circ\) with half-angle formulas. State the quadrant of \(105^\circ\) before choosing either sign.
SOLUTION
Quadrant first: \(105^\circ\) lies between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\) — Quadrant II, where sine is positive and cosine is negative.

\(\cos210^\circ = \cos(180^\circ+30^\circ) = -\cos30^\circ = -\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\). \[ \sin105^\circ = \sqrt{\dfrac{1-\cos210^\circ}{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2+\sqrt3}{4}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2+\sqrt3}}{2} \] (QII sine positive, so the \(+\) root is correct.) \[ \cos105^\circ = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{1+\cos210^\circ}{2}} = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{2}} = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{2-\sqrt3}{4}} = \pm\dfrac{\sqrt{2-\sqrt3}}{2} \] QII cosine negative, so \(\cos105^\circ = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2-\sqrt3}}{2}\).

Cross-check against the sum formula: \(\sin105^\circ=\sin(60^\circ+45^\circ)=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\approx0.9659\), and \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2+\sqrt3}}{2}\approx0.9659\) — the two forms agree.
Final Answer: \(\sin105^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{2+\sqrt3}}{2}\approx0.9659\); \(\cos105^\circ = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2-\sqrt3}}{2}\approx-0.2588\).
PROBLEM 2
Sign selection from a ratio: given \(\cos\alpha = \dfrac{3}{5}\) with \(\alpha\) in Quadrant IV, find the exact values of \(\sin\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}\right)\), \(\cos\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}\right)\), and \(\tan\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}\right)\). State the quadrant of \(\alpha/2\) explicitly, and check \(\tan(\alpha/2)\) against the sign-free formula.
SOLUTION
Locate \(\alpha/2\) first. Quadrant IV means \(270^\circ<\alpha<360^\circ\); halving every part of the inequality gives \(135^\circ<\dfrac{\alpha}{2}<180^\circ\) — Quadrant II, where sine is positive and cosine is negative.

\[ \sin\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}\right) = \sqrt{\dfrac{1-\cos\alpha}{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1-\frac35}{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2/5}{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac15} = \dfrac{\sqrt5}{5} \] (QII sine positive — the \(+\) root stands.) \[ \cos\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}\right) = -\sqrt{\dfrac{1+\cos\alpha}{2}} = -\sqrt{\dfrac{1+\frac35}{2}} = -\sqrt{\dfrac{8/5}{2}} = -\sqrt{\dfrac45} = -\dfrac{2\sqrt5}{5} \] (QII cosine negative — the \(-\) root is forced.)

Sign-free check: since \(\alpha\) is in QIV, \(\sin\alpha=-\dfrac45\) (from \(\sin^2\alpha=1-\frac{9}{25}=\frac{16}{25}\), negative in QIV). \[ \tan\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\sin\alpha}{1+\cos\alpha} = \dfrac{-4/5}{1+3/5} = \dfrac{-4/5}{8/5} = -\dfrac12 \] This matches \(\dfrac{\sin(\alpha/2)}{\cos(\alpha/2)} = \dfrac{\sqrt5/5}{-2\sqrt5/5}=-\dfrac12\) exactly.
Final Answer: \(\sin(\alpha/2)=\dfrac{\sqrt5}{5}\), \(\cos(\alpha/2)=-\dfrac{2\sqrt5}{5}\), \(\tan(\alpha/2)=-\dfrac12\).
PROBLEM 3
Reduction formula, simplify: rewrite \(6\cos^2x - 3\) as a single first-power expression in \(\cos2x\). Verify at \(x=30^\circ\).
SOLUTION
\[ 6\cos^2x-3 = 6\left(\dfrac{1+\cos2x}{2}\right)-3 = 3(1+\cos2x)-3 = 3+3\cos2x-3 = 3\cos2x \] Verify at \(x=30^\circ\): left side \(=6\cos^230^\circ-3 = 6\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)^2-3 = 6\left(\frac34\right)-3=4.5-3=1.5\). Right side \(=3\cos60^\circ=3(0.5)=1.5\). ✓
Final Answer: \(6\cos^2x-3 = 3\cos2x\).
PROBLEM 4
Reduction formula, exact value: find the exact value of \(\cos^2112.5^\circ\) using a reduction formula (note \(112.5^\circ = \dfrac{225^\circ}{2}\)).
SOLUTION
\(\cos225^\circ = \cos(180^\circ+45^\circ) = -\cos45^\circ = -\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\). \[ \cos^2112.5^\circ = \dfrac{1+\cos225^\circ}{2} = \dfrac{1-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}{2} = \dfrac{2-\sqrt2}{4} \] Numeric check: \(\cos112.5^\circ\approx-0.3827\), and \((-0.3827)^2\approx0.1464\); \(\dfrac{2-\sqrt2}{4}\approx\dfrac{0.5858}{4}\approx0.1464\). ✓
Final Answer: \(\cos^2112.5^\circ = \dfrac{2-\sqrt2}{4}\approx0.1464\).
PROBLEM 5 — Explain why
In two or three sentences, explain why the tangent half-angle formula \(\tan(\alpha/2) = \dfrac{\sin\alpha}{1+\cos\alpha}\) never requires a quadrant check, while the sine and cosine half-angle formulas both do.
MODEL SOLUTION
The sine and cosine half-angle formulas are built from a square root, and a principal square root can only report a nonnegative number — so a separate decision has to be made about whether the true value of \(\sin(\alpha/2)\) or \(\cos(\alpha/2)\) is actually positive or negative, which requires locating the quadrant of \(\alpha/2\) itself. The tangent half-angle formula, by contrast, is a plain ratio with no square root anywhere: its numerator \(\sin\alpha\) already carries whatever sign it needs, and its denominator \(1+\cos\alpha\) is never negative (since \(\cos\alpha\ge-1\) always). With the denominator's sign fixed and the numerator's sign already known from \(\alpha\) itself, the ratio's sign falls out automatically — there is nothing left to un-square, and so nothing left to decide by quadrant.
Final Answer: Sine/cosine half-angle formulas involve an un-squared root, requiring a quadrant-based sign decision; the tangent half-angle formula is a sign-carrying ratio (numerator already signed, denominator always nonnegative), so no quadrant check is ever needed.
PROBLEM 6
Judge the claim: a classmate claims, “Since \(\cos150^\circ\) is negative, \(\cos75^\circ=\cos(150^\circ/2)\) must also be negative.” Judge the claim, correct it if it is wrong, and compute the correct exact value of \(\cos75^\circ\).
SOLUTION
The claim is false. A half-angle's sign is decided by the quadrant of the half-angle itself, not the quadrant of the original angle. \(75^\circ\) lies between \(0^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\) — Quadrant I — where cosine is positive. The fact that \(150^\circ\) sits in Quadrant II (cosine negative) is irrelevant to the sign of \(\cos75^\circ\); the classmate reused the wrong angle's quadrant. \[ \cos75^\circ = \sqrt{\dfrac{1+\cos150^\circ}{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2-\sqrt3}{4}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2-\sqrt3}}{2} \] Positive, as the Quadrant I check requires: \(\cos75^\circ\approx0.2588>0\).
Final Answer: Claim false — \(75^\circ\) is in Quadrant I, so \(\cos75^\circ\) is positive: \(\cos75^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt{2-\sqrt3}}{2}\approx0.2588\).
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
Derive a reduction formula for \(\sin^4x\): ① write \(\sin^4x=(\sin^2x)^2\) and substitute the reduction formula for \(\sin^2x\). ② expand and reduce the resulting \(\cos^22x\) term a second time. ③ simplify to \(a+b\cos2x+c\cos4x\). ④ verify numerically at \(x=30^\circ\).
SOLUTION
① \(\sin^4x=(\sin^2x)^2 = \left(\dfrac{1-\cos2x}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1-2\cos2x+\cos^22x}{4}\).

② Reduce \(\cos^22x\) with the same reduction formula, applied to the angle \(2x\): \(\cos^22x = \dfrac{1+\cos4x}{2}\). Substitute: \[ \sin^4x = \dfrac{1-2\cos2x+\dfrac{1+\cos4x}{2}}{4} = \dfrac{\dfrac{2-4\cos2x+1+\cos4x}{2}}{4} = \dfrac{3-4\cos2x+\cos4x}{8} \] ③ Simplified: \[ \sin^4x = \dfrac38 - \dfrac12\cos2x + \dfrac18\cos4x \] ④ Verify at \(x=30^\circ\): directly, \(\sin^430^\circ = (0.5)^4=0.0625\). By the formula: \(\dfrac38-\dfrac12\cos60^\circ+\dfrac18\cos120^\circ = 0.375-0.5(0.5)+0.125(-0.5)=0.375-0.25-0.0625=0.0625\). ✓ The two independent computations agree exactly.
Final Answer: \(\sin^4x = \dfrac38-\dfrac12\cos2x+\dfrac18\cos4x\); verified numerically at \(x=30^\circ\) (both computations give \(0.0625\)).
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
Typing cos(105) should confirm problem 1's decimal value. For problem 7, graphing y = sin(x)^4 and y = 3/8 - (1/2)cos(2x) + (1/8)cos(4x) together should show the two curves sitting exactly on top of each other everywhere.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound. Watch specifically for the signature error this lesson targets: choosing a half-angle's sign from the quadrant of the original angle instead of the quadrant of the half-angle itself (the exact trap problem 6 is designed to expose) — this is a method error, not a slip, and should be flagged even though the set is completion-scored, since the worked key released after the due date is precisely how students self-correct it. Release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).

Quarter / Unit
Q3 · Unit 7
Trigonometric Functions
Lesson
Lesson 7-18
Keys To
Assignment 7-18 · Practice Set: Choosing from the Toolbox
Practice Set · Completion-Scored
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 7-18
Answer Key: Choosing from the Toolbox
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems, for grading and self-correction release. Every simplification and proof below shows the complete strategic path — which identity family was chosen, and why — not only the final line.
PROBLEM 1
Pythagorean combination: simplify \(\dfrac{1}{1+\sin\theta} + \dfrac{1}{1-\sin\theta}\) to a single trigonometric function, squared. Verify at \(\theta=30^\circ\).
SOLUTION
Strategy: a common denominator turns the sum into a single fraction whose denominator is a difference of squares — exactly the shape the Pythagorean identity resolves. \[ \dfrac{1}{1+\sin\theta}+\dfrac{1}{1-\sin\theta} = \dfrac{(1-\sin\theta)+(1+\sin\theta)}{(1+\sin\theta)(1-\sin\theta)} = \dfrac{2}{1-\sin^2\theta} \] By the Pythagorean identity, \(1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta\): \[ = \dfrac{2}{\cos^2\theta} = 2\sec^2\theta \] Verify at \(\theta=30^\circ\): left side \(=\dfrac{1}{1.5}+\dfrac{1}{0.5}=0.6\overline{6}+2=2.6\overline{6}\). Right side \(=2\sec^230^\circ = \dfrac{2}{(\sqrt3/2)^2}=\dfrac{2}{0.75}=2.6\overline{6}\). ✓
Final Answer: \(\dfrac{1}{1+\sin\theta}+\dfrac{1}{1-\sin\theta} = 2\sec^2\theta\).
PROBLEM 2
Disciplined proof: prove \(\dfrac{\sin\theta}{1-\cos\theta} = \dfrac{1+\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\), working from the left side only, naming the identity that does the work.
SOLUTION
Strategy: the right side's denominator is \(\sin\theta\) (first power), while the left side's is \(1-\cos\theta\). Multiplying the left side by a form of \(1\) built from the conjugate \((1+\cos\theta)\) will turn \(1-\cos\theta\) into \(1-\cos^2\theta\), which the Pythagorean identity converts to \(\sin^2\theta\). \[ \dfrac{\sin\theta}{1-\cos\theta}\cdot\dfrac{1+\cos\theta}{1+\cos\theta} = \dfrac{\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)}{1-\cos^2\theta} \] By the Pythagorean identity, \(1-\cos^2\theta=\sin^2\theta\): \[ = \dfrac{\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)}{\sin^2\theta} = \dfrac{1+\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} \] This is exactly the right side. \(\blacksquare\)
Final Answer: Proved by multiplying the left side by \(\frac{1+\cos\theta}{1+\cos\theta}\) and applying the Pythagorean identity \(1-\cos^2\theta=\sin^2\theta\); the left side reduces exactly to the right side.
PROBLEM 3
Double-angle simplification: simplify \(\dfrac{\sin4x}{2\cos2x}\) to a single trigonometric function.
SOLUTION
Strategy: \(4x\) is double \(2x\), so the double-angle formula applies directly with \(2x\) playing the role of the base angle: \(\sin(2\cdot2x)=2\sin2x\cos2x\). \[ \sin4x = 2\sin2x\cos2x \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \dfrac{\sin4x}{2\cos2x} = \dfrac{2\sin2x\cos2x}{2\cos2x} = \sin2x \quad(\cos2x\ne0) \] Verify at \(x=20^\circ\): left side \(=\dfrac{\sin80^\circ}{2\cos40^\circ}=\dfrac{0.9848}{2(0.7660)}=\dfrac{0.9848}{1.5321}\approx0.6428\). Right side \(=\sin40^\circ\approx0.6428\). ✓
Final Answer: \(\dfrac{\sin4x}{2\cos2x} = \sin2x\).
PROBLEM 4
Pattern recognition: evaluate \(\sin75^\circ\cos15^\circ + \cos75^\circ\sin15^\circ\) exactly — without computing \(\sin75^\circ\), \(\cos15^\circ\), \(\sin15^\circ\), or \(\cos75^\circ\) individually.
SOLUTION
Strategy: the expression's shape — \(\sin A\cos B+\cos A\sin B\) — is exactly the expanded sum formula for \(\sin(A+B)\), with \(A=75^\circ\), \(B=15^\circ\). Recognize the pattern before computing anything. \[ \sin75^\circ\cos15^\circ+\cos75^\circ\sin15^\circ = \sin(75^\circ+15^\circ) = \sin90^\circ = 1 \]
Final Answer: \(1\).
PROBLEM 5 — Explain why
Using problem 4 as your example, explain in two or three sentences why recognizing a sum-formula pattern is more efficient than computing each individual value.
MODEL SOLUTION
Computing \(\sin75^\circ\), \(\cos15^\circ\), \(\sin15^\circ\), and \(\cos75^\circ\) individually would require four separate half-angle or sum-formula derivations, each producing an irrational radical value, before those four radicals could even be multiplied and added together. Recognizing that the whole expression is already the expanded right side of \(\sin(A+B)=\sin A\cos B+\cos A\sin B\) collapses all of that work into a single substitution — \(A=75^\circ\), \(B=15^\circ\) — followed by one clean special-angle evaluation, \(\sin90^\circ=1\). The pattern is the whole solution; computing the four pieces separately would have been correct but needlessly slow.
Final Answer: Recognizing the sum-formula pattern replaces four separate radical evaluations with one direct substitution and a single special-angle lookup.
PROBLEM 6
Judge the argument: a classmate “proves” \(\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x\) with one line: “By the Pythagorean identity, \(\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1\), so \(\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x\). Done.” Is this establishing something new, or merely restating an already-known identity in rearranged form? Give one example of a genuinely nontrivial identity from this unit.
MODEL SOLUTION
This is not establishing anything new. \(\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x\) is simply the Pythagorean identity \(\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1\) with \(\cos^2x\) subtracted from both sides — one line of algebra performed on an equation that was already true. No new relationship between the trigonometric functions was proved; the classmate isolated a variable in a statement already established.

A genuinely nontrivial identity, by contrast, is the sum formula itself, \(\cos(A+B)=\cos A\cos B-\sin A\sin B\): it cannot be produced by rearranging the Pythagorean identity's algebra. It requires its own independent geometric argument (a rotation or a distance computation on the unit circle) connecting the trigonometric functions of two separate angles to the functions of their sum — genuinely new information the Pythagorean identity alone could never supply. The double-angle identity \(\cos2\theta=\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta\), which this unit's test derives from that sum formula, is nontrivial for the same reason: it required substituting into an independently-proved formula, not merely rearranging a single equation.
Final Answer: The claim is a rearrangement, not a proof of anything new. A genuinely nontrivial identity: the sum formula \(\cos(A+B)=\cos A\cos B-\sin A\sin B\) (or any double-angle formula derived from it), since these connect two angles' functions to a third in a way algebra on the Pythagorean identity alone cannot produce.
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch: a disciplined proof
Prove \(\dfrac{\cos\theta}{1+\sin\theta} = \sec\theta - \tan\theta\). Work from the left side, multiplying by a form of \(1\) built from the conjugate \((1-\sin\theta)\), and name the Pythagorean substitution. Verify numerically at \(\theta=40^\circ\).
SOLUTION
\[ \dfrac{\cos\theta}{1+\sin\theta}\cdot\dfrac{1-\sin\theta}{1-\sin\theta} = \dfrac{\cos\theta(1-\sin\theta)}{1-\sin^2\theta} \] By the Pythagorean identity, \(1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta\): \[ = \dfrac{\cos\theta(1-\sin\theta)}{\cos^2\theta} = \dfrac{1-\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}-\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \sec\theta-\tan\theta \] This is exactly the right side. \(\blacksquare\)

Verify at \(\theta=40^\circ\): left side \(=\dfrac{\cos40^\circ}{1+\sin40^\circ}=\dfrac{0.7660}{1.6428}\approx0.4663\). Right side \(=\sec40^\circ-\tan40^\circ = \dfrac{1}{0.7660}-\dfrac{0.6428}{0.7660}\approx1.3054-0.8391\approx0.4663\). ✓
Final Answer: Proved by multiplying by \(\frac{1-\sin\theta}{1-\sin\theta}\) and applying \(1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta\); verified numerically at \(\theta=40^\circ\) (both sides \(\approx0.4663\)).
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
For problems 1, 2, 3, and 7, graphing both sides of the identity as separate functions in Desmos should show the curves sitting exactly on top of each other everywhere both are defined — for example, y = cos(x)/(1+sin(x)) alongside y = 1/cos(x) - tan(x) for problem 7.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound. Watch specifically for two signature errors this lesson targets: on problem 4, computing the four individual values instead of recognizing the sum-formula pattern (correct, but defeats the point of the problem — flag it as a missed objective even though full credit stands for completion); and on problems 2 and 7, working from both sides of the equation at once (multiplying across the equals sign) rather than transforming the left side alone into the right — a habit this unit is actively trying to break. Release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).

⭐ Focus Assignment · Method-Graded (2 problems)
Points
Assignment
16 pts
Lesson 7-19
Answer Key: When the Model Hides the Equation
Full worked solutions for all 6 problems. Problems 3 and 4 carry gold-badged scoring guidance for the rubric — those are the only two problems graded for method; the rest are checked for honest completion. Every equation below was re-solved independently and every solution checked against the original, undisguised model.
PROBLEM 1 — Warmup
Solve \(\cos2\theta = \cos\theta\) for \(\theta\in[0,2\pi)\), naming the identity substitution you use.
SOLUTION
Substitute the double-angle identity \(\cos2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta-1\): \[ 2\cos^2\theta-1 = \cos\theta \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; 2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta-1=0 \] Let \(x=\cos\theta\): \(2x^2-x-1=0 \;\Rightarrow\; (2x+1)(x-1)=0 \;\Rightarrow\; x=-\dfrac12\) or \(x=1\).

\(\cos\theta=1 \Rightarrow \theta=0\). \(\cos\theta=-\dfrac12 \Rightarrow \theta=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}\).

Check each against the original equation: \(\theta=0\): \(\cos0=1=\cos0\). ✓ \(\theta=\frac{2\pi}{3}\): \(\cos\frac{4\pi}{3}=-\frac12=\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}\). ✓ \(\theta=\frac{4\pi}{3}\): \(\cos\frac{8\pi}{3}=\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}=-\frac12=\cos\frac{4\pi}{3}\). ✓
Final Answer: \(\theta = 0,\ \dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3}\).
PROBLEM 2 — Warmup
Find the exact value of \(\cos^2105^\circ\) using a reduction formula (note \(105^\circ = \dfrac{210^\circ}{2}\)).
SOLUTION
\(\cos210^\circ = \cos(180^\circ+30^\circ) = -\cos30^\circ = -\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\). \[ \cos^2105^\circ = \dfrac{1+\cos210^\circ}{2} = \dfrac{1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{2} = \dfrac{2-\sqrt3}{4} \] Numeric check: \(\cos105^\circ\approx-0.2588\), squared \(\approx0.0670\); \(\dfrac{2-\sqrt3}{4}\approx0.0670\). ✓
Final Answer: \(\cos^2105^\circ = \dfrac{2-\sqrt3}{4}\approx0.0670\).
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 3
The tide report: \(d(t) = 5 + \cos^2\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{12}\right) - \sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{12}\right)\), \(t\in[0,24)\). Reduce the model, state amplitude/midline/period, solve \(d(t)=5.5\), and close with physical reasonableness.
SOLUTION
① Reduce the model. Let \(x=\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\). The double-angle identity \(\cos2x=\cos^2x-\sin^2x\) applies directly to \(\cos^2x-\sin^2x\), with \(2x=\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\): \[ d(t) = 5+\cos^2x-\sin^2x = 5+\cos2x = 5+\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right) \] ② Amplitude/midline/period. Amplitude \(=1\), midline \(d=5\). Period \(=\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=12\) hours. Since \(24\div12=2\), the model completes exactly two full cycles per day — consistent with a harbor experiencing two high tides and two low tides every \(24\) hours (a real semidiurnal tide pattern).

③ Solve \(d(t)=5.5\): \[ 5+\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)=5.5 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)=0.5 \] Let \(u=\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\). The general solution to \(\cos u=\dfrac12\) is \(u=\dfrac{\pi}{3}+2\pi k\) or \(u=-\dfrac{\pi}{3}+2\pi k\) (equivalently \(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}+2\pi k\)), \(k\) an integer. Converting back with \(t=\dfrac{6u}{\pi}\): \[ t = 6\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)+12k = 2+12k \qquad\text{or}\qquad t = 6\left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right)+12k = 10+12k \] Restricting to \(t\in[0,24)\): \(k=0\) gives \(t=2,10\); \(k=1\) gives \(t=14,22\). \[ t = 2,\ 10,\ 14,\ 22 \text{ hours} \] ④ Physical reasonableness. The model's minimum is \(d=4\) (at \(t=6,18\)) and maximum \(d=6\) (at \(t=0,12\)). The four crossing times split into two matched pairs twelve hours apart: \(t=2\) and \(t=14\) both occur while the depth is falling from a high tide toward the next low tide, and \(t=10\) and \(t=22\) both occur while the depth is rising toward the next high tide. That is exactly the physically sensible pattern — one crossing on the way down, one on the way up, each half-day — that a real, repeating tide should produce.
Final Answer: Reduced model \(d(t)=5+\cos(\pi t/6)\); amplitude \(1\), midline \(d=5\), period \(12\) hr. Depth equals \(5.5\) m at \(t=2, 10, 14, 22\) hours — two rising crossings, two falling crossings, matching a real tide.
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): the double-angle identity \(\cos2x=\cos^2x-\sin^2x\) is named and applied correctly to reduce the model, and the resulting equation \(\cos(\pi t/6)=0.5\) is solved completely and correctly. (2): the reduction is correct but the equation-solving stalls or misses a family of solutions. (0): the model is never actually reduced (student works directly with \(\cos^2\) and \(\sin^2\) terms throughout, or the identity chosen does not match the expression's shape).

Reasoning (4): the general-solution reasoning (\(u=\frac{\pi}{3}+2\pi k\) or \(u=-\frac{\pi}{3}+2\pi k\)) is shown explicitly before restricting to \([0,24)\), and the reasonableness sentence genuinely engages the two rising/falling pairs. (2): the four correct times are found but by pattern-matching against a graph rather than showing the general-solution algebra, or the reasonableness check is generic. (0): times are asserted without derivation.

Presentation & precision (4): the reduction, the amplitude/midline/period statement, the equation-solving, and the four times are each clearly labeled and organized in the order the problem asks; units (hours, meters) carried throughout. (2): organized with a labeling or unit lapse. (0): scattered; the four steps cannot be told apart.

Intellectual honesty (4): the reasonableness sentence is a genuine check against the model's own minimum/maximum, not a rote closing line. (2): reasonableness sentence present but generic ("this seems right"). (0): no reasonableness check, or the pairing claim is asserted without checking whether the depth is actually rising or falling at each time.
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 4
The Ferris wheel inspection: \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi t}{9}\), \(0\le\theta<2\pi\). Find every instant where \(\cos2\theta+\sin\theta=0\), convert to time, and verify one solution against the original equation.
SOLUTION
① Reduce the equation. Substitute the double-angle identity \(\cos2\theta = 1-2\sin^2\theta\): \[ 1-2\sin^2\theta+\sin\theta = 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; -2\sin^2\theta+\sin\theta+1=0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; 2\sin^2\theta-\sin\theta-1=0 \] ② Solve, showing the factoring. Let \(x=\sin\theta\): \[ 2x^2-x-1=0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; (2x+1)(x-1)=0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; x=-\dfrac12 \text{ or } x=1 \] \(\sin\theta=1 \Rightarrow \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\). \(\sin\theta=-\dfrac12 \Rightarrow \theta=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}, \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\) (reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\), sine negative in QIII and QIV). \[ \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6} \] ③ Convert to time using \(t=\dfrac{9\theta}{\pi}\): \[ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}: \; t=\dfrac{9(\pi/2)}{\pi}=4.5 \text{ min} \qquad \theta=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}: \; t=\dfrac{9(7\pi/6)}{\pi}=10.5 \text{ min} \qquad \theta=\dfrac{11\pi}{6}: \; t=\dfrac{9(11\pi/6)}{\pi}=16.5 \text{ min} \] ④ Verify against the original equation (not the reduced form) at \(t=4.5\) min (\(\theta=\pi/2\)): \[ \cos2\theta+\sin\theta = \cos\pi+\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = -1+1 = 0 \;\;\checkmark \] (As a further cross-check, \(t=10.5\) min, \(\theta=7\pi/6\): \(\cos\frac{7\pi}{3}+\sin\frac{7\pi}{6}=\cos\frac{\pi}{3}+\left(-\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=0.5-0.5=0\) — also confirmed.)
Final Answer: \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\), corresponding to \(t=4.5,\ 10.5,\ 16.5\) minutes into the ride. Verified against the original, undisguised equation.
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): the double-angle identity \(\cos2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta\) is correctly chosen and substituted (this is the version of the identity the equation's shape calls for, since it leaves everything in terms of \(\sin\theta\)), and all three \(\theta\)-solutions on \([0,2\pi)\) are found. (2): a different, valid double-angle form is used but not carried through cleanly, or one solution is missed. (0): the equation is never reduced to one function, or an invalid algebraic move (e.g., dividing both sides by \(\sin\theta\), which silently discards the \(\sin\theta=1\) solution) is used instead.

Reasoning (4): the quadratic-in-\(\sin\theta\) is solved by an explicit, shown factoring (not guessed), each \(\theta\) is converted to \(t\) with the conversion formula displayed, and the verification substitutes back into the original equation, not the reduced one. (2): factoring shown but the verification step re-checks the reduced equation instead of the original, missing the point of an independent check. (0): solutions asserted with no algebraic derivation.

Presentation & precision (4): the four numbered steps are clearly labeled and separated, each \(\theta\to t\) conversion shown as its own line, units (minutes) attached to every time. (2): organized with a labeling lapse. (0): scattered; the reduction, solving, and conversion steps blur together.

Intellectual honesty (4): the verification step is a genuine, independent substitution into the original equation (not a restatement of the algebra already used to solve it), and any uncertainty about a step is named rather than smoothed over. (2): a verification is present but merely re-derives the reduced equation instead of testing the original. (0): no real verification, or the check is fabricated to agree with the assumed answer.
PROBLEM 5
The AI cross-examination: give your problem 4 work to an AI tutor, ask it to check your double-angle substitution and whether you found every solution, copy its response, and render your own verdict.
GRADING GUIDANCE (no single correct answer — the response is student-generated)
There is no fixed "correct" AI response to check against — what is graded is the judging. Look for:
  • An actual AI response copied onto the page (two or three sentences), not fabricated or trivial.
  • A verdict that engages the mathematics specifically. Three solutions exist on \([0,2\pi)\): \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{7\pi}{6},\frac{11\pi}{6}\). A common, plausible AI error here would be to divide the reduced quadratic by a factor instead of fully factoring (silently losing the \(\sin\theta=1\) root), or to miss one of the two solutions from \(\sin\theta=-\frac12\) by forgetting that sine is negative in both Quadrant III and Quadrant IV. If the AI's check is itself wrong in one of these ways, the student should refute it by re-substituting the missed \(\theta\) into the original equation and showing it holds.
  • Either outcome earns full credit: a sound refutation of a bad AI claim, or a genuine correction if the AI catches something real (e.g., an arithmetic slip in the \(t=\frac{9\theta}{\pi}\) conversion). What must not appear is a verdict that merely restates "the AI is right" or "the AI is wrong" without checking the specific claim against the factored equation or a direct substitution.
Final Answer: Grade for the quality of the judgment (was every claim actually verified against the factored equation or a direct substitution before ruling?), not for which side of the argument the student lands on.
PROBLEM 6 — Honors stretch
The tide model in three disguises: derive \(d(t)=6-2\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{12}\right)\) from the original using \(\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta\), then evaluate all three forms independently at \(t=3\) hours.
SOLUTION
① Derive the second disguise. Starting from the original, \(d(t)=5+\cos^2\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{12}\right)-\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{12}\right)\), substitute the Pythagorean identity \(\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta\) with \(\theta=\frac{\pi t}{12}\): \[ d(t) = 5+\left[1-\sin^2\!\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)\right]-\sin^2\!\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right) = 5+1-2\sin^2\!\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right) = 6-2\sin^2\!\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right) \] This matches the given second disguise exactly.

② Evaluate all three forms at \(t=3\) (so \(\frac{\pi t}{12}=\frac{\pi}{4}\), and \(\frac{\pi t}{6}=\frac{\pi}{2}\)): \[ \text{Original: } d(3)=5+\cos^2\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\sin^2\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 5+\dfrac12-\dfrac12 = 5 \] \[ \text{Disguise 2: } d(3)=6-2\sin^2\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 6-2\left(\dfrac12\right) = 6-1 = 5 \] \[ \text{Reduced: } d(3)=5+\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 5+0 = 5 \] All three independent computations give \(d(3)=5\).
Final Answer: \(d(t)=6-2\sin^2(\pi t/12)\) derived via \(\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta\); all three forms give \(d(3)=5\) m.
💡 DESMOS CHECK
For Problem 3, graphing the original disguised form of \(d(t)\) alongside \(y=5+\cos(\pi x/6)\) should show identical curves; adding \(y=5.5\) should show four intersection points at \(x=2,10,14,22\). For Problem 4, graphing \(y=\cos(2x)+\sin(x)\) should cross zero at exactly \(x=\pi/2,\ 7\pi/6,\ 11\pi/6\).
📊 GRADING NOTE (Focus Assignment — 16 pts, method-graded on Problems 3 and 4 only)
Problems 1, 2, 5, and 6 are checked for honest, visible completion only — do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound, and release this key after the due date for self-correction. Problems 3 and 4, the two ⭐ method problems, carry the entire 16-point rubric (Understanding / Reasoning / Presentation & Precision / Intellectual Honesty, 4 pts each), applied holistically across both problems together. Budget roughly 1–2 minutes per student for the two method problems, per the course's designated-problems-only grading model. The most common fatal error in Problem 3 is reducing the model correctly but then solving \(\cos u=0.5\) with only the reference-angle solution (\(t=2\)) and forgetting the second family (\(t=10\)) before adding period offsets; the most common fatal error in Problem 4 is dividing the reduced quadratic by \(\sin\theta\) or a similar factor instead of moving everything to one side and factoring, which silently discards a valid solution.
