Unit 7 Applied Task
Answer Key: Daylight by Latitude
Students choose their own two cities and source their own year of day-length data, so there is no single “correct” data table or pair of models. This key gives the structure a correct workbook must show, the general hand-fit method that must be mathematically sound for any two cities, and — unlike a purely open-ended data task — a set of physical relationships between the two models that are right or wrong regardless of which cities the student picked. Grade the physics as firmly as you grade the arithmetic.
PART 1 — DATA SHEET (what the structure must look like)
EXPECTED STRUCTURE
A sheet named Data with two cities' worth of (day-of-year, day-length-in-hours) pairs, at least 12 points per city — monthly sampling (the 1st of each month) is the natural default, but any comparable regular sampling is fine. Each city's source is named in a labeled cell: a national weather service, a government astronomical almanac, or a reputable sunrise–sunset reference site, cited well enough that a grader could find the same table. No invented numbers and no smoothing — real day-length data has small day-to-day irregularities (a minute or two of jitter from how the source rounds sunrise/sunset), and a table that looks too perfectly smooth every single month is a flag to look closer, not a sign of a clean submission.

Latitude separation check: the two cities must be at genuinely different latitudes — not two suburbs of the same metro area. There is no single cutoff, but if the two cities' reported amplitudes (Part 2) come out within about half an hour of each other, the chosen cities were not different enough in latitude for this task's contrast to show up, and that is worth a comment even under completion scoring.
PART 2 — THE HAND-BUILT SINUSOIDAL MODEL (general method for any two cities)
SOLUTION METHOD
For any student's own data, each city's model is built from four quantities read straight off that city's own max and min day length, exactly as the task specifies: \[ A = \frac{\text{max} - \text{min}}{2} \qquad D = \frac{\text{max} + \text{min}}{2} \qquad B = \frac{2\pi}{365} \qquad C = \text{day-of-year of that city's maximum} \] with the model written as \[ y = A\cos\big(B(x - C)\big) + D \] where \(x\) is day-of-year and \(y\) is day length in hours. Note \(B\) is fixed at \(2\pi/365\) for both cities — it is not something either city's data determines independently, since both cities complete one seasonal cycle on the same 365-day orbit. A student who instead back-fits a different \(B\) per city, or uses \(2\pi/12\) (month-indexed) while plotting against day-of-year, has mismatched their model's units to their data and that is a real error to flag, not a stylistic choice.

Concrete verification any grader can run, on any student's own numbers: take the student's own \(A\), \(D\), \(C\) for a city and evaluate their model equation at \(x=C\): \[ y(C) = A\cos\big(B(C-C)\big) + D = A\cos(0) + D = A + D \] Since \(D=\tfrac{\max+\min}{2}\) and \(A = \tfrac{\max-\min}{2}\), this sum is \(A+D = \max\) exactly. So a correct model, evaluated at the student's own day-of-max, must return the student's own recorded max day length — if it doesn't (within rounding), either \(C\) is not really the day of the max in their data, or \(A\)/\(D\) were computed from the wrong max/min, or a sign/formula error crept into the spreadsheet cell. This single check catches the most common hand-fit mistakes without needing to see the student's raw data at all.

Formula-column check: the Model sheet should show one formula (e.g. =$F$2 + $F$1*COS((2*PI()/365)*(A2-$F$3))) copied down the full column, not 12+ separately typed values — and that curve, plotted against the raw scatter points on the same chart, should visibly hug the data. A poor visual fit despite correct arithmetic usually means \(C\) was misread from the data (off by a month or more) rather than a formula error.
PART 3 — PHYSICAL INTERPRETATION (definite right/wrong, regardless of which two cities were chosen)
THIS IS THE ONE SECTION WHERE “IT DEPENDS ON THEIR DATA” DOES NOT APPLY
Every other part of this task is dataset-agnostic — two students can both be fully correct with completely different numbers. Part 3 is different: the underlying orbital mechanics are the same for every city on Earth, so three relationships between the two cities' fitted parameters have a genuinely correct answer. A submission that gets any of the three below backwards has a real conceptual error in the physics, not just a different data choice — treat it accordingly, even under completion scoring.

1. Amplitude must be larger for the higher-latitude city. The sunrise/sunset swing between a location's longest and shortest day grows with distance from the equator, because the same 23.5° axial tilt divides daylight almost evenly at low latitudes (the sun's path across the sky changes little with season near the equator) and very unevenly at high latitudes (near the poles, the tilt can push a location into 24-hour daylight or 24-hour darkness for stretches of the year). So whichever of the student's two cities sits farther from the equator must show the larger \(A\); the city closer to the equator must show the smaller \(A\). If the student's numbers come out the other way, the most likely cause is a max/min mix-up (min entered as max, or vice versa) rather than a genuine data anomaly — check that first.

2. Period must land close to 365 days for both cities. Both cities orbit the same sun on the same schedule, so this one is not latitude-dependent at all — it is fixed by the task's own \(B=2\pi/365\), so it should not even vary between the two models unless the student built \(B\) independently per city, which (per Part 2) is itself a flag.

3. Peaks/troughs must align, unless the two cities are in opposite hemispheres — then they must be roughly six months apart. Two cities in the same hemisphere (both Northern or both Southern) should reach their longest day within a few days of each other, because the same seasonal calendar governs both. Grading branch point: if the student picked a Northern-Hemisphere city and a Southern-Hemisphere city (e.g., something like a European or North American city paired with an Australian or South American one), the two phase shifts \(C\) should differ by roughly half a year (around 180–185 days) — a Southern-Hemisphere summer falls in the Northern-Hemisphere winter. This is the correct outcome for that pairing, not an error, and the student's Answers sheet should explicitly name and explain it rather than treat it as a mismatch. A same-hemisphere pair with phase shifts six months apart, or an opposite-hemisphere pair with phase shifts nearly aligned, indicates a genuine error (wrong max identified, or a hemisphere mixed up) and should be flagged.

Midline (mentioned in the task's own success criteria, same standard): both cities' \(D\) should land close to 12 hours, because averaged over a full year every point on Earth receives almost exactly half daylight and half night regardless of latitude or tilt. A midline that is far from 12 (say, off by more than about half an hour) usually means the max/min values themselves were misread, or the data actually spans less than a full year.
PART 4 — THE AI ROUND
WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER CONTAINS
Three distinct, present pieces, each in the student's own words: ① the original 4–6 sentence defense of why the model's period and phase-shift choices are physically reasonable (not just numerically fitted) — grounded in Earth's orbit and axial tilt, referencing the student's own \(C\) values; ② the AI's critique, pasted in full, not paraphrased or summarized away; ③ a signed critique of that critique naming something specific the AI got right (a real gap or weak spot in the original defense) and something specific the AI got wrong or overstated (a hallucinated claim about orbital mechanics, an invented numeric fact, or an overconfident assertion the student's own data does not support). A submission that only reports agreement with the AI, with nothing conceded and nothing corrected, has not completed the judgment step this task is built around and should not receive full credit on this part — the same standard as the model's Growth on Record key.
HONORS STRETCH — Estimating latitude from amplitude
Using City A's amplitude and an approximate latitude–amplitude relationship, estimate City A's latitude and compare to its actual value.
SOLUTION (approximate — hedge exactly as the task itself hedges)
The task itself is explicit that this is an approximate estimate, not an exact recovery, so the key should be read the same way: as a defensible route to a ballpark latitude, not the precise formula. One reasonable derivation a student or their AI tutor might reach (there are others; do not penalize a different approximate route that is internally consistent and appropriately hedged): the standard sunrise-equation model for day length at latitude \(\varphi\) when the sun's declination is \(\delta\) is \[ \text{day length}(\varphi,\delta) \approx \frac{24}{\pi}\arccos\big(-\tan\varphi\tan\delta\big) \] Evaluating this at the summer solstice, where \(\delta \approx 23.5^\circ\), gives an approximate maximum day length for that latitude; since a city's day length swings roughly symmetrically above and below 12 hours over the year, amplitude \(A \approx \text{max} - 12\), so \[ A \approx \frac{24}{\pi}\arccos\big(-\tan\varphi\tan 23.5^\circ\big) - 12 \] Solving this for \(\varphi\) in terms of a student's own fitted \(A\) gives an estimate of City A's latitude: \[ \varphi \approx \arctan\!\left[\frac{-\cos\!\big(\tfrac{\pi}{24}(A+12)\big)}{\tan 23.5^\circ}\right] \] What to check: the student (or their AI tutor, with the student showing the work) used some internally consistent latitude–amplitude relationship and applied it correctly to their own \(A\) — not that they reproduced this exact formula. Do not require this precision; a cruder proportional estimate, clearly labeled as a rough approximation, is acceptable too, since the task's own honors stretch treats the relationship as something to "find or reason toward," not a known exact law.

Why the estimate should not match the looked-up latitude exactly (the task's own expected discussion): real day-length curves are not perfectly sinusoidal near the poles (the sunrise equation itself becomes ill-behaved as \(\varphi\) approaches 90° minus the declination); atmospheric refraction bends light enough to extend the observed day length slightly everywhere, at every latitude; and any simplified formula — this one included — trades some accuracy for tractability by hand. A student whose estimate lands within a few degrees of the actual latitude, with this reasoning named explicitly, has met the bar; do not expect or require exact agreement.
✅ COMPLETION-SCORING CHECKLIST (10 pts, mirrors the task's Success Criteria)
☐ Three sheets present (Data, Model, Answers); Data sheet holds at least 12 real, unedited data points per city, for two cities at genuinely different latitudes, each with its source named in a labeled cell.
☐ Model sheet shows, for both cities side by side: a scatter chart of day length vs. day-of-year, labeled \(A\)/\(D\)/\(B\)/\(C\) cells, the hand-built model formula copied down a column (not retyped per row), and the model plotted as a smooth curve against the raw data points on the same chart.
☐ Answers sheet states both cities' amplitude, midline, and phase shift in full sentences citing the student's own cells, and correctly explains — per Part 3 above — why the higher-latitude city has the larger amplitude, why both midlines are near 12 hours, why both periods are near 365 days, and why the peaks/troughs align (or are six months out of phase, for an opposite-hemisphere pair).
☐ AI round is complete: original defense, the AI's critique pasted in full, and a signed critique-of-the-critique that concedes at least one real point and corrects at least one AI error or overreach.
☐ Honors stretch, if attempted: some internally consistent latitude-from-amplitude estimate shown with work, compared to the city's actual latitude, and the mismatch discussed with at least one of the task's own named reasons (non-sinusoidal behavior near the poles, atmospheric refraction, or the approximation's own trade-off of accuracy for simplicity).

Answer Key: Unit 7 Test
Full worked solutions for all 11 problems (Part A: 1–8, Part B: 9–10, Part C: 11), for grading against the standing 4-criterion rubric. Every identity manipulation, triangle solve, and trigonometric-equation solution set below was independently re-derived and numerically re-verified — no result was taken on faith from the test page.
📊 POINT ALLOCATION SUMMARY (which problems supply evidence for which criterion)
The rubric is holistic across the whole test (each of the four criteria scored out of 10, 40 pts total) rather than problem-by-problem, but each part carries most of the weight for particular criteria:
  • Understanding of the material (10 pts): primarily Part A (1–8) — reading a transformed graph, a reciprocal-function graph, exact inverse-trig values, a basic trig equation, the Law of Sines, the Law of Cosines with area, the Pythagorean identity, and a sum-formula exact value.
  • Quality of reasoning (10 pts): primarily Part B (9–10) and Part C (11) — the double-angle/reduction identity derived as a genuine logical chain from the sum formula, the SSA ambiguous case fully resolved with the \(h\)-versus-\(a\)-versus-\(b\) comparison explained, and the Part C connection to Unit 4's one-to-one/horizontal-line-test criterion made explicitly, not merely gestured at.
  • Presentation & precision (10 pts): distributed across all parts — neat vertical work, aligned equals signs, exact values kept in radical form where the angle is special, degrees/radians used consistently within a problem, units carried on every applied answer.
  • Intellectual honesty (10 pts): the signed honor line plus honest handling throughout — any problem left incomplete should carry a note of where and why the student stopped, which earns credit here rather than losing it.
📝 PART A — FLUENCY
PROBLEM 1
Reading a transformation: for \(y=3\cos\!\left(2\left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right)-1\), state amplitude, period, midline, phase shift; evaluate \(y\) at \(x=\frac{\pi}{4}\).
SOLUTION
Matching to \(y=A\cos(B(x-C))+D\): \(A=3\), \(B=2\), \(C=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\), \(D=-1\).

Amplitude \(=|A|=3\). Period \(=\dfrac{2\pi}{|B|}=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi\). Midline: \(y=-1\). Phase shift: \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) to the right.

At \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\), the argument is \(2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=2(0)=0\): \[ y=3\cos(0)-1 = 3(1)-1 = 2 \]
Final Answer: Amplitude \(3\); period \(\pi\); midline \(y=-1\); phase shift \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) right. \(y\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=2\).
PROBLEM 2
A reciprocal graph: for \(y=\sec(3x)\), state the period and the two vertical asymptotes nearest \(x=0\) (one positive, one negative).
SOLUTION
\(\sec(3x)=\dfrac{1}{\cos(3x)}\) has the same period as \(\cos(3x)\): period \(=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\).

Vertical asymptotes occur where \(\cos(3x)=0\), i.e., \(3x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}+k\pi\), so \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}+\dfrac{k\pi}{3}\). The two nearest \(x=0\): \(k=0\) gives \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\); \(k=-1\) gives \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}-\dfrac{\pi}{3}=-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\).
Final Answer: Period \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\); asymptotes at \(x=-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) and \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\).
PROBLEM 3
Inverse trig, exact: evaluate \(\arcsin\left(-\frac12\right)\) and \(\arccos\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\) exactly, stating the range each inverse function is restricted to.
SOLUTION
\(\arcsin\) is restricted to the range \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\). We need the angle in that range whose sine is \(-\dfrac12\): \(\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\dfrac12\), and \(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) lies in the range. \[ \arcsin\left(-\dfrac12\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{6} \] \(\arccos\) is restricted to the range \([0,\pi]\). We need the angle in that range whose cosine is \(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\): \(\cos\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)=\cos(\pi-\tfrac{\pi}{6})=-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\), and \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\) lies in \([0,\pi]\). \[ \arccos\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \]
Final Answer: \(\arcsin\left(-\frac12\right)=-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) (range \([-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}]\)); \(\arccos\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\) (range \([0,\pi]\)).
PROBLEM 4
Basic trig equation: solve \(2\sin\theta-1=0\) for \(\theta\in[0,2\pi)\).
SOLUTION
\[ 2\sin\theta-1=0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \sin\theta=\dfrac12 \] Reference angle \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\), sine positive in QI and QII: \[ \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{5\pi}{6} \]
Final Answer: \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\).
PROBLEM 5
Law of Sines: \(A=40^\circ\), \(B=75^\circ\), \(a=12\) (opposite \(A\)). Find angle \(C\) and sides \(b\), \(c\), to the nearest hundredth.
SOLUTION
\(C = 180^\circ-40^\circ-75^\circ = 65^\circ\).

\[ \dfrac{a}{\sin A}=\dfrac{12}{\sin40^\circ}=\dfrac{12}{0.642788}\approx18.6687 \] \[ b = 18.6687\times\sin75^\circ = 18.6687\times0.965926 \approx 18.03 \] \[ c = 18.6687\times\sin65^\circ = 18.6687\times0.906308 \approx 16.92 \]
Final Answer: \(C=65^\circ\); \(b\approx18.03\); \(c\approx16.92\).
PROBLEM 6
Law of Cosines and area: \(a=8\), \(b=10\), included angle \(C=50^\circ\). Find side \(c\) and the triangle's area, to the nearest hundredth.
SOLUTION
\[ c^2 = a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C = 64+100-2(8)(10)\cos50^\circ = 164-160(0.642788) = 164-102.846 = 61.154 \] \[ c = \sqrt{61.154} \approx 7.82 \] \[ \text{Area} = \dfrac12 ab\sin C = \dfrac12(8)(10)\sin50^\circ = 40(0.766044) \approx 30.64 \]
Final Answer: \(c\approx7.82\); area \(\approx30.64\) sq. units.
PROBLEM 7
Pythagorean identity: given \(\cos\theta=-\frac{5}{13}\) with \(\theta\) in Quadrant III, find the exact values of \(\sin\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\).
SOLUTION
\[ \sin^2\theta = 1-\cos^2\theta = 1-\dfrac{25}{169}=\dfrac{144}{169} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \sin\theta=\pm\dfrac{12}{13} \] Quadrant III requires sine negative: \(\sin\theta=-\dfrac{12}{13}\). \[ \tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{-12/13}{-5/13} = \dfrac{12}{5} \]
Final Answer: \(\sin\theta=-\dfrac{12}{13}\); \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{12}{5}\).
PROBLEM 8
Sum formula, exact value: find the exact value of \(\cos75^\circ\) using a sum or difference formula (write \(75^\circ\) as a sum of two special angles).
SOLUTION
\(75^\circ = 45^\circ+30^\circ\). \[ \cos75^\circ = \cos(45^\circ+30^\circ) = \cos45^\circ\cos30^\circ-\sin45^\circ\sin30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\dfrac12 = \dfrac{\sqrt6}{4}-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{4} = \dfrac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4} \] Numeric check: \(\dfrac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}\approx\dfrac{2.449-1.414}{4}\approx0.2588\), matching \(\cos75^\circ\). ✓
Final Answer: \(\cos75^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}\approx0.2588\).
📝 PART B — REASONING (write these as arguments)
PROBLEM 9
Derive an identity from its roots, starting from \(\cos(A+B)=\cos A\cos B-\sin A\sin B\), ending at the reduction formula \(\sin^2\theta=\dfrac{1-\cos2\theta}{2}\); close with why deriving beats memorizing.
MODEL SOLUTION
① Set \(A=B=\theta\) in the sum formula: \[ \cos(\theta+\theta) = \cos\theta\cos\theta-\sin\theta\sin\theta \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \cos2\theta = \cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta \] ② Substitute the Pythagorean identity \(\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta\): \[ \cos2\theta = (1-\sin^2\theta)-\sin^2\theta = 1-2\sin^2\theta \] ③ Solve for \(\sin^2\theta\): \[ \cos2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; 2\sin^2\theta = 1-\cos2\theta \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \sin^2\theta = \dfrac{1-\cos2\theta}{2} \] ④ This derivation connects the sum/difference family (the starting formula) and the Pythagorean identity to produce the double-angle and reduction (power-reducing) formulas. Deriving the reduction formula this way, from two formulas already independently proved, makes it more trustworthy than memorizing it as an isolated fact: if the formula is forgotten, it can be rebuilt in under a minute from results that are secure, closing off the risk of misremembering an unrelated-seeming fact (for instance, confusing the \(+\) and \(-\) signs, or which function gets the \(1-\cos2\theta\) form and which gets \(1+\cos2\theta\)).
Final Answer: \(\cos2\theta=\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta\), giving \(\sin^2\theta=\dfrac{1-\cos2\theta}{2}\). Connects the sum/difference family and the Pythagorean identity; deriving beats memorizing because a forgotten formula can be rebuilt from secure results instead of risked as an isolated fact.
PROBLEM 10
The ambiguous case, fully resolved: \(a=15\), \(b=20\), \(A=35^\circ\). Determine how many triangles, solve every valid one, and explain why SSA (but never SAS/SSS) can have more than one answer.
MODEL SOLUTION
① Compute \(h\) and compare. \[ h = b\sin A = 20\sin35^\circ = 20(0.573576) \approx 11.47 \] Comparing \(h\), \(a\), and \(b\): \(h\approx11.47 < a=15 < b=20\). When \(htwo distinct triangles are possible: side \(a\) is long enough to reach the base line (so a triangle exists), but not so long that it can only swing to one position (which is what happens when \(a\ge b\)) — it can land at two different points along the base, each closing the triangle at a different angle \(B\).

② Solve for every valid triangle. By the Law of Sines: \[ \dfrac{\sin B}{b} = \dfrac{\sin A}{a} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \sin B = \dfrac{b\sin A}{a} = \dfrac{20(0.573576)}{15} = \dfrac{11.4715}{15} \approx 0.76477 \] \[ B_1 = \arcsin(0.76477) \approx 49.9^\circ \qquad\qquad B_2 = 180^\circ-49.9^\circ = 130.1^\circ \] Both are valid: \(A+B_2 = 35^\circ+130.1^\circ=165.1^\circ<180^\circ\), so triangle 2 closes properly.

Triangle 1: \(B_1\approx49.9^\circ\), \(C_1=180^\circ-35^\circ-49.9^\circ\approx95.1^\circ\). \[ c_1 = \dfrac{a\sin C_1}{\sin A} = \dfrac{15\sin95.1^\circ}{\sin35^\circ} \approx \dfrac{15(0.9960)}{0.573576} \approx 26.0 \] Triangle 2: \(B_2\approx130.1^\circ\), \(C_2=180^\circ-35^\circ-130.1^\circ\approx14.9^\circ\). \[ c_2 = \dfrac{a\sin C_2}{\sin A} = \dfrac{15\sin14.9^\circ}{\sin35^\circ} \approx \dfrac{15(0.2570)}{0.573576} \approx 6.7 \] ③ Why SSA can have two answers, but Law of Cosines never does: the SSA setup finds an unknown angle by taking \(\arcsin\) of a ratio, and because sine is positive in both Quadrant I and Quadrant II, two different angles (\(B_1\) and \(180^\circ-B_1\)) can both have the same sine value — and both may be geometrically valid, since neither always exceeds the triangle's remaining angle budget. The Law of Cosines instead finds an unknown angle by taking \(\arccos\) of a ratio, and because every angle of a triangle lies in \((0^\circ,180^\circ)\), where cosine is strictly decreasing and therefore one-to-one, \(\arccos\) always returns exactly one angle for a given ratio — so an SAS or SSS setup can never produce a second, equally valid triangle.
Final Answer: \(h\approx11.47\), and since \(h
📝 PART C — SYNTHESIS (this unit meets Unit 4)
PROBLEM 11
\(\sin\theta=0.6\): find the general solution; state what a calculator returns; connect to Unit 4's one-to-one/horizontal-line-test criterion; close the loop with sine's odd symmetry versus cosine's even symmetry.
MODEL SOLUTION
① General solution. With \(\beta=\arcsin(0.6)\approx36.9^\circ\) as the reference angle, sine is positive in Quadrant I and Quadrant II, so: \[ \theta = 36.9^\circ+360^\circ k \qquad\text{or}\qquad \theta = (180^\circ-36.9^\circ)+360^\circ k = 143.1^\circ+360^\circ k, \quad k\in\mathbb{Z} \] ② What the calculator returns. A calculator's inverse sine key returns \(\arcsin(0.6)\approx36.9^\circ\) — exactly the \(k=0\) member of the first branch of the family in ①, and only that one member.

③ Connect to Unit 4. Both \(\theta\approx36.9^\circ\) and \(\theta\approx143.1^\circ\) are members of the solution family from ①, and both are distinct angles that produce the identical output \(\sin\theta=0.6\). Two different inputs mapping to the same output is precisely what the horizontal line test (Unit 4's certifying criterion for one-to-one) catches: a horizontal line at height \(0.6\) crosses the sine curve more than once over sine's full domain, so sine fails the horizontal line test and is not one-to-one over all reals — meaning "the angle whose sine is \(0.6\)" has no single well-defined answer until the domain is restricted. Restricting sine's domain to \([-90^\circ,90^\circ]\) removes every repeat: on that interval sine is strictly increasing, a horizontal line crosses it at most once, and sine gains the one-to-one property Unit 4 required before a function could be assigned a well-defined inverse. That restricted sine is exactly what \(\arcsin\) computes.

④ Close the loop. Sine is an odd function (\(\sin(-x)=-\sin x\)), symmetric about the origin, so its natural one-to-one stretch is centered at \(0\) and extends equally into positive and negative angles — exactly the symmetric interval \([-90^\circ,90^\circ]\). Cosine is an even function (\(\cos(-x)=\cos x\)), symmetric about the \(y\)-axis, so any interval centered at \(0\) would pair up mirror angles with identical cosine values (e.g., \(\cos(-30^\circ)=\cos(30^\circ)\)) and fail the horizontal line test immediately. Cosine's one-to-one interval must instead run asymmetrically from one side of \(0\) to the other — \([0^\circ,180^\circ]\) — capturing one full monotonic decreasing run with no mirrored duplicate.
Final Answer: \(\theta\approx36.9^\circ+360^\circ k\) or \(143.1^\circ+360^\circ k\). Calculator returns \(36.9^\circ\), one member of the family. Sine fails the horizontal line test over its full domain (two solutions share one output) and gains one-to-one status on \([-90^\circ,90^\circ]\); that interval is symmetric about \(0\) because sine is odd, while cosine's restricted interval \([0^\circ,180^\circ]\) is asymmetric because cosine is even.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC

The whole test is graded against the standing four-criterion rubric, each criterion scored out of 10. Part A supplies most of the evidence for understanding and precision; Parts B and C supply most of the evidence for reasoning.

Criteria What excellent looks like Pts
Understanding of the material Graph features, inverse trig values, the Law of Sines and Law of Cosines, and identity applications are all executed correctly and fluently, with notation exact throughout. 10 pts
Quality of reasoning The identity derivation reads as a real logical chain; the ambiguous case is fully resolved with its reasoning explained; the Part C connection to Unit 4's one-to-one/horizontal-line-test criterion is made explicitly and correctly, not merely gestured at. 10 pts
Presentation & precision Clean vertical work throughout, aligned equals signs, exact values kept in radical form where the angle is special, units carried on every applied answer, pages in order — forty points of work a stranger could follow. 10 pts
Intellectual honesty Honor line signed and honored; work shown as actually done; any problem you could not finish carries an honest note of where and why you stopped — which earns respect here, never punishment. 10 pts
Total: 40 pts
📊 GRADING NOTE (Test — 40 pts, rubric-graded)
Score holistically against the four-criterion rubric printed on the test page (10 pts each). Common partial-credit spots: Problem 1's phase shift reported as \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) instead of \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) (misreading \(B(x-C)\) and dividing the shift by \(B\) a second time) — deduct from Understanding; Problem 2's asymptotes given at \(x=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}\) instead of \(\pm\frac{\pi}{6}\) (forgetting to divide by the coefficient \(3\) inside the argument) — deduct from Understanding; Problem 3 giving \(\arcsin(-\frac12)=\frac{7\pi}{6}\) or another angle outside \([-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}]\) (evaluating sine correctly but not restricting to the inverse function's actual range) — deduct from Understanding; Problem 5 or 6's leg/side ratios swapped (Law of Sines used where Law of Cosines was needed, or vice versa, since both a full-angle and a two-side/included-angle setup appear on this test) — deduct from Understanding; Problem 9's derivation correct through step ③ but the closing "why derive, not memorize" sentence merely restated as "it's easier" without naming that the derivation can be rebuilt from already-proved formulas — deduct from Reasoning; Problem 10 finding only one triangle (stopping after \(B_1\) without testing whether \(B_2=180^\circ-B_1\) also produces a valid angle sum) — deduct from Reasoning, since the problem explicitly asks for every valid triangle; Problem 11③ asserting sine "isn't one-to-one" without explicitly citing the two equal-output angles \(36.9^\circ\) and \(143.1^\circ\) as the evidence, or omitting the explicit horizontal-line-test language from Unit 4 — deduct from Reasoning, since the problem asks the connection to be made explicitly; Problem 11④ asserting the odd/even distinction without explaining why it forces a symmetric versus asymmetric interval — deduct from Reasoning. An honestly noted incomplete answer should never cost Intellectual Honesty points — that criterion rewards the honesty, not the completeness.

Practice Set · Completion-Scored
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 8-1
Answer Key: Charting the Pole
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1
Plot and describe: Plot \(\left(4,\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)\). State which quadrant it lands in and the reference angle you used to get there.
SOLUTION
The angle \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\) (\(150^\circ\)) lies between \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\pi\), so the terminal ray falls in Quadrant II. The reference angle is the acute angle back to the nearest \(x\)-axis, measured from \(\pi\): \[ \pi - \frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{\pi}{6} \] Check by converting to rectangular: \(x=4\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}=4\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=-2\sqrt3\), \(y=4\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}=4\left(\frac12\right)=2\). Since \(x<0\) and \(y>0\), the point sits in Quadrant II. ✓
Final Answer: Quadrant II; reference angle \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\).
PROBLEM 2
Negative \(r\): Plot \(\left(-3,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\), and state an equivalent representation using a positive \(r\).
SOLUTION
A negative \(r\) is plotted \(3\) units out along the ray opposite \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}\), not \(3\) units short of it along the same ray — that opposite ray is \(\frac{\pi}{4}+\pi=\frac{5\pi}{4}\). So an equivalent positive-\(r\) name for the same point is \(\left(3,\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)\).

Check both convert to the same rectangular point: \(\left(-3,\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\to x=-3\cos\frac{\pi}{4}=-\frac{3\sqrt2}{2}\), \(y=-3\sin\frac{\pi}{4}=-\frac{3\sqrt2}{2}\); and \(\left(3,\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)\to x=3\cos\frac{5\pi}{4}=-\frac{3\sqrt2}{2}\), \(y=3\sin\frac{5\pi}{4}=-\frac{3\sqrt2}{2}\). Identical. ✓
Final Answer: \(\left(3,\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\right)\)
PROBLEM 3
Polar to rectangular: Convert \(\left(5,\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\) to rectangular form.
SOLUTION
\[ x = r\cos\theta = 5\cos\frac{\pi}{6} = 5\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) = \frac{5\sqrt3}{2}, \qquad y = r\sin\theta = 5\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = 5\left(\frac12\right) = \frac52 \]
Final Answer: \(\left(\dfrac{5\sqrt3}{2},\ \dfrac{5}{2}\right)\)
PROBLEM 4
Rectangular to polar: Convert \((0,-6)\) to polar form, with \(r>0\) and \(0\le\theta<2\pi\). Reason from the picture, since \(\tan\theta\) is undefined here.
SOLUTION
\(x=0\) means \(\tan\theta=\frac{y}{x}\) is undefined, so the reference-angle shortcut cannot be used — but the point itself makes the angle obvious: \((0,-6)\) sits \(6\) units straight down from the pole, directly on the negative \(y\)-axis. That direction is \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\), and the distance from the pole is \[ r = \sqrt{0^2+(-6)^2} = 6 \] Check: \(6\cos\frac{3\pi}{2}=0\), \(6\sin\frac{3\pi}{2}=-6\). ✓
Final Answer: \(\left(6,\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right)\)
PROBLEM 5
Rectangular to polar: Convert \((2,2)\) to polar form, with \(r>0\) and \(0\le\theta<2\pi\).
SOLUTION
\[ r = \sqrt{2^2+2^2} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt2 \] Both coordinates are positive, so the point is in Quadrant I, and \[ \theta = \arctan\left(\frac{2}{2}\right) = \arctan(1) = \frac{\pi}{4} \]
Final Answer: \(\left(2\sqrt2,\ \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\)
PROBLEM 6
Multiple representations: Give three different polar representations of the point \(\left(4,\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\), using at least one negative \(r\)-value among them.
SOLUTION
Adding a full revolution never moves the point: \(\left(4,\frac{\pi}{3}+2\pi\right)=\left(4,\frac{7\pi}{3}\right)\). For a negative-\(r\) name, flip to the opposite ray and add \(\pi\) to the angle: \(\left(-4,\frac{\pi}{3}+\pi\right)=\left(-4,\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)\). All three name the identical point, since each transformation (full revolution, or opposite direction with negated distance) returns to the same location.
Final Answer: \(\left(4,\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\), \(\left(4,\dfrac{7\pi}{3}\right)\), \(\left(-4,\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)\) — among other valid triples.
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
Convert \((-3,-3\sqrt3)\) to polar form, with \(r>0\) and \(0\le\theta<2\pi\). Show your reasoning for choosing the correct quadrant, not just the reference angle.
SOLUTION
\[ r = \sqrt{(-3)^2+(-3\sqrt3)^2} = \sqrt{9+27} = \sqrt{36} = 6 \] Both \(x=-3\) and \(y=-3\sqrt3\) are negative, so the point lies in Quadrant III — the reference angle alone does not tell you this; it only ever gives an angle between \(0\) and \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), and the sign of each coordinate must be used to place it in the correct quadrant. The reference angle: \[ \theta_{\text{ref}} = \arctan\left|\frac{-3\sqrt3}{-3}\right| = \arctan(\sqrt3) = \frac{\pi}{3} \] Since Quadrant III angles run from \(\pi\) to \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\), add the reference angle to \(\pi\): \[ \theta = \pi + \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{4\pi}{3} \] Check: \(6\cos\frac{4\pi}{3}=6\left(-\frac12\right)=-3\); \(6\sin\frac{4\pi}{3}=6\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=-3\sqrt3\). ✓
Final Answer: \(\left(6,\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)\)
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
Typing (5*cos(pi/6), 5*sin(pi/6)), (0*cos(3pi/2), -6) style checks, and the honors-stretch pair should each land exactly on the given rectangular point. Plotting Problem 6's three representations for \(\left(4,\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\) as three separate points in Desmos (using \(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta\)) should show all three landing on one single dot.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound — watch specifically for the signature error of plotting a negative-\(r\) point closer in along the same ray instead of flipping to the opposite ray (Problem 2), and for skipping the sign/quadrant reasoning on Problems 4 and 7 in favor of a bare reference angle. Release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).

Lesson 8-2
Answer Key: Translating Between Two Languages
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1
Rectangular to polar: Convert \(x^2+y^2=49\) to polar form.
SOLUTION
Recognize \(x^2+y^2=r^2\) directly: \[ r^2 = 49 \;\Rightarrow\; r = 7 \]
Final Answer: \(r = 7\)
PROBLEM 2
Rectangular to polar: Convert \(x=5\) to polar form.
SOLUTION
Substitute \(x = r\cos\theta\): \[ r\cos\theta = 5 \;\Rightarrow\; r = \frac{5}{\cos\theta} = 5\sec\theta \]
Final Answer: \(r = 5\sec\theta\)
PROBLEM 3
Rectangular to polar: Convert \(y=-x\) to polar form, and explain in one sentence why \(r\) disappears from the resulting equation.
SOLUTION
Substitute \(x=r\cos\theta\), \(y=r\sin\theta\): \[ r\sin\theta = -r\cos\theta \;\Rightarrow\; r\sin\theta + r\cos\theta = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; r(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)=0 \] Dividing out the common factor \(r\) leaves \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta=0 \Rightarrow \tan\theta=-1 \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{3\pi}{4}\).

\(r\) disappears because a line through the pole is really a statement about direction, not distance — every point on that line, at every possible distance \(r\) from the pole, shares the same angle \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\). Once \(r\) cancels out of the equation, what is left is purely the fixed angle that describes the whole ray in both directions from the pole.
Final Answer: \(\theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\)
PROBLEM 4
Polar to rectangular: Convert \(r=8\) to rectangular form.
SOLUTION
Square both sides so \(r^2\) appears, then substitute \(r^2=x^2+y^2\): \[ r=8 \;\Rightarrow\; r^2=64 \;\Rightarrow\; x^2+y^2=64 \]
Final Answer: \(x^2+y^2=64\)
PROBLEM 5
Polar to rectangular: Convert \(r=10\cos\theta\) to rectangular form. Multiply by \(r\) first, then complete the square to name the center and radius of the resulting circle.
SOLUTION
Multiply both sides by \(r\) to expose \(r^2\) and \(r\cos\theta\): \[ r\cdot r = 10r\cos\theta \;\Rightarrow\; r^2=10r\cos\theta \;\Rightarrow\; x^2+y^2=10x \] Move the \(x\)-terms together and complete the square: \[ x^2-10x+y^2=0 \;\Rightarrow\; (x^2-10x+25)+y^2=25 \;\Rightarrow\; (x-5)^2+y^2=25 \]
Final Answer: \((x-5)^2+y^2=25\) — a circle centered at \((5,0)\) with radius \(5\).
PROBLEM 6
Polar to rectangular: Convert \(r=-2\sin\theta\) to rectangular form, completing the square to name the center and radius.
SOLUTION
Multiply both sides by \(r\): \[ r^2=-2r\sin\theta \;\Rightarrow\; x^2+y^2=-2y \] Complete the square on the \(y\)-terms: \[ x^2+(y^2+2y)=0 \;\Rightarrow\; x^2+(y^2+2y+1)=1 \;\Rightarrow\; x^2+(y+1)^2=1 \]
Final Answer: \(x^2+(y+1)^2=1\) — a circle centered at \((0,-1)\) with radius \(1\).
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
Convert \((x+4)^2+(y-4)^2=32\) to polar form, simplifying all the way to an equation of the form \(r=\ldots\). (Hint: expand first, and check whether the pole lies on the original circle before you divide by \(r\).)
SOLUTION
Expand first: \[ (x+4)^2+(y-4)^2 = x^2+8x+16+y^2-8y+16 = 32 \;\Rightarrow\; x^2+y^2+8x-8y = 0 \] Substitute \(x^2+y^2=r^2\), \(x=r\cos\theta\), \(y=r\sin\theta\): \[ r^2+8r\cos\theta-8r\sin\theta=0 \;\Rightarrow\; r^2 = 8r\sin\theta-8r\cos\theta \] Check the pole first. The circle has center \((-4,4)\) and radius \(\sqrt{32}\). The distance from the pole to that center is \(\sqrt{(-4)^2+4^2}=\sqrt{32}\) — exactly equal to the radius, so the pole itself lies on this circle. That means dividing by \(r\) below loses no information: the pole is already recovered as a solution of the reduced equation (at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}\), where \(\sin\theta=\cos\theta\), the right side is \(0\)). \[ r = 8\sin\theta-8\cos\theta \]
Final Answer: \(r = 8\sin\theta - 8\cos\theta\)
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
For Problems 5, 6, and 7, graphing both the given equation and the converted equation on separate lines in Desmos should show the two curves sitting exactly on top of each other. For Problem 7 specifically, tracing the graph of r = 8sin(theta) - 8cos(theta) should visibly pass through the pole (origin), confirming the pole-on-the-circle check performed before dividing by \(r\).
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound — watch specifically for the signature error of skipping the multiply-by-\(r\) step in Problems 5–7 (jumping straight to a claimed rectangular equation), and for a rushed or absent completing-the-square step. Release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).

Lesson 8-3
Answer Key: Table, Symmetry, Sketch
Full worked solutions for all 6 problems. Problems 3 and 4 carry gold-badged scoring guidance for the rubric — those are the only two problems graded for method; the rest are checked for honest completion.
PROBLEM 1 — Warmup
Build a table for \(r=2\theta\) at \(\theta=0,\ \frac{\pi}{2},\ \pi,\ \frac{3\pi}{2},\ 2\pi\), and describe the resulting shape in one sentence.
SOLUTION
\(\theta\)\(0\)\(\frac{\pi}{2}\)\(\pi\)\(\frac{3\pi}{2}\)\(2\pi\)
\(r=2\theta\)\(0\)\(\pi\approx3.14\)\(2\pi\approx6.28\)\(3\pi\approx9.42\)\(4\pi\approx12.57\)
The distance from the pole grows in direct proportion to the angle swept, with no repeating or bounded pattern — this is the signature of an Archimedean spiral, winding steadily outward as \(\theta\) increases.
Final Answer: Table as above; the curve is an Archimedean spiral, winding outward with \(r\) growing linearly in \(\theta\).
PROBLEM 2 — Warmup
Test \(r=5-5\cos\theta\) for symmetry about the polar axis, showing the substitution.
SOLUTION
The polar-axis test replaces \(\theta\) with \(-\theta\): \[ r = 5-5\cos(-\theta) = 5-5\cos\theta \] since cosine is an even function, \(\cos(-\theta)=\cos\theta\). The equation is unchanged, so the test passes.
Final Answer: Symmetric about the polar axis.
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 3
Table and symmetry together. Consider \(r=2-2\cos\theta\). ① Test the equation for symmetry about the polar axis, the line \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\), and the pole, showing each substitution explicitly. ② Using whichever symmetry passed, build a table of \(r\) at \(\theta=0,\ \frac{\pi}{3},\ \frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{2\pi}{3},\ \pi\) only, and explain why the symmetry justifies stopping there. ③ Sketch the complete curve, using the symmetry to complete the reflected half. ④ State the angle where the curve passes through the pole and the angle where it reaches its farthest point, and explain how your table shows both.
SOLUTION
① Symmetry tests.
Polar axis (replace \(\theta\) with \(-\theta\)): \(r=2-2\cos(-\theta)=2-2\cos\theta\) — identical to the original, since cosine is even. Passes.
Line \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\) (replace \(\theta\) with \(\pi-\theta\)): \(r=2-2\cos(\pi-\theta)=2-2(-\cos\theta)=2+2\cos\theta\). This is not the same equation as \(r=2-2\cos\theta\) (they agree only where \(\cos\theta=0\)), so the test fails — inconclusive, not disproven.
Pole (replace \(r\) with \(-r\)): \(-r=2-2\cos\theta \Rightarrow r=2\cos\theta-2\). Compared to the original \(r=2-2\cos\theta\), these agree only where \(\cos\theta=1\), not for every \(\theta\), so this test also fails.

② Table using polar-axis symmetry. Since the curve is symmetric about the polar axis, every point at angle \(-\theta\) mirrors the point at \(\theta\) — so a table over \(\theta\in[0,\pi]\) already determines the entire curve; the second half (\(\theta\in[-\pi,0]\), i.e., reflecting through the polar axis) is a guaranteed mirror image, not new information.
\(\theta\)\(0\)\(\frac{\pi}{3}\)\(\frac{\pi}{2}\)\(\frac{2\pi}{3}\)\(\pi\)
\(r\)\(0\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)\(4\)
(e.g., \(r\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=2-2\left(\frac12\right)=1\); \(r\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)=2-2\left(-\frac12\right)=3\).)

③ Sketch. A cardioid with its cusp at the pole along \(\theta=0\) (pointing right, toward the pole side where \(r=0\)), bulging outward and reaching its rounded farthest point at \(\theta=\pi\) (pointing left), and mirrored above and below the polar axis by the confirmed symmetry.

④ Pole and farthest point. The table shows \(r=0\) at \(\theta=0\) — the curve passes through the pole there. The table also shows \(r\) climbing steadily from \(0\) to a maximum of \(4\) at \(\theta=\pi\), the last table entry — that is the farthest point.
Final Answer: Symmetric about the polar axis only (the other two tests fail). Table: \(r=0,1,2,3,4\) at \(\theta=0,\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{2\pi}{3},\pi\). Cardioid, cusp at the pole at \(\theta=0\); farthest point \(r=4\) at \(\theta=\pi\).
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): all three symmetry substitutions are performed correctly and the polar-axis test is correctly identified as the one that passes; the table's five values are all correct; the cusp (\(\theta=0\)) and farthest point (\(\theta=\pi\), \(r=4\)) are both correctly named. (2): the correct symmetry is found but one or more table values are wrong, or the cusp/farthest-point angle is misidentified. (0): a symmetry is assumed without any substitution shown, or the table is built at arbitrary angles rather than the ones that the confirmed symmetry actually justifies.

Reasoning (4): the explanation in part ② correctly connects the polar-axis symmetry to why only \(\theta\in[0,\pi]\) is needed (the rest is a forced mirror image, not new data), and part ④ explains how the table itself displays both features (a zero value and the maximum value) rather than just asserting them. (2): the correct stopping point is used but the justification is thin ("because it's symmetric" with no mirror-image argument). (0): the table's extent is not connected to the symmetry result at all.

Presentation & precision (4): the three symmetry tests, the table, the sketch, and the pole/farthest-point statement are each clearly labeled and easy to follow in order. (2): organized with a minor labeling lapse. (0): scattered; a reader cannot locate which substitution belongs to which symmetry test.

Intellectual honesty (4): both failing symmetry tests are actually shown failing (not silently dropped), and the sketch's reflected half is genuinely built from the confirmed symmetry, not eyeballed. (2): the failing tests are mentioned but not actually carried out algebraically. (0): only the passing test appears on the page, as if the other two were never checked.
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 4
Working backward from features. A polar curve of the form \(r=a+a\sin\theta\) or \(r=a-a\sin\theta\) is known to be symmetric about the line \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\), to pass through the pole exactly once, and to reach a maximum distance of \(6\) from the pole. ① Determine \(a\). ② Determine which sign matches a curve whose cusp points downward (toward \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\)), showing the substitution that proves it. ③ Write the complete equation and verify it by evaluating \(r\) at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\) and at \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\), confirming both the given maximum and the cusp location. ④ In one or two sentences, explain why a curve satisfying the \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\) symmetry test could not have its cusp pointing left or right instead of up or down.
SOLUTION
① Find \(a\). For either form, the maximum value of \(r\) is \(a+a=2a\) (attained where the sine term equals \(+1\) or \(-1\), whichever matches the sign). Since the given maximum distance is \(6\): \[ 2a = 6 \;\Rightarrow\; a = 3 \] ② Find the sign. Try \(r=a+a\sin\theta=3+3\sin\theta\) and substitute \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\), where \(\sin\theta=-1\): \[ r = 3+3(-1) = 0 \] The cusp (\(r=0\)) lands exactly at \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\), pointing downward, as required. (Checking the other sign confirms it does not fit: \(r=3-3\sin\theta\) gives \(r=3-3(-1)=6\) at \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\) — the farthest point, not the cusp, there.) So the correct sign is \(+\).

③ Equation and verification. \[ r = 3+3\sin\theta \] At \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\): \(r=3+3(1)=6\) — matches the given maximum. ✓
At \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\): \(r=3+3(-1)=0\) — confirms the cusp there. ✓

④ Why not left or right. A curve of the form \(a\pm a\sin\theta\) is symmetric about the line \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\) (the vertical axis), and its unique features — the single cusp and the single farthest point — must lie exactly on that axis of symmetry, since any point off the axis would need a mirror partner elsewhere on the curve, which a single cusp or single maximum cannot have. The only two points on the vertical axis are \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\) (up) and \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\) (down), so the cusp can only point up or down — never left or right, which would instead be the signature of a cosine-based (polar-axis-symmetric) cardioid.
Final Answer: \(a=3\); the equation is \(r=3+3\sin\theta\). Verified: \(r\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=6\) (maximum), \(r\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right)=0\) (cusp, pointing down).
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): \(a=3\) is correctly found from \(2a=6\); the \(+\) sign is correctly matched to a downward cusp; the final equation \(r=3+3\sin\theta\) is correct. (2): \(a\) is correct but the sign choice is wrong or unjustified, or a sign error appears in the final equation despite correct reasoning elsewhere. (0): the maximum is treated as \(a\) instead of \(2a\) (giving \(a=6\)), or no attempt is made to distinguish the two sign cases.

Reasoning (4): part ②'s substitution is actually carried out (not merely asserted) and correctly shows \(r=0\) at \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\) for the chosen sign; part ④'s explanation correctly ties the single cusp/maximum to the axis of symmetry. (2): the correct sign is stated but the substitution proving it is thin or skipped; or part ④ asserts the conclusion without the axis-of-symmetry argument. (0): the sign is guessed with no supporting substitution at all.

Presentation & precision (4): all four parts appear as distinct, clearly labeled steps; the verification substitutions in part ③ are easy to check independently. (2): organized with a labeling lapse. (0): scattered; the four parts cannot be distinguished.

Intellectual honesty (4): both verification substitutions in part ③ are genuinely shown reproducing \(6\) and \(0\), not asserted; the sign check in part ② is real, not reverse-engineered from a known answer. (2): the verification is stated as true without the substitution actually shown. (0): the equation appears assumed from the start with the "proof" fitted to it after the fact.
PROBLEM 5
The AI cross-examination: Give your AI tutor the equation \(r=3-3\cos\theta\) with the instruction: “Test this equation for symmetry about the polar axis, the line \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\), and the pole, and state which symmetries hold.” Copy the AI’s response onto your page, then verify each of its three claims yourself by performing the substitution. If the AI claims a symmetry that your own test fails, show the failing substitution and say so; if it misses a symmetry that your test confirms, show that too. Either outcome earns full credit; what is graded is the verification.
GRADING GUIDANCE (no single correct answer — the AI response is student-generated)
The correct, independently-derived answer to check the student's verdict against, for \(r=3-3\cos\theta\):
Polar axis (\(\theta\to-\theta\)): \(r=3-3\cos(-\theta)=3-3\cos\theta\), identical (cosine even). Passes.
\(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\) (\(\theta\to\pi-\theta\)): \(r=3-3\cos(\pi-\theta)=3+3\cos\theta\), not identical to the original in general. Fails.
Pole (\(r\to-r\)): \(-r=3-3\cos\theta \Rightarrow r=3\cos\theta-3\), not identical to \(3-3\cos\theta\) in general. Fails.
This is the identical symmetry pattern as Problem 3 (\(r=2-2\cos\theta\)) — every cosine-based cardioid of the form \(a\pm a\cos\theta\) is symmetric about the polar axis only.

There is no fixed "correct" AI response to check against — what is graded is the verification. Look for:
  • An actual AI response copied onto the page (not fabricated or trivial).
  • All three substitutions actually performed by the student, independent of what the AI said.
  • A verdict that engages the mathematics specifically: if the AI claims the \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\) or pole symmetry holds, the student should catch this and show the failing substitution; if the AI's response matches the correct pattern above, the student should confirm it by performing the same three substitutions themselves and saying so.
  • Either outcome earns full credit: a sound correction of a bad AI claim, or a genuine independent confirmation of a correct one. What must not appear is a verdict that merely restates "the AI is right" or "the AI is wrong" without the student's own three substitutions to back it up.
Final Answer: Grade for the quality of the verification (were all three substitutions actually performed?), not for which side of the argument the student lands on. Independently verified correct result: symmetric about the polar axis only.
PROBLEM 6 — Honors stretch
Build a table for \(r=1+2\sin\theta\) at \(\theta=0,\ \frac{\pi}{6},\ \frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{5\pi}{6},\ \pi,\ \frac{7\pi}{6},\ \frac{3\pi}{2},\ \frac{11\pi}{6},\ 2\pi\). Identify the interval of \(\theta\) where \(r\) is negative, and explain in two or three sentences what that negative stretch does to the plotted curve.
SOLUTION
\(\theta\)\(0\)\(\frac{\pi}{6}\)\(\frac{\pi}{2}\)\(\frac{5\pi}{6}\)\(\pi\)\(\frac{7\pi}{6}\)\(\frac{3\pi}{2}\)\(\frac{11\pi}{6}\)\(2\pi\)
\(r\)\(1\)\(2\)\(3\)\(2\)\(1\)\(0\)\(-1\)\(0\)\(1\)
(e.g., \(r\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=1+2\left(\frac12\right)=2\); \(r\left(\frac{7\pi}{6}\right)=1+2\left(-\frac12\right)=0\); \(r\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right)=1+2(-1)=-1\).)

Solving \(1+2\sin\theta<0\) gives \(\sin\theta<-\frac12\), which holds exactly on \(\left(\frac{7\pi}{6},\frac{11\pi}{6}\right)\) — matching the table, where \(r=0\) at both endpoints and dips to \(-1\) at the midpoint \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\).

Each negative \(r\) in that interval plots on the ray opposite its \(\theta\) — for instance, the point at \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\) with \(r=-1\) actually plots at distance \(1\) in the direction \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\), inside the curve's own upper bulge rather than below the pole. Folding that whole angular stretch back through the pole this way traces a small extra loop inside the main curve, near the top — this equation (\(r=1+2\sin\theta\), with the constant smaller than the coefficient) is a limaçon with an inner loop, and the negative-\(r\) interval is exactly what draws that inner loop.
Final Answer: Table as above; \(r<0\) on \(\left(\frac{7\pi}{6},\frac{11\pi}{6}\right)\). This negative stretch plots on the opposite rays and folds back through the pole, tracing an inner loop near the top of the curve — a limaçon with an inner loop.
💡 DESMOS / EXCEL CHECK
For Problems 3 and 4, graphing r = 2-2cos(theta) and r = 3+3sin(theta) in Desmos should show a cusp at the pole and a rounded farthest point exactly where the table and verification predicted. For Problem 6, graphing r = 1+2sin(theta) should show a visible small loop inside the larger outer loop, appearing in the upper half of the graph — tracing the negative-\(r\) interval found above.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Focus Assignment — 16 pts, method-graded on Problems 3 and 4 only)
Problems 1, 2, 5, and 6 are checked for honest, visible completion only — do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound, and release this key after the due date for self-correction. Problems 3 and 4, the two ⭐ method problems, carry the entire 16-point rubric (Understanding / Reasoning / Presentation & Precision / Intellectual Honesty, 4 pts each). Budget roughly 1–2 minutes per student for the two method problems, per the course's designated-problems-only grading model. The most common fatal error in Problem 3 is asserting the polar-axis symmetry without actually substituting \(-\theta\), or building the reduced table over the wrong interval; the most common fatal error in Problem 4 is taking the given maximum of \(6\) as \(a\) itself instead of \(2a\), or guessing the sign in part ② without the substitution that proves it.

Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 8-4
Answer Key: Reading the Signature
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1
Identify: \(r=9\). State the family, center, and radius.
SOLUTION
A constant \(r\), with no dependence on \(\theta\) at all, is the simplest circle signature — every direction gives the same distance from the pole, which is exactly the definition of a circle centered at the pole itself.
Final Answer: Circle; center at the pole \((0,0)\); radius \(9\).
PROBLEM 2
Identify and verify: \(r=10\cos\theta\). State the family, center, and radius, then verify by converting to rectangular form and completing the square.
SOLUTION
No constant term is added to the cosine term — this is the circle signature \(r=2a\cos\theta\). Matching coefficients, \(2a=10 \Rightarrow a=5\), giving center \((a,0)=(5,0)\) and radius \(|a|=5\).

Verify. Multiply by \(r\): \(r^2=10r\cos\theta \Rightarrow x^2+y^2=10x\). Complete the square: \((x^2-10x+25)+y^2=25 \Rightarrow (x-5)^2+y^2=25\) — a circle centered at \((5,0)\) with radius \(5\), confirming the signature reading exactly.
Final Answer: Circle; center \((5,0)\); radius \(5\).
PROBLEM 3
Identify: \(r=-6\sin\theta\). State the family, center, and radius.
SOLUTION
No constant term — the circle signature \(r=2a\sin\theta\). Here \(2a=-6 \Rightarrow a=-3\), giving center \((0,a)=(0,-3)\) and radius \(|a|=3\). A negative coefficient does not signal a new family; it only reflects the circle's center to the opposite side of the pole.

Check (not required, but confirms the reading): multiply by \(r\): \(r^2=-6r\sin\theta \Rightarrow x^2+y^2=-6y \Rightarrow x^2+(y^2+6y+9)=9 \Rightarrow x^2+(y+3)^2=9\), center \((0,-3)\), radius \(3\). ✓
Final Answer: Circle; center \((0,-3)\); radius \(3\).
PROBLEM 4
Identify: \(r=7+7\cos\theta\). State the family, the cusp’s direction, and the farthest point’s distance from the pole.
SOLUTION
The constant term equals the coefficient of cosine (both \(7\)) — the cardioid signature \(r=a+a\cos\theta\).

Cusp: set \(r=0\): \(7+7\cos\theta=0 \Rightarrow \cos\theta=-1 \Rightarrow \theta=\pi\). The cusp sits at the pole, pointing toward \(\theta=\pi\) (left).
Farthest point: at \(\theta=0\), \(r=7+7(1)=14\), the maximum possible value.
Final Answer: Cardioid; cusp points left (\(\theta=\pi\)); farthest point \(14\) units out along the polar axis at \(\theta=0\).
PROBLEM 5
Identify: \(r=2-2\sin\theta\). State the family, the cusp’s direction, and the farthest point’s distance from the pole.
SOLUTION
The constant equals the coefficient of sine — the cardioid signature \(r=a-a\sin\theta\).

Cusp: \(2-2\sin\theta=0 \Rightarrow \sin\theta=1 \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\). The cusp points up.
Farthest point: at \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\), \(\sin\theta=-1\), so \(r=2-2(-1)=4\).
Final Answer: Cardioid; cusp points up (\(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\)); farthest point \(4\) units straight down at \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\).
PROBLEM 6
Compare: \(r=8\sin\theta\) and \(r=8+8\sin\theta\) share the same coefficient, \(8\). State how the presence or absence of the constant term tells you which family each belongs to, then find each curve’s farthest point from the pole.
SOLUTION
The rule is structural, not about the size of the coefficient: a bare \(r=2a\sin\theta\) (no added constant) is always a circle passing through the pole, while a constant added equal to the coefficient, \(r=a\pm a\sin\theta\), is always a cardioid with its cusp at the pole. The same number \(8\) plays two different roles in the two equations — as \(2a\) in the circle (so \(a=4\)) and as both the constant and the coefficient in the cardioid (so \(a=8\)) — which is exactly why one added term produces such a different shape.

Circle \(r=8\sin\theta\): maximum \(r\) is \(8\), at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\) (this is the point diametrically opposite the pole on the circle, since \(2a=8\)).
Cardioid \(r=8+8\sin\theta\): maximum \(r\) is \(8+8(1)=16\), also at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\).
Final Answer: No constant term ⇒ circle (farthest point \(8\), at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\)); constant equal to the coefficient ⇒ cardioid (farthest point \(16\), at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\)).
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
A polar curve has equation \(r=2a\cos\theta\) for an unknown positive constant \(a\), and it is known to pass through the rectangular point \((6,0)\). Find \(a\), then determine whether \((6,0)\) is the pole, the circle’s farthest point from the pole, or neither — and justify your answer.
SOLUTION
The point \((6,0)\) lies on the positive polar axis, so in polar form it is \((r,\theta)=(6,0)\). Substitute into the equation: \[ 6 = 2a\cos(0) = 2a(1) = 2a \;\Rightarrow\; a=3 \] so the circle is \(r=6\cos\theta\), with center \((a,0)=(3,0)\) and radius \(|a|=3\) — a circle passing through the pole and spanning the polar axis from the pole out to \((6,0)\).

Is \((6,0)\) the pole, the farthest point, or neither? The maximum value of \(r=6\cos\theta\) over all \(\theta\) is \(6\), attained exactly at \(\theta=0\) (since \(\cos\theta\le1\)) — which is precisely the point \((6,0)\). Since this circle passes through the pole (at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\), where \(r=0\)), the point diametrically opposite the pole on the circle is its farthest point from the pole, and that is exactly \((6,0)\). It is not the pole itself (the pole is the origin, distance \(0\)), and since it is confirmed to be the maximum-\(r\) point, "neither" does not apply.
Final Answer: \(a=3\); \((6,0)\) is the circle’s farthest point from the pole (the point diametrically opposite the pole along the polar axis), not the pole itself.
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
For Problems 4 and 5, tracing r = 7+7cos(theta) and r = 2-2sin(theta) in Desmos should show the cusp sitting exactly at the pole in the stated direction, and the farthest point at the stated distance. For Problem 7, graphing r = 6cos(theta) should visibly pass through both the pole and the point \((6,0)\).
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound — watch specifically for the signature error of confusing which angle gives the cusp (\(r=0\)) versus which angle gives the farthest point (\(r\) maximum), and for skipping the required completing-the-square verification in Problem 2. Release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).

Lesson 8-5
Answer Key: Classifying the Snails
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1
Classify and locate: Classify \(r=1+5\cos\theta\) using the ratio \(\frac{a}{b}\), then find every angle \(\theta\in[0,2\pi)\) where \(r=0\).
SOLUTION
Here \(a=1\), \(b=5\), so \(\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac{1}{5}=0.2\). Since \(\dfrac{a}{b}<1\), this limaçon has an inner loop.

Set \(r=0\): \(1+5\cos\theta=0 \Rightarrow \cos\theta=-\dfrac{1}{5}\). This has two solutions in \([0,2\pi)\): \[ \theta = \arccos\left(-\tfrac15\right) \approx 1.7722 \text{ rad} \approx 101.54^\circ \] \[ \theta = 2\pi - \arccos\left(-\tfrac15\right) \approx 4.5110 \text{ rad} \approx 258.46^\circ \]
Final Answer: \(\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac15<1\) — inner-loop limaçon. \(r=0\) at \(\theta\approx1.77\) rad and \(\theta\approx4.51\) rad.
PROBLEM 2
Classify and verify: Classify \(r=4+3\sin\theta\), then show algebraically that \(r\) never equals \(0\) for any \(\theta\).
SOLUTION
Here \(a=4\), \(b=3\), so \(\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac{4}{3}\approx1.33\). Since \(1<\dfrac{a}{b}<2\), this is a dimpled limaçon.

Setting \(r=0\): \(4+3\sin\theta=0 \Rightarrow \sin\theta=-\dfrac{4}{3}\). But \(-1\le\sin\theta\le1\) for every real \(\theta\), and \(-\dfrac43\approx-1.33\) falls outside that range. No value of \(\theta\) can satisfy this equation, so \(r\) is never \(0\) — the curve never touches the pole, consistent with a dimple (a pinch, not a loop).
Final Answer: \(\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac43\) — dimpled limaçon. \(\sin\theta=-\dfrac43\) is impossible, so \(r\ne0\) for any \(\theta\).
PROBLEM 3
Classify: Classify \(r=5+2\cos\theta\), stating the ratio \(\frac{a}{b}\) and comparing it to the convex boundary.
SOLUTION
Here \(a=5\), \(b=2\), so \(\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac{5}{2}=2.5\). The convex boundary is \(\dfrac{a}{b}\ge2\); since \(2.5\ge2\), this limaçon is convex — smooth and egg-shaped all the way around, with no dimple and no loop.
Final Answer: \(\dfrac{a}{b}=2.5\ge2\) — convex limaçon.
PROBLEM 4
Graph a lemniscate: For \(r^2=9\cos2\theta\), find \(a\), state the domain (the values of \(\theta\in[0,2\pi)\) where the curve is defined), and build a table of \(r\) at \(\theta=0,\ \frac{\pi}{12},\ \frac{\pi}{6}\).
SOLUTION
Matching \(r^2=a^2\cos2\theta\): \(a^2=9 \Rightarrow a=3\).

Domain. Real \(r\) requires \(\cos2\theta\ge0\). Over \(\theta\in[0,2\pi)\), the argument \(2\theta\) ranges over \([0,4\pi)\), and \(\cos(2\theta)\ge0\) exactly where \(2\theta\in[0,\frac\pi2]\cup[\frac{3\pi}{2},\frac{5\pi}{2}]\cup[\frac{7\pi}{2},4\pi)\). Dividing by \(2\): \[ \theta\in\left[0,\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right]\cup\left[\tfrac{3\pi}{4},\tfrac{5\pi}{4}\right]\cup\left[\tfrac{7\pi}{4},2\pi\right) \]
Table. \[ \theta=0:\ r^2=9\cos0=9 \Rightarrow r=\pm3 \] \[ \theta=\tfrac{\pi}{12}:\ r^2=9\cos\tfrac{\pi}{6}=9\left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\approx7.794 \Rightarrow r\approx\pm2.792 \] \[ \theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6}:\ r^2=9\cos\tfrac{\pi}{3}=9\left(\tfrac12\right)=4.5 \Rightarrow r\approx\pm2.121 \]
Final Answer: \(a=3\). Domain: \(\theta\in[0,\frac{\pi}{4}]\cup[\frac{3\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{4}]\cup[\frac{7\pi}{4},2\pi)\). Table: \(r=\pm3,\ \pm2.792,\ \pm2.121\).
PROBLEM 5
Find the domain: State the interval(s) of \(\theta\in[0,2\pi)\) for which \(r^2=25\sin2\theta\) is defined.
SOLUTION
Real \(r\) requires \(\sin2\theta\ge0\). Over \(2\theta\in[0,4\pi)\), \(\sin(2\theta)\ge0\) exactly where \(2\theta\in[0,\pi]\cup[2\pi,3\pi]\). Dividing by \(2\): \[ \theta\in\left[0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\cup\left[\pi,\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\right] \]
Final Answer: \(\theta\in\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\cup\left[\pi,\frac{3\pi}{2}\right]\)
PROBLEM 6 — Explain why
In two or three sentences, explain why \(r^2=a^2\cos2\theta\) has no real points for values of \(\theta\) where \(\cos2\theta<0\), reasoning from what solving for \(r\) requires.
MODEL SOLUTION
Solving \(r^2=a^2\cos2\theta\) for \(r\) requires taking a square root: \(r=\pm a\sqrt{\cos2\theta}\). A square root of a real number is only real when the number under the radical is nonnegative, so this equation only produces a real value of \(r\) when \(\cos2\theta\ge0\). When \(\cos2\theta<0\), the right-hand side \(a^2\cos2\theta\) is negative, and no real number squared can equal a negative number — so there is simply no real \(r\) at that angle, and the curve has no point there at all (not a point at the origin, not a point anywhere).
Final Answer: Because \(r^2\) can never be negative, \(\cos2\theta<0\) would force \(r^2<0\), which has no real solution — so those angles simply lie outside the curve's domain.
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
For \(r=3+5\cos\theta\), find the two angles (to the nearest hundredth of a radian, or in exact form if possible) where the curve crosses the pole, then find the angular width of the inner loop — the difference between those two angles. Explain in one sentence what that angular width represents.
SOLUTION
Here \(a=3\), \(b=5\), so \(\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac35<1\) — an inner-loop limaçon, as expected. Set \(r=0\): \[ 3+5\cos\theta=0 \Rightarrow \cos\theta=-\tfrac35 \] \[ \theta_1=\arccos\left(-\tfrac35\right)\approx2.2143\text{ rad}\ (126.87^\circ), \qquad \theta_2=2\pi-\theta_1\approx4.0689\text{ rad}\ (233.13^\circ) \] Angular width of the inner loop: \[ \theta_2-\theta_1 \approx 4.0689-2.2143 = 1.8546\text{ rad}\ (\approx106.26^\circ) \] (Equivalently, using \(\arccos(-x)=\pi-\arccos(x)\), this simplifies exactly to \(2\arccos\left(\frac35\right)\).) Between \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) (the stretch containing \(\theta=\pi\), where \(\cos\theta\) is very negative), \(r\) is negative, and this is exactly the interval of \(\theta\) that traces the inner loop.
Final Answer: Pole crossings at \(\theta\approx2.21\) rad and \(\theta\approx4.07\) rad; angular width \(\approx1.85\) rad (\(106.26^\circ\)) — this is the range of \(\theta\) over which \(r\) is negative and the inner loop is actually traced.
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
Problem 1's curve should show a visible small loop tucked inside the larger outer loop, crossing the pole at the two angles found. Problem 2's curve should never touch the pole at all — only a shallow dimple on one side. Problem 3's curve should be a smooth, egg-like convex shape with no dimple. Problem 4 (r^2 = 9cos(2theta)) should show a figure-eight along the polar axis with blank directions exactly matching the excluded domain; Problem 5's curve should sit along the \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}\) diagonal instead. Problem 7's inner loop should visibly sit inside the outer loop, spanning the same angular range computed above.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound. Watch specifically for students skipping the ratio \(\frac{a}{b}\) step and classifying a limaçon "by eye" instead, and for students who solve the lemniscate domain by guessing rather than by requiring the radicand to be nonnegative. Release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).

Lesson
Lesson 8-6
Keys To
Assignment 8-6 · Practice Set: Predicting Petals
Practice Set · Completion-Scored · includes VR deliverable
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 8-6
Answer Key: Predicting Petals
Full worked solutions for all 6 problems, for grading and self-correction release. The required VR artifact has no single correct answer — see the completion checklist below in place of a fabricated student narration.
🥽 VR ARTIFACT — completion checklist, not a scored answer
The Polar Garden VR Session's two required deliverables (a whiteboard predictions-vs-outcomes snapshot and a narrated spatial-recording link) have no single correct student narration, so this key gives you what to look for rather than an invented example. Do not deduct for phrasing — check for the presence and correctness of these items:
  • Whiteboard predictions-vs-outcomes snapshot present, showing both the \(n=3\) and \(n=4\) predictions written before the outcome, each beside its actual result. The correct outcomes the snapshot must show: \(n=3\) (odd) → 3 petals; \(n=4\) (even) → 8 petals. A prediction of anything other than these two values, if left uncorrected on the sticky note, means the student did not actually verify the outcome in-headset — flag for a quick follow-up conversation rather than a deduction on this completion-scored item.
  • Five labeled garden beds visible in the snapshot's background (circles, cardioids, limaçons, lemniscates, roses), confirming the full polar-family arrangement was completed, not skipped.
  • Shareable recording link present and the link actually resolves to a spatial recording (not a broken or placeholder link). The recording should be a genuine 30–60 second narration explaining, in the student's own words, why \(n=3\) produced only \(3\) petals while \(n=4\) produced \(8\) — the core idea being that for odd \(n\) the negative-\(r\) stretches retrace petals already drawn, while for even \(n\) they land in new, previously unvisited directions (see this lesson's own Common Mistake box). A recording that only states the petal counts without any reasoning about why should be treated as incomplete, the same as a blank written explanation elsewhere on this set.
  • Both artifacts are placed as their own labeled pages at the end of the PDF, after Problem 6, per the submission instructions.
Full credit for this component is presence + genuine content, exactly as with any other completion-scored piece of this assignment.
PROBLEM 1
Predict and verify: Predict the petal count of \(r=\cos(5\theta)\), then build a table of \(r\) at \(\theta=0,\frac{\pi}{10},\frac{\pi}{5}\) to confirm where the first petal begins and ends.
SOLUTION
Predict: \(n=5\) is odd, so the parity rule predicts \(5\) petals.

Verify. \[ \theta=0:\ r=\cos0=1 \qquad \theta=\tfrac{\pi}{10}:\ r=\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2}=0 \qquad \theta=\tfrac{\pi}{5}:\ r=\cos\pi=-1 \] The first petal runs from \(\theta=0\) (the petal's tip, \(r=1\)) to \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{10}\) (where \(r=0\), the petal's edge). From \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{10}\) onward \(r\) goes negative, and (as with every odd-\(n\) rose) that negative-\(r\) stretch reflects back onto a petal already drawn rather than opening a new one.
Final Answer: 5 petals. First petal spans \(\theta=0\) (tip) to \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{10}\) (edge).
PROBLEM 2
Predict and verify: Predict the petal count of \(r=\cos(6\theta)\), then build a table of \(r\) at \(\theta=0,\frac{\pi}{12},\frac{\pi}{6}\) to confirm your prediction.
SOLUTION
Predict: \(n=6\) is even, so the parity rule predicts \(2n=12\) petals.

Verify. \[ \theta=0:\ r=\cos0=1 \qquad \theta=\tfrac{\pi}{12}:\ r=\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2}=0 \qquad \theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6}:\ r=\cos\pi=-1 \] The first petal runs from \(\theta=0\) to \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{12}\). Because \(n=6\) is even, the subsequent negative-\(r\) stretch (from \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{12}\) to \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}\)) opens a genuinely new direction rather than retracing — consistent with all \(12\) potential petals surviving as distinct loops.
Final Answer: 12 petals.
PROBLEM 3
Predict without a table: State the petal count of \(r=3\sin(9\theta)\) and of \(r=3\sin(10\theta)\), using the parity rule alone.
SOLUTION
\(r=3\sin(9\theta)\): \(n=9\) is odd \(\Rightarrow n=9\) petals. \(r=3\sin(10\theta)\): \(n=10\) is even \(\Rightarrow 2n=20\) petals. In both cases the amplitude \(a=3\) sets each petal's length only, never its count.
Final Answer: \(r=3\sin(9\theta)\): 9 petals. \(r=3\sin(10\theta)\): 20 petals.
PROBLEM 4
Compare: Compare \(r=\sin(3\theta)\) and \(r=\cos(3\theta)\). Do they have the same petal count? Do their petals point in the same directions? Justify with the location of each curve's first maximum.
SOLUTION
Both have \(n=3\) (odd), so both have exactly \(3\) petals — same count.

First maximum of \(r=\cos(3\theta)\): occurs where \(3\theta=0\), i.e. \(\theta=0\), so its first petal points directly along the polar axis.
First maximum of \(r=\sin(3\theta)\): occurs where \(3\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\), i.e. \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}\), so its first petal points \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) (\(30^\circ\)) away from the polar axis.

Using the identity \(\sin(3\theta)=\cos\!\left(3\theta-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=\cos\!\left(3\left(\theta-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)\), the sine curve is exactly the cosine curve rotated by \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). So the petals do not point in the same directions.
Final Answer: Same petal count (3 each); different directions — \(r=\sin(3\theta)\) is \(r=\cos(3\theta)\) rotated \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) (\(30^\circ\)).
PROBLEM 5 — Explain why
In three or four sentences, explain why the petals traced when \(r\) is negative land on top of already-drawn petals for odd \(n\), but land in new directions for even \(n\).
MODEL SOLUTION
A negative value of \(r\) at angle \(\theta\) plots at the same location as the positive value \(-r\) at angle \(\theta+\pi\). For \(r=\cos(n\theta)\), shifting \(\theta\) by \(\pi\) gives \(r(\theta+\pi)=\cos(n\theta+n\pi)=(-1)^n\cos(n\theta)=(-1)^n r(\theta)\). When \(n\) is odd, \((-1)^n=-1\), so \(r(\theta+\pi)=-r(\theta)\) — meaning the point traced at \(\theta+\pi\) with value \(-r(\theta)\) lands at the very same point as \(r(\theta)\) at angle \(\theta\); the second half of the sweep exactly retraces the first. When \(n\) is even, \((-1)^n=1\), so \(r(\theta+\pi)=r(\theta)\) — the same \(r\)-value now appears at the diametrically opposite angle \(\theta+\pi\), a genuinely different point, so the negative-\(r\) stretches open new directions instead of retracing.
Final Answer: Because \(r(\theta+\pi)=(-1)^n r(\theta)\): odd \(n\) flips the sign, sending the reflected point back onto an already-drawn petal; even \(n\) keeps the sign, sending it to a genuinely new direction.
PROBLEM 6 — Honors stretch
A single petal of \(r=a\cos(n\theta)\) spans an angular width of \(\frac{\pi}{n}\) in \(\theta\) (from one zero of \(r\) to the next). Use this fact to find the angular width of one petal of \(r=\cos(3\theta)\), then confirm it against your own reasoning about where \(r=\cos(3\theta)\) first returns to \(0\). Explain in one sentence why multiplying this width by the petal count from the parity rule does not always recover exactly \(\pi\) or \(2\pi\), depending on whether \(n\) is odd or even.
SOLUTION
Width from the formula: \(n=3 \Rightarrow \dfrac{\pi}{n}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\).

Confirm. The first petal of \(r=\cos(3\theta)\) is centered at \(\theta=0\) (where \(r=1\), the tip). The first zero after \(\theta=0\) occurs at \(3\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\), i.e. \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}\) — this is only the half-width from the petal's center to its edge. By symmetry the petal also extends from \(\theta=-\frac{\pi}{6}\) to \(\theta=0\), so its full width is \(\frac{\pi}{6}-\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{\pi}{3}\), matching the formula exactly.

Why the product isn't fixed at \(\pi\) or \(2\pi\) uniformly: for odd \(n\), (width)\(\times\)(count) \(=\dfrac{\pi}{n}\times n=\pi\), while for even \(n\), (width)\(\times\)(count) \(=\dfrac{\pi}{n}\times2n=2\pi\) — two different totals, because (per Problem 5) an odd-\(n\) rose only needs half of a full revolution (\(\pi\), not \(2\pi\)) to trace all of its distinct petals once each, since the second half of the sweep exactly retraces the first; an even-\(n\) rose needs the full \(2\pi\), since every part of the sweep produces a genuinely new petal.
Final Answer: Petal width \(=\frac{\pi}{3}\), confirmed by the distance from \(\theta=-\frac{\pi}{6}\) to \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}\). The product is \(\pi\) for odd \(n\) (half a revolution suffices, since the second half retraces) but \(2\pi\) for even \(n\) (the full revolution is needed, since nothing retraces) — so there is no single fixed total; it depends on parity.
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
Problems 1–3 should show exactly the predicted petal count when graphed; dragging a slider for \(n\) in r = cos(n theta) from \(1\) through \(10\) should visibly confirm the odd-matches-\(n\), even-doubles-\(n\) pattern for every value. Problem 4's two curves should look identical in size and shape but rotated \(30^\circ\) relative to each other.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for the VR artifact (per the completion checklist above) plus a genuine, visible attempt at all 6 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the parity reasoning is sound — watch specifically for students who state a petal count only after building the table (reversing the required predict-then-verify order) rather than before. Release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).
