Polar Coordinates & Parametric Equations
Lesson
Lesson 8-7
Keys To
Assignment 8-7 · Focus Set: Reading the Clock Inside the Curve
⭐ Focus Assignment · Method-Graded (2 problems)
Points
Assignment
16 pts
Lesson 8-7
Answer Key: Reading the Clock Inside the Curve
Full worked solutions for all 6 problems. Problems 3 and 4 carry gold-badged scoring guidance for the rubric — those are the only two problems graded for method; the rest are checked for honest completion.
PROBLEM 1 — Warmup
Build a table for \(x=2t+1\), \(y=-t+4\) at \(t=-2,-1,0,1,2\), and state the orientation in words.
SOLUTION
\[ \begin{array}{c|ccccc} t & -2 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ \hline x=2t+1 & -3 & -1 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ y=-t+4 & 6 & 5 & 4 & 3 & 2 \end{array} \] As \(t\) increases, \(x\) increases steadily (\(-3\to-1\to1\to3\to5\)) while \(y\) decreases steadily (\(6\to5\to4\to3\to2\)). The point moves to the right and downward the whole way — consistent with the line's constant slope of \(-\frac12\).
Final Answer: Table above; orientation is rightward and downward (from upper-left toward lower-right) as \(t\) increases.
PROBLEM 2 — Warmup
Build a table for \(x=t^2-2\), \(y=t\) at \(t=-2,-1,0,1,2\), and describe in one or two sentences how the direction of motion changes partway through.
SOLUTION
\[ \begin{array}{c|ccccc} t & -2 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ \hline x=t^2-2 & 2 & -1 & -2 & -1 & 2 \\ y=t & -2 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \end{array} \] The \(y\)-value increases steadily throughout (\(-2\to2\)), but \(x\) first decreases from \(t=-2\) to \(t=0\) (from \(2\) down to \(-2\), the vertex), then increases from \(t=0\) to \(t=2\) (back up to \(2\)). The curve is a sideways parabola (\(x=y^2-2\)): the point moves left and up until it reaches the vertex \((-2,0)\) at \(t=0\), then reverses horizontal direction and moves right and up for the rest of the sweep.
Final Answer: Table above; \(x\) decreases then increases (reversing at the vertex, \(t=0\)), while \(y\) increases throughout.
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 3
Two circles, two directions. Consider \(x=3\cos t\), \(y=3\sin t\) for \(t\in[0,2\pi]\). ① Build a table at \(t=0,\frac{\pi}{2},\pi,\frac{3\pi}{2},2\pi\). ② State the orientation, justifying it from the order the table's points are visited. ③ Build a second table for \(x=3\sin t\), \(y=3\cos t\) over the same domain at \(t=0\) and \(t=\frac{\pi}{2}\), and state whether its orientation is the same or reversed. ④ In one or two sentences, explain how two equations that trace the identical circle can have opposite orientations.
SOLUTION
① Table for \(x=3\cos t,\ y=3\sin t\). \[ \begin{array}{c|ccccc} t & 0 & \frac{\pi}{2} & \pi & \frac{3\pi}{2} & 2\pi \\ \hline x=3\cos t & 3 & 0 & -3 & 0 & 3 \\ y=3\sin t & 0 & 3 & 0 & -3 & 0 \end{array} \] ② Orientation. The points are visited in the order \((3,0)\to(0,3)\to(-3,0)\to(0,-3)\to(3,0)\): starting on the positive \(x\)-axis, moving up into the top of the circle, across to the negative \(x\)-axis, down to the bottom, and back — this is counterclockwise motion.

③ Second table for \(x=3\sin t,\ y=3\cos t\). \[ \begin{array}{c|cc} t & 0 & \frac{\pi}{2} \\ \hline x=3\sin t & 0 & 3 \\ y=3\cos t & 3 & 0 \end{array} \] The points are visited in the order \((0,3)\to(3,0)\) — moving from the top of the circle down to the right side. This is exactly the reverse order of the first curve's opening move (which went from the right side up to the top), so this orientation is reversed (clockwise).

④ Why the reversal happens: swapping the roles of sine and cosine is equivalent to reflecting the parametrization across the line \(y=x\) (or, algebraically, replacing \(t\) with \(\frac{\pi}{2}-t\), which reverses the direction \(t\) effectively runs). Both equations trace the same set of points \(x^2+y^2=9\), but running the angle backward relative to the first parametrization flips the direction of travel from counterclockwise to clockwise.
Final Answer: \(x=3\cos t,\ y=3\sin t\) is counterclockwise; \(x=3\sin t,\ y=3\cos t\) is clockwise (reversed), because swapping sine and cosine reflects the parametrization and reverses the direction \(t\) sweeps the angle.
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): both tables are computed correctly, the first orientation is correctly identified as counterclockwise, and the second is correctly identified as clockwise (reversed). (2): tables correct but one orientation is misjudged. (0): orientation is guessed or read off a mental image of the circle rather than from the table's actual point order.

Reasoning (4): the orientation claim in part ② is justified explicitly by naming the sequence of quadrants/axis points visited (not just asserted), and part ④'s explanation correctly connects the sine/cosine swap to a reflection that reverses direction. (2): the correct orientation is stated but the justification just restates the answer without pointing to the table's order. (0): no real justification connecting the table to the direction claim.

Presentation & precision (4): both tables are clearly labeled by \(t\), the four labeled parts are easy to find in order, and the orientation statements are unambiguous (a reader does not have to guess which way "counterclockwise" refers to). (2): organized with a minor labeling lapse. (0): tables or orientation statements are hard to locate or distinguish.

Intellectual honesty (4): both tables show genuine substitution work, not just final values; the explanation in part ④ is a real argument, not a restated conclusion. (2): tables shown but the explanation is thin or assumed. (0): the orientation appears reverse-engineered from a picture rather than derived from the tables actually built.
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 4
The moving ball. A ball's position \(t\) seconds after being thrown is \(x(t)=15t\), \(y(t)=-16t^2+20t+5\) (feet), for \(t\in[0,1.5]\). ① Find the ball's position at \(t=0.5\) and at \(t=1\), showing full substitution. ② State what \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\) each represent physically. ③ Determine, using only your two computed \(y\)-values, whether the ball is net rising or net falling between \(t=0.5\) and \(t=1\), and justify your answer by comparing the two heights directly. ④ In one or two sentences, explain why \(t\) must represent the same instant in both equations at once, rather than being two separate, unrelated labels.
SOLUTION
① Position at \(t=0.5\). \[ x(0.5)=15(0.5)=7.5, \qquad y(0.5)=-16(0.5)^2+20(0.5)+5=-16(0.25)+10+5=-4+10+5=11 \] Position: \((7.5,\ 11)\) feet.
Position at \(t=1\). \[ x(1)=15(1)=15, \qquad y(1)=-16(1)^2+20(1)+5=-16+20+5=9 \] Position: \((15,\ 9)\) feet.

② \(x(t)\) is the ball's horizontal distance traveled (feet) at time \(t\); \(y(t)\) is the ball's height above the ground (feet) at time \(t\).

③ At \(t=0.5\), height \(=11\) ft; at \(t=1\), height \(=9\) ft. Since \(9<11\), the height decreased over this interval — the ball is net falling between \(t=0.5\) and \(t=1\).

④ \(t\) is the actual time elapsed since the ball was thrown, and the ball occupies exactly one horizontal position and one height at any given instant. If \(t\) were two separate, unrelated labels, the pairs \((x,y)\) would not correspond to where the ball really was at any real moment — the whole point of a shared parameter is that \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\) are evaluated at the identical instant, so together they give the ball's one true position at that time.
Final Answer: Position at \(t=0.5\): \((7.5,11)\) ft; at \(t=1\): \((15,9)\) ft. The ball is net falling between these instants (height drops from 11 ft to 9 ft). \(t\) must be shared because it is the single real-world instant at which both the horizontal and vertical positions occur simultaneously.
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): both positions are correctly computed (\((7.5,11)\) and \((15,9)\)), \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\) are correctly identified as horizontal distance and height, and the rising/falling conclusion (falling) is correct. (2): one position computed with an arithmetic slip that does not change the qualitative rising/falling conclusion, or the physical meaning of \(x(t)\)/\(y(t)\) is stated imprecisely. (0): substitution errors change the conclusion (e.g., ball reported as rising), or \(x\) and \(y\)'s physical roles are swapped.

Reasoning (4): the rising/falling verdict in part ③ is justified by directly comparing the two numeric heights (not by re-deriving calculus or guessing from the equation's shape), and part ④'s explanation correctly argues from \(t\) representing one shared instant. (2): correct verdict but the comparison of the two heights is implicit rather than stated. (0): verdict asserted without reference to the two computed values.

Presentation & precision (4): all four parts are clearly labeled and easy to follow in order; both positions are stated with correct units (feet); the substitution work for each is fully shown. (2): organized with a minor labeling or units lapse. (0): scattered; substitution work cannot be followed.

Intellectual honesty (4): both substitutions are genuinely carried out and shown, not just stated as answers; the falling/rising verdict follows transparently from the shown numbers. (2): final positions given but intermediate substitution steps are skipped. (0): the verdict appears asserted first and the "computed" values adjusted to match it.
PROBLEM 5 — The AI cross-examination
Give your AI tutor the parametric equations \(x=\cos(2t)\), \(y=\sin(2t)\) for \(t\in[0,2\pi]\), with the instruction: “State the orientation of this curve and how many times it traces the unit circle over this interval, showing your reasoning.” Copy the AI's response onto your page, then write your own verdict, checking both claims with your own table at \(t=0,\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{2}\).
GRADING GUIDANCE (no single correct answer — the response is student-generated)
The correct, independently-derived answer to check the student's verdict against: \[ \begin{array}{c|ccc} t & 0 & \frac{\pi}{4} & \frac{\pi}{2} \\ \hline x=\cos(2t) & 1 & 0 & -1 \\ y=\sin(2t) & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{array} \] The points \((1,0)\to(0,1)\to(-1,0)\) move counterclockwise, at double the usual angular speed (since the argument is \(2t\)). As \(t\) sweeps from \(0\) to \(2\pi\), the argument \(2t\) sweeps from \(0\) to \(4\pi\) — two full revolutions — so the curve traces the unit circle twice, counterclockwise.
There is no fixed "correct" AI response to check against — what is graded is the judging. Look for:
  • An actual AI response copied onto the page (not fabricated or trivial).
  • A verdict that engages the mathematics specifically: if the AI misreports the direction, the number of trips (a common error is reporting only one trip, missing the doubled argument), or both, the student should catch this and show the correct table and the correct values (counterclockwise, twice); if the AI's answer is already correct, the student should confirm it independently with their own table and say so.
  • Either outcome earns full credit: a sound correction of a bad AI claim, or a genuine independent confirmation of a correct one. What must not appear is a verdict that merely restates "the AI is right" or "the AI is wrong" without the student's own table to back it up.
Final Answer: Grade for the quality of the judgment (was the table actually built before ruling on the AI's claim?), not for which side of the argument the student lands on. Independently verified correct value: counterclockwise, tracing the unit circle twice over \(t\in[0,2\pi]\).
PROBLEM 6 — Honors stretch
Consider \(x=t-\sin t\), \(y=1-\cos t\) for \(t\in[0,2\pi]\) (you do not need to eliminate the parameter). ① Build a table at \(t=0,\frac{\pi}{2},\pi,\frac{3\pi}{2},2\pi\). ② State whether \(x\) ever decreases as \(t\) increases across this table, and what that tells you about the curve's orientation. ③ Describe, in one or two sentences, the shape the table suggests — where the curve reaches its greatest height, and where it returns to \(y=0\).
SOLUTION
① Table. \[ \begin{array}{c|ccccc} t & 0 & \frac{\pi}{2} & \pi & \frac{3\pi}{2} & 2\pi \\ \hline x=t-\sin t & 0 & \frac{\pi}{2}-1\approx0.571 & \pi\approx3.142 & \frac{3\pi}{2}+1\approx5.712 & 2\pi\approx6.283 \\ y=1-\cos t & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \end{array} \] ② \(x\) increases at every step of this table (\(0\to0.571\to3.142\to5.712\to6.283\)) — it never decreases. Since \(x\) is always moving rightward across the table, the curve is traced left-to-right without ever backtracking, at least at these sampled points (indeed \(\frac{dx}{dt}=1-\cos t\ge0\) for every \(t\), so this holds for the whole curve, not just the table).

③ The table suggests an arch shape: the curve starts at \((0,0)\), rises to its greatest height \(y=2\) at the midpoint \(t=\pi\) (where \(x=\pi\)), then descends symmetrically back down to \(y=0\) at \(t=2\pi\) (where \(x=2\pi\)) — a single rounded arch sitting on the \(x\)-axis between \(x=0\) and \(x=2\pi\), like one hump of a wheel rolling along the ground (this is in fact the cycloid).
Final Answer: \(x\) never decreases across the table — motion is consistently left-to-right, no backtracking. The curve forms one arch: rising from \((0,0)\) to its peak \(y=2\) at \(t=\pi\), then falling back to \(y=0\) at \(t=2\pi\).
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
For Problem 3, tracing (3cos(t), 3sin(t)) and (3sin(t), 3cos(t)) from \(t=0\) to \(2\pi\) with Desmos's \(t\)-slider should visibly move in opposite rotational directions. For Problem 4, tracing (15t, -16t^2+20t+5) from \(t=0\) to \(1.5\) should show the ball's parabolic path, with the traced point sitting exactly at \((7.5,11)\) when \(t=0.5\) and at \((15,9)\) when \(t=1\). For Problem 6, tracing (t - sin(t), 1 - cos(t)) should show a single rounded arch matching the table.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Focus Assignment — 16 pts, method-graded on Problems 3 and 4 only)
Problems 1, 2, 5, and 6 are checked for honest, visible completion only — do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound, and release this key after the due date for self-correction. Problems 3 and 4, the two ⭐ method problems, carry the entire 16-point rubric (Understanding / Reasoning / Presentation & Precision / Intellectual Honesty, 4 pts each). Budget roughly 1–2 minutes per student for the two method problems, per the course's designated-problems-only grading model. The most common fatal error in Problem 3 is asserting an orientation "by eye" from a mental picture of the circle instead of reading it off the table's own point order; the most common fatal error in Problem 4 is reversing which of \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\) represents height versus horizontal distance, or concluding "rising" by misreading which of the two computed heights is larger.

Quarter / Unit

Polar Coordinates & Parametric Equations
Lesson
Lesson 8-8
Keys To
Assignment 8-8 · Practice Set: Translating Back
Practice Set · Completion-Scored
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 8-8
Answer Key: Translating Back
Full worked solutions for all 6 problems, for grading and self-correction release.
PROBLEM 1
Eliminate the parameter: \(x=t-3\), \(y=4t+2\), \(t\) any real number. State whether any restriction applies.
SOLUTION
Solve the first equation for \(t\): \(t=x+3\). Substitute into the second: \[ y=4(x+3)+2=4x+12+2=4x+14 \] Since \(t\) ranges over all real numbers, and \(x=t-3\) also takes every real value as \(t\) does, no restriction is introduced — the rectangular equation describes the entire line.
Final Answer: \(y=4x+14\), no restriction.
PROBLEM 2
Eliminate with a restriction: \(x=\sqrt{t}\), \(y=t-5\), \(t\ge0\). State the domain restriction on \(x\), and check your rectangular equation against the point produced at \(t=9\).
SOLUTION
Since \(x=\sqrt{t}\), squaring gives \(t=x^2\). Substitute into \(y=t-5\): \[ y=x^2-5 \] Because \(x=\sqrt{t}\) is a principal square root, \(x\ge0\) always — this restriction must be carried forward: \(y=x^2-5,\ x\ge0\).

Check at \(t=9\): from the original equations, \(x=\sqrt9=3\), \(y=9-5=4\), so the point is \((3,4)\). Testing this point in the rectangular equation: \(y=3^2-5=9-5=4\). ✓ Matches.
Final Answer: \(y=x^2-5\), \(x\ge0\). Check at \(t=9\): point \((3,4)\) satisfies the equation.
PROBLEM 3
Eliminate using an identity: \(x=2\cos\theta\), \(y=2\sin\theta\), \(\theta\in[0,2\pi]\). Use the Pythagorean identity to find the rectangular equation.
SOLUTION
Divide each equation by \(2\): \(\dfrac{x}{2}=\cos\theta\), \(\dfrac{y}{2}=\sin\theta\). The Pythagorean identity \(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1\) gives: \[ \left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^2+\left(\frac{y}{2}\right)^2=1 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{4}=1 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; x^2+y^2=4 \] Since \(\theta\) sweeps the full \([0,2\pi]\), no piece of the circle is missing — no restriction applies.
Final Answer: \(x^2+y^2=4\), full circle, no restriction.
PROBLEM 4
Eliminate with a restricted range: \(x=2\cos\theta\), \(y=2\sin\theta\), but now \(\theta\in[\pi,2\pi]\) only. State the resulting restriction on \(y\), and check it against the point produced at \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\).
SOLUTION
As in Problem 3, eliminating the parameter still gives \(x^2+y^2=4\) — the identity doesn't know about the restricted domain. The restriction must come from examining \(y=2\sin\theta\) over \(\theta\in[\pi,2\pi]\) directly: on this interval \(\sin\theta\le0\) throughout (it is \(0\) at the endpoints \(\pi\) and \(2\pi\), and negative in between, reaching \(-1\) at \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\)). So \(y=2\sin\theta\le0\) for every \(\theta\) in this range — only the lower half of the circle is traced.

Check at \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\): \(x=2\cos\frac{3\pi}{2}=2(0)=0\), \(y=2\sin\frac{3\pi}{2}=2(-1)=-2\), so the point is \((0,-2)\). Testing: \(0^2+(-2)^2=4\). ✓ And \(y=-2\le0\), consistent with the restriction.
Final Answer: \(x^2+y^2=4,\ y\le0\) (lower semicircle only). Check at \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\): point \((0,-2)\) satisfies both the equation and the restriction.
PROBLEM 5 — Explain why
In three or four sentences, explain why eliminating the parameter from \(x=\sqrt{t}\), \(y=2t+1\) (\(t\ge0\)) and forgetting the restriction \(x\ge0\) produces an equation describing more points than the original parametrization actually draws.
MODEL SOLUTION
Squaring \(x=\sqrt{t}\) to get \(t=x^2\) is a legitimate algebraic step, but squaring is a two-to-one operation: both \(x=3\) and \(x=-3\) square to the same \(t=9\). The original parametrization only ever produces nonnegative \(x\)-values, because \(\sqrt{t}\) (the principal square root) is never negative; the substitution step, however, has no memory of that fact once \(t\) has been replaced by \(x^2\). So the equation \(y=2x^2+1\) alone is perfectly happy to accept negative \(x\)-values too, tracing a full parabola (both left and right halves), when the original parametric curve only ever drew the right half (\(x\ge0\)). Forgetting to reattach the restriction \(x\ge0\) silently doubles the set of points the equation describes.
Final Answer: Squaring \(x=\sqrt t\) to reach \(t=x^2\) loses the fact that \(x\) was always nonnegative, so the resulting equation \(y=2x^2+1\) (without \(x\ge0\)) also accepts negative \(x\), tracing both halves of the parabola instead of only the right half the original parametrization drew.
PROBLEM 6 — Honors stretch
Without eliminating the parameter algebraically, build a table for the cycloid \(x=t-\sin t\), \(y=1-\cos t\) at \(t=0,\frac{\pi}{2},\pi,\frac{3\pi}{2},2\pi\). Describe the resulting shape in two or three sentences, including where it reaches its greatest height and where it returns to \(y=0\).
SOLUTION
\[ \begin{array}{c|ccccc} t & 0 & \frac{\pi}{2} & \pi & \frac{3\pi}{2} & 2\pi \\ \hline x=t-\sin t & 0 & \frac{\pi}{2}-1\approx0.571 & \pi\approx3.142 & \frac{3\pi}{2}+1\approx5.712 & 2\pi\approx6.283 \\ y=1-\cos t & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \end{array} \] The shape is a single rounded arch: it begins at \((0,0)\), climbs steadily to its greatest height \(y=2\) at the midpoint \(t=\pi\) (where \(x=\pi\)), then descends symmetrically back down, returning to \(y=0\) at \(t=2\pi\) (where \(x=2\pi\)). This is the classic cycloid arch — the path traced by a point on the rim of a wheel of radius \(1\) as it rolls one full turn along the \(x\)-axis.
Final Answer: One symmetric arch from \((0,0)\) to \((2\pi,0)\), peaking at height \(y=2\) when \(t=\pi\) (at \(x=\pi\)) and returning to \(y=0\) at \(t=2\pi\).
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
For Problem 2, graphing the parametric form and y = x^2 - 5 {x >= 0} should occupy exactly the same set of points — only the right half of the parabola. For Problem 4, graphing the parametric form and x^2 + y^2 = 4 {y <= 0} should show only the lower semicircle. For Problem 6, graphing (t - sin(t), 1 - cos(t)) with \(t\) from \(0\) to \(2\pi\) should reproduce the table's single arch exactly.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 6 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound. Watch specifically for students who eliminate the parameter correctly in Problems 2 and 4 but skip stating (or checking) the resulting restriction — that check-a-point step is the whole point of the assignment's focus question. Release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).

Keys To
Assignment 8-9 · Practice Set: Two Motions, One Clock
Practice Set · Completion-Scored
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 8-9
Answer Key: Two Motions, One Clock
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems. Every flight time, maximum height, and range below was independently re-solved from the launch data (not copied from the lesson) and numerically re-verified.
PROBLEM 1
Ground launch: \(v_0=32\) ft/s, \(\theta=30^\circ\), \(g=32\) ft/s\(^2\), from ground level. Write \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\); find flight time, maximum height, range.
SOLUTION
Components: \(v_{0x}=32\cos30^\circ=32\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}=16\sqrt3\) ft/s; \(v_{0y}=32\sin30^\circ=32\cdot\dfrac12=16\) ft/s. \[ x(t)=16\sqrt3\,t \qquad\qquad y(t)=16t-16t^2 \] Flight time — solve \(y(t)=0\): \(16t-16t^2=0 \Rightarrow 16t(1-t)=0 \Rightarrow t=0\) or \(t=1\). Flight time \(=1\) s.

Maximum height — at \(t=\dfrac{v_{0y}}{g}=\dfrac{16}{32}=0.5\) s: \(y(0.5)=16(0.5)-16(0.5)^2=8-4=4\) ft.

Range — directly: \(x(1)=16\sqrt3\approx27.71\) ft. By formula: \(R=\dfrac{32^2\sin60^\circ}{32}=32\sin60^\circ=32\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}=16\sqrt3\approx27.71\) ft — the two methods agree, as expected for a ground-to-ground launch.
Final Answer: Flight time \(1\) s; maximum height \(4\) ft at \(t=0.5\) s; range \(16\sqrt3\approx27.71\) ft.
PROBLEM 2
Ground launch, second angle: \(v_0=48\) ft/s, \(\theta=45^\circ\), \(g=32\) ft/s\(^2\). Find flight time and maximum height, exact radical values.
SOLUTION
\(v_{0x}=v_{0y}=48\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}=24\sqrt2\) ft/s. So \(y(t)=24\sqrt2\,t-16t^2\).

Flight time: \(24\sqrt2\,t-16t^2=0 \Rightarrow t\left(24\sqrt2-16t\right)=0 \Rightarrow t=\dfrac{24\sqrt2}{16}=\dfrac{3\sqrt2}{2}\) s.

Maximum height — at \(t=\dfrac{v_{0y}}{g}=\dfrac{24\sqrt2}{32}=\dfrac{3\sqrt2}{4}\) s (exactly half the flight time, as expected for a ground-to-ground launch): \[ y\!\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt2}{4}\right) = 24\sqrt2\cdot\dfrac{3\sqrt2}{4} - 16\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt2}{4}\right)^2 = 36 - 18 = 18 \text{ ft} \]
Final Answer: Flight time \(\dfrac{3\sqrt2}{2}\approx2.12\) s; maximum height \(18\) ft.
PROBLEM 3
Launch height (calculator permitted): javelin, \(h_0=5\) ft, \(v_0=50\) ft/s, \(\theta=40^\circ\), \(g=32\) ft/s\(^2\). Write \(y(t)\); solve \(y(t)=0\) with the quadratic formula for flight time to two decimals.
SOLUTION
\(v_{0y}=50\sin40^\circ\approx32.1394\) ft/s. \(y(t)=5+32.1394t-16t^2\).

Solve \(y(t)=0\), rewritten as \(16t^2-32.1394t-5=0\): \[ t=\dfrac{32.1394\pm\sqrt{(32.1394)^2+4(16)(5)}}{2(16)}=\dfrac{32.1394\pm\sqrt{1352.94}}{32}=\dfrac{32.1394\pm36.782}{32} \] The negative root, \(t\approx-0.145\) s, is not physical (time cannot run backward from launch). Keeping the positive root: \[ t=\dfrac{32.1394+36.782}{32}\approx2.15 \text{ s} \]
Final Answer: Flight time \(\approx2.15\) s.
PROBLEM 4
Range, two ways: \(v_0=80\) ft/s, \(\theta=60^\circ\), \(g=32\) ft/s\(^2\), ground launch. Find range directly and by the shortcut formula; confirm agreement and explain why they must agree.
SOLUTION
\(v_{0x}=80\cos60^\circ=40\) ft/s; \(v_{0y}=80\sin60^\circ=40\sqrt3\) ft/s. \(x(t)=40t\), \(y(t)=40\sqrt3\,t-16t^2\).

Flight time: \(40\sqrt3\,t-16t^2=0 \Rightarrow t=\dfrac{40\sqrt3}{16}=\dfrac{5\sqrt3}{2}\) s.

Range, directly: \(x\!\left(\dfrac{5\sqrt3}{2}\right)=40\cdot\dfrac{5\sqrt3}{2}=100\sqrt3\approx173.21\) ft.

Range, by formula: \(R=\dfrac{80^2\sin120^\circ}{32}=\dfrac{6400\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{32}=100\sqrt3\approx173.21\) ft.

The two methods are guaranteed to agree because the shortcut formula \(R=\frac{v_0^2\sin2\theta}{g}\) is itself derived by evaluating \(x(\text{flight time})\) for a ground-to-ground launch — it is not an independent fact, only a simplified rewriting of the same computation.
Final Answer: Range \(=100\sqrt3\approx173.21\) ft by both methods.
PROBLEM 5
Build the table for Problem 1's ball at \(t=0,\ 0.25,\ 0.5,\ 0.75,\ 1\); circle the maximum-height row and confirm it matches Problem 1.
SOLUTION
Using \(x(t)=16\sqrt3\,t\approx27.713t\) and \(y(t)=16t-16t^2\) from Problem 1:
\(t\)\(x(t)\)\(y(t)\)
000
0.25\(4\sqrt3\approx6.93\)3
0.5\(8\sqrt3\approx13.86\)4 ● max
0.75\(12\sqrt3\approx20.78\)3
1\(16\sqrt3\approx27.71\)0
The circled row, \(t=0.5\), gives \(y=4\) ft — exactly Problem 1's computed maximum height.
Final Answer: Maximum-height row: \(t=0.5\), \(y=4\) ft, matching Problem 1 exactly.
PROBLEM 6 — Explain why
Why does \(x(t)=v_0\cos\theta\cdot t\) contain no acceleration term while \(y(t)\) does? Connect to gravity acting only vertically.
MODEL SOLUTION
Once a projectile leaves the launcher, the only force acting on it (ignoring air resistance) is gravity, and gravity points straight down — it has no horizontal component at all. With no horizontal force, there is no horizontal acceleration, so the horizontal velocity \(v_{0x}\) stays exactly constant for the whole flight; that is why \(x(t)=v_{0x}t\) is a plain linear function of \(t\), with no \(t^2\) term. Vertically, the story is different: gravity constantly decelerates the object on the way up and accelerates it on the way down, which is precisely what the \(-\frac12gt^2\) term captures. Because the same single force is responsible for all of the vertical change and none of the horizontal change, the two coordinates can be modeled as genuinely independent functions of the same clock \(t\) — exactly Galileo's original insight.
Final Answer: Gravity acts only vertically, so horizontal velocity is constant (no acceleration term) while vertical velocity constantly changes (an acceleration term is required).
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
Using Problem 3's javelin, find time to maximum height via \(t_{\max}=\frac{v_0\sin\theta}{g}\); compare double this value to Problem 3's flight time; explain the discrepancy.
SOLUTION
\(t_{\max}=\dfrac{v_{0y}}{g}=\dfrac{32.1394}{32}\approx1.00\) s. Double: \(2(1.00)\approx2.01\) s.

Problem 3's actual flight time was \(\approx2.15\) s — close to \(2.01\) s, but not equal. This happens for exactly the reason Example 2 of the lesson identified: the javelin launches from \(h_0=5\) ft above the ground, so the flight is not symmetric about the moment of launch. The upward half of the motion (from \(5\) ft up to the peak) covers less vertical distance — and takes less time — than the downward half (from the peak all the way back down past \(5\) ft to \(0\)). The formula \(t_{\max}=\frac{v_0\sin\theta}{g}\) never depended on \(h_0\) (it only asks when vertical velocity is momentarily zero), but doubling it silently assumes a symmetric parabola, which a nonzero launch height breaks.
Final Answer: \(t_{\max}\approx1.00\) s; doubled \(\approx2.01\) s, versus the actual flight time \(\approx2.15\) s — the gap is caused by the nonzero launch height breaking the up/down symmetry.
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
For Problem 1, graphing \((16\sqrt3\,t,\ 16t-16t^2)\) with \(t\in[0,1]\) should peak at \(4\) ft and land exactly at \(t=1\). For Problem 4, graphing \((40t,\ 40\sqrt3\,t-16t^2)\) with \(t\in[0,\frac{5\sqrt3}{2}]\) should land at \(x\approx173.2\) ft, matching both range computations.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound — release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it. The most common miss in Problem 3 is reporting the negative root or skipping the quadratic formula in favor of a calculator's root; the most common miss in Problem 4's explanation is asserting the two methods "should" agree without naming that the shortcut formula is itself derived from the direct computation.

Practice Set · Completion-Scored
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 8-10
Answer Key: Rendezvous, Wheels, and Orbits
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems. Every rendezvous system, cycloid evaluation, and orbital-model check below was independently re-solved and re-verified against specific \(t\)-values.
PROBLEM 1
Hiker A: \(x=1+2t,\ y=3t\); Hiker B: \(x=9-2t,\ y=12-3t\). Determine whether they meet, and if so, when and where.
SOLUTION
Set the \(x\)-equations equal: \(1+2t=9-2t \Rightarrow 4t=8 \Rightarrow t=2\).

Set the \(y\)-equations equal: \(3t=12-3t \Rightarrow 6t=12 \Rightarrow t=2\).

Both equations agree on the same \(t=2\) — that agreement is the whole test for a genuine rendezvous.

Position at \(t=2\): Hiker A: \((1+4,\,6)=(5,6)\). Check Hiker B: \((9-4,\,12-6)=(5,6)\). ✓ Both agree.
Final Answer: Yes — the hikers meet at \(t=2\) hours, at position \((5,6)\).
PROBLEM 2
Drones: \(x_1=6t,\ y_1=2t\) and \(x_2=18-3t,\ y_2=1+5t\). Show the \(x\)- and \(y\)-equations demand different \(t\); explain physically.
SOLUTION
\(x\)-equation: \(6t=18-3t \Rightarrow 9t=18 \Rightarrow t=2\).

\(y\)-equation: \(2t=1+5t \Rightarrow -3t=1 \Rightarrow t=-\dfrac13\).

The two equations demand different, inconsistent values of \(t\) (\(t=2\) versus \(t=-\frac13\)), so there is no single moment at which both coordinates agree. Physically, the two drones' flight tracks may still cross somewhere in space (the way two roads cross at an intersection), but each drone passes through that crossing point at a different time — a near miss rather than a collision. The parametric requirement of one shared \(t\) is exactly what distinguishes "paths cross" from "objects meet."
Final Answer: \(x\)-equation gives \(t=2\); \(y\)-equation gives \(t=-\frac13\) — no shared \(t\), so the drones do not meet, even if their paths cross.
PROBLEM 3
A wheel of radius \(1\) ft rolls, tracing a cycloid. Find the traced point's exact position at \(t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\).
SOLUTION
With \(r=1\): \(x(t)=t-\sin t\), \(y(t)=1-\cos t\). \[ x\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{3}-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \qquad\qquad y\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 1-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = 1-\dfrac12=\dfrac12 \]
Final Answer: \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2},\ \dfrac12\right) \approx (0.18,\ 0.5)\).
PROBLEM 4
A wheel of radius \(3\) ft rolls, tracing a cycloid. Find the maximum height of one arch and its horizontal span, exact (\(\pi\)-form) values.
SOLUTION
With \(r=3\), the cycloid's maximum height is always \(2r\) (reached at \(t=\pi,3\pi,\ldots\)), and one full arch spans exactly \(2\pi r\) horizontally (the wheel's own circumference). \[ \text{Max height}=2(3)=6 \text{ ft} \qquad\qquad \text{Span}=2\pi(3)=6\pi \text{ ft} \]
Final Answer: Maximum height \(6\) ft; horizontal span \(6\pi\approx18.85\) ft.
PROBLEM 5
Orbital model \(x(t)=10\cos t,\ y(t)=6\sin t\). Find the rectangular equation; verify the point at \(t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).
SOLUTION
\(\dfrac{x}{10}=\cos t\), \(\dfrac{y}{6}=\sin t\). Squaring and adding: \(\left(\dfrac{x}{10}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{y}{6}\right)^2=\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1\), so \(\dfrac{x^2}{100}+\dfrac{y^2}{36}=1\).

At \(t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\): \(x=10\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}=5\sqrt2\), \(y=6\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}=3\sqrt2\). Check: \(\dfrac{(5\sqrt2)^2}{100}+\dfrac{(3\sqrt2)^2}{36}=\dfrac{50}{100}+\dfrac{18}{36}=0.5+0.5=1\). ✓
Final Answer: \(\dfrac{x^2}{100}+\dfrac{y^2}{36}=1\); the point \((5\sqrt2,\,3\sqrt2)\) at \(t=\frac{\pi}{4}\) satisfies it exactly.
PROBLEM 6 — Explain why
Using the cycloid's definition, explain why the traced point momentarily comes to rest each time it touches the ground, even though the wheel's center keeps moving forward at a constant speed.
MODEL SOLUTION
A wheel rolling without slipping means the point of the rim currently touching the ground is not sliding against the surface at that instant — if it were, the wheel would be skidding, not rolling. "Not sliding relative to the surface" means that point's velocity relative to the ground is exactly zero at that instant, even though every other point on the rim (and the center of the wheel) is still moving forward. As the wheel continues to turn, a different point of the rim becomes the one touching the ground, and it is that new contact point which is momentarily at rest — the "resting" role passes from one point on the rim to the next, rather than staying with any single point, which is why the traced point's own velocity drops to zero only at the specific instants it touches down.
Final Answer: Rolling without slipping means the contact point has zero velocity relative to the ground at the instant of contact, even while the wheel's center keeps moving at constant speed.
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
For Problem 5's ellipse, find the distance from the origin at \(t=0\) and \(t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\). Which is closest, which is farthest, and how does this relate to \(a=10\) versus \(b=6\)?
SOLUTION
At \(t=0\): \(x=10\cos0=10\), \(y=6\sin0=0\). Distance from origin: \(\sqrt{10^2+0^2}=10\).

At \(t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\): \(x=10\cos\frac{\pi}{2}=0\), \(y=6\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=6\). Distance from origin: \(\sqrt{0^2+6^2}=6\).

\(6<10\), so \(t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) is the closest approach and \(t=0\) is the farthest point. This lines up exactly with the semi-axes: the modeled body is closest to the center when it sits along the shorter semi-axis \(b=6\), and farthest when it sits along the longer semi-axis \(a=10\) — the ellipse's extreme distances from its center are always its two semi-axis lengths themselves.
Final Answer: Distance \(10\) at \(t=0\) (farthest); distance \(6\) at \(t=\frac{\pi}{2}\) (closest) — matching \(a=10>b=6\).
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
For Problem 1, graphing both hikers in parametric mode over \(t\in[0,3]\) should show both traced points arriving at \((5,6)\) at the identical slider value \(t=2\). For Problem 5, graphing \((10\cos t,\,6\sin t)\) and tracing should show the closest point to the origin at \(t=\frac{\pi}{2}\) (or \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\)) and the farthest at \(t=0\) (or \(\pi\)), matching Problem 7.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound — release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it. The most common miss in Problems 1–2 is testing only one coordinate equation instead of both; the most common miss in Problem 3 is dropping the \(-\sin t\) term (treating the cycloid as if \(x(t)=rt\) alone) rather than the full \(x(t)=r(t-\sin t)\).

Polar Coordinates & Parametric Equations
Lesson
Lesson 8-11
Keys To
Assignment 8-11 · Focus Set: One Curve, Every Language
⭐ Focus Assignment · Method-Graded (2 problems)
Points
Assignment
16 pts
Lesson 8-11
Answer Key: One Curve, Every Language
Full worked solutions for all 6 problems. Problems 3 and 4 carry gold-badged scoring guidance for the rubric — those are the only two problems graded for method; the rest are checked for honest completion. Every conversion below was independently re-derived and every claimed point re-verified against all three forms.
PROBLEM 1 — Warmup
Convert \(r=4\sin\theta\) to rectangular form and identify the curve completely (center and radius).
SOLUTION
Multiply both sides by \(r\): \(r^2=4r\sin\theta \Rightarrow x^2+y^2=4y\).

Complete the square: \(x^2+y^2-4y=0 \Rightarrow x^2+(y^2-4y+4)=4 \Rightarrow x^2+(y-2)^2=4\).
Final Answer: \(x^2+(y-2)^2=4\) — a circle centered at \((0,2)\) with radius \(2\).
PROBLEM 2 — Warmup
Eliminate the parameter from \(x=3+2\cos t,\ y=-1+2\sin t\) and identify the curve completely.
SOLUTION
Isolate the trig functions: \(\dfrac{x-3}{2}=\cos t\), \(\dfrac{y+1}{2}=\sin t\). Square and add, using \(\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1\): \[ \left(\dfrac{x-3}{2}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{y+1}{2}\right)^2=1 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; (x-3)^2+(y+1)^2=4 \]
Final Answer: \((x-3)^2+(y+1)^2=4\) — a circle centered at \((3,-1)\) with radius \(2\).
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 3
One curve, three languages: \(r=4\cos\theta\). Convert to rectangular (center/radius); derive a parametric form using \(\theta\) as the parameter and state its domain; verify all three forms at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}\); close with which form most quickly reveals the circle passes through the pole.
SOLUTION
① Convert to rectangular. Multiply both sides by \(r\): \(r^2=4r\cos\theta \Rightarrow x^2+y^2=4x\). Complete the square: \(x^2-4x+y^2=0 \Rightarrow (x-2)^2+y^2=4\) — a circle centered at \((2,0)\) with radius \(2\).

② Derive the parametric form. Substitute \(r=4\cos\theta\) directly into \(x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta\): \[ x(\theta)=4\cos\theta\cdot\cos\theta=4\cos^2\theta=2+2\cos2\theta \qquad y(\theta)=4\cos\theta\sin\theta=2\sin2\theta \] using the double-angle identities \(\cos^2\theta=\frac{1+\cos2\theta}{2}\) and \(2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\sin2\theta\). Because the parametrization carries a \(2\theta\), the curve closes after only half the usual sweep: domain \(0\le\theta<\pi\).

③ Verify all three forms at \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\). Polar: \(r=4\cos\frac{\pi}{4}=4\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2}=2\sqrt2\); point \(\left(2\sqrt2\cos\frac{\pi}{4},\,2\sqrt2\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=(2,2)\). Rectangular check: \((2-2)^2+2^2=4\). ✓ Parametric check: \(x=2+2\cos\frac{\pi}{2}=2+0=2\), \(y=2\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=2\). ✓ All three agree at \((2,2)\).

④ Which form reveals the pole crossing fastest? The polar form: setting \(r=0\) gives \(4\cos\theta=0 \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\) directly — the pole crossing is read off the equation in one step. The rectangular form only reveals it if you happen to test \((0,0)\) in \((x-2)^2+y^2=4\) and notice it satisfies the equation; nothing in the equation's form points you there the way \(r=0\) does.
Final Answer: Rectangular: \((x-2)^2+y^2=4\), center \((2,0)\), radius \(2\). Parametric: \(x=2+2\cos2\theta,\ y=2\sin2\theta,\ 0\le\theta<\pi\). All three forms give \((2,2)\) at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}\). The polar form reveals the pole crossing fastest, since \(r=0\) is solved directly.
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): the rectangular conversion (multiply by \(r\), complete the square) and the parametric derivation (substitute into \(x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta\), simplify with a double-angle identity) are both executed correctly, and the domain \(0\le\theta<\pi\) is stated. (2): one representation is correct but the other has a real error (e.g., forgetting to complete the square, or omitting the double-angle simplification). (0): the rectangular conversion is attempted with no direction, or \(\theta\) is not used as the parameter as instructed.

Reasoning (4): the conversion technique is named before use, and the cross-check at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}\) is actually carried out against all three forms (not merely asserted to agree), with the closing sentence genuinely comparing what each representation makes visible. (2): the verification checks only one or two of the three forms, or the closing sentence restates the answer without comparing the forms. (0): no verification shown.

Presentation & precision (4): the four numbered parts are clearly labeled and separated, center/radius stated explicitly, the domain restriction stated as its own line. (2): organized with a labeling lapse. (0): scattered; the three representations blur together.

Intellectual honesty (4): the verification is a genuine independent computation from each of the three forms, not a restatement of the algebra already used to derive them. (2): a verification is present but shortcuts one form (e.g., assuming the parametric point matches without computing it). (0): no real verification, or the point is invented to match rather than computed.
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 4
Drone holding pattern: radius \(6\) nm centered on a beacon at the pole, one loop every \(2\pi\) minutes, starting due east. Write parametric, polar, and rectangular equations; find the position at \(t=5\) min and verify it against the rectangular equation; close with what the parametric form reveals that polar alone cannot.
SOLUTION
① Parametric equations. One loop (\(2\pi\) radians) every \(2\pi\) minutes gives an angular speed of \(\dfrac{2\pi\text{ rad}}{2\pi\text{ min}}=1\) rad/min, so \(\theta(t)=t\). Starting due east (\(\theta=0\) at \(t=0\)) with radius \(6\): \[ x(t)=6\cos t \qquad\qquad y(t)=6\sin t \qquad (t \text{ in minutes}) \] ② Polar equation. \(r=6\). This is especially simple because the flight path is a circle centered exactly on the pole itself — every point on it is the same fixed distance (\(6\) nm) from the beacon, regardless of angle, so no \(\theta\)-dependence appears at all.

③ Rectangular equation. \(x^2+y^2=36\).

④ Position at \(t=5\) min. \(x(5)=6\cos(5)\approx6(0.283662)\approx1.702\); \(y(5)=6\sin(5)\approx6(-0.958924)\approx-5.754\) (5 radians). Verify: \((1.702)^2+(-5.754)^2\approx2.897+33.108\approx36.00\). ✓ (matches \(36\), within rounding.)

⑤ What parametric tells you that polar alone cannot. The polar equation \(r=6\) only records the flight path's fixed shape — that every point on it is \(6\) nm from the beacon — but it carries no information about time. The parametric form \((6\cos t,\,6\sin t)\) additionally tells you exactly where the drone is at any specific moment \(t\), which is precisely what is needed to answer "where is the drone right now?" or to check whether the drone is at a given point at a given time.
Final Answer: Parametric: \(x=6\cos t,\ y=6\sin t\). Polar: \(r=6\). Rectangular: \(x^2+y^2=36\). At \(t=5\) min: \((1.702,\ -5.754)\), satisfying \(x^2+y^2=36\).
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — 4 pts × 4 criteria)
Understanding (4): the angular speed is correctly derived from period and radius (\(\theta(t)=t\)), and all three representations (parametric, polar, rectangular) are correct. (2): the parametric setup is correct but the polar or rectangular form has an error (e.g., \(r=6\) mistakenly written with a \(\theta\)-dependence). (0): angular speed is not derived from the given period (e.g., degrees and radians are mixed, or the period is ignored).

Reasoning (4): the one-sentence explanation for why the polar form is "especially simple" explicitly names the circle being centered on the pole; the \(t=5\) computation shows the trig evaluation and the verification substitutes the computed point into the rectangular equation rather than just re-stating \(r=6\). (2): the polar simplicity explanation is present but generic ("it's just a circle"); the verification is shown but not carried to a numeric check. (0): no explanation given for the polar form's simplicity.

Presentation & precision (4): all five numbered parts are clearly separated and labeled, units (nautical miles, minutes) carried throughout, decimal answers rounded to three places as instructed. (2): organized with a labeling or rounding lapse. (0): scattered; parts cannot be told apart.

Intellectual honesty (4): the \(t=5\) verification is a genuine substitution into the rectangular equation with the actual computed decimal values, not a claim of agreement without the arithmetic shown. (2): verification shown but the small rounding discrepancy (\(\approx36.00\) rather than exactly \(36\)) is not acknowledged as expected from rounding. (0): no verification, or the position at \(t=5\) is asserted without a shown trigonometric evaluation.
PROBLEM 5
The AI cross-examination: give your problem 4 work to an AI tutor, ask it to check your parametric-to-rectangular reasoning and your position at \(t=5\), copy its response, and render your own verdict.
GRADING GUIDANCE (no single correct answer — the response is student-generated)
There is no fixed "correct" AI response to check against — what is graded is the judging. Look for:
  • An actual AI response copied onto the page (two or three sentences), not fabricated or trivial.
  • A verdict that engages the mathematics specifically. The correct position at \(t=5\) is \((1.702,-5.754)\), with \(x^2+y^2=36\). A common, plausible AI error here is treating \(t=5\) as \(5^\circ\) instead of \(5\) radians (since \(t\) was never explicitly labeled a degree measure, but the problem specifies "radians" in its instructions) — this would give the very different, wrong point \((6\cos5^\circ,\,6\sin5^\circ)\approx(5.977,\,0.523)\). If the AI makes this mistake, the student should refute it by re-substituting \(t=5\) as radians and re-checking against \(x^2+y^2=36\).
  • Either outcome earns full credit: a sound refutation of a bad AI claim, or a genuine correction if the AI catches something real (e.g., a rounding slip in the third decimal place). What must not appear is a verdict that merely restates "the AI is right" or "the AI is wrong" without checking the specific claim against the rectangular equation or a direct recomputation.
Final Answer: Grade for the quality of the judgment (was every claim actually verified against the rectangular equation or a direct recomputation before ruling?), not for which side of the argument the student lands on.
PROBLEM 6 — Honors stretch
Repeat Method Problem 3's technique on \(r=8\sin\theta\): convert to rectangular (center/radius); derive the parametric form using \(\theta\) as parameter; verify all three forms at \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).
SOLUTION
① Rectangular. Multiply by \(r\): \(r^2=8r\sin\theta \Rightarrow x^2+y^2=8y\). Complete the square: \(x^2+(y-4)^2=16\) — center \((0,4)\), radius \(4\).

② Parametric. Substitute \(r=8\sin\theta\) into \(x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta\): \[ x(\theta)=8\sin\theta\cos\theta=4\sin2\theta \qquad\qquad y(\theta)=8\sin^2\theta=4-4\cos2\theta \] using \(2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\sin2\theta\) and \(\sin^2\theta=\frac{1-\cos2\theta}{2}\). Domain: \(0\le\theta<\pi\) (same doubling logic as Problem 3).

③ Verify at \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\). Polar: \(r=8\sin\frac{\pi}{4}=8\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2}=4\sqrt2\); point \(\left(4\sqrt2\cos\frac{\pi}{4},\,4\sqrt2\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=(4,4)\). Rectangular check: \(4^2+(4-4)^2=16\). ✓ Parametric check: \(x=4\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=4\), \(y=4-4\cos\frac{\pi}{2}=4-0=4\). ✓ All three agree at \((4,4)\).
Final Answer: Rectangular: \(x^2+(y-4)^2=16\), center \((0,4)\), radius \(4\). Parametric: \(x=4\sin2\theta,\ y=4-4\cos2\theta,\ 0\le\theta<\pi\). All three forms give \((4,4)\) at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}\).
💡 DESMOS CHECK
For Problem 3, graphing \(r=4\cos\theta\) in polar mode and \((2+2\cos2t,\,2\sin2t)\) in parametric mode should sit exactly on top of each other. For Problem 4, graphing the parametric drone path \((6\cos t,\,6\sin t)\) and tracing to \(t=5\) should land at the same point as the hand computation, \(\approx(1.70,-5.75)\).
📊 GRADING NOTE (Focus Assignment — 16 pts, method-graded on Problems 3 and 4 only)
Problems 1, 2, 5, and 6 are checked for honest, visible completion only — do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound, and release this key after the due date for self-correction. Problems 3 and 4, the two ⭐ method problems, carry the entire 16-point rubric (Understanding / Reasoning / Presentation & Precision / Intellectual Honesty, 4 pts each), applied holistically across both problems together. Budget roughly 1–2 minutes per student for the two method problems, per the course's designated-problems-only grading model. The most common fatal error in Problem 3 is stopping at the rectangular form and treating the parametric derivation as optional, or forgetting to restrict the domain to \(0\le\theta<\pi\); the most common fatal error in Problem 4 is evaluating \(\cos(5)\) and \(\sin(5)\) in degree mode on a calculator instead of radian mode, which produces a plausible-looking but entirely wrong point.

Test · Rubric-Graded
Points
Test
40 pts
Unit 8 · Polar Coordinates & Parametric Equations
Answer Key: Unit 8 Test
Full worked solutions for all 11 problems (Part A: 1–8, Part B: 9–10, Part C: 11), for grading against the standing 4-criterion rubric. Every conversion, classification, and general-solution derivation below was independently re-derived and numerically re-verified — no result was taken on faith from the test page.
📊 POINT ALLOCATION SUMMARY (which problems supply evidence for which criterion)
The rubric is holistic across the whole test (each of the four criteria scored out of 10, 40 pts total) rather than problem-by-problem, but each part carries most of the weight for particular criteria:
  • Understanding of the material (10 pts): primarily Part A (1–8) — polar/rectangular point and equation conversion, negative-\(r\) plotting, cardioid/limaçon/lemniscate/rose feature identification, and parametric sketching and elimination.
  • Quality of reasoning (10 pts): primarily Part B (9–10) and Part C (11) — the limaçon classification argued from the ratio test and the computed points together (not asserted), the projectile interpretation explaining what a rectangular equation cannot tell you, and the Part C connection to Lesson 7-8's general-solution method made explicitly, not merely gestured at.
  • Presentation & precision (10 pts): distributed across all parts — neat vertical work, aligned equals signs, exact values kept in radical or \(\pi\)-form where the angle or curve is special, units carried on every applied answer.
  • Intellectual honesty (10 pts): the signed honor line plus honest handling throughout — any problem left incomplete should carry a note of where and why the student stopped, which earns credit here rather than losing it.
📝 PART A — FLUENCY
PROBLEM 1
Point conversion: ① Convert the polar point \(\left(3,\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\) to rectangular. ② Convert the rectangular point \((-2,2\sqrt3)\) to polar, \(r>0\), \(0\le\theta<2\pi\).
SOLUTION
① \(x=3\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=3\left(-\dfrac12\right)=-\dfrac32\); \(y=3\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=3\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}\).

② \(r=\sqrt{(-2)^2+(2\sqrt3)^2}=\sqrt{4+12}=\sqrt{16}=4\). Reference angle: \(\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{2\sqrt3}{2}\right)=\tan^{-1}\sqrt3=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\). The point \((-2,2\sqrt3)\) lies in Quadrant II (\(x<0\), \(y>0\)), so \(\theta=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\). Check: \(4\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}=-2\) ✓, \(4\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}=2\sqrt3\) ✓.
Final Answer: ① \(\left(-\dfrac32,\ \dfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}\right)\). ② \(\left(4,\ \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)\).
PROBLEM 2
Negative \(r\): plot \(\left(-2,\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) by finding its equivalent positive-\(r\) form, then convert to rectangular. Show both steps.
SOLUTION
A negative-\(r\) point \((-r,\theta)\) plots at the same location as \((r,\theta+\pi)\): rotate by \(\pi\) and flip the sign of \(r\). So \(\left(-2,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \left(2,\ \dfrac{\pi}{4}+\pi\right) = \left(2,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{4}\right)\).

Convert \(\left(2,\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\right)\) to rectangular: \(x=2\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{4}=2\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)=-\sqrt2\); \(y=2\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{4}=2\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)=-\sqrt2\).

Cross-check directly from the original negative-\(r\) point: \(x=-2\cos\frac{\pi}{4}=-2\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2}=-\sqrt2\); \(y=-2\sin\frac{\pi}{4}=-\sqrt2\) — identical. ✓
Final Answer: Equivalent positive-\(r\) form: \(\left(2,\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)\). Rectangular point: \((-\sqrt2,-\sqrt2)\).
PROBLEM 3
Equation conversion, both directions: ① Convert \(x^2+y^2=6y\) to polar. ② Convert \(r=4\cos\theta\) to rectangular; identify center and radius.
SOLUTION
① Substitute \(x^2+y^2=r^2\) and \(y=r\sin\theta\): \(r^2=6r\sin\theta\). Divide by \(r\) (the pole, \(r=0\), is already accounted for as a solution of the resulting equation too): \(r=6\sin\theta\).

② Multiply by \(r\): \(r^2=4r\cos\theta \Rightarrow x^2+y^2=4x\). Complete the square: \(x^2-4x+y^2=0 \Rightarrow (x-2)^2+y^2=4\).
Final Answer: ① \(r=6\sin\theta\). ② \((x-2)^2+y^2=4\), center \((2,0)\), radius \(2\).
PROBLEM 4
Cardioid \(r=2-2\sin\theta\): state max \(r\) and where it occurs, state where the curve touches the pole, name the axis of symmetry.
SOLUTION
\(r=2-2\sin\theta\) is maximized when \(\sin\theta\) is minimized, i.e., \(\sin\theta=-1\) at \(\theta=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\): \(r_{\max}=2-2(-1)=4\).

The curve touches the pole where \(r=0\): \(2-2\sin\theta=0 \Rightarrow \sin\theta=1 \Rightarrow \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

A cardioid of the form \(r=a\pm a\sin\theta\) is always symmetric about the vertical axis (the line \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\), i.e. the \(y\)-axis) — the \(\sin\theta\) term is what fixes the axis of symmetry vertically, just as a \(\cos\theta\) term would fix it horizontally.
Final Answer: \(r_{\max}=4\) at \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\); touches the pole at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\); symmetric about the \(y\)-axis.
PROBLEM 5
Classify \(r=4+2\cos\theta\) (inner loop, cardioid, dimpled, convex), showing the ratio test; state max and min \(r\).
SOLUTION
Ratio test on \(r=a+b\cos\theta\) with \(a=4\), \(b=2\): \(\dfrac{a}{|b|}=\dfrac{4}{2}=2\). Since \(\frac{a}{|b|}\ge2\), the limaçon is convex (no dimple, no inner loop).

\(r_{\max}=a+|b|=4+2=6\) at \(\theta=0\); \(r_{\min}=a-|b|=4-2=2\) at \(\theta=\pi\). Since \(r_{\min}=2>0\), \(r\) never reaches zero — the curve never approaches the pole, confirming no inner loop is possible.
Final Answer: Convex limaçon (\(a/|b|=2\ge2\)); \(r_{\max}=6\), \(r_{\min}=2\).
PROBLEM 6
Lemniscate \(r^2=9\sin(2\theta)\): state the number of petals; state the condition on \(\theta\) required for \(r\) to be real.
SOLUTION
A lemniscate always has exactly \(2\) petals (loops), regardless of its coefficient.

Since \(r^2\) must be nonnegative for \(r\) to be a real number, the equation \(r^2=9\sin(2\theta)\) requires \(\sin(2\theta)\ge0\); wherever \(\sin(2\theta)<0\), \(r\) would have to be imaginary, so no curve exists there.
Final Answer: \(2\) petals; requires \(\sin(2\theta)\ge0\).
PROBLEM 7
Rose curve \(r=2\cos(3\theta)\): state the number of petals and the parity reasoning; state the maximum petal length.
SOLUTION
For a rose \(r=a\cos(n\theta)\) or \(r=a\sin(n\theta)\): if \(n\) is odd, the rose has exactly \(n\) petals; if \(n\) is even, it has \(2n\) petals (each petal is traced twice for odd \(n\), while for even \(n\) the curve must sweep twice as far to close, tracing distinct petals on each half). Here \(n=3\) is odd, so the rose has \(3\) petals.

Maximum petal length \(=|a|=2\).
Final Answer: \(3\) petals (\(n=3\) is odd); maximum petal length \(2\).
PROBLEM 8
Parametric sketch and elimination: \(x=2t+1,\ y=t^2-3\). ① Table for \(t=-1,0,1,2\), note direction of motion. ② Eliminate the parameter.
SOLUTION
①
\(t\)\(x\)\(y\)
\(-1\)\(-1\)\(-2\)
\(0\)\(1\)\(-3\)
\(1\)\(3\)\(-2\)
\(2\)\(5\)\(1\)
Since \(\frac{dx}{dt}=2>0\) for every \(t\), \(x\) increases steadily as \(t\) increases — the curve is traced from left to right.

② Solve for \(t\): \(t=\dfrac{x-1}{2}\). Substitute into \(y=t^2-3\): \[ y = \left(\dfrac{x-1}{2}\right)^2-3 = \dfrac{(x-1)^2}{4}-3 \]
Final Answer: Table above; motion is left to right. Rectangular form: \(y=\dfrac{(x-1)^2}{4}-3\).
📝 PART B — REASONING (write these as arguments)
PROBLEM 9
Classify and justify a limaçon: \(r=3+2\sin\theta\). Compute \(r\) at four angles, state max/min; classify with the ratio test and explain what it checks; describe and justify the shape.
MODEL SOLUTION
① Compute \(r\) at the four angles. \[ r(0)=3+2\sin0=3 \qquad r\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=3+2(1)=5 \qquad r(\pi)=3+2\sin\pi=3 \qquad r\!\left(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\right)=3+2(-1)=1 \] Maximum \(r=5\) (at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\)); minimum \(r=1\) (at \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\)).

② Classify with the ratio test. With \(a=3\), \(b=2\): \(\dfrac{a}{|b|}=\dfrac{3}{2}=1.5\). Since \(1<1.5<2\), this is a dimpled limaçon.

What the ratio test is checking: it is really asking whether \(r=0\) has any solution — that is, whether the oscillating term \(2\sin\theta\) is ever large enough in magnitude to cancel the constant term \(3\) and drive \(r\) to (or past) zero. An inner loop can only exist if \(r\) actually reaches \(0\) and would go negative beyond that point, which requires \(|b|>a\) (ratio \(<1\)); here \(|b|=2
③ Sketch/description. Because the ratio sits strictly between \(1\) and \(2\), the curve is neither a sharp-cusped cardioid (which would require \(r=0\) at its minimum) nor a smoothly convex oval (which would require the ratio to be \(\ge2\)) — it is dimpled: a heart-like shape with a shallow inward pinch near \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\), where \(r\) shrinks to its smallest value of \(1\) without ever reaching \(0\). The four computed points bear this out: \(r\) swells to \(5\) at the top (\(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\)), returns to \(3\) at both sides (\(\theta=0,\pi\)), and pinches inward but stays positive at the bottom (\(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\), \(r=1\)) — a gentle dimple, not a cusp.
Final Answer: \(r\) at \(0,\frac{\pi}{2},\pi,\frac{3\pi}{2}\): \(3,5,3,1\); max \(5\), min \(1\). Ratio \(a/|b|=1.5\) ⇒ dimpled limaçon, confirmed by the strictly-positive minimum ruling out an inner loop.
PROBLEM 10
Convert a projectile model and interpret it: \(x(t)=20t,\ y(t)=15t-4.9t^2\) (SI units). Eliminate the parameter; identify shape/concavity; find range two ways; explain why the rectangular equation cannot tell you when.
MODEL SOLUTION
① Eliminate the parameter. From \(x=20t\), \(t=\dfrac{x}{20}\). Substitute: \[ y=15\left(\dfrac{x}{20}\right)-4.9\left(\dfrac{x}{20}\right)^2 = \dfrac34x - \dfrac{49}{4000}x^2 \] ② Shape and concavity. This is a parabola in \(x\) (a quadratic with a negative leading coefficient, \(-\frac{49}{4000}<0\)), so it is a downward-opening parabola — concave down.

③ Range. Set \(y=0\): \(x\left(\dfrac34-\dfrac{49}{4000}x\right)=0 \Rightarrow x=0\) or \(x=\dfrac{3/4}{49/4000}=\dfrac{3000}{49}\approx61.22\) m.

Separately, flight time directly from \(y(t)=0\): \(15t-4.9t^2=0 \Rightarrow t(15-4.9t)=0 \Rightarrow t=\dfrac{15}{4.9}=\dfrac{150}{49}\approx3.06\) s. \[ x\!\left(\dfrac{150}{49}\right) = 20\cdot\dfrac{150}{49} = \dfrac{3000}{49}\approx61.22 \text{ m} \] The two computations agree exactly, \(\dfrac{3000}{49}\) m, because both are really the same statement — where the ball's horizontal position is when its height returns to \(0\) — computed two different ways.

④ Why the rectangular equation can't tell you when. Eliminating \(t\) is exactly what erases the clock: the rectangular equation \(y=\frac34x-\frac{49}{4000}x^2\) records only the relationship between height and horizontal distance, with no trace of how much time it took to get from one point on the path to another. Two balls could trace the identical parabolic path at completely different speeds (a slower horizontal velocity paired with a longer flight time, for instance), and the rectangular equation alone could not distinguish them — only the original parametric functions, with \(t\) still in them, carry that information.
Final Answer: \(y=\frac34x-\frac{49}{4000}x^2\); downward-opening parabola. Range \(=\frac{3000}{49}\approx61.22\) m by both methods (flight time \(=\frac{150}{49}\approx3.06\) s). A rectangular equation has no \(t\) in it, so it cannot record when the ball reaches any point on its path.
📝 PART C — SYNTHESIS (this unit meets Unit 7)
PROBLEM 11
Limaçon \(r=1+2\sin\theta\): find every \(\theta\in[0,2\pi)\) where the curve passes through the pole, using Lesson 7-8's general-solution-then-restrict method; interpret geometrically; classify and cross-check with the ratio test; name the connection to Lesson 7-8.
MODEL SOLUTION
① Find every \(\theta\), by the general-solution-then-restrict method. Set \(r=0\): \[ 1+2\sin\theta=0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \sin\theta=-\dfrac12 \] Reference angle: \(\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac12\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\). Sine is negative in Quadrant III and Quadrant IV, so: \[ \theta = \pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6} \qquad\text{(QIII)} \qquad\qquad \theta = 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{11\pi}{6} \qquad\text{(QIV)} \] General solution: \(\theta=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}+2\pi k\) or \(\theta=\dfrac{11\pi}{6}+2\pi k\), \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\). Restricting to \([0,2\pi)\) (\(k=0\) in each family): \[ \theta = \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6} \] ② Interpret geometrically. These two \(\theta\)-values are exactly the angles at which the traced curve passes through the pole itself — the origin. As \(\theta\) sweeps from \(0\) to \(2\pi\), the curve reaches the pole once at \(\theta=\frac{7\pi}{6}\) and again at \(\theta=\frac{11\pi}{6}\); the portion of the curve traced between those two angles is the limaçon's small inner loop, doubling back through the origin rather than staying out at a distance the way the rest of the curve does.

③ Classify and cross-check. Ratio test: \(a=1\), \(b=2\), \(\dfrac{a}{|b|}=\dfrac12=0.5<1\), so this is a limaçon with an inner loop.

An inner loop exists if and only if \(r=0\) has solutions, because the inner loop is literally the piece of the curve traced while passing through the pole and back out again — if \(r\) never reached \(0\), the curve could never double back through the origin, and there would be nothing to call a loop. The ratio \(a/|b|<1\) is simply the algebraic shortcut that predicts whether \(1+2\sin\theta=0\) has a solution at all (it does exactly when \(|{-a/b}| = \frac12 \le 1\), which is achievable by \(\sin\theta\)); finding the two genuine solutions in ① is not a separate, unrelated fact from the classification in ③ — it is the classification, worked out explicitly rather than merely predicted.

④ Name the connection. The technique used in ① is exactly Lesson 7-8's method for solving a trigonometric equation: isolate the trig function, find the reference angle, place both solutions by quadrant (citing where sine is negative), write the general solution with \(+2\pi k\), and only then restrict to the given interval. Simply reading "where the graph looks like it touches zero" off a sketch would not have been sufficient because a hand-drawn or even a technology-generated sketch can only estimate an angle visually — it cannot guarantee both solutions are found, cannot distinguish a near-miss from an exact zero, and offers no algebraic certificate that these are the only two solutions on \([0,2\pi)\). The algebraic method guarantees exactness and completeness in a way a picture alone cannot.
Final Answer: \(\theta=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\) — the pole-crossings bounding the inner loop. Ratio test \(a/|b|=0.5<1\) confirms an inner-loop limaçon, exactly because \(r=0\) has solutions. Technique: Lesson 7-8's general-solution-then-restrict method for trigonometric equations.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC

The whole test is graded against the standing four-criterion rubric, each criterion scored out of 10. Part A supplies most of the evidence for understanding and precision; Parts B and C supply most of the evidence for reasoning.

Criteria What excellent looks like Pts
Understanding of the material Polar–rectangular conversion, curve identification (cardioid, limaçon, lemniscate, rose), and parametric sketching/elimination all executed correctly and fluently, with notation exact throughout. 10 pts
Quality of reasoning The limaçon classification argument and the projectile interpretation both read as genuine arguments; the Part C connection to Lesson 7-8's general-solution method is made explicitly and correctly, not merely gestured at. 10 pts
Presentation & precision Clean vertical work throughout, aligned equals signs, exact values kept in radical or \(\pi\)-form where called for, pages in order — forty points of work a stranger could follow. 10 pts
Intellectual honesty Honor line signed and honored; work shown as actually done; any problem you could not finish carries an honest note of where and why you stopped — which earns respect here, never punishment. 10 pts
Total: 40 pts
📊 GRADING NOTE (Test — 40 pts, rubric-graded)
Score holistically against the four-criterion rubric printed on the test page (10 pts each). Common partial-credit spots: Problem 1②'s angle placed in Quadrant I instead of Quadrant II (forgetting to check the sign of \(x\) before reporting the reference angle) — deduct from Understanding; Problem 2 skipping the negative-\(r\) rotation-by-\(\pi\) step and instead just reporting \((-2,\pi/4)\)'s magnitude as \(r=2\) without the sign flip — deduct from Understanding; Problem 5's ratio computed backwards (\(|b|/a\) instead of \(a/|b|\)), which would misclassify a convex limaçon as an inner-loop one — deduct from Understanding; Problem 8 reporting the direction of motion as "upward" (looking only at the \(y\)-values, which dip then rise) rather than correctly noting the motion is left-to-right in \(x\) — deduct from Understanding; Problem 9 computing the four \(r\)-values correctly but never explicitly stating why the strictly-positive minimum rules out an inner loop (leaving the ratio test as an unconnected fact) — deduct from Reasoning; Problem 10④ asserting that a rectangular equation "loses information" without specifically naming that it has no \(t\) at all — deduct from Reasoning; Problem 11① skipping the reference-angle/quadrant-placement step and jumping straight to \(\frac{7\pi}{6},\frac{11\pi}{6}\) with no shown derivation — deduct from Reasoning, since the problem explicitly requires the general-solution method to be shown; Problem 11③ asserting the inner loop exists "because the ratio is less than 1" without connecting that ratio back to \(r=0\) actually having solutions (treating the two facts as separate rather than one) — deduct from Reasoning. An honestly noted incomplete answer should never cost Intellectual Honesty points — that criterion rewards the honesty, not the completeness.

Assignment 9-1 · Practice Set: Motion in the Argand Plane
Practice Set · Completion-Scored · includes VR deliverable
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 9-1
Answer Key: Motion in the Argand Plane
Full worked solutions for all 7 problems, for grading and self-correction release. The required VR artifacts have no single correct student narration, so a completion checklist stands in below rather than a fabricated example.
PROBLEM 1
Plot and conjugate: Plot \(z=-4+3i\) and its conjugate \(\overline{z}\). State the coordinates of both points and describe the geometric relationship between them.
SOLUTION
\(z=-4+3i\) plots at \((-4,3)\). Conjugating flips the sign of the imaginary part only: \(\overline{z}=-4-3i\), plotting at \((-4,-3)\).

Both points share the same real part (\(-4\)) and their imaginary parts are opposite (\(3\) and \(-3\)), so \(\overline{z}\) is the mirror image of \(z\) across the real axis — a reflection, not a translation or rotation.
Final Answer: \(z=(-4,3)\), \(\overline{z}=(-4,-3)\); reflection of \(z\) across the real axis.
PROBLEM 2
Add as translation: Compute \((6-i)+(-3+5i)\), then state the translation vector that carries \((6,-1)\) to your answer's point.
SOLUTION
\[ (6-i)+(-3+5i) = (6-3)+(-1+5)i = 3+4i \] The sum plots at \((3,4)\). The translation that carries \((6,-1)\) to \((3,4)\) moves \(3-6=-3\) units in the real direction and \(4-(-1)=5\) units in the imaginary direction — exactly the components of the number being added, \(-3+5i\).
Final Answer: \(3+4i\); translation vector \(\langle -3, 5\rangle\).
PROBLEM 3
Subtract as translation: Compute \((2+7i)-(5+3i)\), then state the translation vector involved.
SOLUTION
\[ (2+7i)-(5+3i) = (2-5)+(7-3)i = -3+4i \] Subtracting \(5+3i\) is the same as adding \(-5-3i\), so the translation vector is \(\langle -5,-3\rangle\) — carrying \((2,7)\) to \((2-5,\,7-3)=(-3,4)\), which matches the computed sum exactly.
Final Answer: \(-3+4i\); translation vector \(\langle -5,-3\rangle\).
PROBLEM 4
Multiply by \(i\): Compute \((5-2i)\cdot i\). Verify by computing \(|5-2i|\) and the modulus of your answer that this operation changed no distance from the origin — only direction.
SOLUTION
\[ (5-2i)\cdot i = 5i-2i^2 = 5i+2 = 2+5i \] Modulus check: \[ |5-2i|=\sqrt{5^2+(-2)^2}=\sqrt{25+4}=\sqrt{29} \qquad |2+5i|=\sqrt{2^2+5^2}=\sqrt{4+25}=\sqrt{29} \] The two moduli are identical, so the point's distance from the origin did not change — only its direction did (a \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise rotation, since \(|i|=1\) contributes no scaling).
Final Answer: \(2+5i\); both moduli equal \(\sqrt{29}\), confirming a pure rotation.
PROBLEM 5
General multiplication: Compute \((2-i)(3+4i)\), fully simplified to \(a+bi\) form.
SOLUTION
\[ (2-i)(3+4i) = 2(3)+2(4i)+(-i)(3)+(-i)(4i) = 6+8i-3i-4i^2 \] Since \(i^2=-1\), the last term becomes \(-4(-1)=4\): \[ = 6+8i-3i+4 = (6+4)+(8-3)i = 10+5i \]
Final Answer: \(10+5i\)
PROBLEM 6
Powers of \(i\): Compute \(i^{7}\) and \(i^{20}\) using the period-4 cycle from this lesson, showing which remainder you used and why.
SOLUTION
The powers of \(i\) repeat with period \(4\) (\(i^1=i,\ i^2=-1,\ i^3=-i,\ i^4=1\), then the cycle restarts), so only the remainder of the exponent after division by \(4\) matters.

\(7 = 4(1)+3\), remainder \(3\), so \(i^7=i^3=-i\).
\(20 = 4(5)+0\), remainder \(0\), so \(i^{20}=i^0=1\) (equivalently, \(i^{20}=(i^4)^5=1^5=1\)).
Final Answer: \(i^7=-i\); \(i^{20}=1\).
PROBLEM 7 — Honors stretch
Multiplying by \(i\) rotates a point \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise. Predict, then verify algebraically, what multiplying by \(-i\) does to the point \(2+5i\) — is it the same rotation, the opposite rotation, or something else entirely? Justify using both the algebra and a distance check.
SOLUTION
Predict: since \(-i\) is the negative of \(i\), it seems reasonable to guess multiplying by \(-i\) undoes the counterclockwise rotation — i.e., rotates \(90^\circ\) clockwise instead.

Verify algebraically. \[ (2+5i)(-i) = -2i-5i^2 = -2i+5 = 5-2i \] Compare to what multiplying by \(i\) would give instead: \((2+5i)(i)=2i+5i^2=2i-5=-5+2i\), the point \((-5,2)\). The \(-i\) result, \((5,-2)\), is not the same point — it is a \(90^\circ\) rotation in the opposite sense. In general, multiplying \(a+bi\) by \(-i\) gives \(b-ai\), i.e. \((a,b)\mapsto(b,-a)\), which is exactly the standard \(90^\circ\) clockwise rotation formula (the formula for counterclockwise is \((a,b)\mapsto(-b,a)\)).

Distance check. \[ |2+5i|=\sqrt{2^2+5^2}=\sqrt{29} \qquad |5-2i|=\sqrt{5^2+(-2)^2}=\sqrt{29} \] The distance from the origin is unchanged, confirming this is a pure rotation with no scaling (since \(|-i|=1\)) — but the direction is the opposite quarter-turn from multiplying by \(i\).
Final Answer: \((2+5i)(-i)=5-2i\). This is the opposite rotation from multiplying by \(i\) — a \(90^\circ\) clockwise turn, not counterclockwise — while the modulus stays \(\sqrt{29}\) in both cases.
🥽 VR ARTIFACT — completion checklist, not a scored answer
The Standing in the Complex Plane VR Session's required deliverables (a powers-of-\(i\) snapshot, a narrated spatial recording link, and a written paragraph) have no single correct student narration, so this key gives you what to look for rather than an invented example. Do not deduct for phrasing — check for the presence and correctness of these items:
  • Powers-of-\(i\) snapshot present, showing all four sticky notes — \(i^1=i\), \(i^2=-1\), \(i^3=-i\), \(i^4=1\) — correctly placed around the origin at \(90^\circ\) intervals. The correct positions the snapshot must show: \(i\) at \((0,1)\), \(-1\) at \((-1,0)\), \(-i\) at \((0,-1)\), \(1\) at \((1,0)\), reached by walking one quarter-turn counterclockwise at a time starting from \(1\). A snapshot with notes out of this order or off the \(90^\circ\) spacing means the student did not actually walk the cycle in-headset — flag for a quick follow-up conversation rather than a deduction on this completion-scored item.
  • Shareable recording link present and the link actually resolves to a spatial recording (not a broken or placeholder link). The recording should be a genuine 30–60 second narration explaining, in the student's own words, what multiplying by \(i\) does to a point in the plane — the core idea being a \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise rotation about the origin that leaves distance from the origin unchanged.
  • Written paragraph present, restating the recording's content in the student's own words with precise vocabulary — at minimum rotation, counterclockwise (or an equivalent \(90^\circ\) turn description), and a statement that the modulus/distance from the origin is unchanged. A reader who never watched the recording should be able to understand exactly what multiplying by \(i\) does from the paragraph alone. A paragraph that only states "it moves the point" without naming the rotation and the preserved distance should be treated as incomplete, the same as a blank written response elsewhere on this set.
  • All three artifacts are placed as their own labeled pages at the end of the PDF, after Problem 7, per the submission instructions.
Full credit for this component is presence + genuine content, exactly as with any other completion-scored piece of this assignment.
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
For Problems 4, 5, and 7, plotting the original point and the computed answer as ordered pairs should show exactly the geometric relationship claimed above: Problem 4 and Problem 7 should each show the two points sitting on the same circle around the origin (equal distance), rotated \(90^\circ\) apart in opposite senses from each other. Problem 5's product has no simple geometric relationship to check beyond the arithmetic itself.
📊 GRADING NOTE (Practice Set — completion-scored)
Full credit (10 pts) for the VR artifacts (per the completion checklist above) plus a genuine, visible attempt at all 7 problems, including the honors stretch. Do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound — release this key after the due date and let students self-correct against it, per the standing 4-criterion standard (understanding / reasoning / presentation / honesty).
