Answer Key: Mixed Set & the Five Languages of the Plane
Full worked solutions for all 9 Part A problems, plus a teacher reference table for Part B's open-ended Field Guide. Problems 4 and 8 carry gold-badged scoring guidance for the rubric — those are the only two problems graded for method; the rest of Part A is checked for honest completion, and Part B is checked against the reference table below.
PROBLEM 1
Line of sight: From a point 120 feet from the base of a lighthouse, the angle of elevation to the top is \(27^\circ\). Find the height to the nearest foot, then state the angle of depression from the top back down to that point and explain why it must equal the angle of elevation.
SOLUTION
The line from the observer to the base of the lighthouse, and the vertical lighthouse itself, form a right triangle with the \(27^\circ\) angle of elevation at the observer, adjacent leg \(120\) ft, and opposite leg equal to the height \(h\): \[ \tan(27^\circ) = \frac{h}{120} \;\Rightarrow\; h = 120\tan(27^\circ) \] \[ h = 120(0.509525\ldots) \approx 61.14 \text{ ft} \]
Angle of depression: the horizontal line at the top of the lighthouse and the horizontal ground at the observer's point are parallel. The line of sight is a transversal crossing both. The angle of depression (measured down from the top's horizontal) and the angle of elevation (measured up from the ground's horizontal) are alternate interior angles formed by that transversal across two parallel lines — alternate interior angles are always congruent, so the angle of depression must equal \(27^\circ\), the same as the angle of elevation.
Final Answer: Height \(\approx 61\) ft. Angle of depression \(=27^\circ\), equal to the angle of elevation because both are alternate interior angles cut from the same transversal across two parallel horizontals.
PROBLEM 2
Two exact values, two arguments: Find \(\tan\!\left(\frac{7\pi}{6}\right)\) and \(\sec\!\left(-\frac{5\pi}{3}\right)\), each with reference angle, quadrant (or coterminal angle), and sign justification.
SOLUTION
\(\tan\!\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)\): \(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\) lies between \(\pi\) and \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\), so it is a Quadrant III angle. Reference angle: \(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}-\pi=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\). In Quadrant III both sine and cosine are negative, so their ratio (tangent) is positive. \[ \tan\!\left(\frac{7\pi}{6}\right) = \tan\!\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{\sqrt3}{3} \]
\(\sec\!\left(-\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right)\): add \(2\pi\) to land on a standard coterminal angle: \(-\dfrac{5\pi}{3}+2\pi = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), a Quadrant I angle (so it is already its own reference angle). In Quadrant I, cosine (and therefore secant) is positive. \[ \sec\!\left(-\frac{5\pi}{3}\right) = \sec\!\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{\cos(\pi/3)} = \frac{1}{1/2} = 2 \]
Final Answer: \(\tan\!\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\)  ·  \(\sec\!\left(-\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right) = 2\)
PROBLEM 3
Building the wave: A sinusoid has maximum \(9\) at \(x=0\), minimum \(-3\), period \(8\). Find amplitude, midline, period, write \(y=A\cos(Bx)+D\), and verify against both the max and the min.
SOLUTION
Amplitude: \(A = \dfrac{\text{max}-\text{min}}{2} = \dfrac{9-(-3)}{2} = 6\).

Midline: \(D = \dfrac{\text{max}+\text{min}}{2} = \dfrac{9+(-3)}{2} = 3\).

Period: given as \(8\), so \(B = \dfrac{2\pi}{\text{period}} = \dfrac{2\pi}{8} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

Since the maximum occurs at \(x=0\) (not the midline), cosine — not sine — is the natural match, with no phase shift needed: \[ y = 6\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{4}x\right) + 3 \] Verify at the max (\(x=0\)): \(y = 6\cos(0)+3 = 6(1)+3 = 9\). ✓
Verify at the min: the minimum of cosine occurs where \(\frac{\pi}{4}x=\pi\), i.e. \(x=4\): \(y=6\cos(\pi)+3 = 6(-1)+3=-3\). ✓
Final Answer: Amplitude \(6\), midline \(y=3\), period \(8\). \(y = 6\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}x\right)+3\); reproduces max \(9\) at \(x=0\) and min \(-3\) at \(x=4\).
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 4
SSA ambiguous case: \(a=15\), \(b=20\), \(A=40^\circ\). Post the guard, solve every surviving case for \(B\), \(C\), \(c\), find each case's area, and deliver a verdict naming which comparison decided the count.

① Post the guard. Compute the height dropped from the side-\(b\) vertex to the baseline: \(h = b\sin A = 20\sin(40^\circ) = 20(0.642788) \approx 12.86\). Compare: \(h\approx12.86 < a=15 < b=20\). When \(hVerdict in advance: two triangles.

② Solve every surviving case. By the Law of Sines, \(\dfrac{\sin B}{b} = \dfrac{\sin A}{a}\): \[ \sin B = \frac{b\sin A}{a} = \frac{20\sin(40^\circ)}{15} \approx 0.85705 \] This gives two candidate angles: the acute solution \(B_1 \approx 58.99^\circ\) and the obtuse supplement \(B_2 = 180^\circ - B_1 \approx 121.01^\circ\). Both survive, since \(A+B_2 = 40^\circ+121.01^\circ \approx 161.0^\circ < 180^\circ\).

Case 1 (\(B_1\approx58.99^\circ\)): \(C_1 = 180^\circ-40^\circ-58.99^\circ \approx 81.01^\circ\). \[ c_1 = \frac{a\sin C_1}{\sin A} = \frac{15\sin(81.01^\circ)}{\sin(40^\circ)} \approx \frac{15(0.98763)}{0.642788} \approx 23.05 \] Case 2 (\(B_2\approx121.01^\circ\)): \(C_2 = 180^\circ-40^\circ-121.01^\circ \approx 18.99^\circ\). \[ c_2 = \frac{a\sin C_2}{\sin A} = \frac{15\sin(18.99^\circ)}{\sin(40^\circ)} \approx \frac{15(0.32538)}{0.642788} \approx 7.59 \]
③ Compute the area of each surviving triangle using \(\text{Area}=\tfrac12 ab\sin C\) (with \(\tfrac12ab = \tfrac12(15)(20)=150\)): \[ \text{Area}_1 = 150\sin(81.01^\circ) \approx 150(0.98763) \approx 148.2 \] \[ \text{Area}_2 = 150\sin(18.99^\circ) \approx 150(0.32538) \approx 48.8 \]
④ Verdict sentence. This data produces exactly two triangles, because the guard comparison placed the height strictly between the two given sides (\(h \approx 12.86 < a=15 < b=20\)) — the classic ambiguous-case signature, and the reason both the acute and obtuse values of \(B\) survive.

⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — anchor for this problem's share of the 16-pt holistic rubric)
Understanding (4): \(h=b\sin A\) computed correctly and compared to both \(a\) and \(b\) to correctly predict two triangles before solving; both Law of Sines cases (\(B_1\) acute, \(B_2=180^\circ-B_1\)) found and both confirmed valid; area formula applied correctly to both cases. (2): method sound but one conceptual slip — e.g., comparing only \(a\) to \(b\) without computing \(h\), or one case's \(C\)/\(c\)/area mis-solved. (0): method doesn't fit the problem — e.g., assuming SSA always yields one triangle, or solving with the Law of Cosines as if two sides and the included angle were given.

Reasoning (4): all four stages (guard, both full case solves, both areas, verdict) are explicit; the verdict sentence correctly names \(h(2): correct values are found but the two-triangle conclusion is asserted rather than tied back to the guard comparison. (0): answers appear with little or no supporting reasoning.

Presentation & precision (4): the four stages are clearly labeled and easy to follow in order; angles in degrees, sides and areas carried to consistent, reasonable precision. (2): organized with a labeling or precision lapse. (0): scattered or illegible; the four stages cannot be followed.

Intellectual honesty (4): both surviving cases are fully worked side by side (not one worked and the other merely mentioned); the verdict is stated plainly and matches the work actually shown. (2): both cases are worked, but one is compressed or under-shown compared to the other. (0): a case is silently dropped or the triangle count is asserted without work.
PROBLEM 5
An identity does the heavy lifting: Solve \(\cos(2x)+\sin x = 0\) on \([0,2\pi)\), naming the identity used and factoring completely.
SOLUTION
Identity used: the double-angle identity \(\cos(2x) = 1-2\sin^2x\) (the form written entirely in \(\sin x\), since the equation already has a lone \(\sin x\) term). \[ (1-2\sin^2x) + \sin x = 0 \] Rearrange into standard quadratic-in-\(\sin x\) form: \[ -2\sin^2x + \sin x + 1 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; 2\sin^2x - \sin x - 1 = 0 \] Factor completely (let \(s=\sin x\)): \(2s^2-s-1 = (2s+1)(s-1) = 0\), so \(s=-\tfrac12\) or \(s=1\).

\(\sin x = 1\) on \([0,2\pi)\): \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
\(\sin x = -\dfrac12\) on \([0,2\pi)\) (Quadrants III and IV, reference angle \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\)): \(x = \dfrac{7\pi}{6}, \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\).

Check all three in the original equation: \(x=\frac{\pi}{2}\): \(\cos\pi+\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=-1+1=0\) ✓. \(x=\frac{7\pi}{6}\): \(\cos\frac{7\pi}{3}+\sin\frac{7\pi}{6}=\frac12+\left(-\frac12\right)=0\) ✓. \(x=\frac{11\pi}{6}\): \(\cos\frac{11\pi}{3}+\sin\frac{11\pi}{6}=\frac12+\left(-\frac12\right)=0\) ✓.
Final Answer: \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2},\; \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\; \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\)
PROBLEM 6
Two curves, two habits: ① Convert \(r=6\cos\theta\) to rectangular form and identify the curve completely. ② Classify \(r=3\sin(4\theta)\) — petal count and length, with the rule used.
SOLUTION
① Multiply both sides by \(r\) before substituting: \[ r = 6\cos\theta \;\Rightarrow\; r^2 = 6r\cos\theta \;\Rightarrow\; x^2+y^2 = 6x \] Complete the square on \(x\): \[ x^2-6x+y^2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; (x-3)^2+y^2 = 9 \] This is a circle, center \((3,0)\), radius \(3\).

② Rule: for a rose \(r=a\sin(n\theta)\) or \(r=a\cos(n\theta)\), the petal count is \(n\) if \(n\) is odd, and \(2n\) if \(n\) is even; the length of each petal is \(|a|\). Here \(n=4\) is even, so the petal count is \(2(4)=8\), and each petal has length \(|3|=3\). Yes, \(r=3\sin(4\theta)\) is a rose: an 8-petaled rose, each petal \(3\) units long.
Final Answer: ① \((x-3)^2+y^2=9\), a circle centered at \((3,0)\) with radius \(3\). ② An 8-petaled rose (n=4 even ⇒ \(2n=8\) petals), each petal length \(3\).
PROBLEM 7
Erasing the clock: \(x(t)=1+2t\), \(y(t)=4-t\) for \(0\le t\le3\). Eliminate the parameter, identify the curve, and describe the motion (start/end points and direction).
SOLUTION
Solve for \(t\) from the \(x\)-equation: \(x=1+2t \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{x-1}{2}\). Substitute into the \(y\)-equation: \[ y = 4-t = 4-\frac{x-1}{2} = \frac{8-(x-1)}{2} = \frac{9-x}{2} \] Equivalently, \(x+2y=9\) — a line (restricted to a segment, since \(t\) is bounded).

Endpoints: at \(t=0\): \(\big(x(0),y(0)\big) = (1,4)\). At \(t=3\): \(\big(x(3),y(3)\big) = (1+6,\,4-3) = (7,1)\).

Direction of motion: as \(t\) increases from \(0\) to \(3\), \(x(t)=1+2t\) is strictly increasing (moving left to right), and \(y(t)=4-t\) is strictly decreasing (moving downward).
Final Answer: \(x+2y=9\) (a line segment). Starts at \((1,4)\) at \(t=0\), ends at \((7,1)\) at \(t=3\); motion is left-to-right and downward.
⭐ METHOD PROBLEM — graded for method against the 4-criterion rubric
PROBLEM 8
One point, five languages: \(P=(2,2\sqrt3)\). Convert to polar, complex trig form, and vector magnitude-direction form; verify all three by converting back to rectangular; close by naming what makes the three forms "the same object."
SOLUTION
① Convert to polar. \(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} = \sqrt{2^2+(2\sqrt3)^2} = \sqrt{4+12} = \sqrt{16}=4\). Since \(x=2>0\) and \(y=2\sqrt3>0\), \(P\) is in Quadrant I, so \(\theta\) is its own reference angle: \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{2\sqrt3}{2}=\sqrt3 \Rightarrow \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\). \[ (r,\theta) = \left(4,\ \frac{\pi}{3}\right) \] ② Convert to complex trigonometric form. Using the same \(r\) and \(\theta\): \[ z = 4\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{3}+i\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\right) \] ③ Convert to vector magnitude-direction form. \(|\vec v| = r = 4\), direction angle \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\). Component form: \(v_x = |\vec v|\cos\theta = 4\!\left(\tfrac12\right)=2\), \(v_y = |\vec v|\sin\theta = 4\!\left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=2\sqrt3\), so \(\vec v = \langle 2,\,2\sqrt3\rangle\).

④ Verify all three by converting back to rectangular.
Polar → rectangular: \(x=r\cos\theta = 4\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 4\!\left(\tfrac12\right)=2\); \(y=r\sin\theta = 4\sin\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 4\!\left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=2\sqrt3\). Reproduces \((2,2\sqrt3)\). ✓
Complex → rectangular: \(z = 4\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + 4i\sin\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 4\!\left(\tfrac12\right) + 4i\!\left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) = 2+2\sqrt3\,i\), whose real and imaginary parts are exactly \((2,2\sqrt3)\). ✓
Vector → rectangular: \(v_x = 4\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=2\), \(v_y=4\sin\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=2\sqrt3\), so \(\vec v=\langle2,2\sqrt3\rangle\), landing at the point \((2,2\sqrt3)\). ✓

⑤ Why the same object, three uniforms: the polar pair, the complex number, and the vector all encode the identical information — a distance \(r=4\) from the origin and a direction \(\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{3}\) — just written in different notations built for different jobs. Polar form makes distance-and-direction facts (and equations of circles, roses, cardioids) easy to read off directly. Complex trigonometric form makes multiplication and rotation easy: moduli multiply and arguments add, so rotating a point becomes multiplying by \(\text{cis}(\alpha)\). Vector form makes addition and composition easy: resultants add tip-to-tail in component form, which none of the other two languages do as naturally.
Final Answer: Polar: \(\left(4,\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\). Complex: \(z=4\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{3}+i\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=2+2\sqrt3\,i\). Vector: \(|\vec v|=4\), direction \(\frac{\pi}{3}\), \(\vec v=\langle2,2\sqrt3\rangle\). All three verified to reproduce \((2,2\sqrt3)\).
⭐ SCORING GUIDANCE (Method Problem — anchor for this problem's share of the 16-pt holistic rubric)
Understanding (4): \(r\) and \(\theta\) correctly found (with quadrant reasoning) for polar form; complex trig form and vector magnitude-direction/component form both correctly built from the same \(r,\theta\). (2): method sound but one conceptual slip — e.g., a quadrant/sign error in \(\theta\), or magnitude and direction angle swapped in the vector form. (0): method doesn't fit the problem — e.g., treating polar \(r\) as an \(x\)-coordinate, or no genuine conversion attempted.

Reasoning (4): each of the three conversions is justified with the correct formula, and all three back-conversions are carried out and explicitly shown reproducing \((2,2\sqrt3)\) — not merely asserted; the closing sentences correctly explain the shared-object relationship and name a distinct operation each form privileges. (2): conversions are correct but one of the three back-conversion checks is skipped or only partially shown. (0): results appear with little or no supporting derivation.

Presentation & precision (4): all five labeled parts (polar, complex, vector, verification, closing sentences) are clearly separated and easy to follow; \(\theta\) is kept as the exact special angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) rather than a rounded decimal. (2): organized with a minor labeling or precision lapse. (0): scattered or illegible; the parts cannot be followed.

Intellectual honesty (4): the back-conversion arithmetic for all three forms is shown in full, exactly as the problem requires ("not just one"); nothing is glossed over. (2): only one or two of the three back-conversions are shown with full arithmetic. (0): back-conversions are asserted with no work shown, or omitted entirely.
PROBLEM 9 — Honors stretch
Find all three cube roots of \(z=8i\) by De Moivre's Theorem, in trig and rectangular form. Treat each as a position vector: verify they sum to zero and form an equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle. Connect to three equal forces at \(120^\circ\) in equilibrium.
SOLUTION
Write \(z=8i\) in trig form: modulus \(|z|=8\), argument \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (\(90^\circ\)), so \(z = 8\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

De Moivre's Theorem for cube roots: the modulus of each root is \(8^{1/3}=2\); the arguments are \(\dfrac{\theta+360^\circ k}{3}\) for \(k=0,1,2\): \[ k=0:\ \frac{90^\circ}{3}=30^\circ \qquad k=1:\ \frac{90^\circ+360^\circ}{3}=150^\circ \qquad k=2:\ \frac{90^\circ+720^\circ}{3}=270^\circ \] Trig and rectangular form of each root (all three angles are special angles): \[ w_0 = 2(\cos30^\circ+i\sin30^\circ) = 2\!\left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}+\tfrac12 i\right) = \sqrt3+i \] \[ w_1 = 2(\cos150^\circ+i\sin150^\circ) = 2\!\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}+\tfrac12 i\right) = -\sqrt3+i \] \[ w_2 = 2(\cos270^\circ+i\sin270^\circ) = 2(0-i) = -2i \] Check (cube each — e.g. \(w_0\)): \((\sqrt3+i)^2 = 3+2\sqrt3i-1 = 2+2\sqrt3i\); \((\sqrt3+i)^3=(2+2\sqrt3i)(\sqrt3+i)=2\sqrt3+2i+6i+2\sqrt3i^2=2\sqrt3+8i-2\sqrt3=8i\) ✓. \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) check the same way.

Treat each root as a position vector from the origin: \(\vec{w_0}=\langle\sqrt3,1\rangle\), \(\vec{w_1}=\langle-\sqrt3,1\rangle\), \(\vec{w_2}=\langle0,-2\rangle\).
Sum: \(\vec{w_0}+\vec{w_1}+\vec{w_2} = \langle\sqrt3-\sqrt3+0,\ 1+1-2\rangle = \langle0,0\rangle = \vec{0}\). ✓

Mutually equidistant (equilateral triangle): each root has modulus \(2\), so all three lie on the circle of radius \(2\) centered at the origin. Distance between each pair: \[ |\vec{w_0}-\vec{w_1}| = \sqrt{(2\sqrt3)^2+0^2} = 2\sqrt3, \quad |\vec{w_1}-\vec{w_2}| = \sqrt{(\sqrt3)^2+3^2} = \sqrt{12}=2\sqrt3, \quad |\vec{w_0}-\vec{w_2}| = \sqrt{3+9}=2\sqrt3 \] All three side lengths equal \(2\sqrt3\) — the three roots form an equilateral triangle inscribed in the circle of radius \(2\).

Connection to equilibrium: three vectors of equal magnitude, spaced \(120^\circ\) apart, summing to the zero vector is precisely the condition for three equal-magnitude forces pulling in those same three directions to hold an object motionless — the net force is zero, so the object is in static equilibrium.
Final Answer: \(w_0=\sqrt3+i\), \(w_1=-\sqrt3+i\), \(w_2=-2i\) (moduli \(2\), arguments \(30^\circ,150^\circ,270^\circ\)). Vectors sum to \(\vec0\); pairwise distances all \(2\sqrt3\) ⇒ equilateral triangle inscribed in the circle \(r=2\). Units touched: 7 (special-angle trig values), 9 (De Moivre's Theorem / complex numbers), 10 (vectors and equilibrium).
💡 DESMOS CHECK (what the graphs should show)
Problem 4: graphing both Law of Sines cases (or plotting the three vertices of each) should show two distinct valid triangles, both with angles summing to \(180^\circ\). Problem 6: switching to polar mode and graphing \(r=3\sin(4\theta)\) should show exactly 8 petals, each reaching out to \(r=3\). Problem 8: plotting the rectangular point \((2,2\sqrt3)\) and the polar point \((4,\tfrac{\pi}{3})\) (Desmos accepts polar coordinates directly) should land in the same spot. Problem 9: plotting the three cube roots as points should show them sitting \(120^\circ\) apart on a circle of radius \(2\), forming a visibly equilateral triangle.

Language Notation What It's Built For Converting to Rectangular Worked Micro-Example (point \((3,4)\))
Rectangular / Cartesian \((x,y)\) Reading coordinates directly — the plane's home base. Already rectangular — this is the language every other row converts to. \((3,4)\)
Polar \((r,\theta)\) Distance-and-direction; equations of circles, roses, cardioids. \(x=r\cos\theta,\ \ y=r\sin\theta\) \(r=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5\), \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(4/3)\approx53.13^\circ\) ⇒ \((5,53.13^\circ)\). Back: \(5\cos53.13^\circ=3\), \(5\sin53.13^\circ=4\).
Parametric \(x(t),\ y(t)\) Motion over time — position as a function of a parameter. Evaluate \(x(t),y(t)\) at the parameter value of interest to get a coordinate pair (or eliminate \(t\) for the full path equation). \(x(t)=3t,\ y(t)=4t\) at \(t=1\) ⇒ \((3,4)\).
Complex / trigonometric form \(z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\) Multiplication and rotation — moduli multiply, arguments add. Real part \(=r\cos\theta=x\); imaginary part \(=r\sin\theta=y\). \(z=3+4i=5(\cos53.13^\circ+i\sin53.13^\circ)\). Back: \(5\cos53.13^\circ=3\), \(5\sin53.13^\circ=4\).
Vector / magnitude-direction \(\vec v=\langle a,b\rangle\); \(|\vec v|\), direction angle Addition and composition — resultants add tip-to-tail. \(a=|\vec v|\cos\theta\), \(b=|\vec v|\sin\theta\) ⇒ component form \(\langle a,b\rangle\), which is itself the rectangular pair. \(\vec v=\langle3,4\rangle\), \(|\vec v|=5\), direction \(53.13^\circ\). Back: \(5\cos53.13^\circ=3\), \(5\sin53.13^\circ=4\).
Completion checklist for Part B
☐ All five rows present (rectangular, polar, parametric, complex/trigonometric form, vector/magnitude-direction)  ·  ☐ All four columns filled for every row (notation, what it's built for, converting to rectangular, worked micro-example)  ·  ☐ The same single point is used throughout every row, and it is a point corresponding to \((3,4)\) — not a different value in different rows  ·  ☐ Each row's own conversion formula is actually applied to its worked example and reproduces \((3,4)\), not just stated in the abstract  ·  ☐ The rectangular row correctly notes that it is the "home base" every other language converts to  ·  ☐ The "what it's built for" column names a genuine operation each language privileges (not a generic "it's useful" restatement).
📊 GRADING NOTE (Focus-style, 16 pts, method-graded on Problems 4 and 8 only)
Problems 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, and 9 (Part A) and the Field Guide (Part B) are checked for honest, visible completion only — do not deduct for arithmetic slips if the method is sound, and release this key after the due date for self-correction; check Part B against the reference table and checklist above rather than any single "model" drawing. Problems 4 and 8, the two ⭐ method problems, carry the entire 16-point rubric (Understanding / Reasoning / Presentation & Precision / Intellectual Honesty, 4 pts each), applied holistically across both problems together — use the per-problem scoring guidance above as the concrete anchor for what each score level looks like on this particular pair. Budget roughly 1–2 minutes per student for the two method problems, per the course's designated-problems-only grading model.

assignments.title: Semester 2 Final Exam
assignments.html:
Semester 2 Final Exam

What this is. One cumulative, hand-written exam covering Units 6–10 (right triangle trigonometry; trigonometric functions; polar coordinates and parametric equations; complex numbers; vectors). Problems are not labeled by unit — recognizing which tool a problem wants is part of the assessment.

Format. One sitting, about 2 hours. Part A — Fluency (7 problems) · Part B — Reasoning (4 problems, written as arguments) · Part C — Synthesis (2 problems that cross units).

Tools. Calculator for arithmetic only. No notes, no lesson pages, no classmates, no AI tools, no solution sites.

Honor pledge. Copy and sign at the top of page 1: “I completed this exam on my own, without help from people, notes, or AI tools.”

Submitting. Work each problem by hand on paper, showing neat vertical work. Photograph or scan every page, combine into one PDF named LastName_FirstName_Precalculus_S2Final.pdf, and upload it here.

Grading. The standing 4-criterion rubric — understanding, quality of reasoning, presentation & precision, and intellectual honesty — at 15 points per criterion (60 points total).

quizzes.title: Unit 6 Check-In: Start of Unit
quizzes.description: Two minutes, before you begin Unit 6. Ungraded — your honest first thoughts help your teacher help you.

questions.text:
This unit's essential question: What does it take to trust a single measured angle enough to act on it — a height, a distance, a direction?

Write down your first answer, before the unit's lessons. There is no wrong answer here.

This unit you will study right-triangle and unit-circle trigonometry — angles in degrees and radians, the six trigonometric functions, and the exact values that anchor them. What is one thing you are curious to find out?

quizzes.title: Unit 6 Reflection: End of Unit
quizzes.description: A few minutes, after the Unit 6 test. Ungraded — honest reflection is the point.

questions.text:
Revisit the essential question: What does it take to trust a single measured angle enough to act on it — a height, a distance, a direction?

Now that you have finished the unit, has your answer changed? Explain.
How confident do you feel in your understanding of this unit's material?
What is one idea, term, or technique from this unit that still feels unclear to you?

This unit's virtue is responsibility. Surveying and navigation problems demand precise measurement because real consequences follow from an inexact angle. Where in this unit did precision itself become part of the mathematics, not just good practice?

quizzes.title: Unit 7 Check-In: Start of Unit
quizzes.description: Two minutes, before you begin Unit 7. Ungraded — your honest first thoughts help your teacher help you.

questions.text:
This unit's essential question: What makes a periodic function's motion disciplined rather than chaotic — and how does an identity prove a claim true for every angle at once?

Write down your first answer, before the unit's lessons. There is no wrong answer here.

This unit you will study trigonometric functions — graphing, modeling periodic phenomena, the Laws of Sines and Cosines, and the identities that let you rewrite one trigonometric expression as another. What is one thing you are curious to find out?

quizzes.title: Unit 7 Reflection: End of Unit
quizzes.description: A few minutes, after the Unit 7 test. Ungraded — honest reflection is the point.

questions.text:
Revisit the essential question: What makes a periodic function's motion disciplined rather than chaotic — and how does an identity prove a claim true for every angle at once?

Now that you have finished the unit, has your answer changed? Explain.
How confident do you feel in your understanding of this unit's material?
What is one idea, term, or technique from this unit that still feels unclear to you?

This unit's virtue is self-government. A periodic function is ordered, disciplined motion that governs itself; an identity proof is disciplined argument that never assumes what it must show. Where did this unit ask you for that same discipline?

quizzes.title: Unit 8 Check-In: Start of Unit
quizzes.description: Two minutes, before you begin Unit 8. Ungraded — your honest first thoughts help your teacher help you.

questions.text:
This unit's essential question: How can the same curve look utterly different depending on whether you describe it by angle-and-distance, by time, or by x and y?

Write down your first answer, before the unit's lessons. There is no wrong answer here.

This unit you will study polar coordinates and parametric equations — a new coordinate system built from angle and distance, and curves traced out by motion over time. What is one thing you are curious to find out?

quizzes.title: Unit 8 Reflection: End of Unit
quizzes.description: A few minutes, after the Unit 8 test. Ungraded — honest reflection is the point.

questions.text:
Revisit the essential question: How can the same curve look utterly different depending on whether you describe it by angle-and-distance, by time, or by x and y?

Now that you have finished the unit, has your answer changed? Explain.
How confident do you feel in your understanding of this unit's material?
What is one idea, term, or technique from this unit that still feels unclear to you?

This unit's virtue is wonder. Roses, cardioids, limaçons, and spirals are strange and beautiful shapes that a simple equation quietly hides. What was the moment in this unit when a curve surprised you?

quizzes.title: Unit 9 Check-In: Start of Unit

questions.text:
This unit's essential question: What did it take for mathematicians to trust a number that eighteenth-century opinion called impossible — and what do we gain by trusting it?

Write down your first answer, before the unit's lessons. There is no wrong answer here.
This unit you will study complex numbers — arithmetic on the complex plane, polar and trigonometric form, and De Moivre's Theorem for powers and roots. What is one thing you are curious to find out?

quizzes.title: Unit 9 Reflection: End of Unit

questions.text:
Revisit the essential question: What did it take for mathematicians to trust a number that eighteenth-century opinion called impossible — and what do we gain by trusting it?

Now that you have finished the unit, has your answer changed? Explain.
How confident do you feel in your understanding of this unit's material?
What is one idea, term, or technique from this unit that still feels unclear to you?

This unit's virtue is courage. Cardano and Bombelli trusted arithmetic on a number their era considered fictional before anyone could say what it truly was. Where did you have to trust a method before you were fully sure why it worked?

This unit's essential question: How do separate magnitudes and directions cooperate to produce one true result?

Write down your first answer, before the unit's lessons. There is no wrong answer here.

This unit you will study vectors — magnitude and direction, addition and scalar multiplication, the dot product, and real applications in navigation and force. What is one thing you are curious to find out?

Now that you have finished the unit, has your answer changed? Explain.
How confident do you feel in your understanding of this unit's material?
What is one idea, term, or technique from this unit that still feels unclear to you?

This unit's virtue is service. A resultant vector is the record of several magnitudes and directions cooperating toward one outcome — forces in balance, a plane's true path through wind. Where did this unit ask separate quantities to serve a shared result?

syllabus_html:
Precalculus Honors — Semester 2

Grading at a glance (as designed — confirm per section)

  • Lesson assignments & applied tasks — 50%. One hand-worked problem set per lesson. Three of each week's four are completion-scored, with worked solutions released afterward for self-correction; the week's marked Focus assignment is method-graded on its two designated problems.
  • Unit tests — 30%. One per unit, taken in the final week of the unit. Hand-written and graded on the standing four-criterion rubric.
  • Semester final — 20%. Cumulative, hand-written, one two-hour sitting during finals week.

Every hand-graded item uses the same four criteria: understanding of the material, quality of reasoning, presentation & precision, and intellectual honesty.

Tools you need

Canvas, the Desmos graphing calculator, Microsoft Excel (applied tasks), ENGAGE VR (select lessons), and your approved AI tutor used within the course's AI norms.

Course readings are adapted from Precalculus 2e by Jay Abramson, OpenStax (Rice University), used under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. The text has been adapted and rewritten for Optima Academy Online.
